News.title: Brit, 43, arrested for attempted murder after ‘stabbing tourist, 21, in chest’ following row outside Magaluf nightclub
News.content:
KNIFE HORROR Brit, 43, arrested for attempted murder after ‘stabbing tourist, 21, in chest’ following row outside Magaluf nightclub







Next

A BRITISH man is accused of stabbing a tourist in the chest after a row in a Magaluf club.

The 43-year-old was arrested on suspicion of attempted murder after the incident in the Spanish party resort in the early hours of Saturday.



His alleged victim, a 21-year-old man from the Czech Republic, was rushed to hospital with serious injuries.

The bloodshed is said to have taken place shortly after the pair got into an argument inside a nightspot in the Majorcan resort near the Punta Ballena strip.



They continued fighting after being thrown out by bouncers until the Brit is alleged to have pulled out a blade and stuck it in his chest.

The victim lay on the ground bleeding profusely as the suspect fled the scene shortly after 5am.

Police obtained a description of the suspect from witnesses and CCTV images showing his face and made the arrest hours later after an officer reportedly recognised the man held as the alleged knifeman.

The Brit remained in custody this morning ahead of a court appearance.

Meanwhile, his alleged victim is being treated in an intensive care unit at Son Espases Hospital in the Majorcan capital Palma.



It was not immediately clear this morning if the unnamed Brit was a tourist or lived locally.

News.title: We’re victims of ‘Britain’s most brazen cowboy builder’ – shock pics, threatening video and his £1m swindle laid bare
News.content:
Next

PHILLIPPA Edgar always dreamed of having the perfect family home.

But for the mum-of-two, her dream quickly turned into a living nightmare when she employed cowboy builder Patrick “Paddy” Hartley.



Phillippa, a quantity surveyor, pictured lazy Sunday mornings with her husband and kids in a new gleaming, open plan, glass-fronted kitchen.

She and her partner had poured their hard-earned savings into turning their four bedroom detached property into a forever-home.

Cruel Hartley didn’t just steal £185,000 of Phillippa’s hard-earned cash – he left her beloved house in a complete mess, open to the elements, and turned her family’s life upside down.



Hartley, 52, traded on fake smiles and grand promises to con 13 households across the North West out of more than £1million.

While his victims were left with structurally dangerous shells, flooding, open ceilings, and crippling debts, rogue builder Hartley took their money and sneered in their faces when confronted.

Now, as the serial fraudster begins a prison sentence, The Sun exposes the devastating wake of destruction left by one of Britain’s most prolific rogue traders.

For 48-year-old Phillippa, whose home is in Poynton, Stockport, the nightmare began in April 2020.

Wanting to create space for her growing family, she hired Hartley for a single-storey rear and double-storey side extension to enlarge the garage of her four-bed detached property.



Hartley shook her hand, flashed a warm smile, and promised the build would take just 10 weeks, slapping a £105,000 price tag on the project.

Trusting the slick operator, Phillippa handed over a staggering £95,000 in instalments over eight months.

But as the weeks dragged into months, her vision of a luxury dream space collapsed into an absolute horror show.

Rather than a stunning showcase home, Hartley left her property as two unfinished, roofless brick shells.

When heavy rain hit Greater Manchester, water cascaded straight into the family’s living space.



In desperate scenes, Phillippa had to rig up an industrial pump inside her own house just to suck out rainwater pooling in the rooms.

“This was supposed to be our dream home – but it became far from it,” a devastated Phillippa recalled.

“Hartley is a conman who knew what he was doing. Lie after lie was told about why work wasn’t complete.



“He then just left the extensions as two brick shells and stole our hard-earned money.

“He left our roof open to the rain, which flooded into our house to the point we set up a pump.

“The situation was extremely stressful and extremely upsetting. It strained everything from my children’s school lives to my marriage. Hartley is a horrid man who deserves to rot in prison.”

To make matters worse, Phillippa was forced to fork out another £89,000 from her own pocket just to hire reputable builders to fix Hartley’s shoddy, dangerous work and make the building structurally safe.

Her grand total loss soared to a jaw-dropping £185,000 – tearing her dream home to absolute ribbons.



Phillippa was far from Hartley’s only victim.

Across the region, the heartless builder operated a systematic scam – overcharging by tens of thousands of pounds up front, abandoning jobs, and declaring himself bankrupt to dodge accountability.

Shocking video footage captured the terrifying moment a disgruntled customer confronted Hartley over his botched work, only for the angry cowboy to aggressively square up to them and raise his arms to fight.



Photos and video taken by distraught homeowners paint a grim picture of his trail of destruction.

One house was left propped up on temporary metal stilts with scaffolding swaying next to windowless, knocked-down walls.

Other footage showed ceilings collapsing under the weight of trapped rainwater because temporary roofs were never fastened down properly.

And homeowners also filmed piles of building materials scattered like rubbish across incomplete, abandoned construction pads.

Another victim, Joanne Dagostina, 42, hired Hartley in November 2021 for a £34,800 extension and kitchen overhaul at her home in Failsworth, Oldham.



Over seven months, Hartley extracted £64,216 from her for extra jobs, including a damp-proof course and a new bathroom.

When Joanne finally sacked the rogue trader in August 2022, a shocked structural engineer revealed the house was a death trap.

Hartley had failed to install crucial steel support beams, leaving the ceiling failing and on the verge of collapsing “at any moment” – threatening to pull her next-door neighbour’s house down with it.



“The blatant lack of care and disrespect to put my family in danger is unforgivable,” Joanne fumed.

She had to fork out another £14,000 to tear up her new kitchen and install the proper steel beams.

“The engineer told me the extension ceiling was failing by 200 per cent and had to be propped up as soon as possible.

“He said it would collapse if we didn’t and if it did it would take the next-door neighbours with it – I was furious.

“I am disappointed with his sentencing as to me it was premeditated and he knew how to take advantage.



In Sale, Trafford, 49-year-old Pelin Akin and her partner Wellington Tsang, 55, handed Hartley £47,500 for a loft conversion and new driveway.

Promised an eight-week turnaround, they were left with no roof and an empty attic for months.

When challenged, Hartley offered a string of pathetic excuses – blaming his workers for being “drunk” or claiming his van needed an MOT.



When Pelin pushed harder, Hartley’s charming persona vanished, replaced by threatening text messages.

“My work suffered, I was signed off with stress,” Pelin revealed. “I added lots of cameras and security to our home just in case he or his representatives decided to visit us.”

The couple had to pay an extra £59,000 to professional builders just to rebuild the roof and fix Hartley’s structural blunders.

Approximately £8,000 of this cost has been to correct Hartley’s work to bring it into compliance with building control requirements.

Perhaps most heartbreaking of all was a family in Bacup, Lancashire, who hired Hartley to build an extension for an elderly relative needing end-of-life care.



Because Hartley abandoned the job, the dying woman was forced to spend her final days in a cold front room with no heating or hot water.

Hartley’s reign of terror finally unraveled when Lancashire County Council’s Trading Standards launched a massive investigation alongside Greater Manchester Police in September 2022.

Investigators uncovered a staggering trail of deceit involving 13 different households.



Facing a mountain of evidence, Hartley eventually buckled at Preston Crown Court, pleading guilty to a string of fraud and consumer protection offences between 2020 and 2023. .

On August 28 a judge sentenced Hartley to three years and nine months behind bars and slapped him with a seven-year Criminal Behaviour Order, banning him from running any private building business.

Judge Jeffries KC said: “It is hardly surprising that the emotional drain on these families is as crippling as the financial one. It must have been obvious to you the real harm that has been caused.”

Victim statements spoke of how families suffered depression and struggled to bring up babies and children with special needs in homes without adequate roofing.

Some took refuge in other peoples’ homes causing families to live apart.



Courts are now launching confiscation proceedings under the Proceeds of Crime Act to strip Hartley of any remaining assets.

Councillor Joshua Roberts, cabinet member for Rural Affairs, Environment and Communities, slammed Hartley as “one of the most prolific and heartless fraudsters” the council had ever prosecuted.

He said: “He deliberately preyed on consumers at some of their most vulnerable moments – especially for the victims that he cherry-picked in Bacup and Rawtenstall.

“He showed them no mercy and left them tens of thousands of pounds out of pocket. For the couple in Bacup, he cost them the chance to make a much-loved family member’s last few months easier. His behaviour was despicable.”

For Phillippa Edgar and the dozens of families whose lives he shattered, the sentence feels like small comfort.



Her dream home may finally be standing, but the psychological and financial scars left by Hartley will take a lifetime to heal.

News.title: Woman sexually assaulted outside Tesco store in early hours attack as cops release CCTV in hunt for man

News.title: Motorist in his 20s arrested for ‘murder’ after man killed on e-bike as cops appeal for witnesses
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

MURDER PROBE Motorist in his 20s arrested for ‘murder’ after man killed on e-bike as cops appeal for witnesses







Next

A MAN has died after a horror e-bike crash as a motorist is arrested on suspicion of murder.

Police were called to the scene in Luton on Friday night where they found the seriously injured victim.



The man was believed to have been struck by a vehicle on Dallow Road and tragically died shortly after.

A man in his 20s has since been arrested on suspicion of murder and remains in custody.



A full murder investigation has been launched by The Bedfordshire, Cambridgeshire and Hertfordshire Major Crime Unit.

Officials have appealed for anyone with information on the incident.

Det Insp Andrew Moralee said: “This was an awful incident which has sadly cost a man his life.

“Our thoughts are with his friends and family who have lost a loved one in such dreadful circumstances.

“Please refrain from sharing any such footage and instead contact police.

“It could also form part of vital evidence in our investigation.”



Anyone with any information has been asked to contact the police website or Crimestoppers anonymously.

News.title: Pilot killed after two planes crash mid-air with one smashing into woodland as urgent probe launched
News.content:
MID-AIR DISASTER Pilot killed after two planes crash mid-air with one smashing into woodland as urgent probe launched







Next

A PILOT has been killed after two gliders crashed mid-air over upstate New York.

One plane plunged into a heavily wooded and remote area, while the other was able to land safely after the collision.



Each aircraft was operated by a single pilot and carried no passengers.

They collided just before 2.30pm on Friday afternoon near Edinburg, a town around 50 miles north of Albany.



It took investigators more than two hours to find debris from the wreck of the Schempp-Hirth Ventus-2B glider.

Helicopters were seen overhead as they scoured the area for traces of the plane.



The crash site was roughly six miles from where the other aircraft, exactly the same model, landed safely at Plateau Sky Ranch Airport.

The body of the pilot, who has not been identified, was found at the scene.

Footage from the crash site showed police surrounding a small plane in a wooded area.

The other pilot escaped without injury, and even went back up in search of the other glider.



Pictures show the survivor‘s plane had some scraping near the nose, but it was otherwise unscathed.

Elayne Wade, owner of the airport where he landed, told the Times Union: “The front end had some damage.

“The pilot is shaken but OK. He just went up in a plane with my husband to find the other glider.”

It is not yet clear what caused the crash, but an investigation has been launched by the National Transportation Safety Board.

They will analyse flight track data, recordings, maintenance records, the pilot’s license and flight history, witness statements and surveillance video.



A preliminary report is expected within 30 days and a final report will follow in the next one to two years.

News.title: Terrifying moment car crashes head-on into another vehicle after driver veers onto wrong side of road
News.content:
Next

THIS is the moment a car crashes head-on into another vehicle after the driver lost control and veered into the opposing lane.

Ethan Loveridge smashed into the unsuspecting car after losing concentration while behind the wheel.



The terrifying moment was captured by dashcam footage of one of the victims.

The 20-year-old Loveridge was driving in his Kia Sorento in Caerphilly in August of 2024 when the crash took place.



Loveridge lost control of the car and veered into the wrong lane where he clipped one car and smashed head-first into Martin Howells’ vehicle.

Newport Crown Court heard how Howells was left suffering from broken bones and fractures which left him out of work for months.



After the smash, Howells was left injured inside his car while passerbys attempted to help him.

He was left dealing with eight broken ribs, a broken nose, a detached bicep, injury to his left shoulder and a rotator cuff, and nerve damage to his neck and shoulder.



In a victim personal statement read to the court, Howells said: “It was a horrific crash that has changed my life forever… I had difficulties with my fingers which has prevented me from playing guitar which is something I love to do.

“I have been diagnosed with PTSD and underwent eight months of psychological therapy.”

Howells added his injuries have left him with extreme weakness in his arms and is now permanently unable to lift anything above shoulder height.

He said: “I was unable to sleep properly and woke up in the night thinking about what could have happened. I was unable to work for 10 months after the collision which had massive financial implications on my wife.

“We had to take a pay holiday on our mortgage for six months and had to use our life savings to make ends meet.



“We had to sell our family home where we have lived for 33 years and our children grew up in that house, we have lifelong memories there. We had to downsize to afford to carry on living.”

Loveridge pleaded guilty to causing serious injury by dangerous driving, possession with intent to supply a class B drug, being concerned in the supply of class A and B drugs and possession of criminal property.

He was sentenced to five years in prison and was disqualified from driving for four years.

News.title: MPs leap from vintage WW2 plane over Arnhem in stunning tribute to heroes involved in biggest air assault in history
News.content:
Next

TWO MPs leapt from a World War Two plane over Arnhem to commemorate the biggest airborne assault in history – that inspired the film A Bridge Too Far.

Ex Special Forces commando Al Carns and Para reservist Bayo Alaba joined veterans, serving troops, firemen and civilians in the act of remembrance.



They jumped from a vintage Dakota C-47 like the ones used Operation Market Garden in 1944.

Some 41,000 allies troops jumped into Nazi occupied Holland to capture a series of bridges from Eindhoven to Arnhem.



Britain’s commander General Bernard Montgomery hoped it would clear the path for an armoured assault and end the war by Christmas.

But the 10,000 troops from UK’s 1st Airborne Division and the Polish 1st Parachute Brigade faced unexpectedly fierce resistance from a Nazi Panzer Corps in Arnhem.



Paras led by Lt Col John Frost secured the northern end of the Arnhem bridge held it for several days – but eventually ran out of ammo before reinforcements arrived.

Carns, a former armed forces minister, said: “A generation ago people sacrificed their lives for everything we have today.

“We never thought we would have war in Europe and now we are seeing the same casualty rates as the Second World War.

“What you are seeing from Russia is an Arnhem every month.”



Bayo, an independent MP, said: “We are paying respect to our forebears.

“I jumped on the 50th anniversary – 32 years ago – with a lot of veterans who were still nimble enough to jump.

“Now we’re are doing it to honour them. We are carrying that baton and remembering that sacrifice.”



Two Dutch firemen from Renkum – the drop zone where the paras landed – also joined Friday’s jump.

Frank Van Rhijn, 33, and Lex Stegink, 33, said they wanted “to remember the guys that jumped in Renkum”.

Frank added: “Renkum is our hometown so this means a lot to us.”

John Todd, 81, from the Pathfinder Parachute Group that organised the jumpers, said: “We have got to keep the memory alive, it should never be lost.

“This is not just a parade, we are doing what those soldiers did all those years ago.”



The former Parachute regiment reservist who made his last jump aged 79, added: “We have got Belgians, Polish, a couple of Australians, Dutch, an American and a lot British.

“We are using the same planes and the same drop zone that the 1st Airborne Division used – the difference we don’t have any flak being thrown up at us and there is no one on the DZ shooting us.”

Terence Millar, a retired airborne sniper, jumped with his late father’s ashes and scattered them in Renkum the drop zone when he landed.



Terence, a former 2 Para sergeant, said he had promised his dad “one last para descent” before he died aged 90.

Terrence, who served 22 years in the regulars and two in the reserves, said: “My father was Sgt Maj Thomas Millar.

He was 90 and served 9 years in the Irish Army and then was 4 Para from 67 to 76.” Terence, who is known as Moose added: “He was the reason I joined. I stayed with him in hospital till he passed away and promised him one last para descent.”



One of his sons had planned to jump but was ill and another son, who is serving in 3 Para, met him on the drop zone.

Moving body-cam footage captured the moment Terence bid his father a final farewell.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

He removed paper packet from his smock and scattered the ashes on the grass in front of his parachute.

He said: “Farewell dad. Airborne dad. Airborne”

News.title: Rape suspect ‘allowed to flee UK while owing taxpayers £200,000’ – as he could still be claiming benefits
News.content:
FREE TO FLEE Rape suspect ‘allowed to flee UK while owing taxpayers £200,000’ – as he could still be claiming benefits







Next

A RAPE suspect who owes £200,000 in taxpayer money was allegedly allowed to flee the UK after police failed to stop him leaving.

Ndumbe Achile Ndumbe claimed hundreds of thousands of pounds in housing benefits despite being a landlord for six houses in Manchester.



The 41-year-old fraudulently claimed £180,000 and was fined another £26,000 in 2025 by the courts after failing to obtain a HMO license.

It is believed Ndumbe flew to Cameroon in January once being released under investigation after being arrested on suspicion of rape in 2024.



It was also revealed that he was allegedly claiming £200 a month in Pip payments.

He pinned this down to mental health struggles and back pain.

An inquiry source told The Times: “This case represents and highlights multiple failures in the system, across the police, the border and Department for Work and Pensions. How was he allowed to leave the country in the first place while being investigated for rape?

“There was evidence he had made previous trips between the UK and Cameroon. He should never have been allowed to keep his passport and leave the country while on bail over a rape complaint.”

When the benefit fraudster was initially arrested in July of 2024 on suspicion of rape, his electronic devices were seized.

His phone, laptop and a camcorder were all confiscated by officials, and possible evidence of further sexual offences was alleged to have been found.



Police expanded their investigation in response to the findings, despite Ndumbe being on police bail for the past two years.

He was also managing six HMOs in Greater Manchester and the freehold owner of two of those properties despite the housing benefit claims.

It was revealed that rent of between £500 and £800 was paid into his account each month.

Ndumbe failed to register the two properties correctly, landing him the £26,486 fine.

Greater Manchester police said in a statement: “Detectives investigating reports of rape have arrested a suspect who remains under investigation and inquiries are actively continuing.



“Specialist agencies continue to provide the victims with support.”

The Department for Work and Pensions and the Home Office have been contacted for comment.

News.title: Harry and Meghan's media treatment echoes what happened to Diana, Earl Spencer tells BBC
News.content:
Speaking to Laura Kuenssberg at his Althorp estate, Earl Spencer was asked if he believed Diana would "identify" with the scrutiny the Duke and Duchess of Sussex face.

"If you look at an article in a tabloid about Diana or the couple that you were mentioning, Harry and Meghan, you know, they can be really, really unpleasant," he replied.

"And I think it would be really beholden on people to learn from Diana's example.

"I'm not here to speak for Harry and Meghan, but for anyone who's being destroyed in this way daily, it must be such a cancerous influence in their life."

He said he saw Diana's "tears of despair" when describing the impact of media coverage on her, adding she was "very, very sensitive to criticism".

Earl Spencer said his sister - who married the then-Prince Charles in 1981 - was "really brought low by all that criticism", describing it as a "pity" to see "echoes of that now" in the treatment of his nephew Prince Harry and wife Meghan.

He also said he thought there was a media perception that he was "on Harry's side" but insisted: "I'm on my deceased sister's sons' side, both of them and if either of them wanted anything, then I'd be equally there for them."

Princess Diana was subject to huge press interest right up until her death in a car crash in Paris on 31 August 1997.

In the eulogy he delivered at her funeral, Earl Spencer accused the media of being on a "permanent quest...to bring her down" and said newspapers had been threatened by her "genuine goodness".

News.title: Watch: Diana's brother says press has 'cancerous influence' on Harry and Meghan's lives
News.content:
Earl Spencer has told the BBC that there are similarities between the way his sister Diana, Princess of Wales and the Duke and Duchess of Sussex have been treated by the press.

He said Princess Diana was "brought low" by press criticism of her and that it is a "pity" to see echoes of that in Harry and Meghan's lives now.

He added that people should learn from Princess Diana's example, and that for anyone being "destroyed daily" by the tabloid press, it must be a "cancerous influence" on their lives.

The full interview with Laura Kuenssberg, Princess Diana: My Sister's Story, will be available on iPlayer from 16:00 and broadcast on BBC One at 18:30 BST on Sunday.

News.title: The deadly new drugs reshaping Scotland's fight against addiction
News.content:
Efforts to bring down Scotland's sky-high rate of drug deaths are being frustrated by the arrival of hundreds of powerful new synthetic substances that experts warn are making the deadly drugs crisis even more dangerous.

In the past three years, there has been an explosion in the supply of new synthetic cannabinoids and opioids, transforming the illicit drugs trade and increasing the risk of fatal overdoses.

Annual figures to be released on Wednesday are expected to show a rise in the number of drug-related deaths in Scotland, which already has an unenviable record as the drugs death capital of Europe.

"The illicit drug supply in Scotland is getting more and more dangerous," said Dr Lorna Nisbet of Dundee University's Leverhulme Research Centre for Forensic Science.

News.title: Major seaside hotel fire that evacuated guests during night treated as suspicious
News.content:
A fire at a seaside hotel where about 280 people were evacuated is believed to have been caused deliberately, police have said.

A total of 26 fire engines were sent to the Grand Burstin Hotel in Folkestone at about 01:05 BST on Saturday, Kent Fire & Rescue Service said.

Kent Police said that the fire was being treated as suspicious and is appealing for witnesses.

"Inquiries into the circumstances are under way," police said.

News.title: Strictly returns with new hosting trio as celebrities find out dance pairings
News.content:
Strictly Come Dancing has returned to the small screen for its 24th series, in a new era for the show as it moves forward with a revamped presenting line up.

Broadcaster Emma Willis, comedian Josh Widdicombe and former Strictly professional Johannes Radebe made their presenting debut on Saturday, taking over from long-running hosting duo Tess Daly and Claudia Winkleman, who left the show last year.

A fresh cohort of famous faces â including actress Melanie Walters and former England footballer Shaun Wright-Phillips â also stepped onto the ballroom floor for the first time.

During the launch show, it was revealed which professional dancers they were paired with.

Stepping out onto the ballroom floor after a huge all-cast opening dance routine, Willis said presenting Strictly was a "genuine honour".

"Josh, you've got moves," proclaimed Radebe, a former professional on the show. While Widdicombe added that it was "a little bit overwhelming" but he was "delighted" to be there.

In a first for the show, celebrity and pro pairings were revealed via three dance routines. It functioned as a musical chairs of sorts, in which the contestants switched partners until the music was paused, and a couple was announced.

News.title: Sex and dating for the sandwich generation - Sharon Horgan on her latest comedy Youth
News.content:
Casual sex. Relationships. Parenting. Sharon Horgan has already seen us through several life stages via hit comedy dramas such as Pulling, Catastrophe and Motherland.

Now, with her latest show Youth, Horgan puts the spotlight on 50-something women, imbued with her trademark tightly balanced mix of hilarity and pathos.

The HBO Max series sees Horgan's character, Alex, gamely attempting to juggle a stressful publishing career while looking after a teenage son and elderly parents. She's part of the so-called sandwich generation, those in midlife who have to juggle caring responsibilities for old and young while often working, too.

And that's not all - Alex is also back in the dating game following a divorce.

I'm curious to know how much of Youth is based on Horgan's own experience. The star is divorced and has two daughters.

"We've all got kids who are kind of adults now and parents who are getting older and ailing in some cases. There is a chunk of my life in there, anâ¦ autobiographical element for sure. But the good thing about writing autofiction is that no one really knows which bits are real and which bits aren't, I guess, except the people [in it]!"

The hit writer, producer and actress mulled over the idea for Youth before going on to make Apple TV's Bad Sisters, coming back to it after the dark comedy ended.

The 56-year-old says she was keen to "write about this particular time in a woman's life... through the lens of a mother of a son".

Horgan wanted the story to be "post-divorce and "menopause adjacent".

"And I wanted it to be a comedy, you know? Because there's a lot that's very funny about our bodies failing!"

But it's not just her comedy chops that have gained her a loyal following - a big factor in Horgan's success over the last 20 years or so is the authenticity she brings to her work.

"I spent a lot of time trying to make it as real and as accurate as possible and trying to put in my faults as a parent and mistakes as a woman, my own sort of anxieties and insecurities," she says.

"I try to put all that in thereâ¦ and hope that's a universal feeling because it's really madly important to me that women, especially, watch it and see themselves reflected back."

She says that Youth "felt like the next stage on" from her popular sitcom Catastrophe.

The series, which first aired in 2015 on Channel 4, followed the lives of 40-somethings Sharon and Rob (played by Horgan and Rob Delaney), a couple who got together suddenly after their brief transatlantic fling resulted in pregnancy.

"This [show] feels part of the same trajectory, almost, which was fun and really helpful when it came to trying to figure out what the tone was, although I hope it's kind of doing its own thing," Hogan explains.

News.title: 'People forget we exist': Why older LGBTQ+ community fears losing identity
News.content:
As a 75-year-old lesbian, Mindy Meleyal has lived through every major milestone in the modern LGBT rights movement, from the start of decriminalisation in 1967 to the first same-sex marriages in 2014.

But now she says this important part of her identity is frequently overlooked due to her age.

She's part of England's older LGBTQ+ community, which a new report suggests often experiences poorer health, more limited finances and greater social isolation than the wider older population.

The report, from the Centre for Ageing Better, says without specialist support, this growing demographic could be forced "back into the closet" when accessing care, warning they may even delay getting the care they need because of concerns about homophobia.

Adam Porter, a housing development manager from the LGBT Foundation charity, says he regularly meets older members of the community in exactly that situation.

"It's very common for people to hide things if they have a carer visiting their home, for example hiding their wedding photos or taking down a trans flag," he says.

"In the case of someone moving into a care environment, that means hiding who they are in their own home, for what could be the rest of their life."

He says he has been "horrified" by some of the stories he has heard meeting older LGBTQ+ people, including some who have had carers offer to "pray for them" regarding their sexuality.

Porter is part of the team behind Kindred House, a first-of-its-kind LGBTQ+ social housing scheme for over-55s, set to open in Manchester next year.

News.title: Analysis: Trump escalates media fight after week of setbacks
News.content:
The president's frustration at the media, however, came after a week of setbacks in which major institutions handed him a series of losses across his agenda.

First, the Supreme Court blocked his plan to restrict mail-in voting ahead of the midterms. This prompted Trump to lash out at the court's justices including those he had appointed. "These are not the people I interviewed to serve on the United States Supreme Court," he said.

The Federal Reserve, the US central bank, then raised interest rates after Trump had spent months arguing they should be cut. This was followed by a judge ordering his administration to give 30 days' notice before making any changes to the Kennedy Center arts venue in Washington DC after the president warned it could be "ripped down".

These headlines, combined with approval ratings that recently sunk to record lows for his second term, suggest Trump is facing challenging political headwinds.

His latest attack on the press, however, raises clear legal questions.

The First Amendment to the US Constitution forbids Congress from "abridging" the freedom of the press. It is language that courts have long interpreted as preventing the government from discriminating against the media based on the content of their coverage.

All three targeted news outlets have promised to file lawsuits challenging Trump's decision.

Although the breadth of this move is unprecedented, it is far from the first time the Trump administration has attempted to limit or deny access to the White House to members of mainstream media outlets.

In his first term, the administration revoked CNN correspondent Jim Acosta's press credentials, setting off a legal battle that was ultimately resolved in the journalist's favour. It also temporarily suspended the pass of a reporter who had a heated argument with White House adviser Sebastian Gorka â a move that also was subsequently blocked by the courts.

Last year, the White House banned reporters for the Associated Press from participating in the president's press pool - which allows media outlets access to smaller in-town and travelling presidential appearances - because the newswire service would not follow Trump's move to rename the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America.

That dispute also led to a protracted - and yet to be fully resolved - legal battle, prompting the White House to change press pool rules to drop the guaranteed spot for all wire services.

News.title: JLR suppliers call for shift to aerospace
News.content:
Major Jaguar Land Rover suppliers have urged the government to help automotive manufacturers move into aerospace and defence, warning that large-scale car production in the UK faces long-term decline.

In an open letter to the prime minister, chancellor and West Midlands Mayor Richard Parker, industry leaders argued Britain's automotive supply chain was "not in decline" but "in the wrong market".

The intervention comes nearly a fortnight after JLR announced plans to cut 4,000 jobs.

The Treasury said it recognised the uncertainty facing workers and was supporting the automotive sector through grants, lower energy costs and investment in electric vehicle production.

JLR has its global headquarters in Coventry and plants in Solihull, Wolverhampton and Halewood.

Signatories to the letter said the redundancies were "the first visible crack" in a UK automotive supply chain supporting about 183,000 manufacturing jobs.

News.title: Maddy Cusack 'more than a number on a shirt' as anniversary falls during inquest delay
News.content:
Sitting on a bench dedicated to her memory, Maddy Cusack's sister and cousin fondly remember her as their sunshine and someone with a real sense of fun.

Olivia Cusack says her big sister was the person "I looked up to my whole life", while for Emily Reilly, her cousin Maddy's the one who "used to get us in trouble with my dad".

But as they come to remember the former Sheffield United footballer on the third anniversary of her death, they're still waiting for answers.

An inquest examining what happened to Maddy Cusack, who was 27 when she was found unconscious at her home in Derbyshire, started in June and should've finished in July.

But it has been paused for months while her former club Sheffield United looks for documents linked to her medical records.

It means her family will have to wait until at least December to hear more evidence, a wait Olivia describes as "extremely overwhelming".

"It is very emotional and you can find yourself frustrated at times," she tells BBC Newsbeat.

"They're very difficult days."

News.title: Michael Marra announced as new Scottish Labour leader
News.content:
He went on to thank his opponents, Joe Fagan and Monica Lennon, and praised them for their ideas about how the party needed to change.

He said: "Joe argued for a politics rooted in people and place, for less control in the centre and more control for local communities. That should be the case in our country and in our party.

"Monica was right to say we need to reconnect with the trade union movement that birthed the Labour party.

"Her record delivering change through parliament is also a template for how Labour should behave in opposition â robust in our criticism of the SNP, yes, but also making our own change."

Marra continued: "Scots know what we are against. They can't tell you what we are for... Social justice. Eradication of poverty. Good work. Good housing. Good public services. The good life for working people. An economy where everyone has a fair chance in life, which redistributes power, wealth and opportunity."

News.title: Tens of thousands of fridge freezers left at docks as household collections suspended
News.content:
People have reported storing broken fridges and freezers in their gardens for months because some council collections have been suspended.

It follows the closure of specialist treatment facilities and a wider shortage of capacity to process cooling appliances, the Local Government Authority (LGA) said.

Recycling company Unimetals, which had dozens of sites in the UK, filed for liquidation in 2025 leaving tens of thousands of fridge freezers at Newport Docks.

The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) said it was working to manage the capacity shortages.

Almost a quarter of Welsh councils say they have suspended household collections of fridge-freezers due to a shortage of space at disposal sites.

Cardiff is one of these and Lee Young, who lives in the city, has been trying to get rid of his broken fridge-freezer for two months.

"I tried to take it to the recycling centre in July but was told it wasn't accepted. Someone said the council would collect it, but they won't either."

It has been sitting in his back garden ever since and he does not know when council collections will resume.

News.title: Davey says Lib Dems are 'firewall against Farage' as conference begins
News.content:
Sir Ed Davey said the Liberal Democrats are "a firewall against Nigel Farage and Reform" as the party's conference began in Brighton.

The Lib Dem leader sought to strike a combative stance as he faced down some criticism from MPs, including one who said publicly that they felt the party was struggling for relevance.

On the first day of the autumn conference, Sir Ed warned an "unholy alliance" between Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch and Farage could turn the UK into a "Trump satellite state".

Addressing speculation about a possible snap election, he said the party was ready to fight and would build its so-called orange wall even higher by winning more than its 2024 record of 72 MPs.

Sir Ed's attention-grabbing stunts helped raise the party's profile ahead of the last election, but recent polling showed 43% of respondents were unclear what the Liberal Democrats stand for, with just over half describing them as "weak".

In an essay, external written ahead of conference, South Cotswolds MP Roz Savage asked: "Why are we as a party struggling for relevance at precisely the moment when so many people feel powerless?"

She urged the party to rediscover its "insurgent spirit" rather than being the "polite custodians of a system that leaves people feeling powerless".

Asked about her comments, Sir Ed said: "No, I heard Roz [Savage], and I really value her, but I think she's wrong on that.

"If you look at our election results up and down the country, we now run more councils than the Conservatives."

He added: "Listen, MPs get elected and they get frustrated because they can't change the world.

"I'm afraid that's the political system. I've been used to it for a little while and people are learning about that frustration."

Speaking on the pebbles of Brighton Beach, Sir Ed told reporters the Liberal Democrats would fight to stop a Reform government.

"One of the things that makes us unique is that we are a firewall against Nigel Farage and Reform," he said.

"Many of the seats he needs to get himself into No 10 are seats that we will defend and indeed win - and we are also able to take seats off the Conservatives, because I really fear that Kemi Badenoch will give the keys to No 10 to Nigel Farage, so we have got to stop the Conservatives as well.

"We have got an historic opportunity to win many more seats and a moral responsibility to stop Reform."

He added a manifesto working group had already been set up in case of an early election "so we'll be ready if it comes early, but, you know, it still could be up to three years away".

Sir Ed insisted his party has a "distinctive position" in British politics, and will use the four-day conference to position it to take on the challenge from Reform as well as its typical rivals the Conservatives, talking up their focus on the NHS and goal of re-joining the EU single market and customs union.

The Lib Dem leader highlighted how six former Conservative cabinet ministers were among 25 Tories to have defected to Reform in the last two years, claiming they were now competing with each other to see who can divide the country more, rather than looking to fix the country's problems.

"An unholy alliance between Farage and Badenoch is the only way either can get into power," he said.

"Together, they want to turn Britain into a Trump satellite state which would trash our NHS, turn our communities against each other, cause untold damage to our environment, and trample over traditional British values of fairness, tolerance, and decency.

"A bigger Orange Wall is the only thing that can stand between Britain and this dangerous experiment, and we will not let them pass."

Davey also attacked the Labour government as having no plan for growth, failing to support families struggling with the cost of living and taxing small businesses "to the brink".

Ahead of a speech to party members, Davey urged Liberal Democrats not to look away from injustice or "human dignity under attack" but to fight back.

News.title: Parents could lose benefits or face prison for child's crimes, minister says
News.content:
Parents could lose their benefits or face prison sentences for their children's crimes under reforms to the youth justice system, a minister has said.

Youth Justice Minister Jake Richards told the Times newspaper the system "should hold parents to account in a proportionate way for ensuring that they play their role in keeping communities safe".

His comments come after the government set out plans in May to strengthen and expand Parenting Orders, which can currently compel parents or guardians to address their child's behaviour by attending counselling sessions or face fines.

Richards said prison sentences would only apply "in the most extreme cases" and would be up to judges' discretion.

He described the proposed changes in England and Wales as part of a "carrot-and-stick" approach.

"Parenting orders are going to make sure that parents are more involved in the process by which we try to turn around young offenders," Richards told the Times.

"Yes, that will have some stick. It could be custodial, or docking benefits - ultimately it will be up to a judge. But we want them to be more involved and that comes with responsibilities as well."

Critics of the proposals say engaging with parents on a voluntary basis is generally more effective in building trusting relationships and providing support.

Jess Mullen, chief executive of the Alliance for Youth Justice which represents more than 70 organisations that advocate for children, previously questioned how putting parents in prison would provide "stability or support for the child".

Andrew Neilson, director of campaigns at the Howard League for Penal Reform, told the BBC: "Reforming parenting orders in this way risks being ineffective at best and counter-productive at worst.

"Criminalising parents is unlikely to help children who need support, and putting them behind bars would only put further strain on a failing prison system that is already bursting at the seams."

When the government white paper was announced in May, then Justice Secretary David Lammy said that strengthening parenting orders would mean "there are real consequences for parents and carers who wilfully fail to support efforts to address their children's behaviour."

He told BBC Breakfast at the time that if a parent was struggling, then the "judge can intervene to make sure that the young person is getting the support that they need and the parent is doing the best that they can".

He also said he expected the power to jail parents to be used "very, very rarely".

Courts are currently required to consider issuing a Parenting Order where a child under 16 has been convicted of an offence.

They can also consider an order for 16 and 17-year-olds if they believe this would help prevent further offences.

The term of the order must not exceed 12 months and breach of a parenting order is a criminal offence with a maximum Â£1,000 fine, according to the Sentencing Council.

However, government statistics show the use of parenting orders has declined in recent years, from more than 1,000 orders in 2009/10 to just 33 in 2022/23.

The government's youth justice reform plans come after Phase One of the Southport Inquiry report found "catastrophic" failures by the parents of the Southport killer Axel Rudakubana and various agencies meant clear chances to prevent the 2024 child murders were missed.

In the interview with the Times, Richards also rejected calls from lawyers to raise the age of criminal responsibility from 10, saying it would undermine "public faith" in the justice system and it was "not a priority at all".

In June, the Bar Council, the representative body for barristers in England and Wales, said the threshold should rise to 14 due to criminalisation at such an early age not being an "effective, proportionate or just response".

The United Nations has previously pointed out the UK has some of the lowest ages of criminal responsibility in the world and that it should rise it to the UN recommendation of at least 14.

On Thursday, ministers met with local leaders and experts in Manchester to discuss how devolution could help reform youth justice.

Additional reporting by AndrÃ© Rhoden-Paul & Shelley Phelps, political correspondent

News.title: Matthew Rhys' sister 'so proud of him' after historic Emmy wins
News.content:
The sister of Hollywood actor Matthew Rhys said her family had been "pinching ourselves all week" following his historic Emmy success.

Rhys became the first person to win two lead acting Emmy prizes in one night, after he was named best lead actor in a limited series for the psychological thriller The Beast In Me, and best lead actor in a comedy for his role in Widow's Bay.

His older sister Rachel Evans, who accompanied Rhys to the ceremony in Los Angeles, said she was starstruck seeing Hollywood royalty at the event, and revealed that she and her brother called their parents afterwards, who were sat at home in their dressing gowns.

"I think we just all giggled for a long time."

News.title: 'Fast, furious and dangerous' - a city's quad bike menace
News.content:
Sitting in his Birmingham city centre apartment, one resident says he can often hear them before he sees them.

The sound of revving engines is followed by groups of quad bikes and off-road motorcycles weaving through traffic, performing wheelies and riding through some of the busiest streets in the city.

"It's only a matter of time until something serious happens," he said.

Videos shared on social media over recent months have captured groups of riders travelling through areas including Hurst Street, Bristol Road and Corporation Street, often with faces covered and no visible number plates.

One video filmed by the resident showed a pedestrian narrowly avoiding being struck as a group rode through the city centre.

"I've watched them and they go through red lights, they just totally ignore the red lights," he said.

"People still cross when the pedestrian lights are green, but they don't even slow down to check.

"They're zigzagging in the middle of cars. No number-plates. It's bad because nobody sees any action happening and it's only a matter of time until something serious happens."

News.content:

Polling is underway on Sunday across two German state elections where projected gains for the far-right AfD threaten to weaken Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s authority and hamper his ability to deliver economic reforms across Europe’s largest economy.

The regional contests are taking place in Berlin, the national capital, and in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, a mostly rural territory in the former communist east that remains economically less affluent.

The voting follows just two weeks after the anti-migration, Russia-friendly Alternative for Germany, or AfD, fell barely short of an overall majority in the small eastern territory of Saxony-Anhalt, giving the movement its strongest opportunity to date to form a far-right regional government for the first time since World War II.

Merz’s leadership was hit hard by his party’s heavy defeat in that 6 September election.

The result stunned a population that had assumed thorough education and robust legal protections enacted after the Nazi era had provided lasting immunity to nationalism and racial ideology.

open image in gallery The top co-candidate of the Greens Werner Graf casts his vote on 20 September in Berlin, during Berlin's state elections ( AFP/Getty )

Further substantial gains for the AfD are expected on Sunday. However, the party lacks any practical path to power in Berlin and faces far tougher resistance from Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania’s centre-left governor than it encountered from Merz’s party in Saxony-Anhalt.

Prospects for Merz’s center-right Christian Democratic Union are bleaker. It could lose the mayor’s office in Berlin.

If things go very badly, it could fail for the first time to win seats in a state legislature anywhere by falling below 5 per cent of the vote in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, where it was already weak.

Merz, 70, became Germany’s leader 16 months ago with promises to turn around an economy that has barely grown in years, but has failed to lift a sullen national mood and has himself become deeply unpopular.

open image in gallery Merz’s authority was severely damaged by his party’s stinging defeat in the 6 September election by AfD — a result that shocked many Germans who had believed their country had developed an immunity to nationalism and assertions of racial superiority after confronting the horrors of its Nazi past through education and laws to outlaw persecution ( Associated Press )

The strong showing of AfD in the Saxony-Anhalt election has further weakened the chancellor's standing on the national level as well, and in the past two weeks there have been calls even from within his own party to replace him as chancellor.

No top-level allies have called publicly for his departure, and many have warned against “personnel debates.”

Apparently anticipating a tough postelection period, Merz abandoned a planned trip to New York next week to attend the U.N. General Assembly. Despite the strong headwinds, he has repeatedly said that he’s determined to stay on and finish his term as chancellor.

Luke Littler has threatened to boycott tournaments in the Netherlands after being booed and whistled during the World Series of Darts Finals in Amsterdam.

The back-to-back world champion faced a hostile environment during Friday’s win over home favourite Danny Noppert and it escalated on Saturday night as referee Charlie Costorphine had to intervene in the last-16 win over Nathan Aspinall.

Littler has taken a stance against volatile crowds before, refusing to travel to European Tour events in Germany as a result of his treatment from fans there.

And he is “100 per cent” prepared to do the same in the Netherlands.

“With the Germans, I haven’t been for a long time, we will have to see in Dortmund whether it changes or stays the same,” he told Online Darts.

“If the Dutch stay like this, then I’m not going to do any Euro tours over there. There’s just no point in me travelling, wasting my time whilst I’m getting booed.

“I just want to play my darts, obviously sign autographs.

“The past two nights, I’ve done nothing, I’ve just walked off stage without thanking anybody. There’s no point thanking everyone when they are booing me.”

open image in gallery Luke Littler and Nathan Aspinall played a thrilling match (Kelly Deckers/PDC)

Despite the bearpit atmosphere, Littler came out on top in a last-leg decider with Aspinall to keep his dream of a clean sweep alive.

The 19-year-old is hoping to become the first man to win all 10 major televised tournaments in a calendar year, having triumphed in the first five.

Welshman Jonny Clayton awaits in the quarter-final on Sunday afternoon.

Central London was at a standstill.

Thousands of stationary black cabs had gridlocked the length of Whitehall, halting traffic around Westminster and the West End.

It was June 2014, and drivers were protesting against a newly-launched private hire service called Uber.

By the following summer, France had cracked down on Uber’s ride-sharing option after disorder saw cars overturned, windows smashed, tires set on fire.

Cab drivers in Paris said they were being undercut by the taxi app and its various services, now ubiquitous in cities across the world, while back home there were complaints about supposed differences in regulations, making competition unfair.

open image in gallery London Black Cab drivers take part in a protest against a new private taxi service 'Uber', a mobile phone app, on the Mall leading to Buckingham Palace in central London on June 11, 2014 ( AFP/Getty )

The emergence of new technologies and the threat they pose to jobs has caused unrest throughout history. But anything that has come before could all pale in comparison with what is to come.

Economist Carl-Benedikt Frey, associate professor of AI & work at the Oxford Internet Institute, paints a bleak picture on how he believes artificial intelligence (AI) will impact the future of work in the UK.

Looking back on the anti-Uber protests, he told The Independent: “That was not a technology that was going to replace them (drivers); that was a technology or company that meant more competition.”

As for the future, “I think civil unrest will come long before mass unemployment”, he added.

The fear that AI will “replace” humans, whether merely on a professional level or in a more fatal sense, is held by many.

In May, research by King’s College London (KCL) revealed that more than half of the British people believe AI will create widespread unemployment – and one in five think it will do so at such a rate which would create civil unrest.

According to Dr Frey, backlash towards AI – whether that is on an environmental level or through the construction of vast data centres – shows it is a “tremendously unpopular technology, even without having produced anything like mass unemployment”.

That sentiment will only deepen once its impact on incomes and livelihoods takes hold further, with new AI models increasingly capable of more and businesses drawn in by their cost-cutting abilities, he believes.

Dr Frey explained: “If AI threatens to reduce people's incomes, even by 5 per cent or 10 per cent – 10 per cent being roughly the amount by which Uber reduced incumbent drivers' incomes - you can see unrest from that as well.

“Taxi services as a share of the entire economy is relatively small; generative AI is a general-purpose technology that will touch on many different industries and occupations, if not all of them.

open image in gallery A taxi blocks the area of Porte Maillot in west Paris, on June 26, 2015, with drivers furious at what they see as unfair competition from Uber ( AFP/Getty )

“Certainly, we can see a lot of discontent and unrest long before anything like mass unemployment materialises.”

A 2024 report by the Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR) found that, without government intervention, nearly eight million jobs in the UK could be lost to AI, leading to a “jobs apocalypse”.

The think tank states that entry-level, part-time, and administrative jobs are the most exposed to being replaced by AI in a worst-case scenario over the next three to five years.

Likewise, at least a million jobs in London are "highly or significantly exposed" to AI, a report published by City Hall in April said.

Last month, the Office for National Statistics said the number of people aged between 16 and 24 not in employment, education or training – so-called Neets – sat at 981,000 from April to June.

It represented a drop from the 1,012,000 Neets in January to March but means that at 13 per cent, the UK’s rate remains among the highest in Europe.

Some places have just one vacancy for every 22 young people, new findings from the IPPR show.

Rotheram in South Yorkshire was found to be the local authority with the fewest suitable vacancies, at just 46 for every 1,000 young people – 58 per cent below the UK average.

This was followed by East Renfrewshire in Scotland (53 per cent below), Broxtowe in the East Midlands (47 per cent), and Newcastle-Under-Lyme in the West Midlands (47 per cent).

The figures illustrate what is a tremendously difficult climate for young people trying to find work – a climate that is only going to become tougher as AI further eats into the job market.

And there is little optimism among young people. In the KCL study, the view that AI-driven unemployment will drive civil unrest rose to a third (34 per cent) among university students.

“I have immense sympathy for young people today”, KCL professor Elena Simperl told The Independent.

“They have already had their lives disrupted by a global pandemic, and now they face the rise of generative AI against a backdrop of wider economic uncertainty”, added Prof Simperl, who co-directs the King's Institute for AI.

However, it is not just jobs for young graduates that AI poses a threat to. According to Dr Frey, the common consensus is that the technology is most threatening white-collar jobs, but its impact will be felt much more widely.

He explained: “It's jobs across the board – in construction, in manufacturing.

“Another story which I think is under-appreciated is that AI allows us as consumers to do more things ourselves. If the boiler breaks down, I would usually call a heating engineer straight away.

“These days, I take a picture of it and see step-by-step with the help of AI if I can fix it myself.

“That is not going to mean widespread unemployment, but it means that many manual trades which we think of as being safe havens from automation might also face income pressures, because that heating engineer loses a job and might then only get the more technically difficult cases.

“That also means that apprentices who learn on the job may not get those easier calls either, which is not going to be good for learning. Those are the more immediate impacts.”

The genie is out of the bottle, however. AI may create jobs but its impact on traditional professions will continue to be felt.

According to Prof Simperl, this means that, assuming the trend of decline in employment continues, we must now think of the required safety nets - as well as re-skilling programmes to adapt to a new and ever-changing world.

“We need to actively guide the trend rather than just letting it happen to us”, she said.

“This means collecting better evidence, but also training both employers and workers to use AI for things they should be using it for, rather than just adopting it blindly and waiting to see what happens.”

open image in gallery Almost 1m young people in the UK are out of work, unemployment or training ( Alamy/PA )

There is also a sociological impact to consider. What would the world look like if millions of people lost their jobs - or job roles which have existed for all of living memory cease to exist?

“I think that would be extraordinarily transformative and challenge a lot of people's identity, sense of purpose, and self-fulfilment”, said Dr Frey.

“It would be a very significant shock.

“At the same time, before the Industrial Revolution, basically everybody worked, but very few people had jobs in the modern sense. We've been in that world to a large degree before, so we know that we can potentially adjust to such a world.

“That would be a more pleasant world where you can do your gardening without depending on it for your living - if a harvest was bad, that would not mean your family was at risk of starving.

“Being on the other side of this, we can potentially get to a better place, but that would be an extraordinarily disruptive transition for a lot of people. It wouldn't be smooth sailing by any means.”

AI-inspired mass unemployment would, naturally, increase pressure on the country’s welfare spending.

Though advocates of the technology suggest it could eventually create a ‘post-work’ world, where the money generated by AI provides a universal income to those made redundant by it, Dr Frey thinks governments must get ready for its impact.

He is unsure whether they are.

Many of these people are already tremendously wealthy; they are probably more interested in writing history than anything else Carl-Benedikt Frey

“I don't think they're prepared for it mentally in the sense that they have policy proposals on the table ready to be implemented when it happens”, he said.

“At the same time, in many ways, we don't have to reinvent the wheel.

“The welfare state exists, and we do have educational systems - we can build on those. There are certainly things that will have to be modified.

“If the labour share of income goes down, obviously, as we tax less income from labour, we will have to tax consumption and capital more, and there are many other things that need to be adjusted.”

Unemployment is not the primary concern related to AI, however.

Researcher Jacob Coxon quit tech giant Anthropic earlier this month, warning that the company and its rivals were “gambling with our lives”, adding those building AI “earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade”.

It is no shock then, that people worry about this technology - and the prospect of it capturing millions of jobs before killing the people that it has made unemployed.

Dr Frey is not convinced he would rather governments would be in control of this technology instead of private companies, but he thinks it is healthy to be skeptical about the motives at play in the AI sphere.

“It's often a correct assumption to assume that somebody doesn't primarily have the public interest in their head”, he said.

“There's a mix of motives. Many of these people are already tremendously wealthy; they are probably more interested in writing history than anything else.

“Money and power are part of it, but legacy and reputation play into it as well.”

He added; “There's a sense that we're lacking accountability, and that's particularly true in places like Britain or Europe, because the firms building these technologies are not here, so our ability to shape this is quite limited.”

The prospect of Ben Stokes reversing his international retirement to play a part in next year’s Ashes has receded after Stephen Fleming said it would be “wrong” to try and change his mind.

Stokes walked away in dramatic fashion earlier this summer after four rollercoaster years as Test captain but has continued playing for Durham, helping his county win the Division Two title with some handy contributions.

He has also signed up for a stint with Adelaide Strikers in the Big Bash League and the idea that he might make a grand return for one last crack at Australia next summer refuses to go away.

open image in gallery Ben Stokes retired from Test cricket this summer (Joe Giddens/PA) ( PA Wire )

Even England’s director of cricket, Rob Key, admitted it would be a “great story” and refused to rule it out.

But England’s new red-ball coach, Fleming, moved to dampen the speculation despite meeting the 35-year-old during his first few days in the country.

“I went up to Durham and spoke to Ben, which was good. He’s really happy and seemed to be really at peace with his decision,” said Fleming, who previously worked with the all-rounder at Chennai Super Kings.

“I’ve worked with Ben quite a bit. We’ve got a really good relationship. He was in a good space. He’d just bowled another 20 overs for Durham with success.

open image in gallery Stephen Fleming is England’s new Test coach (Martin Rickett/PA) ( PA Wire )

“He seems really happy and comfortable with what he’s doing. My view is when a player decides to retire it’s a big decision and I have the utmost respect for that decision so that’s where it sits.”

Speaking later to BBC Sport’s Test Match Special, Fleming suggested he would not be leaning in Stokes to perform a U-turn.

“I respect his decision too much,” he said.

“To try to turn that around and question that is wrong. I know how much goes into that type of decision, and I respect that.”

open image in gallery Ben Stokes’ Ashes career may be in the past (Robbie Stephenson/PA) ( PA Archive )

Although Stokes seems increasingly unlikely to be part of the Ashes, Fleming has no problem at all with the English public’s preoccupation with their oldest rivalry. In fact, he shares it.

“I have an obsession with it as well. New Zealand has obsession with it, we love it,” he said.

“We have a deep desire to beat Australia in everything, as the little cousin. We are linked, and I’m incredibly excited about being part of it.”

“I want to be unhealthy. And unfit. As unfit and unhealthy as possible, actually.”

I doubt you’ve ever heard anyone say this. I certainly haven’t. If anything, the opposite is true.

I walked down my street on recycling day this week and saw plastic boxes filled with protein shakes, supplement tubs, cardboard cartons from meal delivery services and more health-minded products.



It cemented my belief that the vast majority of people want to be healthy and happy, and they’re putting a lot of time, money and effort into achieving it, which should be enough. Yet there is plenty of health data to suggest we’re moving in the other direction.

The 2024 health survey for England found that 66 per cent of adults were either overweight or living with obesity – up from 53 per cent in 1993. But body composition is just one of many signifiers of health.

Perhaps a bigger concern is that, despite an ageing population, the UK’s healthy life expectancy – that is, how long we can expect to live in good health – has fallen in recent years.

On a personal level, as a fitness journalist and coach, I speak to many people who are throwing the kitchen sink at getting fitter only to be left frustrated with a lack of results. But why?

That is the theme of this week’s newsletter.

I posed this question to independent sport and exercise scientist Dr Ash Cox, who raised an interesting point.

Recent Sport England data found the number of adults in the UK meeting government physical activity guidelines is actually on the rise, with the latest figure climbing to nearly two-thirds.

“People participating [in exercise] isn’t necessarily the issue,” he says. “It’s the environment.”

This applies on both the exercise and diet front. Humans, historically, needed to be active to survive – hunting, gathering, seeking out resources and suitable places to sleep. But in the modern world, movement is surplus to requirements.

We work desk jobs, drive home, then unwind from a stressful day with a spot of TV on the sofa, often ordering food on an app when too exhausted to cook. Sitting still is the common denominator.

open image in gallery Shot of a man looking exhausted after his workout ( Getty Images )

A cost-of-living crisis also means many of us are working harder than ever with less cash to splash. We’re left with limited time, energy or money for exercise, with sports clubs and gym memberships often the first expenses to fall by the wayside as we look to conserve finances.

Then we walk into the supermarket to buy food, only to be faced with a barrage of more-ish snacks and packaging covered in tenuous health claims. In a time when money is tight, the most readily available and affordable food is often disproportionately energy-dense and low in genuine nutritional value.

Put plainly: modern life is a minefield, and no normal person could be expected to navigate it without taking a knock to their health.

At this point, I should make clear that nothing in here is accusatory. We’re all trying to be healthy, and we’re all playing this game with a significant handicap.

And while you can manipulate your environment slightly by filling your fridge with pre-chopped vegetables and leaving fitness kit around the house for exercise snacking, wholesale societal changes do not seem to be on the horizon.

So what should we do? Well, if there’s one thing I’ve found the human brain loves, it’s being part of something. Most people also enjoy being a tad rebellious. For that reason, I would like to invite you to join my mini movement revolution.

In it, we are not moving as punishment, or purely as a vehicle for changing the way we look. We are moving because it feels good, because everything is telling us not to, and we are squeezing it in whenever we can as a result.

This does not mean immediately running a marathon. Instead, we’re taking a more playful approach.

Whack on a song and dance while you’re cooking dinner; join in wholeheartedly with your kids’ games; run to the top of a hill, simply because you can; skip up the stairs while swerving the lift; balance on one leg while brushing your teeth; catch up with friends while chucking a frisbee around.

As Dr Cox advises: “All movement adds up. Do the school run on foot; take the stairs when you can, and do it with some intensity; move around the office.

“Dedicated exercise is such a small part of someone’s day, and it has to be squeezed in. But the biggest wins come from habitual physical activity. Put more movement into your life, and go about it with more intent.”

Add this to a nourishing diet – nothing puritanical, just prioritising fruits, vegetables and other foods your grandparents would generally find in their childhood kitchen – and you have a fairly straightforward recipe for better health.

In a world where complexity sells but delivers questionable results, I hope this helps!

England’s new Test coach Stephen Fleming has set his sights on taking the team to number one in the world after kicking off his reign with a “tour of love” across the county game.

The former New Zealand captain was appointed in July but has just taken the reins after sitting out the 3-0 defeat of Pakistan due to family commitments.

He has spent his first week in the country checking in with his captain Joe Root, director of cricket Rob Key and ground hopping with visits to five Rothesay County Championship matches in three days.

open image in gallery Stephen Fleming has started work as England’s new Test coach (Nick Potts/PA) ( PA Wire )

On Saturday he was at Emirates Old Trafford to link up with his predecessor Brendon McCullum, who remains in charge of the white-ball squad.

And he made his ultimate aim clear from day one – lifting the side from fifth in the rankings back to the summit for the first time since 2012 and putting right the nation’s dreadful record in the World Test Championship.

“I would love to be in charge of the number Test team in the world. That would be my aspiration,” he said.

“There have been some really good moments (for this side) but I think there’s more to give. One of the dark arts of coaching is timing and my honest appraisal is that it’s a great time to be the head coach.

“It’s one of the most prestigious jobs in cricket. I was very honoured to be asked. The opportunity to take up this role was one you don’t turn down.”

England have never come to close to reaching the WTC final in four editions since it was launched – and lie sixth in the current table – but Fleming is keen to oversee a change of emphasis when it comes to that competition.

On its importance, he said: “High. England could do much better than that.

“If that’s one of the pinnacle trophies in world cricket, why would we not be trying to get it along with every other marquee event that comes our way? It’s aspirational and that’s why I’m here. That opportunity is real, but there’s a huge amount of work to do.”

That work began with Fleming building – and reigniting – his connection with a domestic game that often felt alienated under the previous regime of McCullum and Ben Stokes.

A title winner with Nottinghamshire in 2005 and a former player of both Middlesex and Yorkshire, he has already embraced the circuit.

“It’s been a tour of love,” he said.

“I have been kissing county coaches’ heads, meeting new players, reintroducing myself to players I played with who are now in positions of authority at counties. I have a deep respect for the county game and what it can offer. It is a key part of English cricket so to reconnect, do some miles on the M1 and immerse myself in that over the last three days has been really good.”

His relationship with fellow Kiwi McCullum will be critical to the success of England’s latest job-share experiment between formats, with the pair not only former team-mates but also firm friends and business partners.

open image in gallery Stephen Fleming was a county champion with Nottinghamshire (John Stillwell/PA) ( PA Archive )

At 53 he is the elder man by nine years and accepted he would be taking the ‘big brother’ role – “yeah, you probably could say that” – in a partnership that will need careful management.

“It’s nice to be in a position to work with him, it’s been a while,” he said.

“It is an advantage that we will be able to talk fairly openly and be robust….we don’t have to spend time getting to know each other as coaches.”

McCullum’s ultra-aggressive style was widely branded as ‘Bazball’, not always fondly, and Fleming was quick to shut down the notion of ‘Flemball’.

“I think that’s a medical condition!” he joked.

News.title: An A to Z guide to what’s in your laundry detergent
News.content:
Laundry is one of those jobs that most of us do on autopilot. Throw a load of washing and your favourite detergent into the drum and wait for the machine to work its magic. Perhaps you’ve never even thought to ask yourself what chemicals you’re putting in with your clothes.

In the UK, detergent brands are legally required to state the use of surfactants and enzymes (the main ingredients for stain removal) in a way that is easy to understand, but you may see additional compounds that leave you scratching your head.

Here, I break down the words on the back of the bottle to help you understand exactly what you’re putting in your washing. Given that I’ve just tested 26 laundry detergents and developed an app to help you clean your clothes better, I’m the best woman for the job.

Below, you’ll find the most common detergent ingredients listed A to Z. If you’ve got a burning question about a laundry buzzword, I should be able to help. Add any in the comments section below.

Anionic

There are two main types of surfactants: anionic and non-ionic. A surfactant has a hydrophilic head that loves water and a hydrophobic tail that hates it. Anionic surfactants have a negative charge on their head, which is what helps lift soils and stains from the fabric, though they’re not so good at getting rid of oils. They create a lot of foam but their effectiveness can be limited by minerals found in hard water, which is why they are paired with non-ionic surfactants.

Bio

Short for biological, this label means that a detergent contains enzymes. These are proteins that break down fats, starches and grease, so use bio formulations when you need to tackle stubborn food stains. They are effective at lower temperatures but they can be abrasive on sensitive skin. If your skin is easily irritated, opt for non-bio, instead.
