World.title: Betel nuts are a top mind-affecting substance. Now there's evidence of ancient use
World.content:
Betel nuts are a top mind-affecting substance. Now there's evidence of ancient use

toggle caption Claire Harbage/NPR

About 600 million people today chew on betel nuts —- the brownish green seeds of certain palm trees that are about the size of a walnut. Betel nut users say they get all kinds of benefits — relief from indigestion, fresh breath, an energy boost.

The medical community notes that long-term betel nut use can damage teeth, increase the risk of heart disease, and lead to oral cancer due to the chemicals within.

Still, many people in Asia and the Asian Pacific are addicted to chewing them. Betel nuts are considered the world's fourth most commonly used mind-affecting substances, after tobacco, alcohol and caffeine.

A new study, published in Science Advances , finds this love affair with betel nuts is nothing new. In fact, it's likely very, very old. By looking at ancient teeth, researchers uncovered what they think is an early stage in the practice, when hunter-gatherers had a habit of sucking on betel nuts, possibly for their painkilling effects.

"It's a chance archaeological discovery that reveals an initial stage in the development of this common drug used today," says Adam Brumm , a professor of archaeology at Griffith University in Australia who led the research, "We think it might have started with hunter-gatherers just sucking on the nuts, almost as though they were gobstoppers ."

Sponsor Message

Outside researchers find the evidence compelling though not conclusive — and further note that drug use has longstanding and deep roots among humanity: The instinct to experiment and expand our horizons with substances is part of human nature, says José Capriles , associate professor of anthropology at Penn State University, who has found drugs used by humans a thousand years ago in South America.

Puzzled by "strange grooves"

How did scientists uncover this ancient betel nut usage? The answer involves two puzzling sets of teeth, fake saliva — and some personal experimentation.

On an archaeological dig in Sulawesi, an island in modern-day Indonesia, Brumm and his colleagues excavated some very old human remains.

They belonged to a hunter-gatherer who lived as far back as 25,000 years. The remains posed a mystery. "There were really strange grooves in the teeth that we couldn't explain," Brumm says.

He emailed other archaeologists — "all of the world's leading experts in ancient dental wear" — soliciting their advice. "None of them could explain how these grooves could have formed," says Brumm.

About 20 miles to the east, they found a second set of teeth from a human who lived up to 8,000 years ago, with similar marks. "The grooves were so deep that they had actually exposed the pulp cavity, the nerve center, of several teeth," Brumm says, describing it as a pattern that likely took decades of repeated wear to form.

Sponsor Message

While hunter-gatherers from that time are known to have used their teeth as tools — holding, breaking, stretching things — none of those uses matched the grooves on these teeth. "We ruled out any type of food they might have been eating, we ruled out the possibility that they were processing plant fibers to make string in their mouth," says Brumm.

Brumm was stumped. Then he remembered another example of distinctive teeth wear, from the colonial period in Europe, America and Australia, when laborers habitually smoked tobacco from clay pipes. "They would have the pipe sticking out of their mouth, Popeye-style," Brumm explains, "Over a lifetime of this habit, they've got a perfectly round notch in their teeth that you can slot the clay pipe stem straight into."

Brumm and his colleagues thought the teeth grooves from Indonesia might originate in a similar habit, one grounded in cultural practices.

The case for the betel nut

In the Asia and Pacific region today, betel nuts are commonly chewed with other chemicals for their combined stimulant effects.

However, the wear patterns on the teeth were consistent with sucking — not chewing — hard, round abrasive objects over many years, Brumm says. He and his colleagues think they've uncovered an early developmental stage in the practice. "We think they were hooked on nut-sucking," Brumm says. Since sucking betel nuts is not common today, Brumm partnered with Professor Roger Papke , a neuropharmacological researcher at the University of Florida, to test whether the action could cause a drug effect ancient humans may have desired.

"We soaked whole betel nuts in artificial saliva, and then introduced the resultant extracts into frog egg cells engineered to produce human brain receptors," Brumm says. They found that the artificial saliva successfully extracted arecoline, an active chemical in the betel nut, and that the brain receptors turned on when they touched the saliva. "We've shown that if you just suck on the nut, there's a physiological reaction that can be released into your bloodstream and then into your brain, and that can alter human brain function," he says.

Sponsor Message

Then they sought to establish that these ancient people actually did it. In addition to matching the shape of betel nuts to the grooves in the teeth, they tested the dental tissues and found traces of arecoline — for which betel nuts are the only known natural source , Papke says.

Brumm also put himself in the mindset of ancient humans and tried sucking on betel nuts himself. "I had to give it a go," he says, "If you gently gnaw on the outside of it, it releases the betel juice. It has this extremely bitter and astringent taste that makes your whole mouth go numb."

He hypothesizes that the numbing, pain-relieving effect was what ancient hunter-gatherers were after. Brumm thinks the betel nut suckers eventually wore their teeth down to the nerve — which he says could have been very painful — leading to more nut-sucking to relieve the pain. "They were essentially caught in this cycle and they were basically addicted to this natural plant drug," Brumm says.

Human nature

Outside researchers say the paper makes a compelling case for ancient betel nut use. "There's evidence for the betel nut causing excessive tooth wear. When you add the chemical evidence, that's pretty much a smoking gun," says Peter Ungar, a distinguished professor of anthropology at the University of Arkansas who studies teeth and was not involved in this study.

"It fits with the bigger picture of our understanding of betel [nut] use and also the cultural dynamics of that time period," says Agustín Fuentes , professor of anthropology at Princeton University.

Others would like to see additional support for the theory. "I wish there was more, I must admit — there are two skeletons that they report," says Capriles at Penn State.

Capriles acknowledges that well-preserved ancient human remains are hard to find, especially in tropical areas where the heat and humidity breaks them down. Still, "more direct evidence would be the actual finding of the nuts, of the seeds, ideally in some form of cultural context," such as a hearth, house floor or burial site, he says.

Sponsor Message

And archaeologists not involved with the study are wary of making assumptions as to why ancient people were attracted to betel nuts. "We have to be very, very careful not to associate our particular assumptions of pain or patterns," says Fuentes, of Princeton. Regarding the researchers' theory that ancient peoples were addicted to betel nuts for their painkilling effects, "I think they're using a contemporary public health and dentistry approach to think about very complicated cultures of the past."

There might have been other social and cultural reasons for the teeth-damaging practice, Fuentes says. After all, people today eat hard candy, open bottles with their teeth, neglect to brush and floss. "All of these things are not directly good for your teeth, but they serve other social [purposes] in other kinds of contexts," he says.

Brumm, the lead researcher, acknowledges there are limitations to the work. "As always with archaeology, you're dealing with vast unknowns," he says, "But we've put a lot of thought into this, and we think this is what was going on."

World.title: Archaeologists are racing to save precious artifacts in Alaska after last year's storm
World.content:
Archaeologists are racing to save precious artifacts in Alaska after last year's storm

toggle caption MaryCait Dolan/KYUK

Last October, remnants of Typhoon Halong swept through western Alaska — causing widespread flooding and displacing over a thousand people in multiple far-flung villages off the state's road system.

In the coastal village of Quinhagak, the storm shook houses and damaged some buildings and infrastructure. And the day after it hit, Jenny Matthew and her husband rode four-wheelers along the torn-up beach, assessing the damage.

The wind and floodwaters had peeled the tundra up like discarded carpeting. And as Matthew scanned the debris, suddenly, something caught her eye.

"I said to my husband, 'Look, what's that?' We stopped. He got up and took it, and it was that bowl," Matthew remembered.

The bowl was wooden and smooth. It was carved by Quinhagak residents somewhere between 400 and 600 years ago and was one of thousands of cultural objects scattered along the coastline.

Sponsor Message

The storm had unearthed it from an archaeological dig site called Nunalleq that sits near the village. It's renowned as one of the best examples of Alaska Native Yup'ik culture before Western contact and serves as an important link to Quinhagak's past. Not only had the storm scattered many objects from the site, it also increased the risks for what was still in the ground by eroding more of the land buffer between the Bering Sea and where these artifacts are buried.

This past summer, a team of archaeologists came to the village for an emergency dig to recover as much as possible before the next big storm.

toggle caption MaryCait Dolan/KYUK

toggle caption MaryCait Dolan/KYUK

Precious objects slowly being excavated

Archaeologists have been working at this dig site since 2009, according to lead archaeologist Rick Knecht. He says that after thawing permafrost revealed significant numbers of these objects in the early 2000s, the village deliberated and decided to try to save these pieces of their culture.

They include hand-carved animals, grass rope, sewing needles, ornate wooden masks and pieces of kayaks.

According to the archaeologists, the frozen ground has helped preserve artifacts composed of organic material, which they say would have likely eroded under different conditions.

The team, Knecht says, is mostly made up of volunteers and has a shoestring budget with funding from the Pacific Northwest Archaeological Society and the Daughters of the American Revolution, among others.

The whole archaeological site is about the size of two Olympic-size pools, but the emergency dig area is smaller, about the size of a backyard pool. It's a hole that has been dug around the buried remnants of several sod houses that date back 400 to 500 years.

toggle caption MaryCait Dolan/KYUK

Digging against time

Charlotta Hillerdal, who has been part of this excavation for over 15 years, was home in Scotland when she heard about the storm damage.

Sponsor Message

"I was crying," Hillerdal said. "It was a horrible feeling."

Knecht said that since the dig began, they've watched the Bering Sea creep closer and closer to the site. Shorelines in this part of Alaska are now more vulnerable to erosion due, in part, to decreasing sea ice and permafrost thaw. Both are fueled by human-caused climate change.

Last October's storm closed the distance even more. Now, at some high tides, seawater can reach into the pit.

"It's every bit as tough as working in front of bulldozers," Knecht explained.

In October, the flooding was so extensive that the site was covered by feet of water. When it receded, it took many valuable objects with it. They're worried that could happen again.

Knecht said they hope to return to the site next summer, though they're still raising the money to do so through a GoFundMe campaign and Quinhagak Heritage Inc., the nonprofit that oversees the dig.

"I'll be damned if I'm going to leave this for the waves," Knecht said. "It's like you might as well take those pieces of artwork we're finding and skip it off into the Bering Sea."

toggle caption MaryCait Dolan/KYUK

"When you know that you come from a people that were so resilient … you get a boost"

At the Nunalleq Culture and Archaeology Center — a museum-style building and lab — these pieces of Quinhagak's past are available for their direct descendants to access, along with the public.

"We all as humans want to know who we are and where we come from, and having the Nunalleq there for us strengthens that," said Elizabeth Church, director of Quinhagak Heritage Inc., which manages the center as well as the dig.

Church said seeing the artifacts exploded onto the beach was traumatic. It underscored the community's desire to steward their ancestors' belongings.

toggle caption MaryCait Dolan/KYUK

"They are interwoven into us as people, and we feel a great sense of responsibility to care for them well, and to take them into the future with us," Church said.

There's evidence of people adapting to environmental change and making technological progress.

"When you know that you come from a people that were so resilient and so capable and so talented and so smart — you get a boost," Church said. "It's amazing."

Sponsor Message

She said that with fall storm season fast approaching, the scramble is urgent to recover what they can of this past.

World.title: UCP riding group demands leadership review as separatist leader criticizes Danielle Smith's unity stance
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A UCP riding association in southern Alberta has formally urged a party vote to review Premier Danielle Smith’s leadership, in the latest sign of simmering frustrations surrounding the Oct. 19 referendum on the province’s future within Canada.

The Highwood UCP association cannot trigger a leadership review on its own. At least 21 additional party constituency groups would need to adopt similar positions to require a special vote on a leader’s future, similar to the internal dissent that ultimately led United Conservatives to prematurely end Jason Kenney’s leadership four years ago.

But the Highwood riding group is not only led by someone who’s also a vice-president on the party’s board, Helen Holder — it also includes Tanya Clemens, co-leader of prominent separatist group Let Alberta Decide.

Clemens defended her support for a leadership review Saturday in a video posted to social media. In it, she said she was motivated largely by the premier’s vocal support for the “stay” option in the referendum.

“I disagree with the adversarial role she has taken toward independence during this referendum, because I believe our highest elected representative should have remained neutral and allowed Albertans to make this decision,” Clemens said in her post.

The pro-independence organizer said she still respects Smith and would likely support her UCP leadership if a review was held today. But Clemens added that Smith’s approach in the referendum’s aftermath “will naturally inform how I will vote in a leadership review.”

Tanya Clemens, speaking at the launch of Alberta independence organization Let Alberta Decide in June in Calgary. (Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press)

Clemens did not reply to CBC News’ interview request.

Let Alberta Decide’s other leader, Keith Wilson, has been supportive of Smith and her decision to give voters a referendum on whether Alberta should remain a Canadian province or plan a subsequent binding referendum on secession. That position was in contrast to the leaders of Alberta Prosperity Project, Jeff Rath and Mitch Sylvestre, who have soured on Smith’s leadership and her pro-unity position.

Sylvestre, himself a UCP riding president in northeast Alberta, told CBC News in May he would organize a party movement to force a leadership review or to make the UCP endorse independence. That stated initiative never showed any public signs of progress.

Highwood is a riding south of Calgary that includes the town of Okotoks. It previously included Danielle Smith’s hometown of High River and she was its MLA for a term last decade when she led the Wildrose Party, but she now represents Brooks-Medicine Hat in the province’s southeast.

Highwood’s current MLA, Affordability Minister RJ Sigurdson, is seeking to distance himself from the decision of his riding’s party association.

“Let me be clear that Premier Danielle Smith has, and will continue to have, my full support,” Sigurdson said in a statement.

“I firmly believe that the decision of the Highwood Constituency Association does not reflect the views of my constituents broadly.”

Highwood MLA RJ Sigurdson has served in Smith's cabinet since 2023. He supports the premier's party leadership. (Jason Franson/The Canadian Press)

United Conservative members gave Smith a resounding endorsement in the last scheduled review — 91.5 per cent support at the 2024 annual party convention. That was before the independence movement became more vocal and organized last year, with many of its leaders, activists and organizers within the UCP.

The next UCP convention is scheduled for late November, after the referendum, but no leadership review is scheduled.

Last week, the Smith government launched a $4 million ad campaign on the 10 referendum questions facing Albertans. While the videos have largely focused on the ballot measures dealing with immigration and constitutional reforms , it referenced the unity question at the end, urging voters to “stand up for a strong and sovereign Alberta within a united Canada.”

While independence remains popular among many backers of Smith’s party, polls have shown the vast majority of Albertans support staying in Canada.

The Alberta NDP contend that public distaste for separatism helped the party flip Calgary-Shaw, a former UCP cabinet minister’s riding, in a by-election last Monday. Some independence advocates, meanwhile, have argued that separatist UCP supporters may have stayed home, turned off by Smith’s pro-unity advocacy.

Holder, the party’s vice-president of fundraising, did not reply immediately to a request for comment on Saturday.

In a statement, a party spokesperson said Smith’s 91.5 per cent score in the leadership review two years ago points to resounding support for her leadership.

“Under her leadership, we are shattering all-time fundraising records, consistently out fundraising the NDP, and drawing sell-out crowds at events across the province,” Dave Prisco said in an email.

“You only see results like that when you have a strong leader with overwhelming support.”

In 2022, the required number of UCP riding associations forced a special general meeting to force a leadership review of Kenney, amid party unrest about the then-premier’s policies on COVID vaccination and other pandemic health measures. The 51.4 per cent support he received was enough for him to remain, but Kenney announced he’d resign as leader because he believed it wasn’t a strong enough mandate to legitimately stay on.

One constituency president leading that anti-Kenney march was Rob Smith, currently president of the party. He did not reply to a request for comment.

Premier Smith didn’t mention any internal party pushback Saturday when she spoke at the Alberta and the West Assembly, a virtual conference focused on the October referendum.

She reaffirmed in her speech that she backs the “stay” option, but emphasized her support for “yes” on the immigration and constitutional questions.

“My advocacy is around the nine questions. I mean, I put nine questions on the ballot because I genuinely want to get a mandate to start working on those things that will fix the country,” Smith told the online event, organized by Preston Manning, former leader of the federal Reform Party.

Former B.C. premier Gordon Campbell, former Reform Party leader Preston Manning and Alberta Premier Danielle Smith appeared at a virtual conference Saturday on Alberta's future within Canada. (Zoom)

The premier also recounted the financial struggles she said Albertans have relayed to her, and that she understands why they’re angry, hurt, and intrigued by independence as a solution.

“So when proud, hard-working people feel their contribution is taken for granted and their livelihood is treated as something to be phased out, some begin to ask a painful question: Does this country actually want us?” Smith said, showing visible emotion as she spoke.

“Even many of those who are voting to remain are fed up. And the Albertans considering the other option are not, for the most part, against Canada or fellow Canadians. They're just heartbroken by it. And that distinction matters.”

World.title: Ed Sheeran apologizes to fans at 1st show since Macklemore dropped over 'Free Palestine' comments
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Singer-songwriter Ed Sheeran took the stage at a Philadelphia stadium Saturday night and addressed the controversy over rapper Macklemore's removal from his tour.

"I'm used to my music being criticized," Sheeran said to the crowd at his first show since Macklemore was dropped over pro-Palestinian comments. "But this week, the criticism was about something much more important, and I've had to take and make difficult decisions, and I am making mistakes, and I'm so, so sorry."

He said he's never wanted to be "an activist musician" and said this incident has put him "in the middle of an important and passionate argument about freedom of speech and the most complex political issue on the planet."

Sheeran called what is happening in Gaza "catastrophic and unjustifiable."

"My heart has been broken by the scale of devastation and loss of civilians' lives, of children's lives," Sheeran said. "And the systemic injustice we're seeing unfold in the West Bank cannot be overlooked."

He said he has been speaking to people across the political spectrum to work out how to make a contribution that helps the victims, admitting he does not know enough about it.

He added that he wants his music and shows to be about unity and humanity, not politics, and said he wants his concerts to be a place where everyone is welcome and can stand beside people with opposing views and just enjoy the music.

Protesters outside

Pro-Palestinian activists had gathered Saturday near Lincoln Financial Field ahead of the show in support of both the Palestinian people and free speech.

Sheeran was alone on stage after his backing band and all of his remaining supporting acts quit his tour in solidarity earlier this week. Sheeran had attributed Macklemore's removal solely to venues and promoters while defending his decision to remain apolitical.

Gillette Stadium owner Robert Kraft, who allegedly led efforts to remove Macklemore as Sheeran's opening act, said Wednesday he is now donating $2 million US to "aid in the region" at the singer-songwriter's request.

Pro-Palestinian activists gathered outside the Philadelphia venue where Ed Sheeran was scheduled to play Saturday evening. (Daniela Ramirez/CBC News)

Ticket prices sag

Tickets for the show were still available for as low as $37 US on Saturday, and Sheeran's website did not list any replacement acts.

Macklemore was dropped from the U.S. leg of Sheeran's tour after chanting "Free Palestine" and expressing solidarity with Palestinians in Gaza and the Israeli-occupied West Bank during a Sept. 5 show in New Jersey.

Philadelphia resident Hillary Steinberg says she bought her tickets for tonight's show a year ago when Sheeran's Loop tour was first announced. But she decided not to go when Macklemore was dropped because she doesn't support "big money dictating what artists can and can't say."

Steinberg says she is no longer a Sheeran fan and doesn't agree with his decision to not stand with his fellow artists, calling it a "betrayal."

"I don't believe anything is without politics," she said.

Philadelphia resident Hillary Steinberg bought tickets for Ed Sheeran a year ago, but chose to protest instead. (Daniela Ramirez/CBC News)

Sheeran fan Christina White says she doesn't like that Macklemore got kicked off the bill for speaking out, but that she's still attending the show. She said thinks it's "a shame" that Sheeran got stuck in the middle of the controversy.

"You come here to see the music," she said. "I don't agree with everything everyone says, but if I like their music, I'm going to come anyway."

For Susan Shulman, there were two reasons to be outside the concert venue Saturday.

"On top of the issue of Palestine, there's the issue of free speech," she said referring to Macklemore's comments, which she described as "very benign."

"And the fact that somebody with a lot of power and money was able to shut that down is just appalling and unfair."

Sheeran said venues had threatened to pull his upcoming performances if Macklemore was not removed as his opening act because of "how Macklemore conveyed part of his message during his performance." He said the decision to remove him was the promoter's, not his.

On stage Saturday, he said, "I am deeply worried about the idea that venues pre-approve content for performers. This happens in so many places that I perform around the world, but it should never happen in the free world."

Kraft, who owns the New England Patriots, was one of the people behind the call for Macklemore's removal, Sheeran confirmed.

WATCH | Protesters gather outside Philadelphia stadium: Protesters gather outside Ed Sheeran's 1st show since Macklemore dropped from tour | Duration closed caption 4:32 Singer-songwriter Ed Sheeran took the stage at a Philadelphia stadium Saturday night in his first show since facing backlash over rapper Macklemore's removal from his tour for saying 'Free Palestine' during a show. CBC News spoke outside the venue with both fans attending the show and pro-Palestinian activists who had gathered in support of the Palestinian people and free speech.

Kraft, a staunch supporter of Israel, said in a statement shared with CBC News Monday that his stadium would "not provide a platform for hate speech," stating Macklemore spread divisiveness through "selective information and ignoring the actions of Hamas."

Macklemore had blamed his removal on Kraft in an Instagram post, claiming the billionaire said the rapper would not be allowed onstage and rallied other stadium owners to threaten to cancel scheduled concerts if he was not taken off the bill. The threats placed Sheeran, his friend, in a difficult position, Macklemore said.

Sheeran takes apolitical stance

Many of Sheeran's supporting acts said they were withdrawing from his tour to stand in solidarity with Palestinians .

In his statement, Sheeran said he was "appalled by the conflict between Israel and Palestine," and called the suffering on "both sides" a "human tragedy."

But he defended his choice not to express his views on the conflict publicly.

"I am not complicit. I have my personal views on this devastating conflict," he wrote.

"Just because I choose not to speak publicly, it doesn't mean I don't have them, and it doesn't mean I don't care."

While promoters and venues wield great power over concert tours, experts say an artist of Sheeran's magnitude generally has the final say about what happens concerning the shows.

Sheeran has performed much of his Loop Tour concerts solo, but he had been joined for several songs at each stop by the Irish folk band Beoga.

Sheeran's other U.S. openers, Danish band Lukas Graham and Irish singer Aaron Rowe, also annouced they were leaving the tour.

Finneas, Billie Eilish's brother and musical collaborator, was due to tour with Sheeran in South America later this year before he too dropped out earlier this week.

World.title: Canada won't pay directly into EU budget under Carney's plan: ambassador-designate
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

As Prime Minister Mark Carney presses toward creating a "unique alliance" with the European Union, Canada's ambassador is ruling out paying directly into the 27-nation bloc's budget.

"We would be very selective," Canada's incoming EU ambassador Jonathan Wilkinson said in an interview with CBC's The House airing Saturday morning. "This is not across the board. It's certainly not membership in the European Union."

But Wilkinson did say there are programs which may require some degree of funding. As an example, he pointed to the EU's Security Action for Europe (SAFE) program, which offers loans to member states for defence investments.

Canada is currently the only non-European country to join the program. Wilkinson said there are other areas for co-operation, like enhancing Canada's ability to sell critical minerals by having Europe make investments in the sector or working with the EU on AI and other digital technologies.

"It's a number of specific areas that the prime minister has described as strategic capabilities — those areas where countries really need to have access to certain things that enable them to actually make sovereign decisions," said Wilkinson, who will be sworn in to his new role in the coming weeks.

Carney formally unveiled his interest in moving Canada closer to the EU during his speech to the European Parliament on Thursday. Some details of his vision were revealed, including:

"Seamless, digital" trade in non-agricultural goods and services.

Canadian membership in Erasmus+ , the EU's program to support education, training, youth and sport in Europe, which includes cross-border student exchanges.

, the EU's program to support education, training, youth and sport in Europe, which includes cross-border student exchanges. Canadian membership in the next generation of Horizon, the EU's research and innovation funding program. Canada has partial access to the current program, which ends after 2027.

Co-operation on computing capacity, broadband connections and AI safety protocols.

Exploring an integrated market for financial services.

Still, it's unclear whether Canada will need to give up anything in return, or whether EU members and the Canadian Parliament would approve the deal. Carney has promised a vote and debate in Parliament on the structure of any alliance with the EU.

Wilkinson said he would be "very cautious" about jumping to conclusions on key concerns some opposition parties have raised, like whether Canada would need to amend migration policies.

WATCH | Carney lays out broad strokes of his plan: Carney pledges deeper ties in EU speech but offers few details | Duration closed caption 3:07 A day after the door was opened for Canada to become an 'associate member' of the EU, Prime Minister Mark Carney delivered a speech at the European Parliament pledging deeper ties with Europe, though questions remain on what that includes.

"Are we talking about mass ability to move across [the two areas]? No, and the idea that somehow it's related to the irregular migrant issues in Europe.… The borders in Canada are so different from Europe," Wilkinson said.

"Canada will retain fully its sovereignty."

European politicians weigh in

Thomas Byrne, Ireland's minister of state for European affairs and defence, told The House the two parties share a lot in common, like commitments to democracy, free trade and the rule of law.

"We know that the U.S.A. is not as committed to the type of tariff-free trade that we support as it used to be. So I suppose we have to develop other connections," Byrne said. "And that brings a level of commonality into us."

Cross Country Checkup is asking: Is Canada more like Europe than the United States? What’s at stake for you if Canada builds closer ties to the EU? Leave your comment here and we may read it or call you back for Sunday's show

Byrne also said what he thinks is being looked at right now is mutual benefits for both parties, not imposing obligations on one another.

WATCH | More about the proposed alliance: ‘No need' for Canada-EU treaties or trade deal: EU member | Duration closed caption 13:55 Prime Minister Mark Carney addressed the European Parliament on Thursday, saying an alliance between Canada and Europe would ‘safeguard our abilities to live our lives as we choose.' Roland Paris, foreign policy adviser to Justin Trudeau when he was prime minister, and Arash Saeidi, a member of the European Parliament, discuss what an alliance between Canada and the European Union could look like.

"We're equal partners across the Atlantic," Byrne said.

But Arash Saeidi, a member of the European Parliament representing France, said he's concerned about the proposal because "if we talk about this, we're going to lose our time and it will last 10 years and we won't do anything."

Instead, Saeidi said, the focus should be doing the work of deepening ties — in areas like diplomacy, culture and academic research — rather than debating a formal process.

The Trump factor

The hitch to Carney's plan is U.S. President Donald Trump, who called the idea of closer Canada-EU ties "laughable" and then threatened new tariffs if it's "a hostile act."

"It's fair to say Europe will act on its own interests," said Fen Osler Hampson, co-chair of the Expert Group on Canada-U.S. Relations.

"There are many Europeans who are already calling for greater European strategic independence from the United States for the same reasons we are."

WATCH | Trump says Canada's move toward EU 'laughable': Trump says closer Canada-EU co-operation is 'laughable' | Duration closed caption 0:25 U.S. President Donald Trump threatened the European Union with 'very serious tariffs' or to 'stop trading' if it makes a trade deal with Canada 'with bad intentions.'

Trump needs to remember that Europe and Canada are major investors in American equity markets, and Canada holds a large chunk of U.S. debt, Hampson added.

"And so when he talks about cutting off trade.… If he acts on it, he's shooting himself in both feet," he said.

Asked whether Trump's threats could scare off the EU from making a deal with Canada, Wilkinson said "I guess it's up to the Europeans," but doubts that will occur.

Canada is not "proposing a third bloc in order to become a great power — only with better manners," Carney said in his speech.

"We do not seek power to dominate others. On the contrary, we are pursuing resilience so no one, no one can control our open markets, impair our sovereignty, threaten our territorial integrity or undermine our freedoms, our democracies, our rule of law."

World.title: Canadian language school files for bankruptcy, leaving students stranded
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Canada's largest private language school filed for bankruptcy on Friday, leaving current and incoming students in limbo.

A notice posted to the International Language Academy of Canada's (ILAC) website says it has ceased operations effective immediately, noting it "no longer has the financial resources necessary to continue operating."

ILAC operated in Vancouver and Toronto, offering a variety of programs including short-term English-language courses, a high school program, and college programs lasting up to two years.

"I’m just really confused and lost," said incoming student José Carlos Chavez, speaking from Guadalajara, Mexico, on Saturday.

Chavez, who works in Mexico as a professional photographer, was supposed to be starting a two-year-long marketing program at ILAC in mid-October.

José Carlos Chavez is supposed to fly to Vancouver next week to start his two-year-long program at ILAC, having paid the school almost $14,000 in tuition. (Submitted by José Carlos Chavez)

His flight to Vancouver is booked for next week.

Chavez says he found out the news from social media. Despite reaching out to the school, he says he has not yet heard back from ILAC directly.

According to receipts Chavez provided to CBC News, he has paid the school almost $14,000 in tuition fees.

He will also have to pay a penalty if he cancels his Vancouver apartment lease now — which will cost him around $1,800.

"Stressed, confused, I don’t know what’s going to happen," said Chavez.

Chavez worries he may have to go into debt and won’t be able to afford studying elsewhere if he doesn’t receive a refund.

"I just hope that the school can ... help me in any possible way," he said.

Chavez, who runs a photography business in Mexico, was supposed to spend the next two years in Vancouver studying marketing. (Submitted by José Carlos Chavez)

The school's notice says it has faced financial challenges over the past three years due to "significant regulatory changes affecting the sector."

Since the federal government started tightening the intake cap on international student permit applications, education providers have been challenged by funding issues.

The number of new students arriving in Canada with study permits has dropped from roughly 293,000 in 2024 to 115,000 in 2025. Between January and July this year, only about 28,000 new students came to Canada with study permits.

Languages Canada, the national language education association that represents and accredits language programs, said the school has 1,362 students.

"The sudden and disorderly closure of Canada’s largest language school is a shock to everyone," said a Saturday statement from the organization’s executive director Gonzalo Peralta.

The statement said Languages Canada will work over the weekend to place current students in alternate equivalent programs.

Incoming students face the unknown

Beatriz Gil runs Truly Canadian Education, a company based in Metro Vancouver that connects international students to Canadian schooling.

She has dozens of clients currently enrolled in ILAC programs in Vancouver and Toronto. For both students and staff, she says Friday was a confusing and upsetting day.

"We were in shock," Gil said, noting she got a call from an ILAC staff member in tears.

Gil said those who were studying at the ILAC high school in Vancouver were asked to take their items and leave the building on Friday.

"They were outside the school with all their belongings asking what’s going on?" she said.

She said their team is working with Languages Canada to transfer current students to other institutions in Vancouver and Toronto.

But for incoming students like Chavez, Gil says she does not know what will happen.

Gil said she is working with one incoming student who had just made her tuition payment to the institution on Thursday — the day before it declared bankruptcy.

"It’s very, very sad for all of them," she said.

ILAC's closure comes just five days after the closure of EC English, a major international English-language school that had operations in Toronto, Vancouver, and Montreal.

"Indeed, there have been closures of many language programs around the world in the last few years," said Language Canada's statement on the ILAC closure.

World.title: 6 people injured after vehicle strikes pedestrians at festival in Saint-Tite, Que.
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Quebec provincial police are investigating after six people were injured after they were struck by a vehicle on the site of the Festival Western de Saint-Tite early Saturday morning.

Police say a collision between a vehicle and pedestrians took place on Saint-Joseph Boulevard in Saint-Tite, about 200 kilometres northeast of Montreal.

Witnesses say police arrived on scene around 4:30 a.m.

The vehicle fled the scene, according to the Sûreté du Québec (SQ). It was later found in the Quebec City region around 5:30 a.m.

The town is hosting the popular Festival Western de St-Tite and three Quebec political leaders are expected on site today as part of their respective campaigns. (Pierre Millot/Radio-Canada)

A man in his 20s was arrested by police and was being questioned by investigators.

The victims, two young women and four young men aged between 17 and 21, were transported to hospital with various injuries, none of which were life threatening, police confirmed later Saturday.

Alcohol is not thought to be involved in the incident, according to a spokesperson for the SQ.

Police said it is unclear if those injured were involved in an argument with the driver.

The town is hosting the popular Festival Western de St-Tite and three Quebec political leaders are expected on site today as part of their respective campaigns.

Festival officials say Saturday's activities will go ahead as planned.

"An isolated incident beyond our control occurred early this morning on Saint-Joseph Boulevard. Our thoughts are with those involved and their families. We wish them a speedy recovery," the organizers said in a statement.

"The safety of our festival-goers, volunteers, and staff remains our top priority. The Festival is a festive event where everyone should feel safe. That's why every effort is being made to ensure this."

WATCH | Police investigation into incident at Quebec festival ongoing: 6 injured after vehicle strikes pedestrians at Quebec festival | Duration closed caption 1:49 Six people were injured after a vehicle struck pedestrians at the Festival Western de Saint-Tite in Quebec early Saturday. Police later located the vehicle in the Quebec City region and arrested a man in his 20s.

Police say Saint-Joseph Boulevard will remain closed to vehicle traffic between Du Couvent and Moulin Streets for most of Saturday as investigators and technicians work on the scene.

Quebec's Domestic Security Minister Ian Lafrenière said that there was no reason to believe that the incident was related to terrorism. He said that there had been an argument among several individuals that escalated.

In an update Saturday afternoon, SQ spokesperson Marc Tessier said the driver of the vehicle was likely to be released later in the day with a promise to appear in court at a later date.

Tessier specified his release would also likely entail conditions.

Quebec leaders react

The early morning incident took place as three Quebec party leaders were expected to attend the festival. The Quebec Liberals (PLQ), Coalition Avenir Québec (CAQ) and the Parti Québécois (PQ) all had stops planned for Saturday.

PLQ leader Charles Milliard said he spoke with members of the festival’s organizing committee to offer them support following what he called “the tragic event.”

“My thoughts are especially with the victims and their families,” he wrote on X. “Despite the confusion and sadness that mark this day, I wish everyone a wonderful festival.”

Police say Saint-Joseph Boulevard will remain closed to vehicle traffic between Du Couvent and Moulin Streets for most of Saturday as investigators and technicians work on the scene. (Pierre Millot/Radio-Canada)

CAQ Leader Christine Fréchette posted her condolences to the victims on X.

“My thoughts are with the victims, their loved ones, and all those affected by the events that took place at the Western Festival in St-Tite. The ongoing investigation will determine the causes of this act,” Fréchette said.

PQ Leader Pierre St-Pierre Plamondon also offered his condolences.

“My thoughts are with the injured individuals, their loved ones, and all those who witnessed the distressing scene in Saint-Tite.,” St-Pierre Plamondon wrote on X.

" Thank you to the first responders who acted quickly. Quebecers should be able to enjoy places where they can gather and celebrate safely."

World.title: ‘Holy moly!’: Rare shark visit to Nova Scotia's Bedford Basin inspires shock and awe
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

It’s been a long time since swimming was encouraged in the Bedford Basin, but that didn’t stop one shark from making a rare and lengthy visit on Friday night.

"I have never seen a shark in the Bedford Basin before. That was a first," said Bedford resident John Calder.

Calder had nearly finished his commute home from work when he came across a crowd standing on the Shore Drive Bridge, which overlooks the basin where it meets the Sackville River.

“I got out of my car to see what was happening and lo and behold, there was two giant shark fins that were protruding from the water,” Calder said Saturday. “Right away, I said: 'Holy moly! That's a shark.'"

According to marine biologist and shark researcher Neil Hammerschlag, who reviewed multiple videos of the shark shared on social media, “it’s clearly a basking shark.”

“They pose no risk to humans, they eat little plankton, and they’re called basking sharks because they often spend time near the surface where they look like they’re basking in the sun,” said Hammerschlag, president of Atlantic Shark Expeditions.

The shark's habit of floating near the surface, combined with the fact that it is the second-largest fish in the world, made it easy to spot once it entered the basin.

However, finding one in such a busy waterway — surrounded by dozens of sailboats and densely populated shores — is highly unusual.

“I think this is a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to see an animal this large so close to shore,” Hammerschlag said.

John Calder says he spotted the shark around 5 p.m. on Friday. (Submitted by John Calder)

Shark spent hours in basin

While Calder watched the shark for only 15 minutes before it swam away, he described it as a moment where time stood still.

“You go about your day, and then all of a sudden there’s a shark, and it’s like everything stops, nothing else is important and you’re just watching mother nature,” he said.

Around 7:30 p.m., Calder's wife, Lisa McCloskey, and his 14-year-old stepdaughter, Audrey Hill, spotted the shark near a dock at the Bedford Basin Yacht Club.

“It seemed kind of surreal,” McCloskey said. “We could almost see our house in the distance, and then we’re watching this massive shark come out of the water and it came near us and almost rolled over so we saw its whole body as well ... it was magical.”

Lisa McCloskey, pictured here with her 14-year-old daughter, Audrey Hill, along with Heather Sangster, Meghan Proude, Mana Wareham, Kathy McCarthy-Murphy and Ben and Lisa Trepanier, says there was a strong feeling of community among those who came down to the Bedford Basin Yacht Club to see the shark. (Submitted by Lisa McCloskey)

For nearly two hours, a growing crowd watched as the shark surfaced and submerged.

“There were probably like 30 or 40 of us, and people were hugging each other when they saw the shark,” McCloskey said. “It really felt like a community event. Everyone was chatting and it was really lovely.”

Hammerschlag said it remains unclear why the shark ventured into the basin. Basking sharks are far more common in open, plankton-rich waters like the Bay of Fundy.

The shark may have been unwell or disoriented, Hammerschlag said, but “unless it washes up on shore,” there's no way to know for sure.

“Either way, it’s a remarkable encounter, and this is a beautiful animal, completely harmless to people, and whoever had the opportunity to see it should consider themselves lucky.”

World.title: Why molasses has long been a sticky point in Canada-U.S. trade, well before Trump's import ban
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A U.S. ban on Canadian molasses imports has resurfaced allegations of sugar smuggling and an industry battle involving a company with a major refinery in Hamilton, Ont.

Spats over dairy, automobiles and booze have become ingrained in the ongoing trade dispute between Canada and the U.S. during President Donald Trump's second term in office. But when the U.S. announced earlier this month that it would ban the import of molasses, it left some scratching their heads.

The ban is due to take effect Sept. 29 alongside bans on motorcycles, most alcoholic drinks and some dairy products.

It comes after months of American sugar producers lobbying their government to raise tariffs on foreign sugar products, saying they're being undercut by cheaper products from other countries.

They're also taking aim at Canadian refineries, who they claim are importing mixes of raw sugar, molasses and water but disguising them as pure molasses as a way to circumvent sugar tariffs and quotas.

'Closing the spigot'

Sugaright, a division of Connecticut-based refiner CSC Sugar, said stopping the flow of watered-down molasses from Canada was a main topic of conversation at the International Sweetener Symposium, a major industry event held in Vail, Colo., this summer.

"Canadian 'molasses' containing substantial sugar is being viewed as a potential sugar-program circumvention problem, and not only does the U.S. sugar industry want the flow to stop, but now the federal government is fully engaged to 'finish the job' of closing the spigot completely," reads an August blog post on Sugaright's website.

The issue appears to stem from a case in the 1990s, when Michigan-based Heartland By-Products mixed molasses with sugar and water at an Ontario facility to import the mixture tariff-free. The company would then refine it a second time in the U.S. to remove the molasses, sell the purified sugar, and ship the molasses back to Canada to reuse in its next batch.

The scheme was legal and approved by the U.S. government, but pressure from the sugar industry and a series of court cases and legislative restrictions forced the company to shut down operations in the 2000s.

Sugar companies' claims of disguised molasses still flowing unchecked from Canada appear to be contradicted by the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) World Agricultural Supply and Demand Estimates report from August, which states that molasses imports for sugar extraction are "on a rapid decline" and are currently projected to be "zero" for next year.

Company says it was targeted

Don Hill, chair of Sucro Can Sourcing, says the latest round of accusations is specifically aimed at his company, which is headquartered in Florida but has its biggest refinery in Hamilton.

"They just don't like the fact that we're legitimately shipping that molasses over to the U.S. And they've chosen to link what we do to what Heartland did 20 years ago, just to create that negative aura — just to cast aspersions and to make it seem all dodgy," Hill told CBC News.

He says his fast-growing company was shipping about 50,000 tonnes of refiners' molasses annually to the U.S., which makes up a fraction of one per cent of the U.S. market — but marks a significant increase from a decade ago, before Sucro entered the picture.

WATCH | Carney responds to import bans: 'We're looking closely' at Trump's import bans and tariffs, Carney says | Duration closed caption 1:03 Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Thursday that the government is looking at U.S. President Donald Trump's recent measures which include bans on Canadian imports including most alcohol products and new 50 per cent tariffs on a series of other products. 'We fully recognize that for individual companies and in individual sectors these are significant, and there's a response there,' Carney said.

U.S. Customs and Border Protection approved Sucro's molasses imports under the Harmonized Tariff Schedule in 2020.

Hill, who is from Toronto but now lives in the U.K., says the sugar lobby has gone "berserk" trying to shut down his operation since then by pulling "every lever possible."

Congress gave the USDA funding as part of the 2024 American Relief Act to test the purity of molasses coming from Canada through Buffalo, N.Y., the route used by Sucro.

The resulting study found signs of "additives or blending," raising concerns about "potential circumvention of U.S. sugar tariff‑rate quotas." It was not officially published by the USDA, but appears to have been made public in an April 20 article on the website of brokerage platform Ag Bull Trading.

The industry has used this study in its arguments for shutting off molasses from Canada and raising tariffs on the product travelling through Buffalo.

Sucro issued a rebuttal to the study, which Hill says does not have "an ounce or shred of legitimate facts behind it." He called for its retraction, citing "glaring mathematical errors," and said he offered data and corrections to the USDA. He said he has not received any meaningful response.

In a statement emailed to CBC News, the USDA said, "This report was not formally published by USDA. There is nothing further to share on the contents."

Sucro stopped importing molasses to the U.S. after completing its latest $135-million refinery in Hamilton in April, Hill says, and has instead been focusing on the Canadian market.

"It just got to the point where the whole market, including the tariffs, including the sugar lobby, has just made everything so toxic and aggravating that there's just no point in even doing it," he said.

Sugar lobby backs ban

The American Sugar Alliance, the main trade association and lobby organization representing major U.S. sugar producers and refiners, emailed CBC News a statement applauding the molasses import ban.

"American sugar producers deeply appreciate President Donald Trump, the U.S. Trade Representative, and the Trump Administration's efforts to ensure that the products being imported into our country under our trade laws are actually the stated products," the statement said.

"The Trump Administration is committed to upholding our laws, restoring fair trade, and putting American farmers and workers first."

CBC News sent follow-up questions regarding Hill's accusations that the group targeted Sucro, but has not heard back.

WATCH | Toronto businesses feeling import ban: Trump hit Canada with new import bans. Here's how GTA businesses are being impacted | Duration closed caption 1:49 U.S. President Donald Trump is banning the import of Canadian alcohol, motorcycles and various other products into the U.S. CBC Naama Weingarten spoke to GTA business owners about how they could be impacted.

David Singerman, an associate professor of history at the University of Virginia and author of Unrefined: How Capitalism Reinvented Sugar, says sugar refining has always been a low-margin, high-volume business.

He says this has inspired a long history of smuggling and tariff manipulation — and also of producers and refiners exerting political power to protect their profits.

Singerman says the lobby's influence gives sugar a "special status" in the American trade system, with a quota system backed up by a minimum price guarantee and high tariffs on foreign imports.

"Any time that there's a threat, or these growers perceive that someone is undercutting the system in some way, they get very nervous and they pick up the phone and call their friends in Washington. And this has been true for a long time," he said.

'Bit of a head scratcher'

Drew Fagan, a professor at the University of Toronto's Munk School of Global Affairs and Public Policy, says U.S. protectionism around its sugar industry is well known. He compared it to Canada's dairy industry, which Trump has frequently lambasted as being unfair to American businesses.

Fagan says there could be several issues at play. Molasses is used in the production of rum and other alcohols, for example, and is also used as feed for dairy cows, which could link it to the booze and dairy bans.

He also says it's not uncommon for lobby groups to use the political climate — in this case, a trade dispute with Canada — to push through long-sought changes.

"Special interests can have a big say if they know which buttons to push," Fagan said.

CBC News contacted the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative to ask for the reasoning behind the molasses import ban but has not heard back.

World.title: Were mosquitos bugging you more than usual this summer? Blame the rain
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

If it felt like mosquitoes were being particularly bad this summer — and hanging around for longer — it might not be in your head.

Some prairie cities saw a mosquito population boom earlier this summer, with some stores in Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta running out of bug spray entirely due to high demand.

Data collected by the City of Edmonton showed the number of mosquitoes in the city was 15 times higher in July compared to the same time last year.

"While these do not represent record high mosquito numbers for our region, they are a stark contrast to the previous two summer seasons, which can magnify public perception," said Peter Daly, a biological sciences technologist at the City of Edmonton.

Saskatoon and Winnipeg also saw higher numbers of mosquitoes in July compared to last year, according to data from those cities.

In southern Ontario, experts say the record rainfall parts of the region saw this summer is likely to blame for the mosquito boom, and why they're still causing itchy red welts well into September.

Fiona Hunter, a medical and veterinary entomology professor at Brock University, said this summer, southern Ontario has seen greater numbers of the Ochlerotatus trivittatus species compared to other years.

Ochlerotatus trivittatus is known as a floodwater mosquito that lays its eggs in low-lying areas filled with water, so the amount of rain southern Ontario has seen this year has created ideal conditions for them, she said.

"Think about all the rain we've had in southern Ontario this year. Soggy fields, low spots in lawns, roadside depressions and other poorly drained areas have repeatedly filled with water," she said.

"That creates lots of potential habitat for this particular mosquito, and probably helps explain why we're seeing so many of them this year."

The species is known to be a very persistent biter, she said.

"So I suspect people are simply coming into contact with this species more often this year, which may be part of the reason mosquitoes seem especially bad right now."

The torrential downpour that pummelled the Greater Toronto Area and many other communities across southern and southwestern Ontario also may have triggered the hatching of a whole bunch of dormant mosquito eggs, said Rosalind Murray, an assistant professor of biology at the University of Toronto.

"And so we might see a little bit of a blip where we have a bit of a boom, especially in places that have major flood flooding like Toronto," she told CBC Radio's Metro Morning.

WATCH | Wet weather extends mosquito season: Mosquito season stretches into September after wet summer in Ottawa | Duration closed caption 1:48 Thanks to heavy rainfall this summer, Ottawa is still seeing high numbers of mosquitoes, even though residents are ready to leave them behind. The CBC's Jenna Legge reports.

Colder temps will drive populations down

But as soon as the region starts to see colder overnight temperatures, the mosquitoes won't be an issue anymore.

"They don't do very well when it's extremely hot, they can dry out. They also are going to die immediately once it gets cold," Murray said.

"Once we start seeing those really cool nighttime temperatures, like below 10 C, we should start to see them peter out. And as soon as we have a frost, they'll be gone."

That's what Alberta has seen happen after a recent cold snap, said Ken Fry, an entomology instructor at Olds College in Olds, Alta.

Edmonton and Calgary experienced a particularly bad mosquito season earlier this summer, driven by a large amount of rainfall early on in the year. But then, he said, mosquito populations "pretty much crashed" due to colder temperatures in recent weeks.

Daly said Edmonton has already seen numbers drop for the most dominant local mosquito species, Aedes vexans, but added that since the city has had a warm fall so far, "we’ve yet to see quite as precipitous drop in their numbers as some other years. "

Fry said the critters might make a reappearance as temperatures are expected to climb back to 20 C or higher over the next week in the region.

"But we won't have the populations, I don't think, anywhere near close to what central Canada is experiencing."
