World.title: Mexico’s week in review: Independence Day fireworks give way to trade deal hopes
World.content:
Listen to this article

Mexico’s Independence Day on Sept. 16 was the focal point this past week, even as less celebratory news circulated. Over the weekend, 21-year-old Spanish exchange student Claudia Tacoronte Aguilera, attending the Autonomous University of Morelos (UAEM) in Cuernavaca, Morelos, was stabbed and killed in Cuautla — the fourth femicide of a UAEM student just this year. On Thursday, Morelos authorities announced the arrest of a suspect, Francisco Javier “N,” but the attack on Tacoronte and the emergency medical response were met with indignation both locally and in Spain.

Also on Sept. 12, Pemex admitted it had contained another oil spill off the coast of Campeche, which the Navy and the state oil company moved quickly to seal and clean up — a contrast to the government’s slower handling of a major spill in February. Meanwhile, the peso spent most of the week trading above 17 to the dollar, weakening toward its worst week since March as markets digested the U.S. Federal Reserve’s decision to raise interest rates for the first time since 2023, narrowing the Mexico-U.S. rate differential.

Didn’t have time to catch this week’s top stories? Here’s what you missed.

Industrial activity posts best growth in years

Mexico’s industrial sector delivered its strongest annual performance in nearly three years in July, with industrial activity up 2.4% in seasonally adjusted terms, according to INEGI — triple June’s 0.8% reading and the best showing since November 2023.

Construction led the gains, climbing 6.7% annually, while mining rose 1.6% and manufacturing grew 1.3%. Month-over-month growth was 0.5%, a second straight month of sequential gains. Still, industrial activity is up just 0.4% for the first seven months of 2026, a modest rebound after a 1.3% contraction in 2025, with manufacturing down 0.7% year-to-date. Economists at Grupo Financiero Monex expect only “moderate” growth ahead, citing USMCA-related uncertainty and U.S. tariffs on vehicles, steel and aluminum.

Coahuila is Mexico’s safest state

For the first time, Coahuila topped INEGI’s national safety perception survey, the 2026 ENVIPE, with just 27.8% of residents calling the state unsafe due to crime — a 9.9-point improvement that pushed Baja California Sur out of the top spot.

Coahuila registered only 100 homicides in 2025, a turnaround from more than 1,100 killings in 2012, when cartels such as Los Zetas and the Gulf Cartel dominated large swaths of the state. Analysts credited beefed-up federal forces and prevention programs. Governor Manolo Jiménez Salinas, in office since December 2023, credited “great teamwork.” Nationally, the picture is less rosy: 74% of adults still consider their state unsafe, and México state overtook Morelos this year as Mexico’s least safe state, with 90% of respondents reporting security concerns.

Mexico’s independence is celebrated at home and abroad

On Tuesday night, President Sheinbaum delivered her second Grito de Independencia from the National Palace balcony before a crowd the Mexico City government estimated at more than 300,000 in the Zócalo, marking 216 years since Miguel Hidalgo’s original Cry of Dolores.

Sheinbaum issued 21 arengas honoring independence heroes including Hidalgo, Josefa Ortiz, Leona Vicario and Vicente Guerrero, alongside Mexico’s Indigenous and Afro-Mexican peoples and migrants abroad, several of whom were included in a national Grito for the first time.

Abroad, Iran marked the holiday by lighting Tehran’s Azadi Tower in green, white and red, the first time the landmark has been illuminated in tribute to Mexico — an occasion the Mexican ambassador to Iran called “a great gesture of friendship.” In New York City, Mayor Zohran Mamdani served as grand marshal of Brooklyn’s Mexican Independence Day parade, days after U.S. Vice President JD Vance mocked a Mexican flag-carrying protester at a Dallas rally.

Antitrust regulators probe Liga MX

Mexico’s National Antitrust Commission (CNA) has opened an investigation into whether Liga MX operates as a monopoly, examining whether a small group is unfairly controlling “affiliation, organization and access” to professional soccer competitions in violation of federal competition law. The probe follows Liga MX’s 2020 decision — upheld through the 2026-27 season by the Court of Arbitration for Sport — to scrap promotion and relegation with the second-tier Liga Expansión and end payouts to lower-tier clubs, a move Liga Expansión officials fiercely disputed. No defendants have been named; the probe can run up to 120 business days and be extended. If wrongdoing is found, Liga MX and its clubs could face fines of up to 10% of annual income.

CFE advances Project Oasis in Baja California Sur

The Federal Electricity Commission unveiled Project Oasis BCS, a solar, battery and green hydrogen initiative meant to bring reliable power to the isolated Mulegé region, which has no direct connection to the national grid and has historically relied on fossil fuels.

The project pairs a 72-megawatt photovoltaic plant with a battery system, electrolyzers to produce hydrogen and fuel cells to convert it back into electricity for use when sunlight is scarce. CFE projects the initiative will serve 40,000 households and cut emissions equivalent to taking more than 31,000 vehicles off the road annually. If completed, it would be CFE’s first-ever green hydrogen power generation project.

Democracy index shows modest gains

According to International IDEA’s annual Global State of Democracy report, released on Tuesday, Mexico’s democracy score edged up slightly in 2025 — Sheinbaum’s first full year in office — rising to 1.778 out of 4 from 1.770 the year before. The country improved in rule of law and participation, held steady in rights and declined in representation, its best-ranked category at 83rd out of 173 nations. Mexico ranked in the top 100 in only one of the four measured categories. The report’s authors flagged rising political polarization and “us versus them” identity politics as threats across Latin America, while separately noting democratic backsliding tied to the Trump administration’s consolidation of executive power in the U.S.

Sheinbaum responds to Trump cartel pressure

Responding to a Trump “presidential determination” pressuring Mexico to take “additional action” against cartels and arrest complicit officials, Sheinbaum turned the spotlight on U.S. drug consumption, asking what Washington is doing to curb domestic drug demand, money laundering and the flow of American-made weapons into Mexico.

“We don’t need to be judged from the outside,” Sheinbaum said, insisting “we know what Mexico’s problems are and we act against them every day.” Trump’s determination, submitted to Congress on Tuesday, named Mexico among 23 countries as major drug producers or transit points and singled out Sinaloa Governor Rubén Rocha Moya — on leave amid U.S. accusations of cartel collusion but still free — as an official Washington wants arrested. The exchange came a week after Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Mexico isn’t doing enough against cartels, even as he acknowledged Mexican efforts had increased.

Record fuel bust in Guanajuato

Authorities announced on Thursday that they had seized 59 million liters of stolen fuel at a property in San José Iturbide, Guanajuato — the largest single-site fuel bust in Mexican history and roughly five times last year’s record seizure in Tamaulipas. The operation traces to a July 3 arrest involving a tanker truck loaded with stolen fuel, which led investigators to the storage facility, capable of holding up to 80 million liters. No arrests had been made as of Friday, and officials say specialized personnel will be needed to safely handle the seized hydrocarbons. Guanajuato’s security minister said the bust would help choke off a funding source for organized crime in a state that has seen four smaller fuel-theft busts this year.

Trade talks hover ahead of US midterms

The fourth round of formal USMCA-related trade talks between Mexico and the United States is tentatively set for next week, with officials on both sides eager to hammer out a deal before U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3, according to sources interviewed by Reuters.

A framework deal would benefit both governments: Trump wants an economic win as he risks losing control of Congress, while Mexico is contending with investor unease and a cooling economy. The push follows the collapse last month of parallel U.S.-Canada trade talks, making the Mexico-U.S. track an effort at an interim bilateral deal.

According to José Medina Mora, president of Mexico’s Business Coordinating Council (CCE), the elimination of Section 232 tariffs, which place duties on aluminum, steel and automobiles, is expected to be a primary focus.

Pups in the news

Rollo, an adopted mixed-breed puppy, is the National Palace’s newest resident, officially tasked with supporting “the emotional well-being of everyone,” per government videos; his brother Theo still awaits adoption, and the palace’s resident cats, including Coco and Zeus, remain in place.

In Morelia, a dog named Maple dressed as a taco stand won the city’s inaugural Patriotic Pup Contest, beating roughly 40 costumed competitors, with runners-up dressed as an elote-and-pork-loin vendor and a pozole bowl nearly twice their size.

Looking ahead

Next week brings a busy convergence of bilateral trade and security missions as well as the potential for currency swings.

The fourth round of USMCA-focused trade talks in Washington, D.C., could yield either a resolution or more setbacks. According to reporting by Politico, a preparatory call between Trump and Sheinbaum on Wednesday may have placed more topics on the discussion table than just Section 232 tariffs. However, Sheinbaum said after the call that “we’re making progress on trade issues.”

Any signs of progress or friction on tariffs are poised to move the peso. Meanwhile, 139 U.S. Army soldiers from the 101st Airborne Division are scheduled to land in Chihuahua on Sept. 20 for 11 days of joint training exercises with Mexican forces at the Centro Nacional de Adiestramiento, the military’s largest training facility.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: Junípero Serra: A complex character with a controversial legacy
World.content:
Standing in the plaza of Jalpan de Serra, a town in Querétaro’s remote, mountainous Sierra Gorda, I gazed up in awe at an enormous, intricately designed mission. Having lived in California for 30 years, I was familiar with the missions, designed by the Franciscan priest Junípero Serra, and for whom one of the busiest freeways in the Bay Area is named. But none of the California missions I’d visited were anywhere near as elaborate and baroque as this structure. In fact, I later learned that the style of the five Sierra Gorda missions is known as “mestizo baroque.”

Junípero Serra, a priest from the island of Mallorca, achieved his dream of becoming a missionary in the Americas at the age of 36, in 1749. After disembarking in Veracruz, he refused to ride horseback to Mexico City, instead journeying on foot the entire 270 miles, despite a severe leg injury. Five months later, he walked another 175 miles from Mexico City to the Sierra Gorda. He used the motto siempre adelante (always forward) to drive his missionary zeal.

In the Sierra Gorda, he evangelized the local population and used the sweat of the Pame, local Indigenous people, to build the five missions that, 250 years later, would become a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

There are several reasons for the dramatic difference in style between the two sets of missions, those in the interior of Mexico and the later ones on the Pacific coast, from Baja California to present-day San Francisco.

Location

The Sierra Gorda missions were close to rich colonial centers, like Mexico City, Querétaro and Guadalajara, which served as supply hubs, as well as to well-established trade routes and ample financial backing from New Spain.

On the other hand, the missions in Alta California (now the U.S. state of California) were built in remote, isolated outposts, thousands of miles from supply ports. Few overland routes existed, which forced Serra to rely on infrequent supply ships.

Skilled labor

In Mexico, the local Pame and other Indigenous artisans had been carving stone for centuries. After being converted, they blended Catholic iconography with Indigenous symbols, creating a hybrid of rich, intricate facades that look as if carved from stone filigree rather than masonry.

In contrast, unskilled workers in Alta California used local sun-dried adobe bricks, timber and river stones, resulting in a much simpler style.

The goal of the missions

In Mexico, the imposing mission architecture was designed to convey permanent control over wealthy interior mining and agricultural zones, whereas in Alta California the missions were built as a military strategy. International law at the time required actual physical settlement to hold a region. Placing missions next to military forts along the coast created a visible barrier against Russian fur traders moving south from Alaska and British explorers from the Pacific Northwest.

Leadership style differences

In addition to architecture, Serra’s way of governing also differed. While he used the same forced Catholic conversion and paternalism in both areas, his treatment of the locals differed. In the Sierra Gorda, he spent nine years learning the Pame language, translating catechisms, teaching European farming techniques and helping the Pames defend their agricultural plots from predatory Spanish soldiers and landowners. And he allowed the well-integrated Pames a high degree of freedom.

In California, however, Serra’s treatment of the Indigenous people was very mixed. On one hand, he wrote letters and reports condemning the violence, rape and mistreatment of native women by Spanish military officers, even walking hundreds of miles to Mexico City to meet directly with the viceroy to secure a “bill of rights” for Indigenous people.

But he was a harsh disciplinarian. Indigenous people were subjected to confinement in crowded, unsanitary conditions; forced labor; and corporal punishment if they tried to leave. Tragically, the isolated missions in Baja and Alta California also became vectors for European epidemic diseases, to which the local population had no immunity, leading to huge population decline, whereas the Pame had already developed relative immunity.

Reactions to Serra’s canonization

Pope Francis canonized Serra in 2015, during a visit to the United States. After such a complicated life, it’s no wonder that his canonization was greeted with very mixed reactions, especially in the U.S. Many traditional Hispanics cheered the decision, seeing it as a long-overdue acknowledgment by the Church of the role the Spanish-speaking missionaries played in bringing the faith to the Americas.

Others condemned the canonization, protesting at the archdioceses in Los Angeles and Washington, D.C., and dubbing Serra the “saint of genocide.” They were also disappointed that Pope Francis canonized Serra when only a few months earlier he had apologized for the “grave sins” committed against Indigenous peoples during the conquest of the Americas.

Mexicans were ambivalent. Because most Mexicans are mestizo — a mix of Spanish Catholic and Indigenous — people wrestled with practicing a deep faith that they loved, yet with the painful awareness that it was introduced through brutal colonial subjugation.

Clearly, Junípero Serra was a complex character. On one hand, he went out of his way to defend Indigenous and women’s rights, yet at the same time betrayed a lack of respect for their human dignity and agency. I suspect he will always be viewed as a complicated historical figure with a controversial legacy.

Louisa Rogers and her husband Barry Evans divide their lives between Guanajuato and Eureka, on California’s North Coast. Louisa writes articles and essays about expat life, Mexico, travel, physical and psychological health, retirement and spirituality. Her recent articles are available on her website, authory.com/LouisaRogers.

World.title: The story of Hotel Mocambo, Mexico’s original luxury beach resort
World.content:
When it comes to tourism in Mexico, one of the most popular options for international visitors is to spend a few nights at a majestic beach resort. From Cancún to Los Cabos, Mexico has established itself as a premier destination for world-class beach getaways, with Mexico’s Ministry of Tourism reporting that nearly half of Mexico’s visitors opt for ritzy coastal areas — where sprawling luxurious properties abound.

The shift toward Mexico’s coastline

The numbers show just how vital Mexico’s top-tier beaches are to its national tourism economy: Despite an overall lower number of visitors this year and a massive blow from U.S. airlines this summer, Cancún still leads the nation in international flight arrivals, accounting for 45% of Mexico’s airport activity as of June, with 4,844,588 reported flight arrivals.

Besides Mexico City, Guadalajara and Monterrey, which are among the 10 most active airports in Mexico, every other visit is largely due to Mexico’s beaches. This year, Los Cabos, Puerto Vallarta, Tulum, Cozumel and Mazatlán have generated the most airport traffic, respectively, with roughly 66% of Mexico’s inbound flights touching down near those beaches.

And yet, Mexico’s identity as a destination for opulent beach resorts originated in a region that is nowadays overlooked, particularly by international visitors. But if you know where to look, a time-travel beach experience awaits along the Gulf Coast, with its own kind of grandeur and charm.

Hotel Mocambo: Mexico’s first grand luxury resort

It’s impossible to overstate the historical significance of Veracruz and its port city, where the Spanish colonization of continental Latin America began in 1519. Over centuries, many of the country’s earliest contributions can be traced back to its Gulf Coast origins, including coffee, jalapeños, vanilla and more.

Add to that list: Mexico’s first grand luxury beach resort.

In 1938, Hotel Mocambo — named after Playa Mocambo, the beach where the hotel was built, and which originally derived from an Afro-Portuguese word denoting the region’s legacy as a refuge for escaped African slaves — began construction, making it among the earliest (if not the first) major beachfront resort in all of Mexico.

A midcentury haven for Mexican stars and cinema

During its heyday, Hotel Mocambo became a national treasure, with famous Mexican actors, musicians and celebrities — including Agustín Lara, Chavela Vargas and Pedro Infante — becoming regulars throughout the midcentury.

In 1943, “María Eugenia,” starring the iconic Mexican actress María Félix (and featuring a cameo from popular Veracruz singer Toña la Negra, who also personally frequented the hotel in those days), was filmed at Mocambo, demarcating the Golden Age of Mexican cinema.

Mocambo began as a 15-room property with a palm tree-studded view of the coastline to be enjoyed from extensive outdoor terrazas, grand staircases, arched hallways and open-air patios. A large outdoor pool and nearby barroom with high ceilings and jacuzzis can be found on separate levels, with a staircase that connects everything and inevitably descends to the beach.

Spanish influence and architectural expansion

The hotel’s walkways are breezy and bedecked with a combination of maritime decorations and Moorish structural features designed by Jesús Martí Martín, an avant-garde architect who was exiled from Madrid, Spain, after the Spanish Civil War. Martín was commissioned by Gov. Miguel Alemán Valdés to lead the hotel’s design atop the highest coastal hill in Boca del Río — the city just south of the port of Veracruz, which sits on the Jamapa River along the Gulf of Mexico — around the time that other beach hotels were starting to sprout up in the Pacific states of Guerrero and Sonora.

Under the governorship of Alemán Valdés, who would go on to become Mexico’s president, Hotel Mocambo aimed to become the first grand-scale beach resort attraction in all of Mexico.

And for a time, it was.

Just two years after opening, the hotel’s first expansion was overseen by another Spanish architect, Enrique Segarra. At one point, the hotel grew to include 110 rooms, though today that number has dwindled to 70 (for context, Mexico’s grandest beach resorts can now exceed more than 2,000 rooms).

Though it is no longer the nexus of Mexican aristocracy that it once was, Mocambo remains an important historical fixture in Mexico’s development as an attractive beach resort destination.

Preserving the legacy of Mexico’s Golden Age

Before Mocambo and the subsequent rise of beach resorts all over Mexico, the country’s most opulent buildings and high-end tourist attractions were centered in Mexico’s cosmopolitan inland cities. Not until Mocambo in Veracruz — and the rise of Acapulco shortly after — did Mexico gain extreme popularity for its prime coastal real estate and beach resort culture.

Ironically, or perhaps symbolically, the once-tranquil escape of Mocambo is now surrounded by modern buildings, major avenues, parking lots and the nonstop bustle of Mexico’s largest port city on the Gulf Coast. One of the neighboring buildings is a recently built high-rise apartment that juxtaposes interestingly with the dilapidated glory of Hotel Mocambo. And the state’s largest and most glamorous mall is within a short walking distance, as modernity has crept up to overtake Mocambo’s place.

Although the paint is faded and signs of decay are apparent in its grand facades, the resort is still worthy of a visit — simply for the pleasure of reliving Mexico’s Golden Age origins of beachside luxury.

Alan Chazaro is the author of “These Spaceships Weren’t Built For Us” (Tia Chucha Press, 2026), “Notes from the Eastern Span of the Bay Bridge” (Ghost City Press, 2021), “Piñata Theory” (Black Lawrence Press, 2020), and “This Is Not a Frank Ocean Cover Album” (Black Lawrence Press, 2019). He is a graduate of June Jordan’s Poetry for the People program at UC Berkeley and was selected as a Lawrence Ferlinghetti Poetry Fellow at the University of San Francisco. His work can be found in NPR, The Guardian, SLAM, GQ, L.A. Times, and more. He is currently based in Veracruz.

Despite the recent weakening from the U.S. Fed interest rate increase, the Mexican peso has been on a tear. Just recently, it was at a multi-year high against the US dollar and below 17.

The peso’s strength has defied just about every single analyst and expert. Even our own MND Peso Index estimates that the peso is nearly 6% overvalued against the dollar.

Recently, I did some analysis and calculated that if the peso had performed since the year 2020 as it did over the previous 25 years, it would currently be at 37 pesos to the US dollar! I wrote about it here: Why isn’t the peso at 37 to the US dollar? A perspective from our CEO.

So how can it be that it is currently trading at less than half of that rate? And can we expect it to devalue again anytime soon?

World.title: The ‘problem’ with Mexico’s 44% growth in exports: A perspective from our CEO
World.content:
A recent headline took just about everyone by surprise: Mexico’s export revenue in July of this year hit US $81 billion, up 44%. Think about that for a moment — an annualized run rate of nearly $1 trillion of export revenue for the country. Last year, exports hit a record $665 billion on 7.6% growth, up from $417 billion in 2020. So far this year through July, exports are up an impressive 27.7%. As a result, Mexico is now firmly the largest exporter to the United States, far surpassing No. 2 Canada and No. 3 China. China had been the leader for years until Mexico overtook it in the years following the COVID pandemic.

One would think that a 44% growth in exports would be exceptional for Mexico and its economy … but is it really as good as it sounds? Let’s dig a bit deeper into the numbers for a better understanding:

1. Most of the growth has come from the category of electrical and electronic equipment and appliances, which increased by a massive 134% in July. For the first time in that month, Mexico’s exports in that category exceeded the category of auto and auto parts. That category had previously led Mexico’s export revenue figures for decades. I recently wrote about that development here: The hottest product on the planet is increasingly made in Mexico: A perspective from our CEO. Automotive exports have been roughly flat year-to-date, and oil exports are actually down. In other words, the vast majority of the export growth is not coming from a diverse set of industries but rather this one segment.

2. Import growth is also booming. Year-to-date, imports are up 25.6%, and in the month of July, imports exceeded exports. Mexico actually had a rare trade deficit in July as imports grew by 45.7%.

3. Mexico has begun to import a massive amount of products from Taiwan, growing by over 200% so far this year and hitting nearly US $40 billion in the first half of the year. For some perspective, Mexico only imported $14 billion from Taiwan in the same period last year. Mexican imports of Taiwanese products increased by only $2 billion in the first six months of 2025, compared to 2024.

4. The massive year-to-date import and export growth numbers are not resulting in an economy that is growing as much as would be expected or hoped. One would think that such a huge increase in exports would dramatically increase production capacity investment and domestic consumption. But neither is happening. Estimates vary, but Mexican GDP is generally only expected to grow in the 1.2%-1.5% range — only half of what is expected in the United States this year.

So what is going on here?

It’s important to look deeper into what is actually happening to these imports and exports, specifically analyzing two measures related to value added:

Domestic value added embodied in the exports (How much Mexican labor is going into the exports?) Mexican-origin content (How much Mexican product is going into the exports?)

What we see is that the rapidly growing electronics category is extremely low in both measures. Said differently, given the high value of the products, the actual amount of Mexican labor and Mexican-origin content going into them is minimal. It is estimated that less than 3% of the exported value of products in this category is Mexican added value — just 3 cents on the dollar! A cynic might say that Mexico is doing little more than receiving the product from Taiwan, adding a “Made in Mexico” sticker and then exporting it — and that cynic wouldn’t be too far from the current reality!

For some perspective, that is barely a tenth of the value that Mexico adds to products in the vehicle segment. Engineering, design, parts manufacturing and assembly in Mexico are all common in that industry. And here is where the real opportunity for Mexico comes in. If Mexico could capture more of the added value in the massive, fast-growing electronics category, it would be hugely impactful on employment in the country. So how can that happen?

Enter the USMCA negotiations. Mexico and the United States have had many rounds of discussions on the updated trade agreement, and despite clear disagreement in certain areas (I’m looking at you, Mexican tomatoes!), increased local content or value added requirements in areas like electronics seems to be an area of agreement and alignment. It is in both countries’ interests to shorten the supply chain and further “de-risk” from China and Taiwan. And it is in both countries’ interests to have more control of the production and supply of such a critical product line.

So will it happen? I am optimistic for a positive outcome given that both countries have similarly aligned interests. Stay tuned to MND as we bring you the developments in this critically strategic area.

Travis Bembenek is the CEO of Mexico News Daily and has been living, working or playing in Mexico for nearly 30 years.

03

What to See & Do

SUNDAY IN SÃO PAULO

Parque Ibirapuera is the day’s hub, open from 5am to midnight with free entry. The MAM shows the 39th Panorama da Arte Brasileira, Depois que tudo foi dito, free on Sundays from 10am to 6pm.

The Oktoberfest runs at the park’s Arena de Eventos from 2pm to 11pm, with entry via Gate 10. It continues until 4 October.

MASP on Avenida Paulista opens from 10am to 6pm, with last entry at 5pm. Admission is R$85 full and R$42 reduced (about US$16.50 and US$8.20).

The Pinacoteca opens from 10am to 6pm at R$40 full and R$20 half (about US$7.80 and US$3.90). Entry is free on Saturdays and every second Sunday, so today is a paid day.

At Pina Luz, the retrospective Ismael Nery: Armadilha Moderna runs until 31 January 2027. Japan House on Avenida Paulista shows Shiro free of charge, from 10am to 7pm.

Farol Santander closes its video game exhibition Player 1 today. The tower opens from 9am to 8pm, with tickets at R$45 and R$22.50 (about US$8.75 and US$4.40).

The Festival da Lua Chinês fills Rua 25 de Março from 10am to 6pm, with free entry. Its programme includes a parade of 100 lion dancers, martial arts and moon cakes.

The Festa de San Gennaro in Mooca runs from 5pm to 10pm on Rua San Gennaro and Rua Lins. Street entry is free, and the festival continues on weekends until 4 October.

The SP Open final at Parque Villa-Lobos pits Spain’s Kaitlin Quevedo against Argentina’s Nadia Podoroska. Podoroska beat second seed Paula Badosa 6-3, 6-4 in Saturday’s semifinal.

The Museu da Imigração in Mooca hosts the free Festival VIVA! Leste Europeu from 10am to 6pm. Tickets are handed out on site, subject to capacity.

04

Getting Around

TRANSPORT

Metrô Lines 1, 2, 3 and 15 ran through Saturday night into Sunday as part of a 24-hour weekend trial. Regular Sunday service runs from 4:40am to about midnight.

CPTM Line 11-Coral trains share platform 2 at Corinthians-Itaquera, Dom Bosco, José Bonifácio and Guaianases until 4pm. The reason is track maintenance, according to Diário do Transporte.

On Line 12-Safira, passengers use platform 1 at São Miguel Paulista, Jardim Helena-Vila Mara and Itaim Paulista from 4am to 7am. CPTM says staff and signs will guide riders.

The single Metrô and CPTM fare is R$5.40 (about US$1.05), in force since 6 January. The municipal rodízio plate restriction applies only on weekdays.

05

Where to Eat

LUNCH & DINNER

The Oktoberfest menu includes a 30-centimetre sausage in three flavours and more than 70 craft breweries. Food service starts when the gates open at 2pm.

The Festa de San Gennaro cantina at Rua San Gennaro 214 charges R$50 on Sundays (about US$9.70). The price covers spaghetti, pizza and bruschetta, and children under 5 eat free.

The Festival da Lua Chinês has traditional food stalls and moon cakes on Rua 25 de Março. The stalls close with the festival at 6pm.

Feira Kantuta in Pari serves Bolivian and Andean food from 11am on Sundays. Entry is free, and each stall charges for its own dishes.

06

Practical Info

GOOD TO KNOW

The MAM is free today, while MASP is free all day on Tuesday. The Pinacoteca’s next free day is Saturday, 26 September.

Don Carlo runs 270 minutes, so the 5pm performance ends late in the evening. Tickets cost R$47 to R$290 (about US$9 to US$56).

Farol Santander sells its last tickets at 7pm, one hour before closing. MASP and the Pinacoteca take last entry at 5pm.

Showers are possible this afternoon and evening, according to the CGE. Carry an umbrella between the park, the museums and the Metrô.

07

Community & Lifestyle

FOR NEWCOMERS

The Virada Esportiva spreads free sport across more than 800 locations today. City Hall says every region of the city has activities.

The Festival da Lua Chinês and the Festa de San Gennaro both offer free street entry today. They showcase the Chinese community in Centro and the Italian heritage of Mooca.

The Oktoberfest includes an amusement park and a pet area, according to Revista Fórum and Passeios. Children up to 11 enter free.

The Festival VIVA! Leste Europeu at the Museu da Imigração is free from 10am to 6pm. It is a family-friendly way to meet the city’s Eastern European communities.

08

Game Day

THE WEEKEND ROUND

São Paulo beat Internacional 1-0 at the Morumbis on Saturday, with Jonathan Calleri scoring a first-half penalty. The club reported a crowd of 25,395 on a night of fan protests.

The defeat leaves Internacional in the relegation zone on 28 points, according to CNN Brasil. Calleri had not scored for two months before the penalty.

Corinthians host Fluminense at 4pm at the Neo Química Arena, live on TV Globo and Premiere. Corinthians sit 14th on 32 points after five straight defeats, according to Terra.

Palmeiras visit Grêmio at 11am in Porto Alegre, live on Premiere. Palmeiras are second on 56 points, according to Exame.

The SP Open final at Parque Villa-Lobos closes the second edition of the WTA 250 event. Quevedo beat Anna Blinkova 6-4, 2-6, 6-4 in her semifinal.

09

Business & Markets

WEEK IN FIGURES

The Ibovespa closed Friday at 185,229.17 points, down 0.41 percent, according to InfoMoney. It fell 1.06 percent over the week, its first weekly loss after four gains.

The commercial dollar ended at R$5.144, up 0.11 percent on the day. Exame and InfoMoney report the same close.

A Datafolha poll released Thursday showed President Lula and Senator Flávio Bolsonaro in a technical tie for an October runoff. InfoMoney put them at 46 and 44 percent, and said the race kept volatility high.

Investors also weighed a newly announced 15 percent increase in Bolsa Família. InfoMoney put its estimated cost at R$22 billion (about US$4.3 billion) for 2027.

Abroad, the Bank of Japan lifted its rate to 1.25 percent, a 31-year high. US Treasury yields rose across the curve, weighing on equities.

10

Plan Ahead

THE WEEK

The CGE warns of storms on Monday afternoon, and Climatempo forecasts gusts up to 58 kilometres an hour. MASP is free all day on Tuesday, from 10am to 8pm.

Don Carlo returns on 22, 23, 25 and 26 September, with the first cast on the 23rd and 26th. The Oktoberfest and the Festa de San Gennaro both run until 4 October.

Wednesday is forecast to be cold and wet, with 36.8 millimetres of rain. Japan House keeps Shiro on show until 25 October.

11

FAQ

QUICK ANSWERS

Is the Pinacoteca free today?

No, because entry is free only on Saturdays and on the second Sunday of each month, and today is the third Sunday. Tickets cost R$40 full and R$20 half (about US$7.80 and US$3.90).

What time do Corinthians play Fluminense?

At 4pm on Sunday at the Neo Química Arena, in round 28 of the Brasileirão. The match is live on TV Globo and Premiere.

What are the Oktoberfest hours today?

From 2pm to 11pm at the Arena de Eventos in Parque Ibirapuera, with entry via Gate 10. Children up to 11 enter free.

Will it rain in São Paulo today?

Climatempo gives a 71 percent chance of rain and 9.7 millimetres, with temperatures from 15°C to 27°C. The CGE expects isolated showers in the afternoon and evening.

How did São Paulo do against Internacional?

São Paulo won 1-0 at the Morumbis on Saturday. Jonathan Calleri scored from the penalty spot in the first half.

What is free to see in São Paulo today?

MAM is free on Sundays, and Japan House is free every day it opens. The Festival da Lua Chinês, the Festa de San Gennaro streets and the Virada Esportiva are also free.

The MIMO Festival plays its second free night at the Circo Voador in Lapa. Capicua and Emicida take the stage at 8pm, and Tinariwen follow at 10pm.

ArtRio closes its 2026 edition at the Marina da Glória, open from 2pm to 8pm. The Semana de Arte do Rio continues across the city until 27 September.

Flamengo host Red Bull Bragantino at the Maracanã at 6.30pm, and Fluminense visit Corinthians at 4pm. Vasco beat Coritiba 5-0 on Saturday.

03

What to See & Do

SUNDAY IN RIO

The MIMO Festival’s second free night opens at 6pm with DJ Machintal at the Circo Voador. Bianca Gismonti and Manuel de Oliveira follow at half past six.

Portuguese rapper Capicua performs with Emicida at 8pm, and Mali’s Tinariwen close the night at 10pm. Entry is free, by order of arrival, with capacity for about 2,000 people.

MIMO also screens Apopcalipse Segundo Baby, a documentary on Baby do Brasil, at Cine Santa Teresa at 8pm. Santa Teresa sits just above Lapa.

ArtRio 2026 ends today at the AXIA Marina da Glória, open from 2pm to 8pm. A 4pm panel brings together carnival artists Leonardo Bora, Gabriel Haddad and Leandro Vieira.

The Semana de Arte do Rio runs from 16 to 27 September, with more than 400 attractions at about 200 venues. Centro is the main hub, around Praça Mauá, Praça XV, Cinelândia and Lapa.

CCBB Rio shows Vik Muniz: A Olho Nu, billed as the largest retrospective of his work, until 12 October. Entry is free, and CCBB is open from 9am to 8pm except Tuesdays.

The Museu do Amanhã at Praça Mauá is open from 10am to 6pm, with last entry at 5pm. It closes on Wednesdays.

Rio Gastronomia fills the Jockey Club in Gávea from noon to 11pm, with more than 30 restaurants and a Ferris wheel. Tickets cost R$46 to R$100, about US$9 to US$19, and the wheel is extra.

04

Getting Around

TRANSPORT

A single metro journey costs R$7.90, about US$1.54, across Lines 1, 2 and 4. The state kept the fare unchanged from 12 April.

The beachfront avenues in Copacabana, Ipanema and Leblon close to cars on Sundays as leisure areas. Expect detours on Avenida Atlântica, Vieira Souto and Delfim Moreira during the day.

The Aterro do Flamengo’s Avenida Infante Dom Henrique also becomes a Sunday leisure area. Allow extra time driving between Centro and the Marina da Glória.

Flamengo’s 6.30pm kick-off will crowd the Maracanã metro station before and after the match. The MIMO night ends late, so ride-hailing is the practical return from Lapa.

05

Where to Eat

LUNCH & DINNER

Rio Gastronomia is the easiest one-stop lunch, with more than 30 restaurants in one place at the Jockey Club. It opens at noon and runs until 11pm.

Lapa is the natural dinner choice before the MIMO shows at the Circo Voador. Eating before 8pm avoids the rush between sets.

Botafogo and Flamengo sit closest to the Marina da Glória for an early dinner after ArtRio. Booking ahead helps on a busy festival weekend.

06

Practical Info

GOOD TO KNOW

Check INEA’s latest bathing bulletin before swimming, as ratings change from week to week. INEA advises staying out of the sea for 24 hours after rain and away from drain outlets.

The MIMO Festival needs no ticket, and entry stops when the Circo Voador reaches capacity. Arrive well before 8pm for Capicua and Emicida.

CCBB exhibitions are free, but tickets are issued at the box office or on ingressosccbb.com.br. CCBB is closed on Tuesdays.

07

Community & Lifestyle

FOR NEWCOMERS

The Semana de Arte do Rio is the city government’s new arts week, spread across museums, squares and theatres. Its free events are an easy way into Rio’s cultural life.

Sunday’s car-free beachfront draws cyclists, runners and families along the Zona Sul. It is one of the city’s most local weekend rituals.

08

Game Day

THE WEEKEND ROUND

Vasco thrashed Coritiba 5-0 at São Januário on Saturday in round 28 of the Brasileirão. The win lifted Vasco to 16th with 31 points, out of the relegation zone for now.

Botafogo lost 2-0 at Mirassol, with Eduardo scoring both goals in the first half. It was Tite’s first match in charge of Botafogo.

Flamengo lead the table with 57 points, one ahead of Palmeiras, and host Red Bull Bragantino at 6.30pm. Pulgar, Paquetá and Samuel Lino are suspended.

Fluminense sit fifth with 45 points and visit Corinthians at the Neo Química Arena at 4pm. Globo and Premiere carry that match, while SporTV and Premiere show Flamengo.

09

Business & Markets

WEEK IN FIGURES

The Ibovespa closed Friday at 185,229 points, down 0.41 percent on the day. It fell 1.06 percent over the week, ending a run of four weekly gains.

The commercial dollar rose 0.11 percent to R$5.144, according to Exame and InfoMoney. It gained close to 0.4 percent over the week.

Among the day’s movers, CSN fell 6.40 percent, while Minerva gained 4.46 percent.

The central bank’s Copom cut the Selic by 0.25 points to 13.75 percent on Wednesday. It was the fifth consecutive cut of that size.

The October election remains a key market driver. A Datafolha poll cited by Exame showed Lula at 46 percent and Flávio Bolsonaro at 44 percent in a runoff scenario.

10

Plan Ahead

THE WEEK

Monday is warm and mostly dry, though Alerta Rio warns of strong gusts. Rain becomes likely on Tuesday, and Wednesday is the wettest day.

The Semana de Arte do Rio continues until Sunday 27 September. Vik Muniz: A Olho Nu stays at CCBB until 12 October.

Rio Gastronomia runs until 27 September at the Jockey Club, then returns from 1 to 4 October. Thursday and Friday sessions start in the early evening.

11

FAQ

QUICK ANSWERS

What is on in Rio today?

The MIMO Festival’s free night at the Circo Voador features Capicua with Emicida at 8pm and Tinariwen at 10pm. ArtRio closes at the Marina da Glória, open from 2pm to 8pm.

Will it rain in Rio today?

No rain is forecast during the day, with temperatures between 20°C and 27°C. Alerta Rio expects strong gusts and possible light, isolated showers at night.

What time is the Flamengo game?

Flamengo host Red Bull Bragantino at the Maracanã at 6.30pm, on SporTV and Premiere. Fluminense visit Corinthians in São Paulo at 4pm.

How much is the Rio metro?

A single journey costs R$7.90, about US$1.54, on Lines 1, 2 and 4.

What time is sunset in Rio today?

Sunset falls at 5.48pm on Sunday.

Key Facts 1.Florianópolis is the best all-round place to live in Brazil for expats in 2026: the safest state capital in the country, a tech scene of about 30,000 foreign residents, and all-in budgets of US$1,250–2,000 a month 2.Curitiba is the value pick (US$800–1,300 a month, top of Brazil’s quality-of-life ranking), São Paulo the career pick (lowest state homicide rate, highest rents), Rio de Janeiro the lifestyle pick 3.Advertised rents run from R$32.51 per square meter in Teresina to R$65.36 in São Paulo (FipeZAP index, August 2026) 4.Exchange-rate basis of this guide: US$1 = R$5.1575 and €1 = R$5.9126 (PTAX closing rate, 18 September 2026, Banco Central do Brasil) 5.The trade-offs are real everywhere: Portuguese is not optional outside expat bubbles, and Brazil’s safety map varies more by state and neighborhood than by city

Where should an expat actually live in Brazil in 2026? For most remote workers and relocatees the answer is Florianópolis, followed by Curitiba for value, São Paulo for careers and Rio de Janeiro for lifestyle — that is the ranking this guide defends with verified rents, budgets and crime statistics. Every figure below carries its source and its month, because a ranking without dated numbers is just an opinion.

How This Ranking Works

Four criteria, weighted toward what expats ask us about most: housing cost (FipeZAP advertised-rent index, July–August 2026), monthly budget (The Rio Times city guides and cost-of-living data, cross-checked against Numbeo and Ookla speed-test aggregates, September 2026), safety (state homicide rates from the Brazilian Public Security Yearbook 2026 and the Atlas da Violência 2026), and the size of the established foreign community. No city wins all four. That is exactly why the ranking exists.

One structural note before the list: Brazil’s visa rules are national, not municipal. Whether you arrive on the digital-nomad visa (VITEM XIV, US$1,500 a month in foreign income or US$18,000 in savings) or another residence track, you can base yourself in any of these cities once approved. Choose on livability, not on paperwork.

The 2026 Ranking at a Glance

Rank City Rent, R$/m² (FipeZAP) Monthly budget, US$ Best for 1 Florianópolis R$60.84 (Jul) 1,250–2,000 Remote work, safety, community 2 Curitiba R$48.91 (Jul) 800–1,300 Value, order, calm 3 São Paulo R$65.36 (Aug) 1,200–1,800 Careers, networking, flights 4 Rio de Janeiro +11.04% YTD (Aug) 1,100–1,700 Beach life, culture 5 Belo Horizonte R$50.14 (Jul) 900–1,400 Food, central location 6 Recife R$64.11 (Jul) 700–1,200 Tech on a budget, Northeast base

Rents are advertised asking prices per square meter from the FipeZAP Residential Rent Index (Fipe/Grupo OLX), city values July 2026 except São Paulo and the Rio trend line, which are August 2026. Budgets: The Rio Times city guides (June 2026) and Numbeo/Ookla aggregates via GetBrazilVisa (September 2026), converted at PTAX 18 September 2026. Budget figures are planning ranges, not quotes.

1. Florianópolis — the All-Round Winner

The island capital of Santa Catarina is the one city that scores high on every criterion at once. The Atlas da Violência 2026 ranks Florianópolis as the safest of all 27 Brazilian state capitals. Santa Catarina sits among Brazil’s three lowest-homicide states, far below the national rate of 19.1 per 100,000 recorded for 2025. The tech and remote-work scene is the densest in the country: roughly 30,000 foreign residents, and the city placed seventh among the world’s fastest-growing remote-work destinations in 2026, with check-ins up about 96 percent (The Rio Times, May–June 2026).

Costs are honest mid-range. Furnished rentals in the popular neighborhoods run R$3,500–7,000 (US$680–1,360) a month, and daily life beyond rent adds about US$520–620. Typical internet: 200–260 Mbps. The downsides are structural: prices and traffic spike hard in the December-to-March high season, the island’s geography makes crossings slow, and winter (June–August) is genuinely cool by Brazilian standards. Book housing months ahead for summer, or sign an annual lease to escape the seasonal premium. Our full Living in Florianópolis guide has neighborhoods and budgets in detail.

2. Curitiba — the Value Pick

Curitiba topped Brazil’s quality-of-life ranking again in 2026 (The Rio Times, May 2026), and it is not hard to see why: organized public transport, walkable core neighborhoods like Batel, a cooler climate, and advertised rents of R$48.91 per square meter — about 25 percent below São Paulo. A comfortable monthly budget runs US$800–1,300, the lowest on this list relative to infrastructure quality.

Paraná’s homicide rate stood at 14.1 per 100,000 in 2024, below the national average, and metro Curitiba homicides fell a further 17 percent in 2025 (state security secretariat). The honest trade-offs: less beach, less nightlife gravity, and a smaller foreign community than Floripa or São Paulo. If your priority is a calm, functional city where money stretches, this is it.

3. São Paulo — the Career Pick

São Paulo is Brazil’s most expensive housing market — R$65.36 per square meter in August 2026, the highest in the FipeZAP index — and its safest state at the same time: 5.7 homicides per 100,000, roughly a third of the national rate, with January–April 2026 posting the state’s lowest robbery and homicide levels since 2001 (SSP-SP/Agência SP, May 2026). You pay for the deepest job market, the best international flight connections, and a food and culture scene with no Brazilian rival.

Budget US$1,200–1,800 a month, and choose neighborhoods deliberately — Pinheiros, Vila Madalena, Itaim Bibi and Moema are the standard expat bases. The real daily risk is phone theft, which still accounts for most robberies even after falling by half over four years. Detail in our Living in São Paulo guide.

4. Rio de Janeiro — the Lifestyle Pick

Rio ranks fourth not on charm but on discipline required. Rents are rising faster than anywhere else in the index — up 11.04 percent in the year through August 2026 — and Zona Sul neighborhoods (Ipanema, Leblon, Botafogo) price close to São Paulo levels. The reward is a daily life no other Brazilian city matches: beach before work, mountains inside the city, an expat community built over decades.

Safety in Rio is a neighborhood question, not a city question, and the state-level statistics sit well above São Paulo’s. Read our Is Rio Safe in 2026? analysis before choosing a district, and the Living in Rio guide for the housing reality.

5. Belo Horizonte — the Underrated Middle

Minas Gerais’ capital rarely leads expat lists, and that is part of the value: advertised rents of R$50.14 per square meter, a nationally famous bar and food culture, a mild highland climate, and a central location between Rio, São Paulo and Brasília. Budgets of US$900–1,400 a month are realistic. The foreign community is smaller and more local-integrated — an advantage if you want to learn Portuguese fast, a disadvantage if you want a ready-made expat scene.

6. Recife — the Northeast Tech Bet

Recife earns its place through Porto Digital, the tech district that made the city the Northeast’s startup capital, and through total monthly budgets that can dip to US$700–1,200. Two honest caveats. First, rents are no longer cheap: R$64.11 per square meter in July 2026, second-highest in this list, because demand concentrates in the same few neighborhoods (Boa Viagem above all). Second, Pernambuco’s state homicide rate of 44.1 per 100,000 (Atlas da Violência 2026) is among Brazil’s highest — Recife is livable with disciplined neighborhood choice, but it is not Florianópolis. This is the ranking’s clearest reminder that Brazil’s regional safety gaps are real.

What the Cheaper Capitals Offer — and Cost

Fortaleza (R$41.66 per square meter) and Teresina (R$32.51, the cheapest capital in the national index) undercut every city above on rent. The trade-off shows up in the safety statistics: Ceará records a state homicide rate of 42.2 per 100,000 (Atlas 2026), and the Northeast as a region posts 31.6 — still Brazil’s highest, even after a 35.5 percent decline since 2017 (Anuário Brasileiro de Segurança Pública 2026). Low rent is real money; we report the full price of it.

The Honest Downsides, Wherever You Choose

Portuguese is not optional. Only about 5 percent of Brazilians speak English (British Council estimate). Outside the expat bubbles of Floripa, Pinheiros and Zona Sul, daily life runs in Portuguese — leases, doctors, bureaucracy.

Bureaucracy is slow everywhere. CPF registration, bank accounts and residence cards take weeks, not days, in every city on this list.

Safety varies by street, not by city brand. Phone theft is the most common expat crime even in São Paulo; our Brazil safety guide for expats covers the habits that reduce it.

Rents are rising in the popular districts. The national index is up 9.16 percent over 12 months (FipeZAP, August 2026), and the increases concentrate exactly where foreigners want to live.

What We Could Not Confirm

City-level homicide rates for 2025 are not yet published for all capitals; where they are missing, we use state-level 2025 data and the Atlas da Violência 2026 capital ranking instead. Monthly budget ranges rely partly on crowd-sourced Numbeo data (September 2026), which we could verify only against our own city-guide reporting. We found no reliable 2026 count of foreign residents for cities other than Florianópolis.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the best place to live in Brazil for expats in 2026?

For most expats, Florianópolis: safest state capital in the Atlas da Violência 2026 ranking, a large foreign community, and mid-range costs. If career access matters more, São Paulo; if budget and calm matter more, Curitiba.

What is the cheapest city in Brazil for expats?

Among the capitals, Teresina posts the lowest advertised rents at R$32.51 per square meter and Fortaleza R$41.66 (FipeZAP, July–August 2026). Of the six ranked cities, Curitiba offers the lowest all-in budgets at US$800–1,300 a month with the strongest infrastructure.

Which Brazilian city is safest for expats?

Florianópolis ranks as the safest of all 27 state capitals in the Atlas da Violência 2026. At state level, São Paulo has Brazil’s lowest homicide rate at 5.7 per 100,000 (Sinesp/Ministry of Justice data). The South region is the safest overall at 11.9 per 100,000 in 2025.

How much money do I need to live in Brazil as an expat?

Plan US$800–1,300 a month in Curitiba, US$1,250–2,000 in Florianópolis, and US$1,200–1,800 in São Paulo, all-in including rent (September 2026 data, converted at US$1 = R$5.1575). Our Cost of Living in Brazil 2026 guide breaks the budgets down line by line.

Do I need to speak Portuguese to live in Brazil?

Yes, for practical purposes. About 5 percent of Brazilians speak English. You can arrive without Portuguese in the nomad hubs of Florianópolis or São Paulo’s Pinheiros, but leases, healthcare and bureaucracy require it — and learning it is the single strongest quality-of-life upgrade available.

Can I work remotely from any of these cities?

Yes. Brazil’s digital-nomad visa (VITEM XIV) requires US$1,500 a month in foreign income or US$18,000 in savings and lets you live anywhere in the country for one year, renewable once. Fiber internet is standard in all six cities, with typical speeds from 150 to 260 Mbps (Ookla-based aggregates, September 2026).

Which city has the largest expat community?

In absolute numbers, São Paulo and Rio de Janeiro host the largest foreign populations. Florianópolis has the densest remote-work community relative to its size, with about 30,000 foreign residents and the fastest growth in 2026.

World.title: Mexico’s Sheinbaum Meets Chihuahua Governor After Row Over US Agents
World.content:

One email, every weekday morning. What moved in Latin American markets, politics and expat life.

MEXICO · SECURITY, 20 SEPTEMBER 2026

Key Facts —The meeting — President Claudia Sheinbaum held a private meeting with Chihuahua Governor Maru Campos at the Ciudad Juárez airport at midday on Saturday, 19 September 2026, despite having said a day earlier that no working session was planned. —The dispute — The two discussed the participation of US intelligence personnel in anti-drug operations in Chihuahua. Two Americans and two Mexican investigators died in a vehicle crash in the municipality of Morelos in April, after an operation against a drug laboratory. —The agreement — Federal and state governments will work jointly through the Secretariat of Governance and the Secretariat of Security. Sheinbaum said that if any law was violated, action must follow — and Campos agreed. —The backdrop — The visit came one day after Sheinbaum confirmed a new call with Donald Trump — the call took place on Wednesday, 16 September — and said a tariff deal is advancing. Formal trade talks resume in Washington on 28 September.

A five-month dispute over US agents operating in Chihuahua has produced its first direct meeting between Mexico’s president and the state’s opposition governor. The outcome is modest but real: a channel for joint work, and an agreement that law violations will have consequences.

President Claudia Sheinbaum. On Saturday she held her 23rd regional accountability event, this time at the Plaza de la Mexicanidad in Ciudad Juárez, across the border from El Paso, Texas. (The Rio Times archive)

What Happened in Juárez on Saturday

Sheinbaum arrived at Abraham González International Airport at midday. Governor María Eugenia Campos Galván, of the opposition PAN party, greeted her there — and the two held a private meeting that had not been on the announced schedule.

On Friday, Sheinbaum had said there would be no working session with the governor. State matters, she had said, would be handled by Interior Secretary Rosa Icela Rodríguez. Saturday’s airport meeting went further than that plan, according to La Jornada’s correspondent in Ciudad Juárez.

After the meeting, Sheinbaum described its core: “We spoke about coordination; what I told her is that in the event there was a violation of any law, action must be taken — she agreed — in case any official of her government acted wrongly, that it proceed.”

The two governments agreed to work jointly through the Secretariat of Governance and the Secretariat of Security, depending on the issue, “for the well-being of the state of Chihuahua,” Sheinbaum said.

The April Crash Behind the Dispute

The disagreement dates to April 2026. Two US personnel and two Mexican investigators died in a vehicle crash in the municipality of Morelos, Chihuahua, following an operation targeting a drug laboratory. Their presence raised questions about the role of American intelligence agents on Mexican soil and who had authorized their work.

Campos described the Americans’ role as “training and assistance” and disputed suggestions that they took part directly in the raid. The conflicting accounts exposed a deeper disagreement between the state and federal governments over how Chihuahua coordinates with US agencies on security matters.

Sovereignty over security operations is a sensitive point in Mexico. Sheinbaum has repeatedly denied reports of unauthorized CIA operations while insisting that any cooperation must respect Mexican law. Saturday’s formula — joint work, with consequences if the law was broken — is the first common position both levels of government have publicly accepted.

What It Means for the Border Economy

Ciudad Juárez and El Paso form one of the largest binational economic zones in North America. Factories, trucking companies and logistics firms on both sides depend on predictable security coordination. A public dispute between the federal government and a border-state governor adds uncertainty that businesses price in quietly.

Campos had requested federal meetings on security, water and cattle exports. Chihuahua shares water resources with the United States, and its ranchers depend on access to US markets. Those files now move to the Secretariat of Governance, which will hold several meetings with the state, according to Sheinbaum.

The timing also matters for trade. One week before formal US-Mexico tariff talks resume in Washington on 28 September, the de-escalation in Chihuahua removes one potential friction point from the table. The Rio Times covered Friday’s confirmation of the latest Trump call and the state of the tariff stack in detail.

What We Could Not Confirm

Whether trade or tariffs were discussed during the airport meeting. Which specific commitments Sheinbaum announced for Chihuahua at the Plaza de la Mexicanidad event itself. The status of any formal investigation into the April crash. And whether the joint channel will produce a written security-coordination protocol — none has been published.

Frequently Asked Questions Why did Sheinbaum meet the governor of Chihuahua in Ciudad Juárez? Governor Maru Campos had requested meetings on security, water and cattle exports. The two also needed to address a months-long dispute over US intelligence personnel operating in the state, after two Americans died in a crash following an anti-drug operation in April 2026. What did Sheinbaum and Campos agree on? Joint work between the federal and state governments through the Secretariat of Governance and the Secretariat of Security. Sheinbaum said that if any law was violated in the US agents case, action must be taken — and the governor agreed. What happened in the April crash in Chihuahua? Two US personnel and two Mexican investigators died in a vehicle crash in the municipality of Morelos in April 2026, after an operation against a drug laboratory. The Americans’ role in the operation has been disputed by the state and federal governments ever since. Does this affect the US-Mexico trade talks? Indirectly. Formal tariff talks resume in Washington on 28 September 2026. Reducing the security dispute between Mexico City and Chihuahua removes one source of friction, but no tariff line has changed and no deal text has been published.

Sources: La Jornada, correspondent report from Ciudad Juárez (19 September 2026); Border Report (18-19 September 2026); KTSM 9 News El Paso (19 September 2026); Reuters (18 September 2026). Quotes from President Sheinbaum as reported by La Jornada.

World.title: Brazil’s Election Two Weeks Out: What Expats Need to Know
World.content:
BRAZIL · POLITICS & ELECTIONS

Key Facts — The date Brazil holds the first round of its general election on Sunday 4 October 2026 — exactly two weeks from today. A runoff, if no presidential candidate wins a majority, follows on Sunday 25 October, three weeks later.

— The race President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva leads first-round polling — the vote actually happening on 4 October — while second-round runoff simulations against Senator Flávio Bolsonaro show a statistical tie, the pollsters’ term for results within the margin of error, not a verdict on the outcome.

— The Abin report A confidential report by Brazil’s intelligence agency Abin, dated late August, rated US pressure on the election as “critical” — leaked this week via Folha de S.Paulo columnist Mônica Bergamo and reported by Metrópoles and CNN Brasil on 19 September. The report describes political pressure; it does not allege tampering with votes or voting machines. Both halves matter.

— The trust gap A Datafolha poll published on Friday 18 September shows distrust of the Supreme Court (STF) at a record 48%, up from 43% in March, in a series running since 2012. The split is partisan: 69% of Flávio Bolsonaro backers distrust the court, versus 22% of Lula voters.

— For expats Voting is for Brazilian citizens only — nothing changes operationally for foreign residents. The economic backdrop: the real closed Friday at 5.1575 per US dollar (PTAX), with the Selic rate at 13.75%.

— This week Both Lula and US President Donald Trump address the UN General Assembly in New York on Tuesday 22 September.

Two weeks from today, Brazil votes. Lula leads the first-round polls, while runoff simulations against Flávio Bolsonaro show a statistical tie; the intelligence agency has privately rated US pressure on the election “critical”; and public distrust of the Supreme Court has hit a record. For the half-million-plus foreign residents who cannot vote, the practical answer is simple — nothing changes on the ground — but the next two weeks will shape the country expats live in. Here is what is actually known, clearly attributed, and what to watch.

An electronic voting machine, in an archive photo. Brazil votes in the first round on Sunday 4 October 2026; a runoff, if needed, follows three weeks later. (Photo: Rio Times archive)

Where the Race Stands

Two weeks out, President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva leads the first-round polls — the vote actually happening on 4 October — while second-round runoff simulations against Senator Flávio Bolsonaro show a statistical tie, meaning the gap between them sits within the polls’ margin of error. Both statements are the pollsters’ own description of their numbers, not a prediction: a first-round lead says who starts ahead; a statistical tie says the runoff race is too close for the surveys to call.

The first round on Sunday 4 October also covers governors, senators and federal and state deputies, but the presidential contest is the one that moves markets and headlines. If no candidate wins a majority of valid votes, a runoff follows on Sunday 25 October, three weeks later.

The Abin Warning — Both Halves of It

A confidential report by Abin, Brazil’s intelligence agency, dated late August, rated US pressure on the election as “critical”. The report entered the public domain this week through Folha de S.Paulo columnist Mônica Bergamo and was reported on 19 September by Metrópoles and CNN Brasil.

Precision matters here, in both directions. The report describes political pressure — statements, diplomacy and leverage from Washington — and rates its intensity as critical. It does not allege tampering with votes or with Brazil’s electronic voting machines. Reading it as proof of interference goes beyond the document; reading it as nothing ignores the agency’s own strongest classification. Both halves of that sentence are what is verified.

Record Distrust of the Supreme Court

A Datafolha poll published on Friday 18 September shows distrust of the Supremo Tribunal Federal at a record 48%, up from 43% in March, in a series the institute has run since 2012. The divide is partisan: 69% of Flávio Bolsonaro supporters distrust the court, against 22% among Lula voters.

The STF is not a bystander in this election. The court has driven the cases against former president Jair Bolsonaro — convicted in September 2025, sentenced to 27 years and serving that sentence since November 2025 — and its justices are central players in the campaign’s arguments. A record distrust number two weeks before voting is part of the climate in which more than 158 million registered voters go to the polls.

What Changes for Expats — Honestly, Little

Voting in Brazil is for Brazilian citizens. Foreign residents — permanent or otherwise — do not vote, and no residency, visa or immigration rule changes on 4 October. Election day is a Sunday; polling stations operate mainly in schools, and normal weekend commerce continues. There is no verified reason to change plans.

What the election does affect is the economic weather expats live in. The real closed Friday at 5.1575 per US dollar (PTAX) after a soft week, and the Selic rate stands at 13.75%. What a Lula or a Bolsonaro victory would mean for the currency is a forecast, not a fact — treat anyone selling certainty on that as selling something.

What Comes Next

On Tuesday 22 September, both Lula and US President Donald Trump address the UN General Assembly in New York — an unusual shared stage two weeks before the vote, given the Abin report’s subject. Then the final campaign stretch to Sunday 4 October. If a runoff is needed, it follows on Sunday 25 October, three weeks later. For daily context, see our daily guide for Sunday 20 September.

Can expats vote in Brazil’s election? No. Voting in Brazilian elections is for Brazilian citizens; foreign residents, including permanent residents, do not vote. Nothing in residency or immigration rules changes on election day. Does anything close or change on 4 October? Election day is a Sunday, so much of the country is already on weekend footing. Polling stations operate mainly in schools, and normal weekend commerce and services continue. No nationwide closures or restrictions beyond the usual election-day routines have been announced. What will the election mean for the real? That is a forecast, not a fact. What is known: the real closed Friday at 5.1575 per US dollar (PTAX), the Selic rate is 13.75%, and Lula leads first-round polls while second-round simulations show a statistical tie. Markets price elections as uncertainty resolves; any specific prediction about the currency’s direction after 4 October is opinion, and we do not publish opinion as fact.

World.title: Bolivia Ends 20 Years of Cheap Diesel: What the 83% Price Rise Means for Expats
World.content:
BOLIVIA · ECONOMY & FUEL POLICY

Key Facts — The headline Supreme Decree 5716, approved on Friday 18 September and in force since Saturday 19 September, raised the retail price of diesel in Bolivia from Bs9.80 to Bs17.95 per litre including VAT — a rise of about 83%, from roughly US$0.89 to US$1.63 per litre.

— The mechanism The decree repeals two earlier decrees (DS 5676 of 16 August and DS 5698 of 1 September) and ties the diesel price to an international reference — Argus ULSD Colonial 62 — with a band of plus or minus 5%, so the price can move in either direction. The price is recalculated on business days.

— What else is in it A 0% import tariff on certain gasoline imports until 31 December 2027, and a flex-fuel incentive running to 30 April 2030. The ministry has five working days to publish the regulation of the price band.

— Why now Fuel subsidies have cost the state around US$55 million a week as dollar reserves ran short. The decree came hours after the Senate approved a US$1.9 billion credit from the IMF (the lower house had approved it on Thursday); officials expect an IMF board vote on 2 October — that date is an expectation, not a confirmed schedule.

— For expats A 40-litre tank now costs Bs718, about US$65. Transport unions had not announced fare changes at the time of writing — expect pressure on bus fares and food prices, but no verified figures yet.

After more than two decades of some of the cheapest diesel in the Americas, Bolivia has let the price jump by about 83% overnight — from Bs9.80 (about US$0.89) to Bs17.95 (about US$1.63) a litre. For expats the direct hit is modest; the indirect effects, through bus fares and food prices, are not yet quantified. Here is what Supreme Decree 5716 actually does, why the government moved now, and what to watch in the coming days.

A YPFB service station, in an archive photo. Supreme Decree 5716, in force since Saturday 19 September 2026, raised the retail diesel price from Bs9.80 to Bs17.95 per litre and tied it to an international reference with a 5% band. (Photo: Rio Times archive)

What Supreme Decree 5716 Does

The decree, approved on Friday 18 September and in force from Saturday 19 September, sets the retail diesel price at Bs17.95 per litre including VAT, up from Bs9.80 — a rise of about 83%. It repeals Supreme Decree 5676 of 16 August and Supreme Decree 5698 of 1 September, the two stop-gap measures of the past five weeks.

Instead of a fixed price, DS 5716 ties diesel to the Argus ULSD Colonial 62 international reference, within a band of plus or minus 5%. The reference price is calculated on business days, and the ministry responsible has five working days to publish the regulation governing the band. In practice this means the pump price can now move in both directions — down as well as up — rather than sitting frozen for years, as it did under the subsidy regime.

The decree also sets a 0% import tariff on certain gasoline imports until 31 December 2027 and extends a flex-fuel incentive to 30 April 2030 — both aimed at private-sector supply, which the subsidy system had crowded out.

Why Now — the Dollar Shortage and the IMF

Bolivia’s fuel subsidies cost the state around US$55 million a week, paid for with dollars the central bank increasingly does not have. The country’s foreign-exchange shortage has made imported fuel — most of what Bolivia consumes — a direct drain on reserves.

The timing is not accidental. The decree came hours after the Senate approved a US$1.9 billion credit from the IMF on Friday (the Chamber of Deputies had approved it on Thursday). Officials say they expect the IMF board to vote on 2 October; treat that date as an expectation, not a confirmed schedule. Fuel-subsidy reform is exactly the kind of fiscal signal an IMF program looks for, and the government has framed the decree as part of stabilizing public finances.

What It Means for Expats

The direct cost is easy to price: a 40-litre tank that cost Bs392 (about US$36) now costs Bs718, about US$65. For expats who drive, that is the whole change for now.

The indirect effects are the real story, and they are honestly unknown at the time of writing. Diesel moves Bolivia’s buses, trucks and farm machinery, so transport unions and food supply chains will feel the increase first. Transport unions had not announced fare changes as of Sunday; any verified figures will matter more than predictions. If you budget in bolivianos, watch bus fares and market prices over the next two weeks rather than assuming the worst on day one.

One structural point in the other direction: because the price now follows an international reference with a 5% band, it can also fall. The era of a price that only goes up by decree is, in principle, over.

The Background — Twenty Years of Cheap Fuel

Bolivia’s fuel subsidies date back more than two decades and were a pillar of the economic model built under the MAS governments. They kept diesel among the cheapest in the Americas, but at the cost of ballooning fiscal spending, smuggling to neighbouring countries, and a refining and import structure dependent on state dollars.

President Rodrigo Paz won the runoff of 19 October 2025 with 54.5% of the vote and took office on 8 November 2025, promising to phase out the subsidy era. The first cuts came in December 2025; the August and September decrees now repealed were interim steps. DS 5716 is the first measure that replaces the fixed-price system with a market-referenced band rather than simply raising the frozen number.

What Comes Next

Three things to watch: the ministry’s band regulation, due within five working days of the decree; the first daily recalculations of the reference price, which will show whether the band actually moves; and the expected IMF board vote around 2 October. Locally, the open question is transport fares — the first union announcements, if any, will set the tone for how the increase lands. The regional picture is in our daily guide for Sunday 20 September.

How much does diesel cost in Bolivia now? Bs17.95 per litre including VAT, up from Bs9.80 — a rise of about 83%. At the official exchange rate of roughly Bs11.01 per US dollar, that is about US$1.63 per litre, up from about US$0.89. A 40-litre tank now costs Bs718, about US$65. Will bus fares and food prices rise? Probably, but no verified figures exist yet. Transport unions had not announced fare changes at the time of writing. Diesel powers Bolivia’s buses, trucks and farm machinery, so pressure on fares and food logistics is the expected channel — watch for official announcements rather than estimates. Can the price go back down? Yes, in principle. Supreme Decree 5716 ties the diesel price to the Argus ULSD Colonial 62 international reference within a band of plus or minus 5%, recalculated on business days. If the international reference falls, the band allows the pump price to fall too — unlike the old fixed-price system, which only ever moved up by decree.

World.title: Costa Rica’s Rebeca Grynspan retakes lead in race to head the UN
World.content:
Costa Rican economist Rebeca Grynspan moved back to the front of the race to become the next secretary-general of the United Nations on Friday. She drew the most support in the Security Council’s third informal straw poll. Grynspan, who leads the UN Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD), received nine “encourage” votes, five “discourage” votes and one “no opinion” among the Council’s 15 members, according to diplomatic sources. The vote took place behind closed doors in New York.



Guyana’s ambassador to the UN, Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett, finished a close second with eight encourage votes, six discourage votes and one no opinion. The two women have drawn the strongest backing across all three rounds. Friday’s result reverses the order of the Aug. 21 poll, when Rodrigues-Birkett led the field. Grynspan had topped the first round on July 30 with 10 encourage votes. That means she returns to first place with slightly less support than she started with.

Argentina’s Rafael Grossi, director general of the International Atomic Energy Agency, received five encourage votes and eight discourage votes. Grossi’s candidacy has the backing of the administration of US President Donald Trump. Senegal’s former president Macky Sall and Uganda’s Olara Otunnu also drew five encourage votes each. Sall received nine discourage votes and Otunnu seven.

Eight candidates remain in the race to succeed António Guterres, whose second five-year term ends Dec. 31. Besides the leading contenders, the field includes former Chilean president Michelle Bachelet, former Ecuadorian foreign minister María Fernanda Espinosa and former Ecuadorian minister Ivonne A-Baki.

Straw polls are non-binding. They allow Council members to signal support or resistance before the body sends a formal recommendation to the General Assembly, which makes the appointment. The Assembly has historically ratified the Council’s choice. The hardest test is still ahead. In the next round, the five permanent members, the United States, China, Russia, France and the United Kingdom, vote on differently colored ballots.

That reveals whether any of them would veto a candidate. A single veto is enough to eliminate a contender, no matter how many encourage votes they collect. To be recommended, a candidate needs at least nine votes in favor and no veto from a permanent member.

That makes discourage votes almost as important as encourage votes at this stage. Compared with the August round, Grynspan gained two votes of support but also added one more vote against her, according to diplomatic sources. The contest is also shaped by the lack of agreement between Washington and Beijing, which have not converged on a consensus candidate. No date has been set for the next round.

A decade ago, the Council formally settled on Guterres in mid-October after several rounds of voting. The next secretary-general will take office in January 2027. Costa Rica’s government has supported Grynspan’s candidacy throughout the process. After meeting with Grynspan and President Laura Fernández in August, Foreign Minister Manuel Tovar said the momentum appeared to favor her.

He added that the race was not over and that the Foreign Ministry was determined to carry the bid through its final stage. If selected, Grynspan would be the first woman to lead the United Nations since its founding in 1945, and the first Costa Rican to hold the post.

World.title: Prime Minister, Special Envoy and Police celebrate National Service Day at HelpAge Center
World.content:
Prime Minister, Special Envoy and Police celebrate National Service Day at HelpAge Center

By Zoila Palma: Today, in honor of Father of the Nation George Cadle Price, Prime Minister John Briceno, Special Envoy Rosanna Briceno, the Orange Walk Central executive and members of the Belize Police Department visited HelpAge center.
