World.title: The cost of having a baby in Europe: Where are essentials cheapest?
World.content:
Most parents describe welcoming a baby as one of the happiest moments in life, but it also comes with a cost. From nappies and feeding to pushchairs and clothes, there is a long shopping list of baby essentials. The bill can be higher than many parents expect.

 

The cost of baby essentials varies significantly across Europe. But how much do parents actually spend? Which countries are the most expensive for baby essentials, and where are they most affordable relative to average wages?

Remitly calculated the annual cost of baby essentials during the first year of a baby’s life, based on prices as of July 2026. It includes 14 staple items across six categories:

Nappy changes (nappies, wet wipes, rash cream),

Bottles (bottle with caps),

Baby formula

Sleep (crib, carrycot, or moses basket, crib mattress, fitted sheets, blankets),

Transport (infant car seat, stroller),

Clothing (bodysuits or onesies, babygrow or pants, socks).

Across 38 European countries, the estimated cost of baby essentials in the first year ranges from €2,813 in the UK to €6,294 in Spain, with a European average of €4,727.

In addition to Spain, first-year baby essentials cost more than €6,000 in the Netherlands (€6,140), Finland (€6,066), Sweden (€6,025) and Switzerland (€6,018).

Costs fall between €5,000 and €6,000 in Luxembourg (€5,665), Italy (€5,609), Lithuania (€5,563), Albania (€5,532), Serbia (€5,509), Montenegro (€5,500), Portugal (€5,337), Slovakia (€5,221), Norway (€5,079) and Iceland (€5,004).

Among the five largest economies, Spain has the highest costs, while the UK has the lowest, at €2,813. Germany (€4,701) and France (€4,393) fall closer to the European average.

Parents in Czechia (€3,211), Romania (€3,385), Latvia (€3,392), Croatia (€3,661), Bulgaria (€3,804) and Bosnia and Herzegovina (€3,844) face some of the lowest baby costs in nominal terms, with all six below €4,000.

Turkey (€4,023), Belgium (€4,084), Malta (€4,118) and Greece (€4,158) are also close to the €4,000 mark, but slightly above it.

Highest spending on clothing, baby formula and nappies

The distribution of costs across the six categories varies widely across Europe. On average, clothing (30.3%), baby formula (25.7%) and nappies (24.5%) account for the largest shares, making up 81% of total first-year costs.

Across the 38 countries, parents spend an average of €1,465 on clothing, €1,187 on baby formula and €1,152 on nappies, bringing the combined cost to €3,804.

The breakdown varies significantly from country to country. Clothing accounts for just 16% of costs in Denmark, compared with 52.5% in Sweden. Its share is also above 45% in the Netherlands, Finland and Ireland.

Baby formula makes up 10.8% of costs in Sweden but 41.3% in Latvia. Its share is also high in Turkey, Denmark and Hungary, where it exceeds 35%.

Nappies account for 12.4% of costs in Turkey, compared with more than 36% in Switzerland and Belgium.

The chart below breaks down how much parents spend on each category during their baby’s first year.

Baby costs as a share of the average wage

Of course, income levels matter when comparing countries, given the wide differences in wages across Europe. So, how much of the average annual wage is spent on baby essentials during the first year?

Remitly’s research compared the cost of baby essentials with average wages in each country. It used the International Labour Organization’s average monthly earnings of employees, adjusted for inflation.

Affordability can also depend on whether both parents work, as well as taxes and family benefits. These can make a big difference as the Euronews article shows.

Across the 36 countries, baby essentials account for an average of 20.9% of annual wages. The share ranges from 5.4% in Belgium to 88.8% in Moldova.

Parents in Albania (66%), Turkey (45.1%), Montenegro (45%), Serbia (41.4%), Bosnia and Herzegovina (36.1%), Portugal (35.7%) and Hungary (34.7%) spend at least one-third of the average annual wage on baby essentials, according to this calculation.

Baby essentials account for less than 10% of the average annual wage in Luxembourg (6%), Denmark (6.7%), the UK (7.5%), Norway (7.6%), Ireland (8%), Switzerland (8%), Germany (8.1%), Austria (8.2%), France (8.5%), Malta (8.9%) and the Netherlands (9.4%).

What about nursery and creche?

This research does not cover nursery and crèche costs, which can be a significant additional burden for parents across Europe.

For example, in 2023, gross childcare fees for two children reached €64,211 in Switzerland, while the Netherlands had the highest figure in the EU, at €39,229, according to the OECD. In Germany, the figure was just €552.

The figures cover centre-based care, meaning childcare provided outside the home in licensed facilities. This includes nurseries, day-care centres, crèches, playschools and parent-run groups, either full or part time.

When net childcare costs for two children are considered, the figure is €10,200 for a single-earner family in Switzerland and €27,551 for a two-earner couple. However, government support can significantly reduce costs for families in some countries, with net costs falling below €5,000, as this Euronews article shows.

World.title: All the direct flight routes from Europe to Central and South America
World.content:
Last week, we looked at all the new airline routes connecting Europe to Canada. Now we thought it was time to look slightly further south – more specifically, at Central and South America.

 

According to the World Tourism Barometer by UN Tourism, both regions saw growth in 2025, with South America up 7% and Central America up 5% year on year.

Destinations in the Americas seeing a big uptick in visitors include Brazil, up a mega 37%, and Guyana, up 24%.

While many airlines offer routes from Europe to these countries via the US, there are still some options for those looking to fly direct.

The best connected airport for travelling to these regions is undoubtedly Adolfo Suárez Madrid-Barajas Airport, with airlines flying from here including Iberia, Air Europa, LATAM and more.

Here, we outline your options in order of the most-to-least visited countries.

Brazil

South America’s largest country had a record-breaking year in 2025, with some 9.3 million international tourists choosing Brazil for their vacation.

It’s little wonder – whether you’re looking to explore the wildlife of the Amazon or party the night away at the Rio Carnival, Brazil has something for everyone.

The country’s most populous city, São Paulo, is home to the best connected airport for those travelling from Europe.

LATAM flies to São Paulo from Madrid, Barcelona, Lisbon, Paris, Amsterdam, Paris and London Heathrow, while TAP Portugal flies there from Porto and Lisbon.

Lufthansa serves this route from Frankfurt and Munich; KLM from Amsterdam; British Airways from London; Air France from Paris; SWISS from Zurich; and Turkish Airlines from Istanbul. Air Europa and Iberia also fly from Madrid.

For those looking to visit Rio de Janeiro, TAP Portugal flies from Lisbon and Porto; Iberia from Madrid; Air France from Paris; Lufthansa from Frankfurt; KLM from Amsterdam; ITA Airways from Rome and British Airways from London. Gol also flies from Lisbon.

You can fly direct to Cartagena from Madrid, Rome, Milan, Amsterdam and Zurich Ricardo Gomez Angel/Unsplash

Colombia

Known for its wildlife, beaches and colonial architecture (and its coffee), Colombia saw 6.2 million international visitors in 2025.

The capital Bogotá will most likely be your main point of entry. There, you can make your way through the culinary wonders of Colombia, explore the street art scene and climb Cerro de Monserrate for spectacular views, or head out of the city to Chingaza National Park.

Avianca flies to Bogotá from Madrid, Barcelona, Paris and London Heathrow; Air France from Paris; Lufthansa from Frankfurt; Edelweiss Air from Zurich; KLM from Amsterdam; and Turkish Airlines from Istanbul.

Alternatively, Cartagena with its UNESCO-listed fortress and walled city is served by airlines including Plus Ultra and World2Fly, which both fly from Madrid; Neos from Rome and Milan; KLM from Amsterdam; and Edelweiss Air from Zurich.

Chile

Another country bursting with things to do, Chile is known for its dramatic Patagonian landscapes, its stargazing spots in the Atacama Desert, and its volcanoes, with six million tourists descending on its attractions last year.

You can fly direct to the capital Santiago with Iberia from Madrid and Barcelona; from Paris with Air France; from London with British Airways; and with LATAM from Madrid.

Argentina

Last year, 5.7 million tourists headed to Chile’s next-door neighbour Argentina for its diverse landscapes and as a jumping off point for visits to Antarctica.

You can fly to the capital Buenos Aires with Aerolineas from Madrid or Rome; with Lufthansa from Frankfurt; with Air France from Paris; with KLM from Amsterdam; and with ITA Airways from Rome. Air Europa, Iberia and Plus Ultra also fly there from Madrid.

Peru's Machu Picchu is a bucket list destination – and you can fly to the country's capital direct from Madrid, Barcelona, Paris and Amsterdam Victor He/Unsplash

Peru

A bucket list destination for many thanks to Machu Picchu, Peru offers lots for history lovers, with Inca, Chavín, Moche, and Nasca sites for you to discover alongside Spanish colonial architecture. Around 3.4 million tourists visited last year.

You can reach the capital Lima with Iberia from Madrid and Barcelona; with Air France from Paris; and with KLM from Amsterdam. Air Europa, LATAM and Plus Ultra also fly from Madrid.

El Salvador

Some 3.4 million people chose to visit El Salvador last year, thanks to its archaeological sites, brilliant beaches and volcanoes.

You can fly to San Salvador with Iberojet and Iberia from Madrid, and with Iberojet from Barcelona.

Costa Rica has some 5% of the world’s biodiversity Adrián Valverde/Unsplash

Costa Rica

Another popular choice for wildlife lovers, Costa Rica is known for its national parks and protected areas, with the country containing some 5% of the world’s biodiversity. Around 2.9 million tourists arrived in 2025.

You will most likely fly into the capital San José, which is served by Iberia and Iberojet from Madrid; Edelweiss Air from Zurich; Air France from Paris; Lufthansa from Frankfurt; KLM from Amsterdam; and British Airways from London.

Guatemala

Some 2.5 million tourists headed to Guatemala last year in search of its Mayan archaeological sites, Lake Atitlán and colonial architecture.

You can fly direct from Madrid to Guatemala City with Iberia.

Uruguay

Boasting beautiful beaches and a quieter pace of life compared to its larger neighbours, 2.5 million people headed to Uruguay in 2025.

You can reach the capital Montevideo from Madrid with Air Europa, Iberia or Plus Ultra, and from Barcelona with Iberia.

Panama

Beyond the Panama Canal, Panama offers beaches, snorkelling opportunities, spectacular waterfalls and awe-inspiring hikes, with some 2.3 million visitors discovering the country last year.

You can fly direct to Panama City with Air Europa and Iberia from Madrid; Air France from Paris; KLM from Amsterdam; and Turkish Airlines from Istanbul.

Paraguay

More waterfalls await in Paraguay, along with UNESCO-listed Jesuit missions, and little chance of overtourism, with two million visitors in 2025.

Your only option to fly direct is from Madrid with Air Europa.

Tourists head to Ecuador to explore the Galápagos Islands Unsplash

Ecuador

Best known for the Galápagos Islands, where Charles Darwin came up with his theory of evolution, Ecuador offers wildlife in abundance for visitors (including the 1.3 million visitors who came here in 2025).

From Madrid, Air Europa, Iberia and Euroairlines fly direct to the capital Quito, while KLM flies here from Amsterdam.

Bolivia

Around 1.1 million were drawn in by Bolivia’s attractions last year, such as the Salar de Uyuni, the world’s largest salt flat, the ruins of Tiwanaku and the UNESCO-listed city of Potosí.

Both Air Europa and BoA (Boliviana de Aviación) fly direct from Madrid.

Honduras

Getting firmly into the underexplored part of the region, Honduras welcomed 920,000 international tourists in 2025 who came for the coral reefs, beaches, and archeological sites.

Two cities have direct flights from Europe: Comayagua, which you can fly to with Iberojet from Madrid or Barcelona, and San Pedro Sula, which is served by Air Europa from Madrid.

Guyana

Just 290,000 people visited Guyana last year, but those who did make the journey were rewarded with Georgetown’s unique food scene and the spectacular Kaieteur Falls.

KLM flies direct to Georgetown from Amsterdam.

Suriname

Just next door, Suriname offers jungle exploration for those who come here, including the 220,000 people who visited in 2025.

You can fly direct from Amsterdam to Paramaribo with KLM or Surinam Airways.

French Guiana

Last but not least, just 70,000 international tourists made it to French Guiana last year. The overseas department of France is perhaps currently best known for being home to the Guiana Space Centre, the European Space Agency’s spaceport, but it also offers an opportunity to explore the country’s dark past at Devil's Island, a former penal colony.

You can fly to Cayenne from Paris Charles de Gaulle with Air France, or from Paris Orly with Air Caraïbes.

Top tips for planning your trip

While many routes mentioned above are served daily, you can use websites like flightconnections.com to see which days of the week different airlines operate the flights on, and this website will also flag if a route is seasonal.

If you’re planning on flying with Iberia, don’t forget the Spanish flag carrier offers a stopover programme that will allow you to spend up to 10 days in Madrid before or after your trip.

Be sure to check travel advisories for the country you are planning to visit. Many countries are currently telling citizens to avoid trips to Venezuela, for example, but there are also alerts in place for parts of Ecuador, Colombia and others.

World.title: Sweeping raids leave Turkey’s LGBTQI+ community fearing what comes next
World.content:
Turkey has jailed dozens of people pending trial as a sweeping crackdown on LGBTQI+ groups widens, prompting international condemnation and protests outside Turkish embassies on Friday.

Advertising

By Thursday, courts in several provinces had jailed at least 82 people following raids on LGBTQI+ organisations, clubs, cafes and homes.

The cases include LGBTQI+ activists and members of rights groups as well as people accused of prostitution, drug offences and other crimes. Not everyone jailed is accused of gay rights advocacy.

The United Nations human rights office has called on Turkey to uphold human rights without discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity and to immediately release anyone arbitrarily detained.

Protests were held outside Turkish embassies in cities including Paris, Brussels, London, Oslo and Washington on Friday.

The crackdown began on Saturday, when police carried out coordinated raids targeting nine LGBTQI+ organisations. Justice Minister Akin Gurlek said legal action was being taken against 162 people, nine associations and 13 businesses in 15 provinces.

Turkey arrests dozens in ongoing crackdown on LGBTQI+ groups

Mass detentions

The raids prompted protests across Turkey, including outside Istanbul’s main courthouse on Tuesday. Police broke up the demonstration and detained more than 100 people, including journalists. They were later released.

“I am here because I want to say that LGBTQ+ friends are not alone in this country,” said Ayse, a protester who asked to be identified only by her first name.

“I want to support them and to stay in solidarity with them, which is not easy these days in Turkey, but they are not alone, and we are not alone, and we will be here until the end.”

Opposition DEM Party parliamentarian Ozgul Saki remained at the protest, protected from arrest by parliamentary immunity.

“This oppression against LGBTQ+ people is an attempt to compress society into a single type; to build an Islamist, Turkish, racist society,” Saki said. “Those who are here say, 'No! Society will live equally, freely and honourably with all its diversity,' and that's why they were all detained.”

The operations have been defended by Gurlek, from President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s conservative Justice and Development Party (AKP).

“No criminal organisation, abuse network or illegal activity which targets children, youths or families will be tolerated,” Gurlek posted on social media.

Among the organisations affected was Istanbul-based SPoD, which provides psychological support to LGBTQI+ people.

“As a community, we were expecting that such an operation would come one day. But we didn't imagine it as that violent, that much unlawful,” said a SPoD representative who asked to remain anonymous.

“They raided our office; I think four or five have been detained, and they are still in custody. What will happen to the LGBTQ+ community after this day? Like they can implement a kind of informal criminalisation upon our community, so my personal feeling is an immense feeling of uncertainty.”

Surge in anti-LGBTQ disinformation targets Pride in Europe

Obscenity allegations

Homosexuality has been legal since the foundation of the Turkish republic in 1923, but authorities are using an obscenity law as part of the crackdown.

“All of our board members are detained due to the allegations of obscenity,” said Yildiz Tar of Ankara-based KAOS GL, Turkey’s leading LGBTQI+ news portal.

“They look into our social media account, and our news articles are seen as obscene because, for example, there is one picture of two women kissing, and they see that it's obscene. So that is why they have been detained.”

The measures resemble actions taken against LGBTQI+ communities in Russia and Egypt, Tar said.

“It's very similar to Russia and Egypt, like the things they want to do is very similar to anti-gay propaganda laws, and there were huge operations, and people got detained,” Tar said.

“So it's very similar to both countries. And actually, like the Turkish government is very fond of Putin's way of dealing things.”

The crackdown has also drawn condemnation from the European Union and international human rights groups.

“It's an attempt to show LGBTQ+ people as immoral and against the family. But in fact, none of this does anything to protect the family at all,” said Emma Sinclair-Webb, who leads Human Rights Watch’s Turkey office.

“It's all about discrediting and stigmatizing people for their sexual orientation or gender identity.”

Turkey marks a decade since the coup that never was, but never really ended

Wider crackdown

The arrests form part of a broader crackdown on people regarded as opposing the government, Sinclair-Webb said.

“This operation should be set in the context of a very wide crackdown on anybody who is regarded as oppositional to the government, whether in terms of being politically or in terms of their lifestyle or their outlook… there is a general attempt by the government to impose as well as, you know, ideological conformity on people, lifestyle,” Sinclair-Webb said.

President Erdogan routinely refers to LGBTQI+ people as perverts and has stepped up his rhetoric ahead of much-rumoured early elections. Gurlek has called on prosecutors to increase investigations into the LGBTQI+ community, fuelling fears of further arrests.

The crackdown has also prompted condemnation across Turkish civil society, with trade unions, doctors’ associations and opposition parties voicing their opposition.

For Tar, that support offers some hope amid fears over what could follow for Turkey’s LGBTQI+ community.

“If this attack won't be stopped, it would mean a lot of maltreatment and torture; it can also cause hate crimes; it incites hatred inside the country too,” Tar said. “And it will mean that you cannot be openly queer; if they succeed in their operation, that is a really, really hellish scenario.”

World.title: A doubleheader feast!
World.content:
This week on The Sound Kitchen it’s a doubleheader: you’ll hear the answers to TWO quiz questions, as well as TWO “Listener's Corner" with Paul Myers, and of course, Erwan Rome’s “Music from Erwan”. So sit down, relax, and join the banquet! Just click the “play” button above to join the feast.

Advertising

Hello everyone!

As noted on the show, I am retiring on 1 October. Unfortunately, The Sound Kitchen is retiring too – I will not be replaced.

We’ve had a great time together all these years, haven’t we?

Click here to listen to past Sound Kitchen podcasts.

I know you will all stay loyal to RFI English – our service has so much to offer. We’re small, but my colleagues are firebrands!

For example, we have wonderful podcasts: Spotlight on France, with journalists Alison Hird and Sarah Elzas; Melissa Chemam’s insightful Spotlight on Africa, and our International Report, usually sent to us by one of our foreign correspondents. We also have an award-winning bilingual series – an old-time radio show, with actors (!) – to help you learn French, called Les voisins du 12 bis.

Remember, podcasts are radio, too! As you see, sound is still quite present in the RFI English service. Please keep checking our website for updates on the latest from our team of journalists. You never know what we’ll surprise you with!

To listen to our podcasts from your PC, go to our website; you’ll see “Podcasts” at the top of the page. You can either listen directly or subscribe and receive them directly on your mobile phone.

And don’t forget, in addition to our audio bilingual series, you can also learn French through our website “Le Français facile avec rfi”. In addition to online lessons, there are news broadcasts in slow, simple French, with exercises to practice what you’ve heard.

Go to their website and get started! At the top of the page, click on “Test level”, and you’ll be advised on the best-suited activities for your level, according to your score.

Do not give up! As Lidwien van Dixhoorn, the head of the “Le Français facile” service, told me: “Bathe your ears in the sound of the language, and eventually, you’ll get it”. She should know – Lidwien is Dutch and came to France hardly able to say “bonjour,” and now she heads this key international award-winning RFI department – so stick with it!

For the quiz on 24 January: I asked you a question about the Africa Cup of Nations, and an article sent to us by Paul Myers, who was there. You were to re-read his article “Senegal outwit Morocco to claim 2025 Africa Cup of Nations”, and send in the answer to this question: At the 2026 World Cup, which took place in the United States, Mexico, and Canada in June, in which group did Morocco play, and in which group did Senegal play?

The answer is, to quote Paul’s article: “Morocco will play in Group C against Brazil, Scotland and Haiti.

Senegal will feature in Group I with France, Norway, and the team that emerges from the intercontinental play-off in March.”

In addition to the quiz question, there was the bonus question: “What is your favorite day of the year? Why? What is it about that day that makes it your favorite?”

The winners are: RFI Listeners Club member Dipita Chakrabarty from New Delhi, India. Dipita is also the bonus question winner.

Also on the list of lucky winners this week are Muhammed Naved, a member of the International DX Radio Listeners Club in West Bengal, India; Muhammad Abdullah, a member of the RFI Online Visitors Club in Sahiwal, Pakistan; RFI Listeners Club member Rodrigo Hunrichse from Bio-Bio, Chile, and last but not least, RFI English listener Sakila Musarrt from Chapainawabganj in Bangladesh.

Congratulations winners!

For the quiz on 31 January: You were to listen to our podcast “Spotlight on France”, the brainchild of my colleagues Alison Hird and Sarah Elzas. I hope you listen to it regularly, it’s really quite good.

On their programme number 138, Alison reported on La Ménardière, an alternative living arrangement for seniors in the village of Bérat, close to the southern French town of Toulouse. The aim of the project is for seniors to live and grow old together, contributing to society for as long as possible, and to delay – or avoid – the moment when people are forced into institutional care.

The answers you were to send in were: How many residents can live at La Ménardière, and what is the selection process?

The answer is, to quote Alison: “La Ménardière can house up to 20 residents. The selection process to become one is rigorous. Candidates stay for trial weekends and, if they decide to join, they must then complete a six-month probation period.”

The bonus question you answered that week – suggested by Murshida Parvin Lata, the co-chairman of the Sonali Badhan Female Listeners Club in Bogura, Bangladesh – was: “Which daytime temperature do you prefer: cold or hot? Why?”

The winners are: RFI Listeners Club member Father Steven Wara, who lives and serves in the Cistercian Abbey in Bamenda, Cameroon. Father Steve is also the winner of this week’s bonus question.

There’s long-standing RFI Listeners Club member Zenon Teles, who is also the president of the Christian – Marxist – Leninist – Maoist Association of Listening DX-ERs in Goa, India, as well as another faithful Sound Kitchen listener – and club member – Radhakrishna Pillai from Kerala State, also in India.

Moving over to Bangladesh, Anjana Parvin – she’s the secretary of the very active Shetu RFI Listeners Club in Naogaon. And last but not the least, club member and my fellow dinosaur, Alan Holder, from England’s Isle of Wight.

Congratulations winners!

Here’s the music you heard on this week’s programme: “Take the A Train” by Billy Strayhorn and Duke Ellington, performed by Duke Ellington and his orchestra; the “AFCON 2025 Official Intro Theme – Africa Cup of Nations Morocco 2025” by Othmane Laaouina; “What a Wonderful World” by Bob Thiele and George David Weiss, sung by Louis Armstrong; “The Cakewalk” from Children’s Corner by Claude Debussy, performed by the composer, and “Étincelles”, Op. 36, No. 6 by Moritz Moszkowski, played by Alexander Zhou.

I’ll talk to you next week, 26 September, for our final Sound Kitchen together. You’ll hear the answers to the questions about the Grammy Awards Lifetime Achievement Awards and the Benin Bronzes, as well as your responses to the bonus questions on "The Listener’s Corner" with Paul Myers, so be sure and tune in.

Until then, fare thee well!

World.title: A city at the crossroads of history: Unearthing Gaza's ancient heritage
World.content:
Before Gaza became synonymous with conflict, it was a place where merchants sold wine from local vineyards, pilgrims crossed continents, fishermen set out before dawn, and generations of families lived between sea and desert. RFI explores its deep history.

Advertising

Sitting on the coastal corridor linking Egypt, the Levant, the Arabian Peninsula and the Mediterranean, the port city has always been a strategic crossroads.

Like many places around the Mediterranean, Gaza's identity wasn't built by a single people or culture. It was shaped by generations of arrivals, departures and exchanges.

As the Mid-East Junction podcast returns from a six-year hiatus, we'll trace the city's history from the age of the Philistines until the creation of Israel in 1948.

In this first episode of season 3, a Gazan archaeologist, a historian, and a professor of contemporary Arab people shed light on Gaza’s little-known yet fascinating ancient history.

Mid-East Junction is produced by RFI's English-language service. This episode was mixed by Vincent Pora.

World.title: In cosmopolitan Berlin, elections still closed to foreigners
World.content:
A quarter of Berlin residents will have no say in the German capital's city-state election because they lack citizenship. That's the highest proportion of residents excluded from the election yet, and many are unhappy.

Abdu, an Egyptian software developer, ended up in Germany's capital more or less by chance seven years ago. "I wouldn't say I chose Berlin," he told DW. "It was just that the company that offered me a job was here."

But now he loves it. The culture is "better than any other city I have experienced," he said. That's partly because of its diversity, but he also likes the way Berliners approach life. "They're more interested in living than just working," he said. "Here I feel life is more relaxed, and this also offers the opportunity for people to get more creative."

But there's plenty about the city that he's not particularly happy with, including Berlin's rapidly rising rental prices, and the notoriously opaque bureaucracy is a constant source of annoyance. "I myself would like to start my own business, but it is difficult because of all the bureaucracy," he said.

In general, Abdu is dissatisfied with Berlin's current government, a conservative-led coalition of the Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) — but the trouble is, as a non-German national, he has no say in deciding whether it should stay in office or not. That is particularly frustrating at the moment, when the streets are bristling with campaign posters ahead of the election on September 20.

"We are people who pay taxes, but we don't have any representation at all, even on local level," he said. "The cuts to health care and German courses, for example, affect me directly."

Berlin initiative helps immigrant moms find their feet To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Berlin: Bigger and more international

The German capital is growing and becoming more international. While the voting population in the upcoming election will be bigger than ever — mainly because the voting age has been lowered to 16 — so is the number of the disenfranchised.

Of Berlin's population of 3.9 million, a full quarter — around 976,000 adults — cannot vote because they don't have German citizenship. That number has doubled since 2011.

This is partly because of Germany's political structure. In Germany and across Europe, citizens of other EU countries can vote in municipal elections. In London, people from Commonwealth countries can do the same as long as they have UK residency. Spain, meanwhile, also has reciprocal voting agreements with several non-EU countries — in South America and elsewhere — that allow their citizens to vote in municipal elections, including for the mayors of Madrid and Barcelona.

Berlin's Sunday election is not a municipal one. Since Berlin is one of Germany's 16 federal states, it is holding a state election, which means that voting rights are more restricted. Berlin's municipal elections, where EU citizens are allowed to vote, only decide who governs the city's individual districts, and their political influence is limited.

The disenfranchisement is particularly acute in central Berlin. For that reason, Stefanie Remlinger, Green Party mayor in the district of Mitte, has organized a "symbolic election" for the non-Germans in her area — some 135,000 adults out of a population of 365,000. The initiative invites foreigners to vote at 15 ballot stations over a two-week period in early September to "raise awareness for the issue of voting rights for all."

"Mitte is an extremely heterogeneous district with a very international population," Remlinger told DW via video call from her office. "We have people from 170 different countries living here, and a lot of them don't have the right to vote. It's important to us to signal to those people that we value their opinions, that we see them."

Around a third of adults in Stefanie Remlinger's district don't have German nationality Image: Annette Hauschild

Germany's 'rightward shift'

Getting people to vote in a meaningless election is a tough sell. Remlinger said she expected only a few hundred people to take part, and, anyway, she thinks the political climate in Germany is not exactly immigrant-friendly at the moment. Even in cosmopolitan Berlin, the anti-immigrant Alternative for Germany (AfD) is currently polling in second place, with nearly 20%.

"We as the Greens would liberalize voting rights even more, but I don't see the general debate in Germany going that way," she said. "We're fighting a rightward shift and a lot of hostility to immigration, and I think the chances of changing something on that issue right now are very bad."

To illustrate the state of the current debate, Remlinger mentioned a recent panel discussion she was part of, where a politician from the neoliberal Free Democratic Party (FDP) — a party that calls itself socially liberal — said voting rights shouldn't be opened to foreigners because they might start their own parties and take over the government. "And that from someone from the FDP!" said Remlinger, exasperated.

Abdu is also aware of this anti-immigrant shift in German politics. In fact, he said, that was one of the reasons he was considering leaving Germany altogether. "All the parties are trending right-wing, so it's getting more hostile," he said.

How Berliners are reshaping their city for the future To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Is expanding voting good for the economy?

From an economic perspective, it might be considered a shame if qualified people like Abdu decided to leave Germany. The country lacks workers. The government estimates that the country will be short of about 440,000 workers by 2029, and even the AfD leadership claims it has nothing against immigrants who contribute to the economy.

Though some German cities and local authorities do have an elected advisory board for non-German residents, offering immigrants a real vote is frequently seen as a step too far.

Remlinger herself thinks that the best path to enfranchisement is not to offer foreign nationals voting rights, but to make it easier for immigrants to become German citizens.

That happens to be another one of Abdu's complaints about Berlin: "I applied for citizenship two years ago, and I didn't get any response," he said.

Germany has recently tightened citizenship rules again. Last year, Chancellor Friedrich Merz's government reversed the three-year "fast-track" citizenship option introduced under his predecessor, Olaf Scholz. Still, the government did keep another of Scholz's reforms, which allows people to apply for citizenship after only five years of residency.

More and more Berliners are in fact becoming German: 2025 saw about 39,000 people naturalized in the capital, 17,000 more than in 2024.

That avenue is still closed for Abdu, but in the meantime, a little more political participation would go a long way. "If I could vote, I would reconsider leaving, to be honest, because then I could affect things, but now I'm just like a bank machine — they come to me and take half of my salary."

Edited by: Rina Goldenberg

World.title: India news: PM Modi says developing nations unfairly blamed for emissions
World.content:
09/20/2026 September 20, 2026 Developing nations unfairly blamed for emissions, Modi tells climate conference

Prime Minister Narendra Modi has said developing countries are unfairly held responsible for carbon emissions despite their comparatively low per-capita output.

Modi made the remarks on Saturday as he inaugurated a two-day international conference on environmental and climate governance in New Delhi, organized by India's National Green Tribunal.

Speaking at the opening of the "Future of Environment and Climate Dynamics" conference at Vigyan Bhawan, Modi said, "We know that often the responsibility for carbon emissions is wrongly placed upon developing countries... the historical truth is that India's contribution per capita carbon emission is less than half of the global average."

"In developed countries, per capita carbon emissions are six times higher than in India."

He said India has consistently raised this point at global forums, including at the 2015 Paris climate summit, adding that India is the only G20 nation to have met its Paris commitments ahead of schedule.

The remarks come weeks after devastating floods hit India's northern neighbor, Nepal, killing over 1400 people. Nepal contributes roughly 0.1% of global greenhouse gas emissions, making it what the World Bank calls a "negligible contributor to climate change."

The conference, which ends Sunday, brings together judges and environmental officials from 17 countries as well as Indian Supreme Court and High Court judges, senior bureaucrats, and representatives of state environmental authorities, according to the Prime Minister's Office.

World.title: Germany news: Doctors offer Oktoberfest flu jabs
World.content:
09/19/2026 September 19, 2026 High-profile Jewish representative calls for AfD ban

Knobloch, seen here at a DW interview, survived Nazi pogroms in the 1930s Image: DW

Charlotte Knobloch, the former president of the Central Council of Jews in Germany, has reiterated her call for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) to be banned.

"A lot about the AfD reminds me today about the path the Nazis took to power," the 93-year-old Knobloch told the daily Augsburger Allegemeine.

She said the party "teems with Jew-haters and extremists" — something she said had already existed before, "but once, such parties disappeared from the scene very fast."

This would not be the case with the AfD, she said: "It has broad support in the population, not least with young people."

The party spouts hatred, including "hatred of Jews," she said.

"Unfortunately, no one has managed to clamp down on it so far, so it needs to be banned," she said, even if this is "perhaps difficult legally."

Knobloch called on voters in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania on Sunday to "read the newspaper, listen to the radio and watch TV; then you can't help seeing that the AfD is a profoundly anti-democratic party."

She also warned that Jews in Germany were "literally under fire once more," with much reminding here of the 1920s and early 1930s.

"There is hatred of Jews from right, from left and from the Muslim milieu," she said.

Knobloch herself was recently the target of a death threat following the AfD's landslide victory in the state of Saxony-Anhalt two weeks ago.

World.title: Decolonizing perceptions about Africa
World.content:
A UN resolution to redraw the global map to project the African continent more accurately, national initiatives to decolonize schools and a campaign to present positive developments are changing the way Africa is seen.

The Correct the Map resolution to promote map projections that more realistically reflect the true size of continents endorsed by the United Nations in New York at the beginning of September was a huge success for the African countries that led the campaign. In the General Assembly, 164 member states voted to encourage the use of Equal Earth projection and other equal-area maps instead of the 16th-century Mercator projection.

Robert Dussey, the foreign minister of Togo, which sponsored the Correct the Map campaign at the UN, spoke of a "feeling of pride."

Correct the Map is also supported by the African Union.

"Finally, Africa is fighting to regain its place in the community of nations," he told DW. "The place it has been reserved to this day is unfair. It does not correspond to Africa's reality, not in historical, geographical or economic terms."

Dussey made clear that the debate about global maps was also clearly about symbolically redrawing the maps of facts and knowledge, culture and identity and redressing misperceptions about political and economic realities and power.

Trump's US only state to reject UN resolution

The only UN member state that rejected the resolution was the United States, whose president Donald Trump has engaged in various acts of political symbolism, having issued orders for places to be renamed on maps which he would presumaby also like to redraw Trump has signed executive orders to rename the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America, and Lake Ontario as Lake America.

The UN resolution, meanwhile, is part of a broader, global trend, as French historian Romain Tiquet from the African Worlds Institute (IMAF) told DW.

"Since the late 2000s and early 2010s, there has been a great deal of debate about the decolonization of knowledge — in universities, museums and cultural institutions, as well as within social movements and civil society."

He said many questions were being explored: "Who established the categories through which we conceptualize the world? From which locations? And what power dynamics result from this? And cartography fits right into this context."

The Equal Earth map is aimed at a more accurate representation of the world Image: Equal Earth/Handout/AFP

Mali breaks with former colonial power France

Many African states have also been trying to free the school systems from colonial influence, often for political reasons.

In October 2025, the Malian government decided to remove French history from the school curriculum. The decision was made to stop teaching about the French Revolution but to focus on Malian history and the other ancient West African kingdoms.

In just a few years, the country's military government has made a clean break with the former colonial power. Mali ended its military cooperation with France in 2022, and French soldiers began to withdraw from the country. Burkina Faso and Niger did the same and the three formed the Alliance of Sahel States in 2023.

Philemon Mtoi from Tumaini University Makumira in Tanzania said Mali had made an important step: "As a historian, I believe that a country without a strong understanding of its own history is like a country without clear leadership and direction. This decision is important because it seeks to strengthen patriotism and foster a stronger sense of national identity."

By investing in the research and preservation of African history, Mali — like Africa as a whole — was making a strong contribution to global scholarship, Mtoi explained.

He spoke of "reclaiming and documenting African histories from an African perspective" and said that this was not only "an act of decolonization" but also an "important step toward intellectual independence."

Mtoi said that many other African countries, such as Ghana, Namibia, South Africa and Kenya, had adopted a similar approach. He added that his own country, Tanzania, had also made major changes to the school curriculum recently. He said that "Tanzanian history and ethics" was now a compulsory subject that had replaced global history and that it would be taught in Swahili, the country's national language.

The historian warned, however, that knowledge of other countries and histories should not be erased. He said it was important to acquire a profound knowledge of significant events in global history, such as the French Revolution, but that this could be done at a later stage.

How German merchants shaped Africa's fate To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

#NotWaiting campaign to abolish stereotypes

School education in a formal setting is only one part of the puzzle. The non-profit Africa No Filter was one of the organizations behind the Correct the Map campaign. It works to challenge and change harmful narratives about Africa.

In a report titled "The cost of media stereotypes to Africa," it says that "Africa could be losing up to $4.2 billion (€3.6 billion) annually in inflated interest payments due to biased media coverage."

Francois Bouda, an officer for arts and culture at Africa No Filter, said that media outlets continued to portray Africa as being poor, corrupt and crisis-ridden. The new campaign #NotWaiting is meant to change this perception.

"We are addressing Africans because we, too, need to change the way we view the African continent. We've accepted the image of a continent incapable of taking care of itself, one that is poor and has no opportunities. We've internalized this and come to believe it, even though many positive things are happening. First of all there has to be an internal change," said Bouda.

How the Berlin Conference spurred the colonization of Africa To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

'Millions of ordinary people doing extraordinary things every day'

The #NotWaiting campaign is part of a larger movement, which aims to highlight positive developments and initiatives in Africa, to focus on political programs and actors, to counter crisis-reporting.

It comprises figures on the continent and in the diaspora, people who are "not waiting for an external hand to dictate what path to follow," said Bouda.

"This is good for Africans," he said, adding that there were many actors but that the only problem was that they "aren't visible."

The campaign is about Africans themselves painting a positive picture of Africa as a continent on the move, about people sharing stories, which are not curated by international institutions or media outlets.

"We've been building all along," says a video clip to promote the campaign. "From village roads to crowded cities, across the 54 countries that make up the continent, millions of ordinary people doing extraordinary things every day."

This article, to which Sandrine Blanchard and Jean-Claude Abalo contributed, was originally written in German.

World.title: Germany: Polls open in two key state elections
World.content:
Skip next section Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania election guide: What you need to know

09/20/2026 September 20, 2026 Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania election guide: What you need to know

Manuela Schwesig (SPD) and Leif-Erik Holm (AfD) participate in a TV debate Image: Jens Büttner/dpa/picture alliance

In Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, the fight is between the Social Democrats (SPD) led by the popular Manuela Schwesig and the far-right Altnerative for Germany (AfD).

The 52-year-old Schwesig has made it her mission to beat back the advance of the AfD, which is polling at around 37%, ahead of the SPD at 33%.

"The situation is serious," Schwesig told DW recently. "The AfD would harm our economy; they would harm our social cohesion. Their crude way of speaking, their hate and incitement, is tearing our society apart; there's a renewed propensity for violence, and that will affect us women in particular."

Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania is a largely rural state in Germany's northeast Image: Tasneem Zahra/DW

What to watch out for in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania

Besides keeping tabs on whether the AfD comes out on top, all eyes are also on how the CDU performs in the state.

CDU is the conservative Christian Democratic Union party that is chaired by the chancellor of the country, Friedrich Merz.

His party is polling at around 7% in the state, which is slightly above the 5% threshold required by a party to enter state parliament.

In the 2021 elections, the CDU had just 13.3% of the vote.

If the CDU fails to achieve the 5% threshold, there's going to be immense pressure on Merz to fight for his job.

Who are the main candidates?

SPD: Manuela Schwesig, also the incumbent state premier.

AfD: Leif-Erik Holm is the AfD's candidate for state premier, whom the party would put forward to head the state government if it can form one, while Enrico Schult is the AfD's candidate leading the party's election campaign in the state. Holm is the better-known candidate out of the two.

CDU: Daniel Peters, who has been the chair of the CDU parliamentary group in the state parliament.

The Left (Die Linke): Simon Oldenburg, who is the current minister for education in the state.

What's the likeliest scenario?

Even if the AfD comes out on top in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, that's not a guarantee that it will govern the state.

In Germany's parliamentary system, a party needs a majority in the state parliament or coalition partners to elect a state premier.

That means that the AfD could be pushed to the sidelines if other parties reject cooperation with it under the so-called "firewall" policy.

World.title: Germany: Is it possible to replace the chancellor?
World.content:
Chancellor Friedrich Merz's record-low approval ratings have emboldened his opponents. There are three ways to remove a chancellor from office in Germany.

It is the hot topic this week in Berlin: Does German Chancellor Friedrich Merz still have the backing of his own party, the Christian Democrats (CDU), and the coalition partners, Bavaria's Christian Social Union (CSU) and the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD)? Will he be ousted? How would that work? Can he just step down?

Support for the chancellor has reached a record low: In the latest Deutschlandtrend representative survey, conducted by pollsters Infratest-Dimap for German public broadcaster ARD in early September, only 13% of respondents said Merz was doing a good job.

In early September, Merz's CDU suffered a resounding loss in the state of Saxony-Anhalt's parliamentary election, seeing the party's result halved from the 2021 election.

The election result has reinforced criticism of Merz, even from within his own ranks, and his communication style, which frequently alienates his audience.

But Merz remains chancellor. What are the options to change that? Germany's constitution, the Basic Law, grants the position a strong standing. German chancellors are not so easy to unseat.

Option 1: Resignation

Merz himself can decide to resign for any reason. That would not necessarily mean the end of the coalition government he leads. An example: In May 1974, then Chancellor Willy Brandt of the SPD resigned after a spy from communist East Germany (DDR) was discovered to have been working in his inner circle. The governing parties, the SPD and the business-oriented Free Democrats (FDP), quickly agreed to continue their alliance.

Only 10 days later, Finance Minister Helmut Schmidt, also of the SPD, was elected as the new chancellor. To do this, an absolute majority of all lawmakers in the Bundestag, the lower house of parliament, was needed (not only those present during the vote). This majority is called the "chancellor majority". Schmidt achieved the necessary majority, eventually got reelected and remained head of the German government for 8 years.

How likely is Merz to step down? Today's chancellor seems determined not to give up.

Option 2: A constructive vote of no-confidence

If a new majority were formed through alliances in the Bundestag or if a chancellor fell so far out of favor that their own supporters no longer believed in them, the instrument of a "constructive vote of no-confidence" could come into play. That means the majority of lawmakers vote in favor of a new candidate for chancellor.

An example: Helmut Schmidt of the SPD, lost the support of his junior coalition partner, the FDP, in 1982. The FDP wanted to push through changes to economic policy, which Schmidt rejected. They joined forces with the conservatives from the CDU and CSU, and jointly put CDU leader Helmut Kohl forward as a new chancellor. He won a majority in parliament, replaced Schmidt and moved into the chancellor's office where he remained for 16 years.

The probability of this happening in Merz's case is very remote. The conservatives and Social Democrats do not want to end their coalition. There is no clear rival candidate for Merz. North Rhine-Westphalia's State Premier Hendrik Wüst of the CDU is seen as a possible successor, but has not made a step forward. Besides: The CDU is usually very loyal toward its political leaders; ousting the chancellor via a vote of no-confidence on the open stage of the Bundestag is simply unthinkable for most conservative lawmakers.

Option 3: A confidence vote

Germany's parliament cannot simply dissolve itself and call new elections. Lawmakers can, however, call a confidence vote on the chancellor and his government. Several chancellors have already used this mechanism, coupling it with a vote on a contentious issue.

As chancellor in November 2001, Gerhard Schröder (SPD) put forward a confidence vote in the Bundestag and linked it with the question of whether his government should deploy the German military to Afghanistan to support the NATO mission led by the United States following the September 11 attacks. Schröder won, remained in office and continued with his military policy.

Merz has already said he sees no point in calling for a confidence vote. There are also no signs of large breakaway movements from members of his coalition in Parliament.

If a chancellor loses a confidence vote, the Bundestag can be dissolved and fresh elections called. Following the defeat in the Bundestag, the chancellor can ask the German President to dissolve parliament and call voters to the polls. The president is not obliged to do so, but usually does.

It seems that Merz has ruled out this option. Neither the SPD nor the conservative Union (of CDU/CSU) are interested in calling new elections at a time when their approval ratings are low.

So will the government remain the same? Right now, it seems so. However, things have been so dynamic in recent days and weeks in Berlin political circles that nothing should be ruled out.

This article was originally written in German.

World.title: Dutch police disperse violent far-right protest in The Hague
World.content:
After violence broke out, Dutch riot police dispersed hundreds of far-right protesters in The Hague. Prime Minister Rob Jetten said that the demonstrators had chanted "abhorrent" far-right and antisemitic slogans.

Dutch riot police on Saturday clashed with approximately 500 far-right protesters who chanted antisemitic slogans at a rally in The Hague city center.

The protesters threw fireworks and other projectiles at the police.

According to AFP reporters on the scene, police used baton charges and specialist dogs to break up the demonstration.

What do we know about the protest

The "We Are the People" rally was organized to protest government policies, particularly those related to immigration.

Protesters had planned to march through the city, but local authorities banned the march when violence broke out in the park where protesters were gathering. Authorities then ordered the demonstration to break up.

The police said that they arrested 24 people and used water cannons to disperse the rioters. They added that further investigations are underway.

The police broke up the demonstration using batons and police dogs Image: Mouneb Taim/AP Photo/picture alliance

How did the authorities react

On X, Prime Minister Rob Jetten said that the demonstrators had deliberately sought confrontation with the police and had chanted "abhorrent" far-right and antisemitic slogans.

Meanwhile, Justice Minister David van Weel called for an "extremely firm" response to the "disgusting scenes" that occurred at the protest.

Van Weel said demonstrators made Nazi salutes, chanted antisemitic slogans, attacked police, and threw fireworks at riot officers.

Saturday's unrest occurred one year after riots broke out during a right-wing demonstration.

During clashes between black-clad protesters and police, a police car was set on fire, and the headquarters of the centrist D66 party — whose leader, Rob Jetten, is now prime minister — was attacked.

Edited by: Saim Dušan Inayatullah

World.title: Summer of 2026 broke records in Europe, and caused deaths
World.content:
The summer of 2026 was not only the hottest on record in Europe, it also saw a record number of people die. More than 16,000 are thought to have died because of the heat in Germany alone.

The summer (June to August) of 2026 was the warmest in Europe since records began, beating the record set in 2003, according to the Copernicus Climate Change Service,

Not only that, Germany's DWD weather service says that there was an "unprecedented" number of hot days this year. "On average across Germany,there were about 22 hot days with temperatures of at least 30 degrees Celsius and about five very hot days with temperatures of at least 35 degrees Celsius," the DWD wrote in in a press release at the end of August.

The estimated number of heat-related deaths also reached unprecedented levels, with at least 16,300 people dying by the end of August, even if few of them died directly because of the heat, but rather as a consequence of underlying health conditions exacerbated by the heat.

The figures were compiled from a statistical correlation between the number of deaths recorded by Germany's Federal Statistical Office and the temperatures measured by the DWD during a specific period.

Heat-related deaths in Germany are more likely if the average weekly temperature reaches 20 degrees Celsius or more. This is the average of all hourly temperatures recorded in a week, including at nighttime.

This year, the average weekly temperatures in the country rose above the 20-degree mark several times. It was particularly hot at the end of June, when the average weekly temperature reached above 26 degrees between the 22nd and 28th of the month.

Why Europe's extreme summers are getting worse To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Excess mortality during heat waves

Though it is not possible to determine a cause of death using statistics, researchers and medical professionals have a good understanding of how heat affects the human body, and there is widespread consensus that excess mortality during heat waves is possible.

"It was not just the high temperatures on the thermometer that were important, but also how long the heat lasted and the fact that it hardly cooled down at night," said Andreas Matzarakis, professor of environmental meteorology at Freiburg University.

Many people have trouble sleeping on hot nights. Yet, getting enough sleep is important so that the body can recover from the heat and stress of the day.

Matzarakis said that the severity of heat stress was not related solely to air temperatures. Humidity, solar radiation and wind also played a role — and what is known as the 'felt' temperature. He said that humidity and still air could place a heavy strain on the body, even in moderate temperatures.

Powerful El Nino set to bring extreme weather To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Underprivileged most vulnerable

The less privileged members of society were also among the most vulnerable, said Martin Röösli, environmental scientist at the Swiss Tropical and Public Health Institute in Basel. "They are more likely to live in homes that are not well insulated or are more likely to work outdoors."

A large proportion of those who died because of the heat probably had only a short life expectancy left, due to their age and medical conditions, but Röösli said that there was a consensus that "some of the deceased could have lived for a long time and were simply in a fragile state at the time of the heat wave."

For Alexandra Schneider, a meteorologist and epidemiologist at the Helmholtz center in Munich in southern Germany, the deaths that occurred during the heat waves were very likely not only because of the "harvesting effect," which describes "how a heat wave causes very vulnerable individuals in particular to die a few days or weeks prematurely."

Had this been the case, there would have been a deficit of mortality in the following weeks, which did not happen. Thus, she believes, a significant proportion of those who died could have lived on for months or even years.

This article was translated from German.

World.title: Más de 1.000 menores aún deambulan por Ceuta: entre la guerra política y el limbo
World.content:
Los mil menores que aún viven en la calle en Ceuta pasan los días atrapados en un limbo con verbo propio: deambular. Aunque los recorridos son variables, esos niños y niñas comparten un trayecto que realizan a diario aunque el resultado no varíe. Primero acuden en grupos pequeños al corazón de la ciudad, a la Jefatura Superior de la Policía. Pero jamás logran entrar. “Que os vayáis, ya os lo dije ayer y anteayer, no estamos filiando”, les chilló un agente a un grupo de chicos de no más de 14 años.

La escena tuvo lugar el jueves, pero se repite en bucle cualquier otro día en la ciudad. Esta vez, además, una de las intérpretes de la comisaría salió a darles en dariya (variedad dialectal del árabe hablada popularmente en Marruecos) alguna razón más para el rechazo: “No podemos identificaros hasta que no haya instalaciones dónde llevaros. De momento, no hay sitio en ninguna. Si queréis, preguntad allí directamente”, les dijo. Los niños se fueron, aunque ella y ellos saben la respuesta que les aguarda en los centros de menores como Piniers, al suroeste de Ceuta: “Aquí no hay sitio, id a la Policía y ellos os dirán”. Y este grupo de niños, o cualquier otro, volvió a rebotar entre negativas, hasta que por la noche el deambular se detiene para buscar algún sitio dónde dormir.

Otros sí que lograron techo. Dos semanas después de la entrada masiva, el Ejecutivo ceutí —competente de la tutela de los menores—, empezó a realojar muy poco a poco a niños y adolescentes en establecimientos improvisados. Hasta ese momento habían transitado a su suerte desde que lograron entrar solos en Ceuta en la ciudad autónoma. La avalancha y la falta de atención de las administraciones les dejó en condiciones de insalubridad extremas en los asentamientos improvisados o en los solidarios de Sidi Embarek o El Príncipe.

Aún así, las escenas de niños tirados en cualquier acera se han repetido durante semanas en medio de la emergencia humanitaria y la resistencia del PP a que sean derivados a la península. Porque la capacidad de Ceuta para acogerles reventó con el cruce: solo hay disponibles 22 recursos de acogida en una ciudad cuyos servicios sociales están más que saturados.

Antes de julio había ya unos 700 menores no acompañados en el sistema de acogida ceutí, a los que se sumaron en torno a 1.300 que cruzaron entre el 30 y el 31 de ese mes. La ciudad autónoma, en cálculos del Ejecutivo central, tiene disponibilidad solo para 29 plazas ordinarias y cuando una comunidad excede por tres sus recursos puede solicitar la situación de contingencia migratoria y los menores tienen que ser realojados obligatoriamente en la península. Ahora son 2.200 menores filiados.

En ese grupo, que tiene nombre y rostro, se encuentra Youness, de 16 años. Quien, como muchos otros, ya se han rendido de ese deambular entre la Policía y los centros en busca de techo y filiación. El miércoles por la noche, en la playa de El Trampolín, contaba que también había dejado de pasar el tiempo con otros grupos de menores para repetir el peregrinar. Fue a la playa buscando a sus vecinos de Castillejos y se quedó a vivir con ellos en una de sus tiendas. “¿Tú crees que me podré colar en el campamento del puerto cuando lo abran?”, preguntaba. Youness se refería a lo sucedido en el anterior realojo de migrantes, el de las inmediaciones de Loma Colmenar. Aunque estaba destinado solo a hombres adultos, varios menores se pusieron en la fila y lograron plaza. “Este es menor, pero bueno, déjale y ya haremos el papeleo después”, susurraba uno de los responsables del traslado.

La guerra política de los menores

El mismo miércoles en el que Youness se rendía, en el Congreso de los Diputados se desataba la batalla política. “Pregúntele a Vivas”, respondió el presidente Pedro Sánchez a los periodistas cuando le interpelaron en los pasillos por los menores. Se refería al presidente de Ceuta, el popular Juan Jesús Vivas, que ha virado radicalmente su discurso y ahora demanda que todos sean devueltos a Marruecos. Pero sobre todo que ninguno de los que ya están en centros sea derivado a la península, donde 11 comunidades están gobernadas por sus compañeros de partido, cuatro en coalición con Vox. La ultraderecha presiona con el repudio a la inmigración como su gran bandera.

Enfrente, el Ministerio de Juventud e Infancia da como mucho al PP dos meses antes de forzar, con la ley en la mano, los traslados. De producirse, no solo resolvería la situación de los que ya están en acogida en esos centros, sino también de los otros mil que esperan esa plaza libre que nunca llega.

Youness no la logró tampoco en los centros de adultos. Antes de llegar al campamento del puerto, cuando los migrantes esperaban sentados en el suelo a la espera de que la Policía les organizara para entrar, una de las responsables de la entidad que gestiona el campamento distinguió entre ellos a dos gemelos con sudaderas azules claramente menores de edad. Les retiró de la fila y repitió la operación en el resto de grupos. Hizo lo mismo con otra decena, Youness entre ellos. Les sentaron en la acera, a la espera de que terminara el realojo. Pero, ¿dónde llevarlos si no hay plazas libres en los centros? De acuerdo a la legislación, es el área de menores de Ceuta quien ostenta su tutela, pero para eso es necesaria su correcta filiación. Y con los recursos tan saturados, todavía hay decenas sin registrar. Todos los ven, pero todo avanza como si no existieran.

El área de menores de la ciudad navega también este otro limbo y busca plazas sueltas en los centros ya habilitados, estirando su capacidad más allá del límite. Cuando las encuentra, les filia y acoge. Pero sigue siendo insuficiente: hay cientos en las calles y algunos también en las casas. Desde finales de julio, alguno vecinos de las barriadas más humildes acogieron bajo sus techos a muchos de ellos, y aunque continúa pasando cincuenta días después, el perfil ha variado. Los más pequeños, los vulnerables y las niñas fueron los primeros grupos en ocupar las plazas de los primeros centros de menores que se habilitaron, aliviando los acogimientos solidarios de los vecinos.

Pero ahora los menores atrapados en el limbo de las calles son mayoritariamente varones, con edades entre los 14 y los 17, y estos refugios provisionales y vecinales escasean cada vez más. Así que lo menores tienden a agruparse entre ellos, haciendo piña en las calles ceutíes, lo más lejos posible de la frontera con Marruecos. Aunque es ilegal expulsarles, muchos dicen haber presenciado a militares forzando a otros menores a cruzar el puesto fronterizo, obligándoles a firmar el retorno voluntario a su país. De las expresiones que manejan en español, hay una que repiten con convicción: “Marruecos no, militares no”, dicen.

Otra de ellas es “soy menor”. Dos palabras que usan como escudo cuando, por su aspecto adulto y su cercanía a la mayoría de edad, son frecuentemente tomados por adultos. Ellos enseñan sus pasaportes verde oscuro y señalan la fecha de nacimiento: 2009, 2010 algunos; otros, 2011 o 2012. Los ofrecen a quien interpreta que les puede decir algo más que “no hay sitio” y le preguntan “¿dónde voy?“, pero las respuestas escasean en el limbo.

Lo único parecido a una certeza es la pulsera naranja de sus muñecas. La repartió hace algunas semanas la Cruz Roja para organizar el reparto de comida diario en la Playa de Trampolín, para evitar el tráfico de alimentos y que los que ya duermen en asentamientos se pusieran también en la fila. Esa es la única cola en la que estos adolescentes tienen sitio asegurado, en la cabecera. Junto a mujeres y niños, son los primeros en recibir las bolsas blancas de la organización.

Expulsiones y reagrupación

El Gobierno y el PP coinciden en que, una vez que se filie a estos menores, la reagrupación familiar en Marruecos es una prioridad. Sin embargo, tanto la normativa española como la europea son garantistas con los derechos. Es un proceso que requiere de tiempo y se tramita individualmente. Hay que identificar a su familia, escuchar qué quiere el menor... En cualquier caso, y pese a las manifestaciones públicas de Rabat asegurando que acogerá de vuelta a todos los adultos y menores, no siempre facilita los retornos. Antes de la avalancha, Ceuta había resuelto la reagrupación de 668 menores que hasta entonces no habían sido aceptados por el reino alauí, indican fuentes de la administración ceutí.

En lo tocante a los menores del cruce de finales de julio, no fue hasta este lunes cuando empezaron a tramitarse 10 expedientes de repatriación. El mando único encabezado por el ministro de Política Territorial, Ángel Víctor Torres, espera las primeras resoluciones el próximo miércoles.

Detrás de todo ese ruido político, los técnicos de la ciudad autónoma siguen trabajando en la tramitación de los expedientes para intentar una reagrupación familiar en Marruecos altamente improbable, lo que aboca a su derivación a territorio peninsular. El Ministerio de Juventud e Infancia ha planteado dos fórmulas: convenios de colaboración entre comunidades autónomas o la obligación de aplicar el artículo 35 de la ley de extranjería. A través de la primera vía salieron 5 niñas la semana pasada rumbo a Navarra, gobernada por el PSOE. El Gobierno de Vivas tuvo que autorizar su salida pese al argumento de que si se marchan a la península habrá un “efecto llamada”. En las próximas semanas, a los expedientes completados podrá aplicarse la segunda vía, la obligación de las comunidades autónomas de realojar a los menores.

Y mientras llega, más limbo. Para Youness, para Yasim, que vive en otro asentamiento en el Polígono de El Tarajal, o para Samir, que comparte mantas cada noche con otros 10 menores junto a la planta desalinizadora, entre las playas de Trampolín y Benítez. Parece una lengua de tierra con un muro blanco frente al mar, pero en realidad es tierra de nadie.

World.title: El mapa de Ceuta 50 días después de la entrada: más de 10.000 migrantes entre centros y asentamientos informales
World.content:
El desalojo del viernes es el último cambio en una ciudad donde, además de los 8.300 migrantes alojados en instalaciones oficiales, hay más de 4.000 en las calles y en los campamentos improvisados

Este viernes se cumplieron 50 días desde que irrumpieron más de 80.000 personas en Ceuta, una ciudad situada en la costa norte del continente africano con una población acostumbrada a las noticias de inmigración y al sonido de las sirenas acudiendo a la frontera con Marruecos. Durante unas horas, la mañana del 30 de julio, la frontera española dejó de existir. Se abrieron las puertas para evitar una tragedia humana mayor —hubo casi 100 muertos— y, aunque hasta 70.000 personas regresaron a Marruecos por el mismo camino en las siguientes horas, según datos del Gobierno, más de 10.000 siguen atrapadas, en una especie de limbo. Esperan a saber si podrán quedarse en territorio español o serán devueltos a Marruecos, como prometieron tanto el Gobierno como la ciudad autónoma al inicio de la crisis.

Ceuta tiene 83.000 habitantes viviendo en casi 20 kilómetros cuadrados de superficie. Con un mapa enfrente, la ciudad se asemeja a un brazo derecho con un puño entreabierto que apunta hacia el Estrecho de Gibraltar y cuyo hombro está cosido a la frontera marroquí. En la muñeca estarían las Murallas Reales y el istmo, la franja de tierra que conecta la península de La Almina con el resto del continente africano. “Con el pulgar y el índice se podrían formar los diques del puerto y en los dedos corazón, anular y meñique quedaría el monte Hacho”, explica un periodista veterano de la ciudad. El resto de la mano, la parte central, sería el centro de la ciudad, donde reside gran parte de los funcionarios, y con población occidental y bien remunerada, mientras conforme se entra en la zona oeste, donde está el Campo Exterior, hay barriadas de mayoría árabe-musulmana más castigadas por el paro, la infravivienda y el fracaso escolar.

Los ceutíes, que ya vivieron una entrada multitudinaria en 2021 —en aquella ocasión cruzaron unas 10.000 personas— revivieron el día 30 de julio una pesadilla. En cuestión de horas, la ciudad en la que vivían, con su seguridad, tranquilidad y espacios públicos, como parques, jardines o playas, dejó de existir.

Desde entonces, el Gobierno y la Ciudad Autónoma, de quien depende la tutela de los menores migrantes no acompañados, han buscado y acondicionado, muy poco a poco y con gran contestación ciudadana, parcelas y espacios disponibles con los que dar a estos migrantes unas condiciones de vida dignas y que también sirvan para agilizar los trámites administrativos que resuelvan su situación legal en España. Estos centros de acogida temporal también son claves para aliviar la presión migratoria en la ciudad, con una densidad poblacional que se acerca a la media de Madrid.

La cantidad de migrantes que se asentaron provisionalmente en Ceuta es una gran incógnita que se despeja muy poco a poco. El Gobierno central y la Ciudad autónoma tienen albergadas a más de 8.300 personas en centros oficiales (6.100, algunos de ellos menores con familiares) y recursos para menores migrantes (2.200). En torno a muchos de ellos, además, se ha creado un cinturón de otros asentamientos improvisados, migrantes que viven ahí por si se libera una plaza o porque se sienten más seguros cerca de los centros. Así, instalaciones de acogida como las naves del Tarajal o La Hípica, tienen en sus inmediaciones campamentos de unas 300 personas el primero, y un centenar en el segundo.

Aunque los más numerosos son los asentamientos informales como la Playa de El Trampolín, donde hay al menos 2.000 migrantes y el Ejecutivo estima que entre 700 y 1.000 menores todavía pernoctan en las calles. Además, otras 5.482 personas han abandonado voluntariamente la ciudad desde la segunda semana de agosto; unos 300 han sido expulsados por haber cometido algún tipo de delito o altercado; y otros 100 han desistido voluntariamente de su solicitud de asilo.

Pero todavía quedan zonas grises. Nadie se atreve a poner un número a los migrantes que viven escondidos en las zonas de los montes, alojados con familiares o repartidos en bajos de urbanizaciones que soportan la mayor presión migratoria, sobre todo las del extrarradio. Entre esas barriadas, se encuentran las del Príncipe Alfonso y Príncipe Felipe, San José-Hadú, Almadraba, Los Rosales, Juan Carlos I y Recinto. El centro de la ciudad, donde se encuentran los edificios administrativos y de renta más alta, se han mantenido en una burbuja.

El mapa de la renta en Ceuta dibuja un contraste claro entre el centro y los extremos de la ciudad. Los valores más altos, por encima de 27.700 euros de media por cada miembro del hogar de una zona, se concentran en el entorno del puerto y en el barrio de Manzanera-Otero. A medida que uno se aleja de esa zona central, la renta baja: barrios como Príncipe Felipe, Juan XXIII, Hadú o Erquicia, en la periferia sur, están entre los que registran los valores más bajos, por debajo de 12.800 euros.

Tener una fotografía fija de dónde se concentran los migrantes pasado este tiempo resulta complicado porque están en permanente movimiento. Los centros de acogida temporal del Gobierno les dan techo y comida mientras se resuelven los trámites legales, con plazos máximos estipulados de 12 semanas desde la formalización de la solicitud de protección internacional. La Policía ha echado a rodar un engranaje que tiene el núcleo de operaciones en el Centro de Atención Temporal de Extranjeros (CATE) de El Tarajal, con cerca de un centenar de agentes que ya han iniciado los trámites para más de 1.900 personas. El proceso, tasado y muy garantista, incluye la posibilidad de recurrir ante la Audiencia Nacional.

“Ceuta es una ciudad pequeña, pero compleja, con muchos planos”, explica Fernando Trujillo, profesor de la Facultad de Educación, Economía y Tecnología de Ceuta, un campus que pertenece administrativamente a la Universidad de Granada. Después de pasar más de 30 años en la ciudad autónoma, defiende que esas capas tan características de la ciudad han hecho que la crisis se viva con prismas y comportamientos diferentes. En ella conviven cuatro culturas (cristianos, musulmanes, que están entre el 40% y el 45%, y minorías hebrea e hindú), y una fuerte presencia de funcionarios (en enero había 9.800 empleados públicos, 4.000 de ellos de Fuerzas Armadas y Fuerzas de Seguridad del Estado); y también caballas (gentilicio coloquial de los ceutíes) de varias generaciones.

La sensación de abandono del Gobierno por parte de los ceutíes es general. “Es algo simbólico, como el miedo, y no se ha restaurado”, se lamenta Trujillo. “La contienda política, la desunión entre ciudad y Gobierno, también hace daño”, añade. “Hay un clima muy negativo, también por la sensación de que no se haya hecho nada en los últimos cinco años, desde la crisis de 2021, nada para prevenir, ni para actuar en caso de que se repitiera”, añade Carlos Rontomé, sociólogo y director de la UNED en Ceuta.

Quienes se compadecen del drama humano que se vive en sus calles se sienten señalados. “Se está criminalizando y deshumanizando al inmigrante”, valora un técnico que trabaja con asociaciones humanitarias en la ciudad y que pide no ser identificado. “Con el lenguaje que se emplea, da igual que sean adultos o menores, porque no se ve a personas, sino a invasores”, añade. De su trabajo de campo, incide en la lentitud e inacción de las Administraciones, especialmente teniendo en cuenta que pasado todo este tiempo sigue habiendo familias viviendo en la calle con niños pequeños, y que todavía no tienen ni unas mínimas condiciones sanitarias, como aseos. “La comunidad musulmana está actuando de otra forma, están siendo solidarios”, considera. El pleno estallido de la crisis murieron 82 personas ahogadas y aplastadas por la multitud que intentaba acceder por el espigón fronterizo. Todos han sido enterrados en la ciudad autónoma. Marruecos también ha confirmado la muerte de otros 14 migrantes durante el cruce multitudinario.

Gran parte de los migrantes se refugiaron desde las primeras horas en barriadas en las que vive población musulmana. Muchos vecinos les han ayudado, aunque esto no quiere decir que no estén también al límite. “No todos muestran su malestar o protestan de la misma forma”, añade Rontomé, que fue vicepresidente segundo de la Ciudad Autónoma de marzo de 2020 a junio de 2023 con el Gobierno de Juan Jesús Vivas, del PP. También hay gente que se aprovecha de los migrantes, que les explota laboralmente o les hospeda en condiciones insalubres.

En una ciudad en la que es habitual escuchar el castellano y el dariya (dialecto del árabe que se habla en Marruecos), se dan situaciones en las que los ceutíes árabes elevan la voz mientras hablan en castellano para que se sepa que son de la ciudad autónoma y no se den malentendidos. “Aunque no se verbalice, hay un deseo muy poderoso en la ciudad de que no se rompa la convivencia”, considera Trujillo. Un grupo de vecinos prendió fuego a varias tiendas de migrantes en la Playa de Benítez hace tres semanas y tanto el Gobierno como la ciudad lanzaron mensajes para cortar de raíz la violencia. “Reaccionaron diciendo ‘Esto no es Ceuta”, añade el profesor.

Migrantes se instalan en el nuevo centro de acogida de Los Rosales, a 14 de septiembre de 2026, en Ceuta. Marcos Moreno (Europa Press) El centro de Loma Margarita, el 21 de agosto.
