World.title: Renovated University Campus Worth Over €50 Million Opens in Zagreb
World.content:
September the 19th, 2026 – A newly renovated university campus worth over €50 million has opened as part of FER in Zagreb.

After two years of extensive works, Buildings B and C of the campus of the Faculty of Electrical Engineering and Computing of the University of Zagreb (FER) were solemnly opened. The complete renovation amounting to €50 million excluding VAT was co-financed with European Union funds from the Solidarity Fund and the Recovery and Resilience Facility. Poslovni reports that this concerns an area spanning 18,000 square metres in Unska Street that includes five modern amphitheatre lecture halls with a capacity of 900 seats, 153 office rooms and 26 classrooms and laboratories for teaching. The newly opened FER premises were visited by representatives of the state leadership, the City of Zagreb, the University of Zagreb and prominent entrepreneurs, members of the Faculty’s Alumni Board.

FER Dean Prof. Vedran Bilas, PhD, said that the investment in the renovation is the initial phase of the campus development, which was last expanded at the end of the 1980s, when the faculty had almost half as many employees, fewer study programmes and many times fewer research projects than today.

“Generations of professors and students before us built this institution, its competences, significance and values. FER is a synonym of excellence in the Croatian public, academic and business community. This renovation and this ceremony are stations on a path that continues. The Faculty has an experienced and proven team and capacity for the implementation of complex infrastructure projects, ready to continue cooperation with the Ministry of Science, Education and Youth on campus development projects,” Bilas said and announced a new spatial expansion: “The Government of the Republic of Croatia, through a Loan Agreement with the World Bank, is financing the preparation of the main project for the reconstruction of Building A, which will be completed by the end of this year. The reconstructed building will have three underground and nine above-ground floors, five more than now.”

Prime Minister Andrej Plenković praised the Faculty’s results and emphasised its contribution to society.

“By renovating these buildings we aren’t investing merely in space, but in Croatia’s ability to understand, shape and lead the technological changes that in the decades ahead will determine the economic strength, security and technological independence of states. FER is one of the central places where Croatia creates knowledge for the digital age, and we count on its professors, researchers and students also in responding to the challenges of artificial intelligence, cyber security and quantum computing. Our vision is clear: Croatia must not be only a user of other people’s technology, but must develop and export its own high value-added solutions,” said Prime Minister Plenković.

“Through patient work, persistence and joint action we have arrived at a result that benefits our teachers and those most important for our future, and that is our students. I believe that the Faculty in the renovated premises will develop new visions and continue to lead in the IT sector and digital transformation, recognising what society and the state need,” said Rector of the University of Zagreb, Prof. Stjepan Lakušić, PhD.

The FER team responsible for the implementation of the renovation guided representatives of the Government, Prime Minister Plenković, Minister of Construction and State Property Branko Bačić, Minister of the Economy Ante Šušnjar and other high-ranking guests through the newly renovated premises, and the tour ended on the 13th floor with a spectacular panoramic view of the whole of Zagreb. The contractor for the extensive works was the construction company TROMONT d.o.o., and a complete energy, fire-protection and multimedia renovation was carried out.

The programme and celebration of the opening will continue in the afternoon. From 18:00 a parking party for friends, fellow citizens and neighbours is planned on the FER car park in Unska Street, with musicians Duška Brčić, Vjeko Ključarić, Filip Rudan, young up-and-coming bands and the Disco section of KSET.

World.title: “Forever Chemicals” Found in Lika Water Following Waste Scandal
World.content:
September the 19th, 2026 – So-called “forever chemicals” have unfortunately been found in Lika water following the shameful hazardous waste scandal.

The Croatian Institute of Public Health (HZJZ) and the Public Health Institute of Lika-Senj County have published the results of extraordinary water sampling in the Lika area. Index reports that the results have revealed that dangerous PFAS compounds, so-called “forever chemicals,” were found in two private wells downstream from an illegal waste dump near Gospić, but they assure the public that the pollution is exclusively of a local character and that water from the public water supply is not endangered.

the chemicals were found in two wells near the illegal waste dump

According to the HZJZ statement, from the 20th of August to the 9th of September water was sampled from 43 private facilities – 38 wells, three cisterns and two springs. The Institute states that in one well in the immediate vicinity of the dump a concentration of PFAS compounds of 0.3018 µg/L was recorded, which is three times higher than the maximum permitted limit of 0.1 µg/L. In the second well 0.0265 µg/L was measured, which is within the permitted limits. HZJZ claims that the owners of the disputed wells are connected to the public water supply and do not use that water for drinking. As for the other findings, the Institute claims that in 33 facilities only “usual microbiological pollution characteristic of untreated water” was recorded, while elevated physical-chemical values in a further 10 samples are attributed to the natural properties of the karst, and not to the dumped waste.

the people of lika feel betrayed by the government

The statement comes at a moment when the scandal surrounding the illegal burial of as many as 37,000 tonnes of hazardous waste in Divoselo and Benkovačko Selo near Gospić has grown into a first-class political scandal. HZJZ Director Krunoslav Capak personally sits on the newly established Scientific Council of Prime Minister Andrej Plenković, a body that the government formed precisely with the aim of “correctly interpreting” in public the dramatic findings of the USKOK investigation into the pollution of soil and waters in Lika. The documents that Plenković’s Scientific Council is supposed to put into the “correct context” were signed by authorised institutions and are quite exact.

The expert examination by the “Josip Juraj Strossmayer” Water Institute for the Divoselo location established that the water passing immediately under the dump carries 89 percent of the total detected plastic, while upstream it is clean. 737 micrograms of Styrofoam per litre were measured, and the presence of Teflon from the group of “forever chemicals” (PFAS) was also recorded, with the expert’s note that the Lika River is a directly connected water body.

the prime minister is at the council’s helm

Although formally composed of professors from technical and natural science faculties, the Council has been placed under the direct authority of the Prime Minister. According to the government decision, the sessions are convened and chaired by Plenković himself, operational tasks are carried out by his office, and there are no prescribed obligations for the publication of minutes, expert conclusions or any dissenting opinions of members. The entire manoeuvre of forming the Council is taking place at a time when the remediation is only being prepared, and political pressure on the ruling party is growing after a mass protest in Zagreb and a drop in HDZ’s rating.

is there any real reason to panic?

Despite this, HZJZ persists in the claim that there is no reason for panic. They state that the fact that such compounds were not found in other wells across the county proves that it is “pollution of a local character in a narrower circle.” They also repeat that private wells in any case do not fall under regular state supervision and that the responsibility lies with the owners themselves. The Institute finally states that all regular tests confirm that water from the public water supply in the entire Lika-Senj County area, as well as on the islands of Pag and Rab, is completely health-safe and that they will continue monitoring the situation on the ground.

World.title: Estonian experts say social media should be improved for children instead of banned
World.content:
The European Union is discussing a safe‑internet regulation that includes several restrictions planned for minors' use of social media. While EU plans propose setting a minimum age of 13, Estonian social scientists argue that blunt bans will not solve all problems and may even create new ones.

Tallinn University media professor Indrek Ibrus is critical of the EU initiative, saying the planned restrictions conflict with children's fundamental rights.

"In my opinion, it's generally a pretty bad idea," Ibrus said, explaining that it ignores the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child. "Children must have opportunities for self‑expression and free access to information to support their development and identity. Any age‑based restriction on access to information essentially disregards children's rights," Ibrus said.

According to Ibrus, the European Commission is effectively giving up by proposing restrictions.

Indrek Ibrus. Source: Siim Lõvi /ERR

"Instead of working on these environments, these platforms, these spaces in a way that would make them safe and suitable for children, the European Commission throws up its hands and gives up. They don't have the strength to deal with regulation, even though the regulatory framework — the Digital Services Act — already exists and simply needs to be enforced. In a sense, children are being sacrificed because of the Commission's own inability," he said.

University of Tartu media studies professor Andra Siibak agreed that relying solely on bans and restrictions is not the best solution, highlighting the need to change platform business models. Siibak said it is positive that the EU demands concrete measures from service providers to make platforms more protective of children's rights, well‑being and privacy.

Like Ibrus, Siibak pointed out that all these recommended changes are already written into earlier EU regulations — whether the Digital Services Act or the AI Act. "The European Union itself must start thinking carefully about how to demand these changes from platforms and monitor that they actually implement them," Siibak said.

Andra Siibak Autor/allikas: ERR/Lauri Varik

Tallinn University participation‑culture professor Katrin Tiidenberg warned against overly rigid bans, citing Australia's experience.

"Based on what we know from Australia and how their ban doesn't actually work, children under 16 are still online, which mainly means we don't know what they're doing on social media or where they're logged in," Tiidenberg said.

One of the biggest questions surrounding the EU Kids Act is how to verify users' ages without massively violating people's privacy.

Ibrus sees major risks in age verification. "It may be a direct privacy intrusion, and it may also be harmful in the sense that platforms could use identification for more precise profiling of users, which can be dangerous in several ways," he explained.

Ibrus added that although the EU is developing a digital wallet solution that could provide secure infrastructure in the future, any restrictions must be approached with extreme caution.

Siibak also noted that finding a reliable and transparent age‑verification method is currently difficult. Attempts with facial‑recognition software have not worked, and young people easily bypass restrictions using, for example, their parents' documents.

"We know from Australia's experience how skillfully young people bypass such age‑assessment apps and solutions. To access a platform, they show their parents' documents or take a photo with a famous footballer's poster in the background instead of showing their own face. Young people certainly have many ways to get around such systems. Finding a method acceptable to all member states will be a very difficult discussion," Siibak said.

Katrin Tiidenberg Autor/allikas: Priit Mürk/ERR

Tiidenberg also stressed that mechanical age‑verification methods bring risks. "It's a very important issue, because if it means a child must log in with an ID card, then it means everyone must log in with an ID card. We want to avoid mass surveillance and monitoring of which sites we visit and who does what. In my view, maintaining freedom is important," Tiidenberg said.

"That doesn't mean age verification cannot be done in a reasonably safe way, but the method must be developed very carefully and not by quickly trusting the first private company that says: 'Look, I built you a solution,'" Tiidenberg said.

Experts say protecting children and young people on social media should focus on improving the platforms themselves.

Tiidenberg highlighted the need to pressure platforms to create well‑being‑oriented and responsible design. This means placing strong emphasis on curbing addictive algorithms — for example, giving users the option to choose between a chronological feed and recommendation algorithms. She also supports separate child‑ and youth‑friendly accounts (for example, ages 13–15) where harmful content is automatically limited.

Ibrus reminded that in addition to tightening rules, it is important to support young people's digital skills and critical thinking instead of creating artificial barriers that do not actually protect them online.

"Instead of bluntly banning communication environments because they may involve certain risks, those risks must be addressed. Platforms must be adapted, regulated, existing regulations enforced, and at the same time media literacy must be developed for different age and social groups," Ibrus said.

Tiidenberg added that digital skills are important, but a person can be both competent and helpless at the same time — including children.

"Critical awareness is very important, but obviously children have different self‑regulation abilities at different ages. Even many adults do not have very good self‑regulation. You may know something is harmful to you, but you still may not be able to avoid certain social media content," she said.

"Skills are important — they are part of the toolkit — but they are not enough if we allow user interfaces to be designed manipulatively, because they still measure the user's slowing finger while scrolling. If we do not regulate how quickly systems must respond when I say that I or my child does not want to see certain content, then digital skills alone are of little use," Tiidenberg added.

On Thursday, the European Commission adopted the safe‑internet regulation (EU Kids Act), which increases children's online safety in the EU. The package includes proposals to ban social media use for children under 13 and to require companies providing online services to create safe accounts for children.

Under the proposal — which EU member states and the European Parliament will negotiate — accounts for children aged 13–15 would be under parental control.

Social media and video services, online games and AI‑based companions and chatbots intended for users under 18 would be subject to a list of permitted and prohibited activities.

World.title: Reintroduced dormice face a fox that moved to predator‑free island
World.content:
The garden dormice released on Suur‑Pakri Island this summer to rewild the species have encountered an unexpected co‑inhabitant who may consider the newcomers gourmet food.

The garden dormouse (Eliomys quercinus), a native Estonian species, went extinct in Estonia due to human activity. The exact cause is unknown. The last wild garden dormouse was seen in 1986. Around the same time, the species disappeared from neighboring countries as well. This summer, the first small colony was released on Suur‑Pakri Island.

"When we last left the island a couple of weeks ago, more than half of the 20 animals released were definitely alive. For a small zoo animal, that's a surprisingly good result. We're optimistic that maybe they'll even survive until spring," said ecologist Marko Mägi.

"Since it's a small animal with a very short lifespan and could end up in a predator's jaws during winter — even though it sleeps through winter — we don't know whether any of them will still see daylight in spring," Mägi noted.

Suur‑Pakri was chosen for reintroduction because it lacked predators.

"Last autumn we carried out control surveys and studied small mammals to determine whether the island was safe for garden dormice. At that time we could say there were no predators that would threaten them. We had a very harsh winter that covered the sea with ice, and a fox easily crossed over to the island," Mägi explained.

"This summer we discovered that a fox is indeed on the island. We saw it on trail cameras, and it was also spotted running through the forest. Now we're curious to see what happens by spring: will the fox win, or the garden dormice?"

"Although the garden dormouse is active at night and gladly climbs trees, where a fox cannot reach, their paths may still cross. But fortunately for the dormice, the island has plenty of other small rodents that interest the fox more. For the fox, the garden dormouse would be a true gourmet meal," Mägi said.

World.title: Kelly Sildaru second in New Zealand as winds cancel final
World.content:
Estonian freestyle skier Kelly Sildaru kicked off her competition season with a second-place finish at the Snow League event in Cardrona, New Zealand.

The season-opening event saw Sildaru overcome Australian Indra Brown in her first halfpipe duel, scoring 77 points on her opening run and 74 on her second, while her opponent's best was 72.

Sildaru, 24, is competing in the Snow League's World Challenge format, where teams of four comprise a male and female snowboarder alongside a male and female freestyle skier. She is part of Team Europe together with Finnish freestyle skier Jon Sallinen and snowboarders Queralt Castellet (Spain) and Jonas Häsler of (Switzerland).

The win sent her into the final, but strong winds forced the cancellation of her duel with Challengers team representative Mischa Thomas. The winner was decided on semifinal results, where Thomas had scored 83 and 91.

Sildaru earned seven points for Team Europe with her second-place finish, and her team finished second overall on 27 points. The Challengers team won with 37, Team Asia-Pacific were third with 22 and the North Americans fourth with 14. Finley Melville Ives and Ryusei Yamada also took victories alongside Thomas.

The next Snow League event takes place in Aspen, Colorado, in early January, with the World Cup season starting ahead of that in Innsbruck, Austria, in late November.

Estonian freestyle skier Henry Sildaru, Kelly's brother, was drafted to XC Golden State for the X Games' new team league and will team up with Eileen Gu.

World.title: Wandering cat Kurri covers 15,000 kilometers in two months
World.content:
Kurri, adopted from a shelter, has over the years become a travel‑loving wanderer with six summer road trips behind him.

Recently the cat traveled 15,000 kilometers in two months, braving mountain roads, passing through 14 countries and reaching Armenia.

"Kurri was offended with me for three days. Normally he comes to my lap and sleeps next to me at night, but he just ignored me. He was so upset that we were home and not going anywhere anymore. No more daily excitement."

Now nine years old, Kurri came into owner Katri Bagirov's life from a shelter where she volunteered helping cats find new homes. "I was also a foster home for a while. That winter there were many cats in quarantine. Kurri was in the worst condition, so I took him under my care, took him to the vet, and it turned out he had pneumonia. I nursed him back to health and started looking for a home for him. Soon the thought started ticking that maybe I wanted him myself, and we began looking for ways to adopt him," said Bagirov, whose life involved a lot of travel.

"He didn't really fit my lifestyle, but since my mother offered to take care of Kurri when I'm away, the decision was made," she added.

Kurri was not born a travel cat. At first, even a single car ride was a challenge. "I didn't even have the idea back then that a cat could travel like this. I thought he could come with me to the countryside, visit friends and family. I trained him that first spring with a harness, leash and car. It was a huge headache. He got sick easily, he was anxious, had diarrhea. My car was covered in plastic and newspapers before I started training him more consciously," Bagirov recalled. Today Kurri crawls into her travel suitcase with little trouble and is ready to go.

"Nearly three years passed, covid came, we wanted to go on vacation and ruled out any flights. We decided to go by car, and there was nowhere to leave Kurri. We thought he'd come along, and if needed, we'd just turn back. We drove through Germany, France, Spain and Portugal. And I was surprised how much he walked. He walked through entire villages. Small villages, but still," Bagirov laughed.

This year's trip was Kurri's sixth summer road journey. It was the longest so far and, for the first time, took them to the Caucasus. Traveling with Kurri are Katri, Katri's mother and her husband. Travel planning largely revolves around the four‑legged family member.

"We function as a travel group because we are Kurri's people, and all our trips revolve around him. At least in recent years. We choose everything based on Kurri," Bagirov explained.

"In the European Union it's simple: you need to microchip the animal, have a pet passport and a rabies vaccination. Leaving the EU gets a bit more complicated. You need a health declaration, which basically means a stamp in the pet passport confirming the animal is healthy and has had parasite treatment," Bagirov said.

Before confirming accommodation, they check with potential hosts what they think about having a cat stay overnight. "So far the experience has been very positive. Problems have been with larger hotels that have their own rules and conditions. If it's not allowed, then it's not allowed. But smaller accommodations have generally let Kurri into the room. Very surprising. It's much easier to walk in and ask than to search online," Bagirov noted.

World.title: Märt Meesak: Only devoted die‑hards will keep working in the food service sector
World.content:
Eating out is not a luxury, and only the true fanatics of the foodservice sector — those who have not yet given up — will continue operating, writes Märt Meesak.

ERR recently published an extensive overview of the state of Estonia's foodservice industry. Nearly every month, if not every week, brings news of restaurants closing. The reasons are always the same: costs exceed revenue. Estonia has the highest VAT on food and dining out in Europe after Denmark — roughly twice the EU average.

What makes me especially disheartened about the arguments coming from leading politicians is the claim that "the strongest will survive," or that eating out is a luxury. Even worse is the suggestion that the sector is not a significant part of Estonia's economy, so why worry about it. In reality, the entire sector is speeding toward a crisis — if it isn't already there.

The tourism sector is one of the most beneficial for the state. A functioning tourism industry brings in foreign money through visitors, who also pay taxes on everything they consume here (VAT, labor taxes, alcohol excise, fuel excise).

Thanks to tourism, many other businesses get work: laundries, courier companies, security firms, cleaning companies, farmers, manufacturers. The list is long, because the economy is a system of connected vessels. Tourists also take taxis, rent cars, and so on. All these companies provide jobs and pay taxes.

Eating out should not be a luxury, as some politicians imagine. In a normal society that aims to grow a healthy middle class, eating out should be the rule, not the exception. Dining out offers people culinary experiences, healthier eating options, and a way to relieve stress.

"Dining out offers people culinary experiences, healthier eating options, and a way to relieve stress."

It is certainly healthier for an office worker to eat at least one warm meal a day rather than snack on store‑bought ready food. Stepping out of the office during a stressful day is already beneficial, and going out in the evenings is good for mental health. We talk about Estonia's mental‑health problems, yet we prevent people from improving their well‑being in a natural way. Eating out is also a social activity — in the internet age, meeting people face‑to‑face and feeling happy is irreplaceable. That's how we climb higher on happiness indexes.

The sector employs professionals trained in Estonia's public education system — funded by taxpayers. They work with passion to create something exciting. The fact that people can work with heart and offer something good to others is a value worth preserving. And there are many more reasons.

But the situation is serious: no business is a social project — it must be profitable. Unless we want to return to Soviet‑era canteens. Too often, foodservice business owners work 24/7, and their health and well‑being matter too. Doing this work at zero profit — or even at a loss — is not sustainable. And so doors close. It's nice to provide jobs and pay taxes, but the owner must also receive some benefit.

Profit margins in the foodservice sector have collapsed to near zero. According to the Estonian Hotel and Restaurant Association's 2026 data, average profitability has fallen from four percent to about one percent.

Politicians' counterarguments against lowering VAT have been predictable. They claim that a VAT reduction would not reach consumers, and that restaurateurs would pocket the difference as huge profits. Let's break that claim down.

The sector's annual turnover is under one billion euros (it fell 1.6 percent last year). Estonia has roughly 2,500–3,000 active food‑and‑drink establishments. That means an average annual turnover of €300,000–€400,000 per business (about €25,000–€33,000 per month). With a one‑percent profit margin, the average annual profit is €3,000–€4,000 euros — about €300 per month.

Even if we optimistically use the former four‑percent margin, the situation is still bleak. A four‑percent margin means €14,000 profit per year — €1,166 per month. In many establishments, the owner works behind the stove or counter, meaning this is essentially their monthly income.

Compare that to Estonia's average salary, which is over €2,000. The imbalance and unsustainability are obvious. And if the owner wanted to pay themselves a salary, social tax and unemployment insurance would reduce it further — leaving around €600.

Show me a government official willing to work around the clock for that amount. The owner must take full financial responsibility, pay all employees on time, and transfer all state taxes down to the second.

Even if part of the VAT reduction stayed with the business, it would not be a crime if the owner could earn €1,000 instead of €600. The business could regain investment capacity, improving working conditions for employees. If the business does better, wages rise — which benefits the entire economy. And when Estonia's economy improves, tax revenue increases.

Let's not kill off a sector that provides so much value we often don't notice at first glance. Only the "crazy ones," the devoted die-hards, remain in the catering sector — everyone else has already given up. Let's support our people and our businesses.

World.title: Gallery: More than 50 Estonian artists take stock of what matters now
World.content:
What matters to Estonian artists right now? A major new exhibition at Tallinn's Haus Gallery offers 51 perspectives through nearly 60 never-before-displayed works.

"From the Artist's Perspective" opened Thursday, marking a new curatorial project that Haus Gallery hopes to turn into an annual tradition: a dialogue between artists and the public around issues they see as important right now.

The exhibition was assembled through an open call that drew dozens of professional artists from across generations.

With few restrictions on medium or format, artists were invited to submit one to three recent works that represented something personally meaningful to them, reflecting a significant personal position or worldview.

None of the works had been previously exhibited, and artists were asked to personally provide a few lines contextualizing each work and its significance in terms of the show. These accompanying texts, the gallery said, form an important part of the project and are included on site as well as on their website.

Nearly 60 works were ultimately selected, bringing together different artistic perspectives as well as their common threads to provide a unique collective portrait of the present moment.

Rather than imposing a single interpretation, the exhibition leaves viewers to consider what Estonian artists are depicting, what moves them and why.

51 Estonian artists

Haus Gallery, which has been active on Estonia's art scene since 1997, says the project is rooted in its conviction that art can map our emotional history and reflect what takes place in society through the personal but broadly resonant perspectives of individual artists.

Curated by Piia Ausman, the exhibition features 51 artists, including Vano Allsalu, Jaan Elken, Mall Nukke, Marko Mäetamm, Maarit Murka, Liisa Jugapuu, Mari Früling, Tiit Pääsuke, Laurentsius, Katariin Mudist, Liisa Mudist, Mari Roosvalt, Külli Suitso, Lisa Add and Valeri Vinogradov.

"From the Artist's Perspective" will remain on view through October 24.

World.title: Vaba Lava seeks additional €250,000 to keep Narva theater open
World.content:
Estonian independent theater Vaba Lava is considering closing down its Narva location, saying current state funding is not enough to run it sustainably.

Vaba Lava receives more than €300,000 a year from the state for theater activities, but says that is no longer enough to produce Estonian-language theater in Narva.

The largely Russian-speaking border city requires translated performances, carefully selected repertoire and drastically lower ticket prices, even as its district heating costs soar as the highest in Estonia. The theater says the current funding model does not account for any of these factors.

"They tell us we're so very needed, that we're doing incredibly important work, but then there's essentially no follow-through," said Vaba Lava founder and director Märt Meos, adding that in his role, he can no longer take on that kind of five-year commitment.

"At this level of funding, we can no longer continue the contract," Meos added.

The Ministry of Culture acknowledges the importance of Vaba Lava's presence in Estonia's third-largest city, which has no state theater. Earlier plans to establish a joint foundation with the state fell through, however, leaving Vaba Lava to compete for operating grants.

Marie Anett Heinsalu, a theater adviser at the ministry's Art Department, said not much else can be done about those grants.

"Unfortunately, there's really no other way around it; the application needs to score higher, and if there are fewer recipients, the amount of funding could also increase," Heinsalu explained, adding that neither the ministry nor the theater have any control over that.

Time to decide

Vaba Lava's lease for its Narva location expires next year, but a decision on extending it needs to be made this fall. The theater says it needs at least €250,000 more in state funding to stay in Narva.

"We have to make these plans a year or two ahead, and right now, we don't know whether we'll still be here on August 1, 2027," Meos said.

The ministry says any additional funding would ultimately require a political decision.

If the political commitment exists, Heinsalu said it may be possible to find additional funding for the Narva theater through other measures.

"But we can't do that until we know how state budget negotiations turn out," she added.

Estonia's 2027 state budget talks are expected to wrap up next week.

World.title: Tõnis Saarts: Herem could save the Reform Party — or deliver a fatal blow
World.content:
Martin Herem may unintentionally determine whether the Reform Party retains its last strong card of competence going into the next elections — or whether it enters the campaign with the most battered reputation in its history, writes Tõnis Saarts.

The recent turmoil surrounding national defense and the Ministry of Defense is not just another leadership or trust crisis for the Reform Party, but a far more fundamental challenge. Defense policy was the party's last truly credible area of competence; its reputation for sound economic policy has long since eroded. The ministry scandal has seriously shaken confidence in their core field of expertise.

Bringing in Martin Herem as minister carries a major risk for the party. A highly independent minister could, by revealing new problems, deliver a fatal blow to the Reform Party's already fragile credibility in defense policy. Or, conversely, through effective and constructive work, he could restore trust.

Before the 2023 elections, the Reform Party was highly successful in convincing voters of three things.

First, that they were the most competent party on economic issues — the ones who bring prosperity and keep public finances in order.

Second, that under their leadership, the welfare state — pensions, family policy, healthcare, education — was in safe hands and would not face cuts.

Third, and perhaps most importantly, that they were the most reliable force in countering the Russian threat, with strong security and defense expertise unmatched by their competitors.

The party's once‑dominant image of economic competence has now been heavily devalued. Years of economic stagnation, tax hikes, and fiscal problems have stripped it of its former strength.

Their credibility in welfare policy remains, but defending the welfare state has never been the Reform Party's ideological hallmark. It cannot serve as the sole foundation for the next election campaign. That left defense competence and the ability to counter the Russian threat as their strongest remaining pillar.

The scandal at the end of Hanno Pevkur's term cracked that pillar. It still stands — barely — but another shake caused by a new scandal could topple it entirely.

"Bringing in Martin Herem as minister carries a major risk for the party."

This is where the "Herem factor" comes in. On one hand, the Reform Party made a brilliant PR move by bringing in the field's most respected expert to clean up its failures. If Herem puts things in order, they will be in order for the government and the Reform Party as well. On the other hand, if he starts digging deeper into decisions and non‑decisions of recent years, he may uncover something that delivers a devastating blow to the party's credibility.

There are three possible scenarios.

In the first, Herem enthusiastically begins to fix the field but discovers that leadership, information flows, and procurement processes have been in disarray for years. Worst of all would be if some issues date back long enough to show that the Reform Party has not managed its key policy area properly despite its polished public façade.

In the second scenario, the Reform Party feels tempted to strike back at Herem, hinting that he himself was commander of the EDF during the same period and shares responsibility. A blame‑shifting ping‑pong begins. This would be the worst outcome: trust in national defense would suffer, and both the governing party and Herem would end up in the public's "mud league." Meanwhile, hands would be rubbed together across the eastern border.

The third scenario — the one the Reform Party hopes for — is that Herem fixes the problems, and although some credit goes to him, the political beneficiary is the Reform Party. They could launch a pre‑election narrative: "Yes, we made mistakes, we admitted them, we brought in the best minds to fix the field, and the job got done. And what do you, the conservatives, have to offer in response?"

It is difficult to predict which scenario will unfold. One thing is clear: over the next six months, Herem will not only determine how well Estonia's national defense is managed. He may also decide whether the Reform Party retains its last strong competence card for the next elections — or whether it enters the campaign with the most damaged reputation in its history.

If the Reform Party is left with no policy area in which a significant share of voters believes they outperform others, they have real reason to fear the next elections.

World.title: Washington Institute urges sanctions on Maliki, and Ameri over disarmament delays
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – A policy analysis published by the Washington Institute for Near East Policy has recommended that the United States prepare targeted individual sanctions against former Iraqi Prime Minister Nouri Al-Maliki and Badr Organization leader Hadi Al-Ameri if both figures continue obstructing federal efforts to disarm armed factions.

The study, authored by former U.S. Assistant Secretary of State David Schenker and reported by the 964 Network, argues that the two veteran political leaders—who collectively command 47 parliamentary seats within the ruling Coordination Framework—remain entrenched in maximalist positions rather than facilitating genuine state control over weapons, particularly following high-profile cross-border drone strikes against regional energy targets.

The analysis highlights that while Al-Maliki previously pledged to defuse factional tensions and avert collisions with Baghdad’s sovereign agenda, Iranian-backed groups within the Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF) subsequently launched an explosive drone barrage on September 10 targeting Saudi Arabia’s East-West crude pipeline near Yanbu, Riyadh, and Medina.

The assault, which temporarily disrupted up to 4–5 million barrels per day of transit to the Red Sea, directly undermined Coordination Framework claims of having neutralized escalation risks, exposing the fragility of domestic political assurances.

Schenker notes that Al-Maliki narrowly escaped U.S. Treasury designations during the first Trump administration and warns that continued efforts to replace disarmament with ambiguous “containment” models—akin to Lebanese political formulas surrounding Hezbollah—should trigger direct U.S. financial designations against both Al-Maliki and Al-Ameri.

The policy paper comes as Prime Minister Ali Faleh Al-Zaidi approaches his self-imposed September 30 deadline to monopolize arms under sovereign command—a date that coincides with the scheduled conclusion of the U.S.-led International Coalition’s mission in Iraq.

While moderate factions like Asa’ib Ahl al-Haq and Kata’ib Imam Ali offered preliminary disarmament concessions, and Muqtada Al-Sadr agreed to absorb Saraya Al-Salam into the regular military, hardline elements led by Kata’ib Hezbollah, Harakat Hezbollah Al-Nujaba, and Kata’ib Sayyid Al-Shuhada have openly resisted.

Bolstered by summer visits from IRGC Quds Force Commander Esmail Qaani, these groups have conditioned disarmament on non-starter demands, including dissolving the constitutionally recognized Kurdish Peshmerga, expelling Turkish forces, and enshrining PMF benefits by statute, while proposing unacceptable workarounds such as storing heavy weaponry in Iran or maintaining private depots under a nominal two-year activity freeze.

To reinforce Baghdad’s authority and protect vital regional energy corridors, the Washington Institute urges the White House to pursue calibrated pressure rather than sweeping economic embargoes, outlining several immediate policy steps:

World.title: Iraq’s University of Technology explores academic partnerships in Spain
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq’s University of Technology conducted high-level academic discussions on Saturday, September 19, 2026, with Spain’s University of Seville and University of Granada, aiming to broaden bilateral research cooperation, facilitate student and faculty exchanges, and launch joint scientific projects.

According to an official university statement carried by INA, the institutional visit was led by the President of the University of Technology, Mohsen Nouri Hamza, heading a senior academic delegation as part of the institution’s broader strategy to expand global academic engagement.

At the University of Granada, Hamza met with University Rector Pedro Mercado Pacheco to review frameworks for institutional collaboration and advance a draft comprehensive Global Agreement designed to govern future academic and scientific ties.

The delegation held additional technical sessions with Irene Pedreira Romero, Director of International Projects and Networks, and Leandro Di Stasi, Director of Internationalization at the International School for Postgraduate Studies.

Deliberations centered on establishing joint research initiatives and leveraging opportunities under the European Union’s Erasmus+ program to facilitate bilateral mobility for researchers, instructors, and graduate students, including hosting Iraqi postgraduate candidates in Spanish laboratories to carry out specialized thesis work.

The mission to the University of Seville focused on technical and engineering disciplines aligned with national development priorities. Talks concentrated on joint projects in renewable energy, industrial catalysts, advanced materials, structural engineering, and sustainable architectural design.

The Iraqi delegation—which included Dean of the College of Architecture Abbas Ali Hamza, Dean of the College of Electromechanical Engineering Ghassan Abdul Hussein Bilal, Materials Engineering faculty member Mohammed Al-Zuhairi, and Electromechanical Engineering faculty member Sundus Samir Jumaa—agreed to establish specialized bilateral research teams aimed at supporting sustainable development through academic innovation.

World.title: Four key clashes conclude Iraq Stars League matchday 8 on Saturday
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Four decisive fixtures will wrap up Matchday 8 of the Iraq Stars League on Saturday evening, September 19, 2026, setting the stage for high-stakes clashes spanning the title chase, mid-table consolidation, and redemption campaigns.

The evening action kicks off at 6:45 PM Baghdad time with two simultaneous fixtures. Ghaz Al-Shamal takes on Newroz in an encounter where both clubs will battle to secure maximum points and strengthen their footholds in the league standings. At the same hour, perennial title contenders Al-Quwa Al-Jawiya meet Diyala, determined to bounce back from recent dropped points, rediscover winning form, and reignite their domestic momentum.

The focus shifts to the summit of the table at 9:00 PM when league leaders Al-Karma host Zakho at Al-Jawlan Stadium. Al-Karma enters the contest intent on protecting their prime position at the top of the standings and sustaining their strong run of form, while Zakho aims to disrupt the leaders and secure a valuable away result to bolster their points tally.

Matchday 8 concludes at 9:30 PM with Al-Shorta welcoming Al-Kahrabaa at Al-Shorta Stadium. Returning swiftly to domestic duties following their midweek AFC Champions League Two continental fixture, the hosts will target all three points in front of home supporters, while an ambitious Al-Kahrabaa side seeks to capitalize on any fatigue to claim an upset.

World.title: US dollar surges past 160,000 IQD amid US liquidity pressures and market slump
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The U.S. dollar crossed the 160,000-dinar threshold across Iraq’s parallel currency markets during opening trading on Saturday, September 19, 2026, marking a sharp depreciation of the domestic currency as market liquidity contracted under geopolitical and fiscal strains.

Bureaus in Baghdad posted selling prices of 160,000 dinars per $100 against buying rates of 159,500 dinars, while trading in Erbil, the capital of the Kurdistan Region, reflected a parallel surge, settling at 159,650 dinars for sale and 159,100 dinars for purchase.

The widening spread against the Central Bank of Iraq’s official peg of 131,000 dinars follows reports of heightened U.S. Treasury pressure and restrictions on monthly physical cash shipments from Iraq’s oil revenue reserves held at the U.S. Federal Reserve.

Washington has reportedly conditioned the continuity of unhindered dollar liquidity flows on Baghdad’s progress in disarming Iran-aligned armed factions and meeting the critical September 30 deadline, which coincides with the scheduled conclusion of the International Coalition’s military presence.

The resulting cash shortage has fueled market speculation, with local traders and currency dealers warning that selling rates could climb toward the 170,000-dinar mark if physical inflows remain constrained.

The monetary volatility has begun depressing consumer sentiment across the country ahead of the month-end deadline. Households across Iraqi governorates have visibly shifted toward precautionary saving and defensive spending, prioritizing essential food commodities while curtailing expenditures on discretionary goods and leisure services.

Foot traffic and commercial turnover have contracted noticeably across cafes, restaurants, and retail markets—even extending to school stationery vendors preparing for the upcoming academic term—choking domestic cash flow and deepening liquidity bottlenecks across the real economy.

World.title: Iraq Customs clarifies duties on pharmaceuticals, vitamins, and supplements
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The Iraqi General Authority of Customs asserted on Friday evening, September 18, 2026, that the formal classification of imported commodities and the determination of their corresponding Harmonized System (HS) codes and tariff bands remain the exclusive legal jurisdiction of the customs authority.

In a statement received IraqiNews.com, the authority clarified the operative tariff schedules for healthcare products, noting that certified pharmaceutical products are levied at a baseline duty of 0.5%, while vitamins and dietary supplements face duties of either 5% or 10% based on technical categorization.

Customs regulators emphasized that receiving testing clearances or regulatory approvals from the Ministry of Health does not automatically classify a product as a pharmaceutical medicine for border assessment purposes.

The authority underlined that health sector certifications fulfill domestic safety compliance requirements, whereas border taxation, HS code designation, and duty assessments are determined strictly through official statutory tariff tables and active customs regulations.

Under the declared tariff structure, conventional pharmaceuticals formally categorized under recognized medical subheadings qualify for the lower 0.5% rate.

Conversely, vitamins and nutritional supplements are evaluated individually based on their specific chemical formulation, physical composition, and technical commodity descriptions, subjecting them to standard 5% or 10% duty brackets rather than pharmaceutical exemptions.

The authority reiterated that brand names, marketing designations, or laboratory review bodies do not dictate tariff bands, which rely solely on technical HS documentation.

The regulatory clarification addresses recurring friction between border revenue authorities and the domestic healthcare market regarding import costs. In January 2026, the General Authority of Customs confirmed a 1% tariff adjustment on medical supplies, dismissing claims of a ten-fold duty increase flagged by the Iraqi Syndicate of Pharmacists as an unintentional clerical error.

The latest customs advisory establishes clear statutory boundaries between health testing protocols and fiscal border valuations, maintaining firm oversight over revenue collection on non-essential health and wellness supplements entering the country.

World.title: Iraqi Election Commission monitors Russian elections in Moscow
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – A senior delegation from Iraq’s Independent High Electoral Commission (IHEC), headed by the Chairman of the Board of Commissioners, Judge Omar Ahmed Mohammed, commenced official international election monitoring duties in the Russian Federation on Friday, September 18, 2026.

The delegation, which includes Chief Electoral Officer Hussein Abdul-Sada Baheer and Board of Commissioners member Abbas Farhan, is participating as accredited international observers for the Russian State Duma parliamentary elections running through September 20, following a formal invitation extended by the Central Election Commission of the Russian Federation.

IHEC confirmed in an official statement that the visit is designed to enhance institutional cooperation, facilitate knowledge exchange on electoral administration, and examine international frameworks for staging large-scale voting processes.

Alongside their direct oversight roles, the Iraqi delegation is taking part in the international forum entitled “Elections in Times of Turmoil,” an expert convening addressing technical, logistical, and administrative mechanisms required to organize and secure democratic balloting under exceptional operational constraints and shifting geopolitical realities.

As part of their official itinerary, the Iraqi commissioners initiated field inspection rounds across several designated polling stations to observe on-the-ground voting workflows firsthand.

The monitoring tour focused on evaluating voting machine operations, logistical organization, ballot management, and queue protocols inside voting centers. IHEC noted that participating in high-level overseas monitoring missions forms a core element of its strategy to benchmark international best practices, integrate comparative operational knowledge, and refine Iraq’s domestic technical and administrative capacities for future electoral cycles.

World.title: Iraq and France work on energy pipeline to Europe
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — France is working with Iraq and Jordan on a pipeline project to transport Iraqi oil and gas to European markets, French President Emmanuel Macron said days after Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Falih al-Zaidi visited Paris for discussions on energy and investment.

Macron stated that the initiative was part of attempts to secure an alternate energy supply for Europe, since the Middle East crisis interrupts conventional shipping routes and raises oil and gas costs.

Iraqi official media said that the planned pipeline would take Iraqi energy via Jordan to European markets.

The statement comes after Al-Zaidi’s official visit to France from September 13 to 14, during which he met with Macron at the Élysée Palace.

The two leaders addressed diversifying energy supply pathways in the wake of delays to Iraqi oil shipments and increased pressure on global energy markets.

During the visit, Iraq and TotalEnergies, a French energy giant, agreed to initiate negotiations on further energy projects, including gas supply collaboration.

TotalEnergies is also looking for a share in the multinational consortium implementing the proposed Basra-Baniyas pipeline, which would give Iraqi petroleum an alternative route from southern oilfields to Syria’s Mediterranean coast, circumventing the Strait of Hormuz.

Chevron, TI Capital, and UCC Holdings of Qatar are all members of the partnership.

The projects highlight Iraq’s quickening efforts to diversify export routes after interruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, which revealed the risk of depending mainly on southern marine terminals for petroleum shipments.

Macron said that Middle Eastern turmoil has exacerbated Europe’s energy challenges, making alternative oil and gas suppliers even more crucial.

France is also advocating for more international cooperation on energy stockpiles and supply, while prices stay high.

For Iraq, new pipeline links via Jordan and Syria might give alternate routes to European clients while lessening its vulnerability to outages in the Arabian Gulf.

World.title: England can build on World Cup ‘spirit’, says Tuchel
World.content:
London – Thomas Tuchel said England will build on the “fantastic spirit” of their World Cup campaign as he targets glory on home soil at Euro 2028.

The England boss was speaking at Wembley after naming a 27-man group for a four-game Nations League camp, starting with a clash against world champions Spain on September 26.

It comes just nine weeks after the end of the World Cup, where England conceded two late goals in a painful semi-final defeat by Argentina.

Real Madrid defender Trent Alexander-Arnold and Chelsea forward Cole Palmer were the headline picks after both were controversially overlooked for the World Cup.

Tuchel also included Liverpool’s teenage winger Rio Ngumoha, uncapped Bournemouth midfielder Alex Scott and Everton defender Jarrad Branthwaite in his first squad since the tournament in North America.

A number of players who were in the World Cup squad including John Stones, Djed Spence, Dan Burn, Jordan Henderson and Dean Henderson missed out through injury.

Former Chelsea and Paris Saint-Germain boss Tuchel said he did not see the Nations League as a new start, instead focusing on continuity.

“I feel that it’s not a new beginning that we are starting now, so we build on a solid and very valuable foundation, and the target is to win the home Euros,” he told reporters on Friday.

Euro 2028 will be co-hosted by England, Scotland, Wales, and Ireland.

The German said his side’s ultimate failure at the World Cup had left him unfulfilled but stuck by his squad picks.

“I had a lot of sleepless nights, but I had not one sleepless night about our selection, because I was more than seven weeks with this group of players, and they were nothing but fantastic,” he said.

“I think the spirit that we built and the mentality that we showed brought us to the place that we got.”

Tuchel said Palmer had impressed for Chelsea early in the season.

“He has his numbers back, he has assists back, he has decisive goals back, so that’s why he’s in the squad and I think he has a point to prove,” he said.

“The same goes for Trent. He was never off the list, he was never in a non-selectable class, and he has this chance to show, to be the best version of himself.”

Tuchel said it was his “duty” to play Manchester United midfielder Kobbie Mainoo after he failed to feature for a single minute at the World Cup.

The England boss welcomed the challenge of taking on Spain at Wembley.

“We feel the gap is closing and we feel that we are close and we want a proof of point,” he said.

“The stadium is sold out, it will be very exciting, the motivation cannot be higher to play against the world champions.”

England also play the Czech Republic twice and Croatia once during the upcoming international window.

World.title: J&K: Fire damages Mata Vaishno Devi helipad terminal in Reasi
World.content:
NEW DELHI: A fire broke out at a helipad terminal in Katra, the base camp for pilgrims visiting the Mata Vaishno Devi Shrine in

's Reasi district, early Sunday, officials said.

The fire started around 3:15 am, apparently due to a short circuit, and was brought under control within 30 minutes through the joint efforts of terminal staff, security personnel and fire and emergency services, officials said, according to news agency PTI.

The helipad terminal, an important transit point for pilgrims travelling to the shrine atop the Trikuta hills, was closed at the time of the incident.

Some computers at the ticket counter and a coffee shop were destroyed in the fire, officials added.

The extent of the damage is being assessed. No casualties have been reported so far.

More details are awaited.

World.title: Toll rises to 31 as 22-hour standoff ends at Pakistan police line HQ
World.content:
What began on Friday as a suicide blast at the compoundâs perimeter gate rapidly developed into an active siege

NEW DELHI: The death toll from the attack on the police lines headquarters in Kohat, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, rose to at least 31, with over 100 injured, as military and police forces concluded the 22-hour-long stand-off Saturday noon.What began on Friday as a suicide blast at the compound's perimeter gate rapidly developed into an active siege after at least seven operatives from the Ittehad-ul-Mujahideen Pakistan (IMP) group breached the counter terrorism department (CTD) and intelligence facilities. In a turn of events, the operatives, once inside, managed to reach the facility's weapons depot, released many detained terror suspects, and armed some of them to fight the Pakistani personnel, sources said.Despite a large deployment, heavy gunfire was exchanged through Friday night and Saturday morning. A military command with the infantry division was used to direct the Pak govt's operation, but strong resistance from inside the lockdown zone prolonged the multi-building standoff, leaving scores wounded and critical.Among those killed were SP Akbar Shinwari, a deputy SP and Dr Israel Orakzai, head of the pediatrics department at Kohat hospital.A few civilians also died in the exchange of fire.Special Service Group (SSG) Zarrar unit and infantry division had to be pressed into service to end the siege and clear the compound. Khyber Police claimed to have neutralised eight of the attackers. The facility, which has been facilitating establishment of new terror camps in KPK region, was struck Friday afternoon with a vehicle-borne improvised explosive device (VBIED), enabling multiple suicide attackers to force their way inside the premises shooting indiscriminately.

World.title: Morning-after pills may get 4 boxed warnings
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Morning-after pills containing levonorgestrel may soon carry four prominent boxed warnings. Govt has proposed that the pills should be labelled clearly as meant only for emergency use, not as regular contraception, not as abortion pills and not as protection against HIV or other sexually transmitted infections.

The proposed warnings will also caution that frequent use may lead to side effects and advise users seeking regular contraception to visit a health facility or a registered medical practitioner.

Dr Megha Tiwari, Consultant, Obstetrics and Gynaecology, Kailash Hospital & Neuro Institute, said emergency contraceptive pills are an important and safe option when used appropriately, but concerns arise when they start being treated as routine contraception.

"We do see women taking it repeatedly after unprotected intercourse, sometimes without understanding that it can disturb the menstrual cycle and cause temporary bleeding irregularities, nausea or anxiety around a delayed period," she said.

"The bigger issue is misinformation. Some women believe the pill can terminate an existing pregnancy, while others assume it offers protection against HIV or other sexually transmitted infections, which it does not," Tiwari said.





She added that the proposed warnings were less about creating fear around emergency contraception and more about ensuring women understood its correct role as a backup method after contraceptive failure, rather than a replacement for regular contraception or condoms.

Join conversation Commentsâ Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

The Ministry of Health and Family Welfare has proposed the changes through a draft amendment to Drugs Rules, 1945, covering levonorgestrel tablets of 0.75 mg and 1.5 mg.

The warnings would have to appear prominently both on the packaging and the package insert.

The proposal also seeks to add levonorgestrel tablets 0.75 mg and 1.5 mg as a specific entry under Schedule K of Drugs Rules, along with conditions relating to their exemption from sale-licence requirements.

However, the warnings are not yet mandatory. The notification is a draft, with 30 days invited for objections and suggestions.

Aadhar mandatory for LPG refills

NEW DELHI: Govt has made biometric Aadhaar authentication mandatory for subsidised domestic LPG refills from Oct 1, reports Atul Mathur.The Union petroleum ministry said nearly 90% of consumers have already completed the authentication process. World.title: India to make 350 kmph bullet trains by 2030, match Japan's E10
World.content:
The current cost of the project works out to around Rs 399 crore per km

Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: India will manufacture indigenous high-speed or bullet trains with a design speed of 350 kmph (B35) by 2030, matching Japan's next-generation E10 series trains that are scheduled for production the same year, according to the railway ministry's Cabinet proposal seeking approval for the revised cost of the Mumbai-Ahmedabad High-Speed Rail (MAHSR) project.Cabinet has approved the revised cost of the project at over Rs 2 lakh crore, nearly double the original estimate prepared in 2015, and the expenditure of nearly Rs 1 lakh crore escalated cost will come from budgetary support.TOI has learnt that the ministry informed the Cabinet it has initiated the process to develop B35 trains after the Japanese side conveyed in Dec 2024 that production of existing E5 series trains was being phased out. It mentions that Japan indicated that production of E10 trains would begin in 2030 and they would be ready for operations by 2034. Officials said deployment of E10 trains would be explored when they become available.The ministry has said that manufacturing of indigenous B28 high-speed trains has been taken up and India will also develop its own Bharat Train Control System (BTCS). The move mirrors China's indigenous CTCS signalling and train control system, which manages speed, spacing and safety across conventional and high-speed rail networks.As per the ministry, sharp increase in project cost from earlier Rs 1.1 lakh crore is largely due to a more than three-fold rise in land acquisition cost to about Rs 19,700 crore; a nearly 50% increase in infrastructure cost to over Rs 1 lakh crore, and around 100% escalation in spending on trains and signalling systems compared with the 2015 estimate.The current cost of the project, excluding future Japanese trains, works out to around Rs 399 crore per km.Initially, the Mumbai-Ahmedabad corridor will operate with B28 trains having a design speed of 280 kmph, while their maximum operating speed will be "249 kmph". BEML has received contracts to manufacture 32 B28 trains.Two prototype trains are expected to be ready for trial runs in the first quarter of 2027. BEML informed the BSE on Friday that it has received a separate Rs 5,400-crore contract to manufacture 15 additional B28 trains. The full 508-km Mumbai-Ahmedabad High-Speed Rail corridor is targeted for completion by Dec 2030.

World.title: As monsoon withdrawal begins, season may end with 10% deficit
World.content:
Monsoon withdrawal has begun

The deficit in rainfall

Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: The southwest (summer) monsoon, which has so far reported a nationwide deficit of 15% in cumulative (June 1-Sept 19) rainfall, started withdrawing from west Rajasthan Saturday, as against the normal date of Sept 17, IMD has said.The line of withdrawal Saturday passed through Ramgarh, Mohangarh, Phalodi and Khajuwala. "Conditions are also favourable for further withdrawal from some more parts of Rajasthan and some parts of Punjab and Saurashtra and Kachchh over the next three-four days," said the Met department.The monsoon normally starts withdrawing from Sept 17 and the process ends on Oct 15 - a few days ahead of the onset of the winter monsoon in peninsular India.As many as 14 states, including Bihar, Punjab, Haryana and all five peninsular states, have reported a rain deficit of more than 20% so far. The current situation shows that the monsoon season is likely to end on Sept 30 with an overall deficit of more than 10% in the country as a whole - a level of rain deficiency which is considered a drought - even as the low pressure area and subsequent depression over east central Bay of Bengal may cause good rain in east India and coastal Odisha next week.Although the sowing of kharif (summer-sown) crops has progressed well despite the El Nino-linked rain deficit, it does not mean the crop sector is out of danger as regional variations and the skewed timing of rainfall may impact overall yield and sowing during next crop (rabi) season. El Nino, a climatic phenomenon involving the warming of ocean surface temperatures in central and eastern equatorial Pacific, is invariably associated with a harsh summer and weak monsoon in India.Acreage data Friday shows that though the overall sown area for all kharif crops has declined this year by just a little over 1%, water-intensive paddy - the most important seasonal crop that accounts for the most acreage - reported a decline of nearly 4% compared to the corresponding period last year.

World.title: The Blue Collar Uniform Hub of Chennai aligns with the times and grows bigger
World.content:
Sydenhams Road in Periamet is the “wardrobe” for blue-collar workers. On this oft-crowded thoroughfare, from the point where the Greater Chennai Corporation’s headquarters (Ripon Building) begins to the point where the Nehru stadium almost ends, around thirty shops, some found in a cluster and others spaced apart, provide passersby with a peek into this wardrobe.

There is something for almost every front-line worker under the sun. Uniforms for security personnel; safety jackets for those working amidst traffic; safety helmets for construction workers; gear tailored for housekeeping staff and conservancy workers; shoes, boots, caps and belts associated with the police force; general caps; and laboratory coats. Let not that “and” hoodwink the reader into thinking this list is exhaustive. It hardly is. Bulk orders placed by corporates, government agencies, education institutions and construction companies, among others, as well as individual purchases sustain this business. And for novelty, orders sometimes fly in from cricket leagues and franchises.

This visual side of Sydenhams Road is familiar for old timers, and it remains its dominant feature. For the superficial eye, little has changed. Can that be said about the eye that has been taking in this “scenery”, day in day out, for years, and even decades? Has anything in the market shifted significantly? As it was established in 1945, United Uniform is probably at an advantage while taking that question. It operates from a shop built into the historic Periamet mosque, established in 1838 by hides and skins traders. After Independence, the mosque would go through two reconstruction exercises, and that would give birth to these shops, partly defining the lower reaches of the mosque on one side. Kashifullah Khan, the third-generation owner of United Uniform, observes this shop was constructed in 1956. At that time, United Uniform was functioning from what was called ‘Red Building’ in Moore Market with the founder and Kashifullah’s grandfather, Hafizullah Khan at the helm.

Kashifullah recalls that the enterprise shifted to its current location in the early 1980s following the much-discussed Moore Market fire, an event that led to the scattering of Moore Market traders dealing in various goods to the nooks and crannies of Madras.

On the question of changes, Kashifullah draws attention to the facade of his shop and those of others in the mosque complex. These shops are noticeably below road level, even coming across as basement shops. With a barely concealed chuckle, he remarks that these shops were once above road level; successive road-laying exercises have got them where they are. In every other aspect, according to him, these small enterprises constituting a segment of the unauthorised sector have been on an upward trajectory.

“There are now more shops in this line of business than ever before,” states Kashifullah, adding the changes have had to do with the major buyers’ mindset, and thankfully, meeting those new expectations is hardly a tough ask.

On the dominant category sold by these shops through the decades, Kashfullah points out that in the 1980s, the focus was largely on police-related products, and then a shift happened, with greater attention now being accorded to medical items, the coats, then NCC and Scouts uniforms and accessories. From the 2010s, safety gear is the major grosser: safety shoes, jackets and helmets easily constitute the highest-selling category, he states. Yet another noticeable shift has to do with the choice of material for the making of shoes. Around 15 to 17 years ago, the scales tipped in favour of rexine over leather. And Kashifullah believes this change has been driven primarily by “large-scale manufacturing of rexine in Gujarat and Haryana. Some people even import rexine from Korea and China.”

If one parsed through the resilience of these shops, one factor emerges strongly, a bond that goes beyond a common trade. Kashifullah puts a ballpark number on the shops in this line of business on Sydenhams Road, thirty-five, and adds that out of that, around 90 per cent of them are run by those that are part of his extended family. He admits there is competitive pricing, but there is also cooperation. In this climate, sourcing items not in one’s stock from others is possible.

One senses a strong sense of connection and continuity best epitomised by Kashifullah himself. He is essentially a techie, having had a long stint in the IT industry, and he peeled himself from it to keep a family legacy going. He joined this business four years ago following his father Shafiullah’s death in 2022.

The narrative about connections and continuity gains greater ground as more conversations are initiated with these tradespeople. At Khaleel Cap Mart, a misnomer, as they sell uniforms and accessories in addition to caps, Quraishi, 45, who first came to the shop at age 12 during his school days, remarks that the name ‘Cap Mart’ is a reminder of those early years. The shop originally specialised in caps, from turbans and Muslim prayer caps or Kufis to Kashmiri caps. As customer requirements changed. So did the shop’s inventory. One of the shop’s most distinctive products is not necessarily the most conspicuous. Its cotton mosquito nets are made in the traditional way and remain popular among police personnel at various police residential quarters. Depending on the bed type, they cost between ₹500 and ₹1,500. Started by Khaleel Ur Rahman, the shop is now run by Quraishi and his brother Nayeem. Quraishi echoes Kahifullah’s sentiment that this business is on an even keel.

Speaking for the tradespeople in his line of business on Sydenhams Road, Quraishi observes digital buying has left no dent in their business. “Individuals might buy a cap online; for bulk orders, they come to us.”

(Old Markets, New Trends is a column that features markets that have continued to retain their hold on people’s mindspace despite the shifting sands of fads. Through entities that have been around for a long time, it seeks to find out what makes these markets tick)

World.title: CM Rekha Gupta, former CM Kejriwal among those to get notices amid Delhi SIR
World.content:
Delhi Chief Minister Rekha Gupta and former Chief Minister Arvind Kejriwal were among 33.1 lakh electors in the Delhi draft electoral roll for whom notices have been generated, either because of “logical discrepancies” in their voter details or because their details were not mapped to the previous Special Intensive Revision (SIR) exercise.

Also Read: Delhi draft electoral roll: names flagged for 11 ‘logical discrepancies’

The Delhi Chief Electoral Officer on Friday (September 18, 2026) published the list of electors flagged for discrepancies. Those on the list will have to get their documents verified to feature in the final roll.

Other prominent names to figure in this list include former Vice President Jagdeep Dhankhar and his wife Sudesh Dhankhar, former Supreme Court judge Justice Madan B. Lokur, former Union Minister Kapil Sibal and his wife Promila Sibal, former Union Minister Subramanian Swamy, Delhi Minister Parvesh Sahib Singh, former Delhi BJP president Virendra Kumar Sachdeva, historian Romila Thapar, and New Delhi MP Bansuri Swaraj.

While Congress MP Abhishek Manu Singhvi is also on the list, the slot for the reason his name was flagged was left blank.

CM’s documents validated

Ms. Gupta’s name figures in the list of electors flagged for notices in Part Number 123 of the Shalimar Bagh Assembly constituency. The Election Commission’s (EC’s) software flagged her name for an “age gap of less than 15 years between a parent and progeny”.

Economist Bibek Debroy, who passed away in 2024, flagged for notice in Delhi SIR

Later on Saturday, the electoral registration officer (ERO) of Shalimar Bagh said that following a physical verification of documents at Ms. Gupta’s address, her name has been validated for inclusion in the final electoral roll. “In accordance with the standard operating procedures of the Election Commission of India (ECI), a Notice was issued to the elector & physical field verification was conducted by the designated Booth Level Officer (BLO),” a press note said.

The system also flagged Justice Lokur’s name, saying the age gap between him and his grandfather was not more than 40 years. Justice Lokur is a voter in the Malviya Nagar constituency.

Delhi Minister Mr. Singh's name was flagged for “self-name mismatch”, which means a mismatch between the name given during the current SIR process and the previous roll. Mr. Sachdeva’s name was also flagged for “self-name mismatch”.

There are 11 categories of such discrepancies in Delhi, including a mismatch in names between the current and previous rolls, more than six progeny being linked to the same parent, an age gap of less than 40 years between a voter and a grandparent, and a mismatch in the father’s name or the relative to whom an elector has been linked. Similar categories of mapping anomalies have been identified by the EC in SIR exercises in other States.

Around 19.3 lakh electors in Delhi have been flagged for such “logical discrepancies”.

‘No mapping’ category

Mr. Kejriwal’s name, along with those of his parents, Gobind Ram Kejriwal and Gita Devi, wife Sunita Kejriwal and son Pulkit Kejriwal, has been flagged under the “no mapping” category. The names of Mr. Dhankhar and Ms. Dhankhar, Mr. Sibal and Ms. Sibal, Mr. Swamy, and Ms. Thapar were also flagged in this category.

Another name to figure in this category was that of Ms. Swaraj, the daughter of former Union Minister and Delhi Chief Minister Sushma Swaraj and former Mizoram Governor Swaraj Kaushal.

This category covers electors whose details, or those of a close relative, could not be linked to the previous SIR roll during the enumeration exercise.

Electors in the no-mapping category will have to establish their eligibility by submitting documents from the 12 documents prescribed by the EC for the verification process.

A senior election official said prominent leaders and other well-known personalities would not be required to visit hearing centres. EROs will prepare a list of such cases and direct booth-level officers (BLOs) to visit their registered addresses to verify and resolve the discrepancies, the official said.

The 33.1 lakh electors who have received notices constitute roughly one-third of the 97.5 lakh electors included in the draft roll. The verification and disposal of these cases are to be completed by October 29, while the final electoral roll is scheduled to be published on November 4.

World.title: Asian Games 2026 LIVE: Elavenil Valarivan leads India’s shooting charge with double silver on opening day
World.content:
India began its Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games campaign with a strong showing in shooting, securing silver in the women’s 10m air rifle team event. Elavenil Valarivan, Sonam Maskar and Vidarsa Vinod finished second behind China, which set a world record with 1904.2 points. Elavenil also claimed individual silver, scoring 252.4 in the final, while Japan’s Hinata Taichi won gold with an Asian Games record 253.0.

Also read: India open shooting campaign with silver in women’s 10m air rifle team event

India also enjoyed impressive starts in hockey, MMA and table tennis. Deepika scored eight goals as the Indian women’s hockey team thrashed Uzbekistan 19-0 in their opening Pool B match. Suchika Tariyal assured India of a medal by reaching the women’s Traditional MMA 60kg semifinals with a 2-0 win over Mongolia’s Altanchimeg Baigalmaa. Meanwhile, India’s women’s table tennis team defeated Indonesia 3-0 in its opening Group F fixture.

Also read: India women open table tennis campaign with 3-0 win over Indonesia

The 20th Asian Games officially opened in Nagoya on September 19 and will run until October 4, featuring around 11,000 athletes from 45 nations competing across 43 sports and 469 gold-medal events. India will aim to build on its record 107-medal haul at Hangzhou 2023, including 28 gold medals, while seeking to defend its cricket and kabaddi titles. The men’s hockey team will also enter the competition as defending champions.

Also read: Full India schedule with key events

(With agency inputs)

World.title: Five injured in attack by neighbours
World.content:
Five members of a family, including two children, were injured when their neighbours attacked them in Benakatti in Yaragatti taluk in Belagavi district on Saturday (September 19, 2026) night.

Family members of Rudrappa were attending a funeral when a neighbour began abusing them. When Rudrappa objected to it, around a dozen members of the neighbour’s family came to Rudrappa’s house and beat him up.

They also beat up his wife, brother and children. The injured have been admitted to the district hospital where they are undergoing treatment. Doctors told the police that they were out of danger.

A case has been registered.

World.title: Delhi Police head constable, wife found dead in Narela; children find flat locked from inside
World.content:
A Delhi Police head constable allegedly strangled his wife before ending his life at their second-floor flat in Narela on Saturday (September 19, 2026), police said. The couple were found dead in the same room.

The deceased were identified as Head Constable Monu, 40, who was posted in North district, and his wife Meenu, 35.
