World.title: Eumir Marcial sits out 2026 Asian Games after latest pro win
World.content:
POWER. Eumir Marcial in action for the Philippines in the 2025 Southeast Asian Games.

Eumir Marcial is skipping this Asian Games edition owing to the 'tight timeline' that requires him to promptly fly to Nagoya, Japan, from San Diego, United States, where he scored a third-round knockout win over Omar Ulises Huerta

MANILA, Philippines – The power Eumir Marcial showcased in his latest professional fight will not be on display at the Asian Games.

The Olympic bronze medalist is sitting out this edition of the continental showpiece owing to the “tight timeline” that requires him to promptly fly to Nagoya, Japan, from San Diego, United States, where he scored a third-round knockout win over Omar Ulises Huerta on Saturday, September 19 (Sunday, September 20, Manila time), to keep his professional record unblemished at 8-0.

Association of Boxing Alliances in the Philippines president Marcus Jarwin Manalo said he spoke to Marcial after the bout, and they agreed that it would be best for the pride of Zamboanga to skip the Asian Games and allow himself to rest and recover.

“It would be very hard for him to immediately transition from a professional fight in the US, into long-distance travel to Nagoya with 16-hour time difference, and then into another high-level boxing competition with such a short recovery period,” Manalo said in a statement released on Sunday.

“Boxing is a physically demanding and inherently risky sport, and adequate time to rest and recover is extremely important, and we do not want to compromise Eumir’s health and safety because of the tight timeline.”

Losing Marcial is a major blow to the Philippines’ hopes of ending a 16-year gold-medal drought in Asian Games boxing, considering his performances in the last two editions.

Marcial fell short of gold in the 2023 staging in Hangzhou, China, where he suffered a contentious unanimous decision loss to home bet Tuohetaerbieke Tanglatihan in the men’s 80kg final.

He also bagged bronze in the men’s 75kg class at the 2018 edition in Jakarta, Indonesia.

But for Manalo, it was a necessary move, with Marcial’s long-term career in mind.

“Eumir himself was very much looking forward to the opportunity to represent the flag once again. This is therefore a difficult decision for everyone involved,” said Manalo.

“However, representing the Philippines is not only about stepping into the ring. It is also about making responsible decisions that protect our athletes and allow them to have long, healthy careers.”

Marcial is still slated to represent the country at the Asian Indoor and Martial Arts Games in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, in December.

“We sincerely hope for understanding that this decision was made with Eumir’s best interests in mind. His commitment to Philippine boxing and to representing the country has never been in question,” said Manalo. – Rappler.com

World.title: Day jobs and dreams: Dubai OFWs chase indie film spotlight
World.content:
Despite the demands of their regular jobs, these passionate Dubai OFWs pursue unpaid acting projects, with some even earning recognition at international film festivals

DUBAI, United Arab Emirates – Some 70 overseas Filipino workers (OFWs), whose day jobs range from hairdressers and grocery store merchandisers to office clerks, teachers, DJs, and finance professionals, have pursued their dream of acting on camera with the help of an award-winning Filipino indie director who brought them together and produced films for competition.

No one gets paid, including the director, and the films explore alternative themes seldom found in the mainstream.

“Cinema has never been simply about entertainment,” said Francis L.J. Gacer, director and founder of Kikoman Films (KMF), an independent production outfit. “It is about bearing witness.”

Francis, fondly called “Direk Kiko,” said he has been engaged in filmmaking for the past 10 years because “every Filipino has a story worth telling, and every voice deserves to be heard.”

And so the KMF, a UAE-licensed “creative sanctuary” for migrant artists where every talent can “flourish,” hopes to discover more experiences that “could become stories…voices [that could be heard on] the screen.”

The production house has been the go-to place of OFWs wishing to hone their acting talents.

Actor Ron Jordan de Ocampo Actresses Pamela Villadiego and Trixie Mae Tautuan

“I wanted to continue growing as an actor and be part of a community of people who genuinely love filmmaking,” said Pamela Villadiego, who works in the marketing department of a company while freelancing as a DJ.

“Acting has been part of my life since I was young, and being in Dubai didn’t make me want to stop. Instead, I wanted to find a way to continue telling stories and challenging myself as an artist.”

Pamela has won Best Actor in the American Golden Picture International Film Festival (AGPIFF), Southeast Asia International Film Festival (SEAIFF), and the Sweden International Film Festival (SIFF) for her role as a human trafficking victim in the 45-minute, true-to-life short film Alimbukay (Nausea). The film also won Best Psychological Film in the recent Emirates Film Festival (EFF).

“I have upcoming films this year, Sa Manlulupig and When Life Gives You Lemons, which we will shoot this month. Aside from acting, I’ve also been involved behind the scenes, particularly in production as camera woman,” said Pamela.

Gudelia “Lia” Rodriguez said she was just a curious bystander when she found herself playing a role.

“Acting has always been one of the things on my bucket list and I really thought it was a long shot, but here I am. Never did I imagine that a dream, at my age, may come true,” she said.

“I joined because it gives ordinary people a chance to shine, explore their creativity and discover talents they may not even know they have,” added Lia, who has been working in finance for the past 24 years.

Lia Rodriguez

Lia played a role in the award-winning horror film Batingaw, where she played the lead character’s sidekick. She also appeared as an extra in Alimbukay and in 100 Uploads.

“There are two lined-up films where I am part of this 2026 for scheduled shooting as well,” Pamela shared

Another artist, Trixie Mae Tautuan, works as an administrative assistant at a trading company. She has starred in three short films — Alimbukay, Sa Paghupa ng Unos, and Salamism — and remains busy shooting other projects this year.

“At first, it was not in the plan. A friend just had me tag along to an acting workshop. I tried it out of curiosity, and, at the same time, for experience since I’m fond of movies. I thought there was nothing to lose anyway,” Trixie said.

Also looking for something new to do on her weekends, hairdresser and makeup artist Jessica Leano Miranda replied to a KMF social media casting call.

“As I am an artist doing hair and makeup, I worked in an Arabic TV Channel here in Dubai years ago and I love watching movies, I got so interested to try it,” she said.

Jessica so far has two films under her belt: Tahan Tahanan, her first supporting role where she played a grandmother left to take care of a physically-challenged grandchild; and Batingaw, where she won an EFF acting award.

Jessica Leano Miranda KMF director and founder Francis L. J. Gacer

Amor Nano Matildo, a finance and logistics assistant at a manufacturing company for 16 years, said acting is one of her “passions in life” and a dream she hopes to conquer.

“I joined Kikoman Films because the films I’ve seen have meaning and sense, and also lessons,” she said.

Amor has played roles in four films last year: Bidyo-Oke, Remember Mercy, Paghupa ng Unos, and Tilamsik sa Dakilang Apoy. She’s busy shooting two films this year: Ang Dalisay and Reasong Razon.

Amor Nano Matildo

Ron Jordan de Ocampo, a supermarket shelf stocker by day, has likewise become a regular actor for KMF, playing roles in 12 films.

“Each project has given me valuable experience and helped me grow as an actor,” he said.

Becoming an actor was “already a dream” for De Ocampo, who has always loved watching movies, especially indie films, even when he was still in the Philippines.

One of the most intense films De Ocampo has appeared in is Tilamsik sa Dakilang Apoy, where he starred as a former New People’s Army (NPA) combatant who, having been afflicted with a medical condition in the hills, returned home to his wife and daughter.

In playing the role, De Ocampo won Best Actor at the Global India International Film Festival (GIIFF) and Most Promising Actor at EFF.

He also won Best Actor in two other films, Apo and Malakaya, at the World Film Carnival Singapore (WFCS) and the Gully International Film Festival (GIFF).

Ron Jordan de Ocampo

What started as a dream became a passion for De Ocampo, who met his wife at KMF.

“And now we have our baby girl, Baby Melon, who has also become part of some of our film experiences,” De Ocampo shared.

The actors said time management plays an important part in their task, as they memorize and practice the scripts after work on weekdays and shoot the film on weekends.

Since KMF’s inception in 2016, more than 25 film productions have reaped awards and recognition in various festivals in France, USA, Russia, Singapore, India, Turkey, Czech Republic, Spain, Philippines, Sweden, Italy, Hungary, and UAE, among others.

Direk Kiko, who usually comes up with ideas for the scripts, said 12 films are being lined up for 2027. He also supervises the acting workshops.

The director noted that plans are also underway to open KMF to non-Filipino talent, building on the six foreign members already among its 76-strong roster.

“Whenever I drive, I record my voice and speak of an idea for a story. Also, most of the time, I keep a small notebook and a pen in my bag,” said Direk Kiko, who also works as a producer and designer at a big retail firm. His superiors at the company support him, he shared, even attending last month’s KMF Gala Night.

“I still remember writing a script on the plane on my way back to Dubai from Saudi Arabia and the film eventually won awards in Kalayaan Independence Day celebration.” He also listens to nationalistic and progressive songs, the director said, “and from there, ideas flood me.” – Rappler.com

Some quotes have been translated to English for brevity.

World.title: How to know if you can trust an AI’s answer to your question
World.content:
It might be useful to sort AI answers into an ‘answer typography’ of four broad types: factual, interpretive, constructive, and strategic

I recently typed a simple question into Google search: How much screen time is too much for teenagers? Instead of presenting links, as Google had been doing for many years, it gave me an AI-generated answer.

The artificial intelligence agent cited a number, then complicated that reply, noting that quality and balance of time could matter more than the number of hours, and that “too much” time could depend on a teenager’s sleep, exercise, school demands and mood.

I tried another search: Should I take a daily aspirin? This time the AI answer presented me with medical information, warned about risks and offered more tailored guidance if I provided my age and medical history.

These were good replies. What interested me was that they were different kinds of replies.

Debate about AI answers has focused on accuracy: Did the system get the answer right? That matters, but accuracy is only one test. Each kind of answer requires a user to judge something different.

I find it useful to sort AI answers into an “answer typography” of four broad types: factual, interpretive, constructive, and strategic.

A factual claim can often be checked against a source. An interpretation can be accurate and still reflect choices about which evidence matters. A construction can be well reasoned and still be wrong for the person receiving it. A beautifully written strategic document may not be true. Yet AI presents all four types of answers in much the same fluent, authoritative form; the differences are easy to miss.

I’m university librarian and dean of libraries at the University of Virginia who leads national efforts to develop AI competencies for library professionals, and I consult widely on AI literacy. I first proposed the typography in the Journal of Academic Librarianship.

The four categories are not airtight boxes. A response from an AI agent can reflect several types. That said, I describe each type of answer below, and offer guidance for deciding whether a reply is ready to use or needs more investigation.

Which answer is Google giving you?

A factual answer makes a claim that can, in principle, be checked against evidence. When was the University of Virginia founded? What is the chemical symbol for gold?

To determine whether a factual answer is robust enough for you to use, verify the claim against an appropriate source. If the answer cites a source, follow that link instead of simply treating the answer itself as proof.

An interpretive reply is built on evidence, but there is not a single takeaway. How much screen time is too much for a teenager? Does remote work raise productivity? The answer depends on what evidence is included, what is left out and how disagreement is understood.

Google’s initial answer to my screen-time question indicated that two hours was a limit for teenagers. Then it noted that pediatric guidance puts more weight on the quality and context of screen use than on simple hours. The American Academy of Pediatrics says there is no exact recommended amount for teens and emphasizes the kind of screen use and what activities it might be displacing. A question that looked numerical turned out to require interpretation.

To assess interpretive answers, do more than check facts. Ask yourself what evidence the system emphasized, what it left out and whether another defensible interpretation exists. A useful follow-up question to present to the search engine is: “What is the strongest evidence for a different conclusion?”

Constructive answers are made rather than discovered. Ask AI to draft a cover letter, write a eulogy, suggest a lesson plan or reorganize a paragraph — there is no single correct result.

You can judge the response by considering purpose, audience and voice. A eulogy can be grammatically perfect and still sound nothing like the person delivering it, or it may land flat on family members hearing it. It may not capture the deceased person well, either. Consider these kinds of effects as you read.

Strategic questions ask what to do. Should I take a daily aspirin? Should I buy the house? The answers combine information with judgment about goals, risks, trade-offs and personal circumstances.

My aspirin search shows why context matters. Google warned about risks, told me to consult a medical professional and offered more tailored information if I provided my age, cardiovascular history and risk of bleeding. That caution matches the US Preventive Services Task Force guidance. It says the decision to start low-dose aspirin for prevention of heart attacks and strokes should be individualized and weigh cardiovascular benefit against bleeding risk.

For strategic answers, ask what the system would need to know before its advice could reasonably apply to you individually. Consider the stakes, the alternatives and whether a qualified person should be involved. For the aspirin question, a useful follow-up would be: “What details about my age, medical history or bleeding risk could change this advice? What should I discuss with my doctor before deciding?” The final judgment remains yours because you are the person who has to live with the outcome.

The first question after an answer

My questions began as ordinary Google searches. I did not open a chatbot. The AI-generated responses simply arrived, and links were appended.

The responses were useful. Google added context, acknowledged complications and offered tailored guidance if I supplied additional information. Within each response, though, the type of answer could change. Reporting what a medical guideline says is different from deciding how it applies to a particular person. A fluent response can move between those types of answers without a noticeable change in voice.

As a user, try to recognize what kind of intellectual work the AI agent did for a response you receive. Consider whether the interpretation is persuasive or the advice fits your circumstances.

Before asking whether an AI answer is right, ask a more basic question: What kind of answer is this? The type will tell you what to do next. – Rappler.com

Leo S. Lo is a dean at the University of Virginia.

World.title: [Just Saying] Phantom judges in the impeachment court
World.content:
Constitutional provisions must never be fragmented and parsed into isolated words and phrases, each assigned a standalone meaning detached from the whole

Article XI Section 3(6) of the 1987 Constitution provides:

The Senate shall have the sole power to try and decide all cases of impeachment. When SITTING FOR THAT PURPOSE, the Senators shall be on OATH OR AFFIRMATION. When the President of the Philippines is on trial, the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court shall preside, but shall not vote. No person shall be convicted without the concurrence of two-thirds of ALL MEMBERS OF THE SENATE.

A. The Transformation: Oath and Sitting Status

A senator does not automatically become an impeachment judge by virtue of holding legislative office. Section 3(6) mandates a structural metamorphosis: Senators become trial judges only when they take a separate oath or affirmation and officially convene by “sitting for that purpose” — specifically, “to try and decide.”

Therefore, the phrase “all the Members of the Senate” qualified to vote on conviction must refer exclusively to the pool of Senators who accomplish two elements: 1. Taking their oath and 2. actively sitting in the impeachment court. Both must concur. Non-accomplishment of one excludes a senator or a senator judge from “all members of the Senate.”

Because Section 3(6), Article XI of the 1987 Constitution was directly transplanted from prior constitutional texts, its construction does not depend on the speculative intent of the 1986 Framers, but on the plain, ordinary understanding of the People who ratified it. And even if there were deliberations regarding the provision, still the so-called intention of the framers must yield to the understanding of the people.

To the ratifying public, the choice of the word “sitting” in the phrase “sitting for that purpose” was not casual legalese; it is a deliberate, everyday term chosen because it naturally conveys a dual purpose:

1. The Dual Meaning of “Sitting”

The term “sitting for that purpose” seamlessly captures both the legal capacity and the physical act required of an impeachment adjudicator:

Capacity to Act as a Judge (De Jure Authority):

In popular understanding, a judge “sits” on the bench when invested with jurisdiction. When a senator takes the required special oath or affirmation, they undergo a constitutional metamorphosis — stripping off their pure legislative identity to assume the legal capacity of a judicial officer. “Sitting for that purpose” marks the assumption of this distinct judicial office.

Mandated Presence in Conducting the Trial (De Facto Exercise):

Simultaneously, “sitting” is a factual descriptor. An ordinary citizen understands that a court cannot “sit” in a vacuum. To be “sitting” means to be physically present, in the chair, actively conducting and hearing the proceedings. A judge who is absent is not “sitting.”

By fusing these two concepts into a single term easily understood by the public, the text establishes that legal capacity without physical presence does not constitute “sitting,” and therefore cannot qualify a Senator to be counted among the baseline of “all the Members of the Senate” who “try and decide” the case.

Simply, judicial power of a court which is a “trier of facts” which, in turn is the attribute of an impeachment court cannot be divorced from its exercise. And its exercise requires presence.

B. Elucidation Across Four Perspectives

Historical perspective

Historically, Anglo-American trial tradition — from which this constitutional text was borrowed almost verbatim — treats a tribunal as a body that operates only when its members physically “sit” in court. To the public that ratified the Constitution, the term “sitting” carried the settled historical weight of court sessions: a tribunal “sits” when its judges gather in person to take evidence. The phrase was retained precisely because its historic, dual meaning — signifying both judicial session and physical attendance —was well established in public consciousness.

Constitutional perspective

Synthesizing the text, Section 3(6) creates a strict operational sequence:

1. The Oath/Affirmation: Grants the senator the capacity to act as a judge.

2. Sitting for the Purpose: Combines that judicial *capacity* with actual presence in the tribunal.

3. To Try and Decide: Dictates the action permitted only to those who are currently “sitting.”

If “all the Members of the Senate” were interpreted as a raw count of all elected legislators regardless of presence, the phrase “sitting for that purpose” would be rendered redundant surplusage. Constitutional interpretation dictates that every word must be given effect. “Sitting” qualifies the baseline of senators to only those who possess both the judicial capacity and the active presence during the trial.

Practical perspective

From a practical and common-sense perspective — the exact lens through which the ratifying public viewed the text — a person cannot “try” a case they did not watch or hear. The duty “to try” requires observing witnesses, evaluating demeanor, and weighing live evidence. The word “sitting” vividly communicates this physical necessity. The ordinary voter understood that you cannot judge a trial from afar; “sitting” requires being in the room where the trial takes place.

Political perspective

Politically, the double meaning of “sitting” prevents a grave constitutional abuse: the participation of “phantom judges.” If capacity alone were enough without mandated presence, politically aligned Senators could skip the trial, avoid hearing damaging evidence against an ally or opponent, and emerge at the final hour merely to vote. The requirement of “sitting” — meaning both holding the sworn capacity and maintaining actual presence — ensures that only those who endured the burden and public scrutiny of the bench are empowered to render judgment.

Conclusion

The ratifying people understood “sitting” in its common, intuitive sense. By retaining this exact word from previous Constitutions, the text enshrines a clear rule: to be counted among “all the Members of the Senate” who decide an impeachment, a senator must have taken the oath to gain the capacity of a judge, and must be actively present (“sitting”) in the trial court.

Constitutional provisions must never be fragmented and parsed into isolated words and phrases, each assigned a standalone meaning detached from the whole. A text adopted verbatim across generations must be construed as an integrated, seamless structure, interpreted continuously in the light of the Constitution’s enduring principles — chiefly due process, which demands that those who decide must actually hear the evidence, and participatory democracy, which requires active, transparent, and accountable engagement rather than passive partisan head counts.

It is entirely understandable that the ouster of a high official elected by the sovereign people should carry a heavy measure of difficulty. However, difficulty must never be equated with absurdity. The claim advanced by some sectors — that fixing the two-thirds threshold to an inflexible 16 senator-judges saves the impeachment process from political manipulation — may sound superficially plausible. Yet, if applied, forcing such a rigid number regardless of how many senators actually qualify, take the oath, and sit for the trial produces an irrational implementation that is far more destructive of the constitutional process itself.

Isolating the phrase “all the Members of the Senate” from its constitutional anchors — “sitting for that purpose” and the requirement of a distinct oath — shatters this holistic design. Departing from these fundamental rules of interpretation produces an obviously absurd result: an impeachment court where non-attending, unsworn, or non-participating legislators can decide the fate of a trial they never witnessed. Such an outcome subverts the foundational guarantees of judicial fairness and democratically accountable governance, yielding a practical impossibility that only a clever manipulation of semantics can ostensibly justify. – Rappler.com

Mel Sta. Maria is former dean of the Far Eastern University Institute of Law. He teaches law at FEU, the Ateneo School of Law, the University of Sto. Tomas, Pamantasan ng Lungsod ng Maynila, University of Makati, and Manuel L. Quezon University. He also hosts shows on both radio and YouTube, and has authored several books on law, politics, and current events.

World.title: PH earns first 2026 Asian Games medal with historic bronze in soft tennis
World.content:
MEDALISTS. The Philippine women's tennis team of (from left) Hilary Paas, Princess Catindig, Bien Zoleta, Christy Sañosa, Shyryn Salazar deliver in the 2026 Asian Games.

The quintet of Bien Zoleta, Princess Catindig, Hilary Paas, Shyryn Salazar, and Christy Sañosa make history as the Philippines secures its first-ever podium finish in Asian Games soft tennis

MANILA, Philippines – It did not take long for the Philippines to break the medal ice at the Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan.

Less than 24 hours after the opening ceremony, the country won its first medal courtesy of the women’s soft tennis team, which bagged a bronze despite its 2-0 loss to defending champion Japan in the semifinals at the Higashiyama Park Tennis Center on Sunday, September 20.

Aside from delivering the Philippines’ maiden medal in this edition of the continental showpiece, the quintet of Bien Zoleta, Princess Catindig, Hilary Paas, Shyryn Salazar, and Christy Sañosa made history as the country secured its first podium finish in Asian Games soft tennis.

“It’s such an overwhelming feeling because this isn’t just for us, it’s for the Philippines, especially knowing that we’re the first ones to get a medal. We hope this can boost the morale of other national athletes who will be competing in the coming days,” Zoleta told reporters in a mix of Filipino and English.

“We really worked to win this, especially here in the Asian Games. For us in soft tennis, this is our Olympics. So to win a medal here means so much to us.”

The Philippines started its campaign with a 3-0 win over Mongolia and a 2-1 victory over Thailand.

Although it wrapped up the preliminary round with a 0-3 loss to Chinese Taipei, the Philippines still earned a top-two finish in Group B to advance to the semifinals and assure itself of a medal.

In the semifinals, Japan — which ruled the women’s team event in three of the last four editions, including the last two — displayed its dominance.

Zoleta and Catindig absorbed a 5-0 loss to Rena Temma and Kiho Miyamae in the opening doubles match before Sañosa fell to Ayaka Iwakura, 4-0, in singles play, paving the way for Japan to return to the finals.

But the defeat did little to wipe the smiles off the Filipinas’ faces as the country finally broke through in a sport that made its Asian Games debut in 1994.

“We are very, very proud and very, very happy to win a medal for the country,” said Zoleta. – Rappler.com

World.title: Local cavers confront fear, discover hidden world in Samar
World.content:
STUNNING. Cavers pose in front of giant columns inside Teta Cave, part of the Langun-Gobingob Cave System.

What begins as an adventure into one of the Philippines’ largest cave systems becomes a firsthand journey through fear, discovery, and wildlife — and a reminder that Samar’s underground landscapes are worth exploring and protecting

CALBIGA, Samar – For nearly an hour, Michael Salingsing, a 57-year-old teacher at Samar National School, sat patiently on a camp chair beside his tent near the mouth of Langun Cave, his Sony A7 IV camera pointed toward the dark opening.

He was waiting for the 5 pm bat exodus.

Then the first bats appeared.

Soon, the quiet of the late afternoon gave way to the sweeping movement of thousands of bats emerging from the cave and disappearing into the fading Samar sky.

Salingsing kept his camera trained on them. For him, the wait was part of the experience.

“It’s a different experience,” Salingsing said between shots.

Local cavers make their way into the Gobingob Cave entrance. Photo by Ricky Bautista

Fear to fascination

For YouTuber Genesis Fortaleza, a member of the Calbayog Mountaineering and Outdoor Group (CMOG), the experience began with a different challenge: fear.

He had been hesitant to enter Langun-Gobingob, not only because of its reputation as the largest known cave system in the Philippines, but also because of the dangers he imagined waiting in the darkness.

He decided to go in anyway.

Fortaleza brought sets of lightings and a 360-degree camera, recording the cave’s formations and the bats circling near the campsite.

He had initially overthought the possible dangers of entering the cave, but eventually realized that unless he confronted his fear, he would never know what beauty was hidden below the surface.

The journey was far from easy. The group descended steep sections, negotiated slippery rocks, walked through knee-deep mud and guano, and stood before towering formations that have developed over extraordinarily long periods.

With the guidance of the Speleo Samar PH team, however, the journey became more manageable. Once inside, the fear gradually gave way to fascination.

Fortaleza described the cave as another dimension, a quiet world of extraordinary beauty that is not easily seen by everyone.

“Minsan, kailangan mo talagang tumawid sa sarili mong dilim para lang makita ang totoong liwanag (Sometimes, you have to cross your own darkness to see the true light),” he said.

A caver descends a 30-meter cliff with the help of a rope and a cave guide. Photo by Ricky Bautista

An adventurer but first-time caver, Jennifer Pallones admitted that the darkness was also something to overcome.

Pallones, also a teacher, said she was afraid to enter the cave, and it took a friend who had joined the activity to persuade her to try. She eventually went in.

After completing the experience, Pallones said she now felt ready to join another cave activity, having overcome her fear of enclosed or confined spaces.

For Hope Doblon and other participants, the defining challenge came during a steep vertical descent.

“It was tough, but I’m glad I’ve survived it,” Doblon, a city government employee, said. “This is surely an addition to my caving experience, especially since I have a fear of heights.”

Light filters through the cave. Photo by Jennifer Pallones A picturesque camping site inside the cave. Photo by Jedee Magoncia

Enormous chambers

Langun-Gobingob in Barangay Panayuran in Samar’s Calbiga town is not an ordinary cave. It’s recognized as the largest known cave system in the Philippines, with an explored area reported at about 2,968 hectares and 12 immense chambers extending across roughly seven kilometers.

For people entering it for the first time, however, statistics quickly become secondary. Inside, the numbers become walls.

They become towering formations disappearing into darkness, enormous chambers swallowing the beam of a headlamp, and passages that make the outside world feel impossibly far away.

Participants Aura Anne Rose Tan, Rhea Libungan, Joel Lauron, Albert Dagal, and Jedee Magoncia, along with the other members of the group, experienced that underground landscape firsthand.

“Grabe, once-in-a-lifetime experience talaga ito, di na kami uulit (This is a once-in-a-lifetime experience, we won’t do this again),” participants joked as they confronted the steep wall descent.

The humor eased some of the tension, but the physical challenge was real.

The author, Ricky Bautista, poses in front of a towering stalagmites inside the Langun-Gobingob Cave. Contributed photo Genesis Fortaleza poses in amazement at ‘The Stage,’ a striking flowstone formation. Contributed photo

Caving is not simply walking into a hole in the ground. It requires preparation, knowledge of the environment, appropriate equipment, teamwork and respect for the limitations of both the people and the cave.

The participants also got to experience the technical side of caving through a rope-assisted descent of a steep vertical section.

“Grabe, hindi kami na-orient beforehand na may ganito pala (We weren’t oriented beforehand that we’ll do something like this),” participants joked while trying to negotiate the descent.

For some, it was physically demanding. For others, it was a test of nerve.

Doblon’s fear of heights made the descent particularly challenging.

“It was botake (short for bonggang atake or major heart attack) and tough, but I’m glad I’ve survived it,” he said.

The bat exodus at Langun Cave. Photo by Ricky Bautista

The experience left participants with a deeper appreciation of the skills and discipline involved in moving through underground environments.

Caving requires more than physical strength. It demands judgment.

A misplaced step can have consequences. A careless movement can damage a fragile formation. An inexperienced visitor can put both himself and his companions at risk.

That is why responsible caving places equal importance on safety and conservation.

Bats, crabs, gobies

The timing of the activity wasn’t coincidence. The Speleo Samar PH Inc. joined the global observance of the first International Day of Caves and Karst on September 13, an annual observance proclaimed by UNESCO in 2025.

The organizers introduced participants to cave management and responsible caving, including the importance of minimizing disturbance to cave formations and wildlife.

For the visitors at Langun-Gobingob, the bats should not be merely part of the attraction as they’re using the cave as a roost and the surrounding landscape as part of the habitat they depend on.

Deep inside the cave, pale freshwater crabs have also adapted to life underground.

Samar is known to harbor cave-dwelling freshwater crabs of the genus Sundathelphusa, some of which show adaptations associated with subterranean environment, including reduced eyes, lighter pigmentation and elongated legs.

A cave-adapted freshwater crab. Photo by Ricky Bautista

The cave is also known for the blind cave gobies or the Caecogobius cryptophthalmus, a specie first documented during the 1987 Samar speleological expedition.

Such creatures offer a glimpse into an ecosystem that exists largely beyond human sight — and a reminder that every deeper exploration can reveal more of what remains to be understood and protected beneath Samar’s limestone.

Tourism with responsibility

The growing interest in caves can create opportunities for local communities.

Cave tourism can support guides, transport providers, accommodation, food services, and outdoor groups. It can encourage visitors to explore rural communities and create new opportunities for environmental education.

But tourism also brings pressure. More visitors mean more footsteps, more waste, and greater potential disturbance to wildlife and fragile formations.

A cave formation that took thousands of years to develop can be damaged in seconds.

Repeated disturbance can affect bats and other cave-dependent species.

Waste left underground can persist long after visitors have gone.

And because karst landscapes can contain interconnected underground drainage systems, disturbances on the surface can affect places below ground that visitors may never see.

The 13 locals who journeyed through the Langun-Gobingob in Samar on the International Day of Caves and Karst on September 13. Contributed photo

That is why responsible cave tourism requires more than opening a cave to visitors. It requires trained guides, proper equipment, visitor orientation, safety protocols and clear conservation rules.

It also requires visitors to understand that they are entering an ecosystem, not merely an attraction.

The challenge is not to keep people away. It is to teach people how to enter without damaging what they came to see.

For the 13 people at the Langun Cave that day, they came in with different fears and expectations, but came out with different stories to tell.

The darkness revealed a world they had never known firsthand. It was not empty. It was alive.

And their responsibility now is to make sure it stays that way. – Rappler.com

Ricky Bautista was Rappler’s Aries Rufo Journalism Fellow in 2023.

World.title: White House turns away CNN, MS NOW, Politico reporters after Trump’s ban
World.content:
TRUMP. US President Donald Trump looks on after disembarking Air Force One as he arrives at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland, US, April 12, 2026.

The three news outlets have signaled that they may contest the ban on the grounds that it conflicts with the US Constitution's First Amendment protections for free speech and a free press

The White House on Saturday, September 19, denied access to journalists from CNN, MS NOW, and Politico, following through with US President Donald Trump‘s announcement that he would ban them from the building’s grounds.

All three news outlets separately said their teams’ press passes were confiscated on Saturday morning when their journalists went to the White House. They have signaled that they may contest the ban on the grounds that it conflicts with the US Constitution’s First Amendment protections for free speech and a free press.

A CNN statement on Saturday called the ban “an illegal assault” on its constitutional right to do journalism without interference from the government. In separate statements, MS NOW and Politico said they would “defend our First Amendment rights.”

MS NOW said it intends to “take any and all steps necessary to defend our First Amendment rights and the essential role of independent journalism in our democracy.”

CNN and MS NOW said they would continue reporting on the Trump administration, and Politico said it stands by its reporters covering the White House.

A social media post by Trump on Friday accused the outlets of “reporting FAKE NEWS” and said that they “shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States.”

He added, “Other Fake News Media Outlets to follow.”

Speaking to reporters in the Oval Office on Friday, September 18, Trump answered a question about what he meant by other outlets by describing the New York Times and the Washington Post as examples of “fake news,” although he did not specifically say he would ban them from the White House.

The New York Times in a statement called Trump’s latest ban “yet another retaliatory and unconstitutional threat” and said the newspaper “stands in support of the news organizations being unfairly targeted by the president.”

The Washington Post in a statement on Saturday said its access to the White House is a “non-negotiable constitutional right,” and called the president’s actions “a clear form of intimidation meant to silence coverage.”

Trump previously has tried to keep certain news outlets or specific journalists out of press gatherings.

Last year he banned the Associated Press from the pool of reporters that cover his movements because the news agency did not adopt Trump’s preferred name for the Gulf of Mexico after the president instructed the executive branch to call it the Gulf of America. AP has challenged the ban.

In his first term, Trump’s White House sought to revoke or suspend the credentials of Playboy correspondent Brian Karem and CNN’s Jim Acosta, but federal judges ordered their ⁠White House press passes restored. – Rappler.com

World.title: Itogon Mountain Village builds a home for love above the clouds
World.content:
DIVINE. The Chapel of the Mountains at Itogon Mountain Village opens to sweeping views of the surrounding ridges, with wood, glass, and greenery allowing the landscape to remain part of the space.

The Bernabe family bets that people will leave the city for the mountains, where Itogon Mountain Village builds a home for love above the clouds

ITOGON, Benguet – You notice the mountains before almost anything else.

They appear through the glass walls, between the pines beside the cabins, and behind the altar of a wooden chapel where nearly every direction opens to another ridge.

At Itogon Mountain Village, the view is not decoration. It is the point.

The three-hectare property in Barangay Loacan has grown from a small family café into a mountain destination with cabins, an events venue, and a nonsectarian chapel designed around an almost 360-degree view of the Cordillera landscape.

On September 19, after weeks of habagat rain, the sun finally returned. The timing coincided with the property’s first wedding open house, Love Above the Clouds, but the experience made clear why people had begun coming here long before the flowers, gowns, and reception tables arrived.

The Bernabe family made a simple bet: that people would leave the city for the mountains, and that the mountains themselves were enough.

EVENTS. Montesierra Events Place at Itogon Mountain Village is designed for weddings, family celebrations, and other gatherings, with the mountain landscape visible through its wide glass windows. Photo by Mia Magdalena Fokno

It started with coffee

Itogon Mountain Village did not begin with plans for weddings. It began with Café Stella.

“We started off very small,” said lawyer Rish Bernabe, one of the family members behind the property.

There were about six employees and only around 15 items on the menu, she recalled. Their father had envisioned a café down the mountain, while the family, which had long spent holidays in Baguio and the surrounding highlands, took on the challenge of running it.

Opening outside Baguio was a gamble. The place is almost half an hour away from the city, so “building up a business here was really a risk,” Rish said. Then people came.

The café gained attention on social media, and a kitchen designed for a modest number of customers suddenly had to feed far more. So they expanded the kitchen, upgraded to commercial equipment, hired more workers, and opened more of the building.

From a handful of employees, the enterprise eventually grew to around 80, according to the family.

Customers then began asking to reserve the café for private events. Closing the restaurant for an entire celebration was difficult, so the family expanded again.

Cabins followed. Then the Chapel of the Mountains. Then Montesierra, a dedicated events space.

What started as somewhere to eat had become somewhere people wanted to stay, gather, and mark important days.

VIEW. A guest cabin at Itogon Mountain Village shows how existing pine trees were preserved and incorporated into the design, with the structure built around them rather than cutting them down. Photo by Mia Magdalena Fokno

Building around the mountain

The growth could easily have changed what drew people there. But the Bernabes say they tried not to let that happen.

Glass dominates much of the architecture so that the surrounding mountains remain visible. Buildings and roads were adjusted around existing trees whenever possible, they said.

One tree remains standing in the middle of a road because the family refused to cut it.

“This is the yamang lupa that made us come here,” Rish said. “So we really have to preserve it and celebrate it.”

That approach is most evident at the Chapel of the Mountains.

Wooden pews face an altar framed by glass, pines, and distant slopes. Light falls through the roof. Turn to either side, and the landscape remains part of the room.

On that sunny September afternoon, after a long stretch of rain, no manufactured backdrop could really compete.

The chapel is also deliberately non-sectarian. It is not accredited by the Roman Catholic Church to host Catholic sacramental weddings, management clarified after earlier confusion over a ceremony held there.

Rish said the couple involved had already been legally married in Manila and that the ceremony at the chapel was symbolic.

“We respect the rules of the diocese,” she said.

The space remains open to other ceremonies consistent with legal and religious requirements.

Its openness, then, is not only architectural. It gives couples and families from different traditions a place to celebrate in their own way.

MOUNTAIN. Wedding bells outside the Chapel of the Mountains at Itogon Mountain Village, framed by pine trees and the steep slopes of Itogon. Photo by Mia Magdalena Fokno

Love beyond weddings

That idea of inclusion was central to the September 19 gathering.

“Today is about love, and not just romantic love,” said Suzy Mejia Bernabe, who handles marketing and sales for the family enterprise.

She spoke about weddings, birthdays, anniversaries, reunions, and other milestones, but also about creating a place where people could “slow down and reconnect.”

The family says it works with local suppliers, uses local produce when possible, and invites local makers, artists, and cultural performers to take part in events. That puts the property within a broader effort by Itogon to build tourism around its landscape and culture.

The municipality has long been associated with gold. Its own historical account traces gold working in the area to Indigenous communities before the colonial period, while large-scale mining later shaped much of the town’s modern history.

Today, Itogon’s tourism program also promotes nature and culture, with environmental sustainability, heritage preservation, and local employment among its stated goals.

The setting comes with limits. Itogon is rugged mountain country, with 74.6% of its land classified as having slopes steeper than 50%, according to the municipal government.

The Bernabes know building here is different from building on flatter ground. The terrain dictates what can be done, where structures can go, and sometimes which trees have to stay exactly where they are.

Perhaps that is why the place works. It does not feel as though the mountain was flattened to make room for a destination. In places, the destination appears to have negotiated with the mountain.

Looking up

For generations, Itogon has been known for what lies beneath its mountains: gold.

Itogon Mountain Village asks visitors to look up instead. At the pines growing beside the buildings. At the ridges beyond the glass. At a chapel where mountains remain visible behind the altar.

The family started with a small café and the uncertainty that anyone would drive this far from the city. But now, people come not only for coffee, but to stay, celebrate, marry, or simply spend a few hours where the mountains are allowed to remain the biggest thing in the room.

Perhaps the distance is not something visitors have to overcome after all. Perhaps it is part of the point. – Rappler.com

World.title: Making of World No. 1: Elena Rybakina’s Journey
World.content:
ASTANA – On Sept. 12, Kazakhstan’s Elena Rybakina defeated Aryna Sabalenka 6-4, 5-7, 6-2 in the US Open final to claim the third Grand Slam title of her career.

The victory ended Sabalenka’s 19-match winning streak at the tournament and completed a remarkable rise for Rybakina. A few days before that, she became the world No. 1, the 30th woman in WTA history to reach the top of the rankings and the first player representing Kazakhstan to do so.

Rybakina had technically secured the No. 1 ranking before the final, after defeating Zheng Qinwen in the quarterfinals. But winning the title made the achievement even more significant.

It was also an unexpected conclusion to a tournament that had begun with uncertainty. Rybakina arrived in New York after spending a week away from the court because of a left-foot injury. She had retired during the first set of her Cincinnati match against Iga Swiatek, and that tournament could have given her an earlier opportunity to reach the top of the rankings.

Instead, she reached No. 1 in New York.

“I don’t want to put too much pressure on myself,” Rybakina said before the final, explaining that regardless of the result, she would still have other opportunities ahead.

The Grand Slam

Before 2026, the US Open was Rybakina’s least successful Grand Slam tournament.

Across eight previous appearances, she had never advanced beyond the fourth round. This time, however, she defeated Thea Frodin, Jessica Bouzas Maneiro and Yuliia Starodubtseva before overcoming former champion Naomi Osaka.

Her quarterfinal against Zheng Qinwen became another test of her ability to recover. Rybakina lost the opening set but fought back to win the match.

The semifinal against Coco Gauff followed a similar pattern. After losing the first set 3-6, Rybakina won the next two 6-4, 6-4 to reach her first US Open final.

Three consecutive comeback victories were significant for a player whose game has often been associated with a straightforward formula: a powerful serve, flat groundstrokes and an aggressive style of play.

In New York, she demonstrated another side of her game: the ability to adapt, recover and win when a match does not follow her preferred script.

A tennis player almost by accident

Rybakina was born in Moscow on June 17, 1999. She initially tried several sports with her elder sister Anna, including gymnastics and figure skating. Tennis came later.

Because of her height, gymnastics and figure skating eventually became less suitable, and her father, who was interested in tennis, suggested that she try the sport. She was six years old.

Rybakina trained first at Dynamo and later at Spartak, where she worked with former Top-10 player Andrei Chesnokov and former world No. 100 Evgenia Kulikovskaya.

For years, she did not have an individual coach. Until the age of 15, she trained in a group of around eight players and later in a smaller group of four.

Her daily schedule also looked different from that of many young elite athletes. She spent roughly two hours on tennis and another three hours on physical preparation while attending a regular school rather than a specialized sports school.

This became an important part of her development. Rybakina was not raised through one of the highly structured tennis academies that produce professional players from an early age. Much of the work that would eventually turn her into an elite athlete came later.

From junior success to an uncertain future

Rybakina entered the ITF junior circuit in November 2013, at the age of 14.

Her strongest junior season came in 2017. By the end of that season, she was ranked No. 3 in the world among juniors. But her path was not always smooth.

At the 2016 US Open junior tournament, Rybakina fainted because of low hemoglobin and withdrew in the first round. According to her account, her family did not receive sufficient assistance from representatives of the Russian Tennis Federation at the tournament.

After the incident, her parents decided that she would no longer travel to tournaments without them.

That created another problem: the cost.

Professional tennis requires constant travel, accommodation, coaching and tournament expenses. Her family could not indefinitely finance that lifestyle on its own.

As a result, Rybakina and her family seriously considered another route of moving to the United States or Canada, studying at a university and playing college tennis.

For a teenager who would eventually become world No. 1, a professional tennis career was still far from guaranteed.

The decision that changed her career

In 2018, shortly before turning 19, Rybakina received Kazakh citizenship and switched her sporting representation from Russia to Kazakhstan.

The initiative came from her father, Andrey Rybakin, who was born in Almaty. He contacted the Kazakhstan Tennis Federation, which offered financial support in exchange for her representing Kazakhstan.

Rybakina chose that opportunity instead of pursuing university tennis in the U.S.

The change affected her career in practical ways. The support allowed her to travel to tournaments, build a professional team and most importantly, work with a full-time coach who could accompany her on the tour.

In February 2019, Croatian coach Stefano Vukov became her coach. He was the first coach in her career to regularly travel with her to tournaments.

Rybakina later described Kazakhstan’s support as crucial.

“They believed in me,” she said in an interview with the WTA. “I was not so good when they offered. So they believed in me and they’re helping me a lot.”

The decision therefore meant more than simply changing the flag next to her name in the rankings. It came at a moment when Rybakina had to decide whether tennis would remain an after-school activity or become her profession. With Kazakhstan’s support, she chose the latter.

The first signs of a breakthrough

Rybakina’s first major breakthrough on the WTA Tour came in St. Petersburg in 2018.

After winning her first WTA-level match, she moved up from around No. 450 to No. 268. The following year brought an even bigger step. In July 2019, Rybakina won her first WTA title in Bucharest, which pushed her into the Top 100 for the first time, at No. 65. She ended the season ranked No. 37.

Then came 2020. Rybakina reached five finals during the season, more than any other women’s player that year, and won the title in Hobart. By the time the COVID-19 pandemic interrupted the tennis season, Rybakina had risen to No. 17 and become the first Kazakh player to enter the WTA Top 20.

In 2021, she reached her first Grand Slam quarterfinal at Roland Garros, defeating Serena Williams on the way, and finished fourth at the Tokyo Olympics.

Rybakina was no longer simply a promising young player. She was becoming one of the strongest players on tour.

Wimbledon 2022: the title that changed everything

The biggest moment of her career came at Wimbledon in 2022. At 23, Rybakina became the first player representing Kazakhstan to win a Grand Slam singles title.

The victory also created a complicated situation because Wimbledon had banned Russian and Belarusian players following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Rybakina had been born in Moscow and had represented Russia as a junior, leading to considerable discussion around her nationality and sporting identity.

There was another unusual consequence: Wimbledon did not award ranking points that year. As a result, winning the tournament did not improve Rybakina’s ranking in the way a Grand Slam victory normally would.

She ended 2022 ranked No. 22 and did not qualify for the WTA Finals.

From Grand Slam champion to a Top-3 player

The next major step came in 2023. Rybakina reached the Australian Open final and then won two WTA 1000 titles, in Indian Wells and Rome. In June, she reached a career-high No. 3 in the WTA rankings.

But the following two years were less straightforward. Injuries and health problems affected her schedule, while changes to her coaching team added another layer of uncertainty.

She split with Vukov after the 2024 US Open and briefly worked with former Wimbledon champion Goran Ivanisevic. She later reunited with Vukov, who was subsequently suspended by the WTA for 12 months. Rybakina also worked with Davide Sanguinetti during this period.

While she had fallen to No. 11 in April 2025, the year of 2025 became another turning point.

At the 2025 WTA Finals in Riyadh, Rybakina entered the tournament as the final qualifier among the eight players. She then won the entire tournament without losing a match. The victory brought her back into the world’s Top 5 and gave her the biggest title of her career since Wimbledon.

2026: the season that took her to the top

Rybakina began 2026 by winning the Australian Open. Rybakina won 6-4, 4-6, 6-4 in a match against Sabalenka to claim her second Grand Slam title.

She later won in Stuttgart and reached the finals in Indian Wells and Toronto.

When she arrived in New York, she was ranked No. 2. The gap between Rybakina and Sabalenka at the top of the rankings had become one of the central storylines of the season.

Rybakina secured the No. 1 ranking after defeating Zheng Qinwen in the quarterfinals. But she still had two matches to play.

“You never know how long you’re going to stay. I want to win the titles still in tournaments, so all my thoughts are just for the next match,” she said.

That mentality carried her through the semifinal against Gauff and into the final against Sabalenka.

Rybakina’s victory over Sabalenka in the US Open final completed perhaps the most successful season of her career.

She became a three-time Grand Slam champion, won her first US Open and became the first world No. 1 in the history of Kazakh tennis.

Rybakina said she would like to win the French Open one day and complete a career Grand Slam. The achievement matters, she said, but she does not want to spend too much time thinking about it. There will always be another tournament, another opponent and another problem to solve.

That perspective is consistent with the story of her career.

Rybakina was not a child prodigy who was destined for the top from the beginning. She started tennis because other sports were not a good fit. She trained without an individual coach for years. At 17, she was still considering university instead of professional tennis.

Her career changed when Kazakhstan offered her the support needed to make professional tennis financially and logistically possible. From there, the progress came step by step and the ranking is only one part of the story. The girl who once played tennis simply because it was something to do after school had become the best-ranked women’s player in the world.

And, for Rybakina, there was still another match ahead.

World.title: Asian Games Open in Nagoya as Kazakhstan Targets Bigger Medal Haul
World.content:
ASTANA – The 20th Asian Games opened in Japan on Sept. 19, bringing together thousands of the continent’s top athletes. Kazakhstan is represented by 558 athletes competing in 35 of the 43 sports on the program, reported the Ministry of Tourism and Sports.

The opening ceremony was held in Aichi Prefecture and Nagoya, and the Games run through Oct. 4.

More than 15,000 athletes are expected to compete for medals in 469 events across 43 sports, spanning both Olympic and non-Olympic disciplines. Several competitions will also count toward qualification for the 2028 Olympic Games, either by awarding direct quota places or points toward Olympic rankings.

Paris 2024 Olympic judo champion Yeldos Smetov and national table tennis team member Sarvinoz Mirkadirova carried the Kazakh flag at the opening ceremony. Smetov is a three-time Olympic medalist, having also won silver at the 2016 Rio Games and bronze at Tokyo 2020, while Mirkadirova is a multiple Kazakh champion and medalist on the WTT Feeder circuit.

The scale of Kazakhstan’s delegation reflects a broader push ahead of the Games to strengthen the national team system. The ministry said foreign specialists with international experience and modern training methods had been brought into the preparation process, with the longer-term goal of developing domestic coaching expertise as well as improving results at major international competitions.

The country won 80 medals, including 10 gold, 22 silver and 48 bronze, at the previous Asian Games in Hangzhou, finishing 11th in the medal standings. Ahead of the competition in Japan, the ministry has set a target of 99 medals. Meeting that goal will depend on sports in which Kazakhstan has traditionally been competitive in Asia, including boxing, wrestling, judo, fencing and shooting. But several of the country’s leading medal contenders arrive in Japan with another layer of pressure, according to the National Olympic Committee press office. Many will be facing opponents they already know from Olympic finals, world championships and previous Asian Games.

Familiar rivals

One of the examples comes in men’s team épée, where Kazakhstan and host Japan have developed one of the continent’s strongest fencing rivalries.

Japan beat Kazakhstan in the semifinals of the 2018 Asian Games, while Kazakhstan took silver and Japan gold at the following edition. A few years later in the semifinals of the 2025 world championships, Japan edged Kazakhstan 42-41 before going on to win the title.

A year later, Kazakhstan won its first men’s team épée world championship, defeating Ukraine 45-40 in the final. It also won the 2026 Asian championship, with Japan finishing second.

That means the two teams arrive at the Asian Games as winners of the past two world championships.

Boxing

Boxing brings another major regional test, particularly against Uzbekistan.

Kazakhstan finished first at the inaugural World Boxing Championships in Liverpool in 2025 with seven gold medals, while Uzbekistan won six. Kazakh and Uzbek male boxers won in 10 weight categories at the tournament, setting up the possibility of several high-profile rematches in Japan.

Among them is Aibek Oralbay, who defeated Uzbekistan’s Jakhongir Zokirov in the over-90-kilogram final in Liverpool.

Aida Abikeyeva could also renew her rivalry with Uzbekistan’s Navbakhor Khamidova after the pair finished first and second at major international events over the past year.

Torekhan Sabyrkhan could again face Japan’s Sewonrets Okazawa after defeating him in the 70-kilogram world championship final in Liverpool.

Another major Kazakh medal contender is Nazym Kyzaibay, one of the most decorated athletes on the team. The Paris 2024 Olympic bronze medalist has repeatedly reached the podium at major international tournaments and took silver at the 2025 world championships while competing in the 48-kilogram division.

In Nagoya, Kyzaibay moves up to 54 kilograms, where she faces a particularly strong field. Her potential rivals include reigning world champion Huang Hsiao-wen of Chinese Taipei, Paris Olympic silver medalist Pang Chol-mi of North Korea, South Korea’s Olympic bronze medalist Im Ae-ji and Japan’s Tokyo Olympic bronze medalist Tsukimi Namiki.

Namiki also has a history with Kyzaibay: the Japanese boxer defeated her in the semifinals of the 2022 Asian championships, giving a potential meeting in Nagoya the added dimension of a rematch.

Olympic champions

Kazakhstan also brings considerable experience into the judo competition.

Smetov, the reigning Olympic champion in the 60-kilogram division, could again face Chinese Taipei’s Yang Yung-wei. Yang won silver at the Tokyo Olympics and gold at the previous Asian Games, while Smetov defeated him in the Paris 2024 Olympic quarterfinals on his way to the title.

Smetov is himself a former Asian Games champion, having won gold in Incheon in 2014.

Abiba Abuzhakynova gives Kazakhstan another strong medal opportunity in judo. She won silver at the previous Asian Games and has since added bronze at the 2024 world championships and silver in 2025, giving her three senior world championship medals.

Some of Kazakhstan’s most intriguing contests could come against Japanese athletes competing before a home crowd.

In Greco-Roman wrestling, Demeu Zhadrayev could meet Japan’s Nao Kusaka in a rematch of the Paris Olympic final. Zhadrayev took an early lead back then before Kusaka came back to win 5-2 and claim Olympic gold. Both return in the 77-kilogram division in Japan.

In breaking, Amir Zakirov could renew his rivalry with Japan’s Shigekix, or Shigeyuki Nakarai. Zakirov beat the Japanese star at the Breaking for Gold World Series in Kitakyushu in 2023, while Shigekix later won Asian Games gold in Hangzhou and became world champion in 2025. Both also competed at the Paris Olympics.

Medal chances

Kazakhstan’s medal ambitions extend beyond its traditional strengths in boxing, wrestling and judo.

Skeet shooter Assem Orynbay enters the Games after beating China’s Jiang Yiting at the World Cup in Almaty in May, where Orynbay hit 33 targets in the final, equaling the world record.

In athletics, former world champion Norah Jeruto could line up against Bahrain’s Olympic champion Winfred Yavi in the women’s 3,000-meter steeplechase. Yavi won the world title in 2023 and Olympic gold in Paris, while Jeruto was world champion in 2022.

Rhythmic gymnast Akmaral Yerekesheva arrives after a breakthrough first senior season. She won three medals at the 2026 Asian championships and finished sixth in the all-around at the world championships, putting her among Kazakhstan’s emerging medal prospects in Nagoya.

The men’s water polo tournament carries another long-running rivalry.

Kazakhstan won six Asian Games titles between 1994 and 2018, including one-goal victories over Japan in the finals in both 2014 and 2018. Japan reversed the balance in Hangzhou, beating Kazakhstan 15-13 in the group stage before winning gold, while Kazakhstan finished with bronze.

The two sides are drawn together again and are scheduled to meet Sept. 26.

Olympic Games official website describes China, Japan and South Korea as “three traditional powerhouses at the Asian Games.”

“Those three National Olympic Committees have won the most gold medals between them at every single Asian Games since 1978, with 1974 the last time one of those three NOCs did not win at least the third-most gold medals at the Games,” reads the website.

World.title: Kulans Released Into Wild in Ile-Balkhash Reserve
World.content:
ASTANA – A group of kulans has been released into the wild in the Ile-Balkhash State Nature Reserve as part of Kazakhstan’s efforts to restore the species’ population and return it to its historical range.

The animals were transferred from Altyn Emel National Park and released into their natural habitat, reported the Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources. Specialists will monitor the kulans’ adaptation, movements and condition following the release.

The kulan, a wild relative of the domestic donkey, is native to the steppes and semi-deserts of Central Asia. In Kazakhstan, the species disappeared from most of its historical range in the first half of the 20th century, largely due to hunting and habitat loss.

Conservation efforts have gradually helped rebuild the population. In recent years, Kazakhstan has expanded reintroduction programs to several protected areas, including Ile-Balkhash and Altyn Dala.

In October 2024, 24 kulans were transported 2,139 kilometers from Altyn Emel National Park to the Altyn Dala Nature Reserve. The 50-hour journey was part of efforts to develop safer methods for relocating wild animals over long distances.

The Ile-Balkhash reserve has become one of the key sites for restoring native wildlife. The area is part of a wider ecosystem restoration project that includes the return of species alongside measures aimed at creating suitable conditions for the future return of the Turan tiger.

The reintroduction of kulans is intended to strengthen natural ecosystems as well as increase the number of animals in the wild. As large herbivores, kulans contribute to the functioning of steppe and desert habitats by influencing vegetation and forming part of the food chain.

The latest release marks another step in Kazakhstan’s broader biodiversity conservation strategy, which increasingly focuses on restoring species in their historical habitats and rebuilding entire ecosystems rather than protecting isolated animal populations.

World.title: Kazakhstan Eyes Cross-Border QR Payments as India’s UPI Offers Blueprint
World.content:
MUMBAI – Kazakhstan is moving toward expanding its domestic QR-payment infrastructure across borders, with India among 11 countries identified for potential cross-border QR-payment cooperation. The initiative comes as cashless payments continue to account for the overwhelming majority of transactions in Kazakhstan.

According to the National Bank of Kazakhstan, 84 million payment cards were in circulation as of Aug. 1, with debit cards accounting for 81.6% and credit cards for 15.5%. In July, transactions using cards issued by Kazakh banks reached 19.9 trillion tenge (US$44.4 billion), covering 1.3 billion transactions.

Non-cash transactions accounted for 17.6 trillion tenge (US$39.3 billion) and 1.3 billion transactions, increasing 8.4% in value and 7.5% in number compared with July 2025. Internet and mobile banking comprise 77.6% of the number and 89.6% of the value of non-cash payments and money transfers, while POS terminals accounted for 21.9% and 10%, respectively.

The figures provide a growing domestic base for Kazakhstan’s efforts to make QR payments interoperable across borders.

Kazakhstan launched its national Interbank Mobile-Payment System on July 19, allowing customers of participating banks to make real-time interbank transfers and payments using phone numbers and a single QR code. The system enables merchants to accept payments from customers of various participating banks without installing new equipment.

The next step is to make such payments work across borders.

India’s UPI model

India offers one example of how a nationally interoperable payment infrastructure can evolve into a cross-border service.

Speaking to foreign journalists in Mumbai on Sept. 16, Sonal Asnani, head of Asia Pacific at NPCI International Payments Limited (NIPL), outlined how India developed the Unified Payments Interface (UPI) from a domestic payment infrastructure into a system with international applications.

UPI, operated by the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI), is a payment infrastructure rather than a standalone application or card. It connects banks, fintech companies and customers through a common framework, allowing users to make payments through different applications while maintaining interoperability.

“It’s not an application, it’s not a card. It’s a payment layer,” Asnani said, explaining the basic architecture of UPI.

According to Asnani, one of the key factors behind UPI’s expansion has been the division of roles across the ecosystem. The Reserve Bank of India acts as the regulator, NPCI operates the national payment infrastructure and establishes standards, banks hold customers’ accounts and funds, while fintech companies develop customer-facing services.

This model has allowed users to make payments through various applications while relying on the same underlying infrastructure.

From domestic payments to international use

NPCI created NIPL in 2020 to take Indian payment technologies and expertise to international markets.

One of its main areas of activity is cross-border merchant payments. Under UPI Global Acceptance, Indian users can make QR-based payments at participating international merchants directly from UPI-enabled applications.

Asnani noted that users can scan a participating local QR code and review the transaction amount, exchange rate, and applicable fees before completing the payment.

She said NPCI International currently works with 11 countries on international merchant-payment acceptance.

The model allows an Indian traveler to use a familiar UPI-enabled application abroad rather than relying exclusively on cash or international payment cards.

“For example, when I travel to other countries, I can scan the local QR with my UPI app and still make a payment,” Asnani said.

For Kazakhstan, which is developing cross-border QR arrangements with India and other countries, interoperability could provide a similar mechanism for travelers and merchants.

The practical question, however, is how two national payment systems can be connected while preserving their respective regulatory and technical frameworks.

Asnani highlighted that such partnerships require due diligence and compliance procedures, while the presence of an established QR-payment ecosystem in the partner country can make integration more straightforward.

“Wherever there is a high level of QR adoption, and there is a QR system, it becomes natural for us to collaborate,” she said, describing the factors considered when establishing international partnerships.

Beyond QR payments

NPCI International’s activities extend beyond merchant payments. The organization also works on cross-border person-to-person remittances and provides technology to countries seeking to develop their own domestic payment infrastructure.

Asnani said some countries have adopted elements of India’s technology to develop sovereign instant-payment or card systems rather than building such infrastructure entirely from scratch.

That approach differs from simply connecting two existing payment systems. It involves sharing technological infrastructure and experience with countries that are developing or upgrading their own national payment systems.

Kazakhstan has a well-developed digital payments ecosystem. The next step is to connect its existing infrastructure with international payment networks while ensuring seamless interoperability and maintaining regulatory oversight.

The potential use cases extend beyond tourism. Cross-border QR payments could facilitate transactions for travelers, small businesses and merchants. At the same time, interoperability between payment systems could also support broader economic and financial links between Kazakhstan and its partner countries.

The country’s growing domestic use of digital payments provides a substantial base for such expansion. In January-July, QR-code payments within Kazakhstan accounted for 2.34 billion transactions worth 11.8 trillion tenge (US$26.3 billion), according to National Bank data.

As Kazakhstan moves from domestic QR interoperability toward international connectivity, India’s experience offers one possible path. This involves building common infrastructure, allowing banks and fintech companies to compete at the customer level, and using interoperable standards to make the payment experience seamless for users.

World.title: News Digest: Rybakina’s US Open Triumph, Kazakhstan-South Korea Ties and Oil Export Strategy
World.content:
ASTANA – The Astana Times has selected articles from global media outlets covering Kazakhstan. This week’s foreign media digest highlights Elena Rybakina’s U.S. Open victory, strengthened Kazakhstan-South Korea cooperation, Astana Arena’s selection to host the 2028 UEFA Super Cup, and Kazakhstan’s efforts to diversify its oil export routes.

S. Korea, Kazakhstan sign MOU on preservation of historic sites linked to Korea’s independence movement

South Korea and Kazakhstan have signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) to help better preserve historical sites in the Central Asian country that are linked to Korea’s independence movement against Japan’s 1910-45 colonial rule, Seoul’s veterans ministry said Wednesday, Yonhap reported on Sept. 16.

“Under the MOU, the two countries agreed to systematically preserve the historical records and cultural value of historical sites related to Korea’s independence movement while also strengthening academic exchanges. There are 25 historical sites related to Korea’s independence movement in the central Asian country, according to the ministry,” reads the article.

Seoul Cyber University chairman receives Kazakhstan’s Order of Dostyk

Lee Sang-kyun, chairman of Seoul Cyber University (SCU), received Kazakhstan’s Order of Dostyk, recognizing his contributions to expanding online education and promoting friendly cooperation between Korea and Kazakhstan, reported The Korea Times on Sept. 16.

Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, who visited Korea this week for the first Korea-Central Asia Summit, personally presented the order to Lee on Monday. The Order of Dostyk is one of Kazakhstan’s highest state honors, awarded to figures at home and abroad for contributions to peace, friendship, international cooperation and social harmony.

U.S. Open final: Elena Rybakina smothers Aryna Sabalenka to dethrone reigning champion

For the second time this year, Elena Rybakina is a Grand Slam champion after defeating Aryna Sabalenka. The 27-year-old from Kazakhstan toppled Sabalenka 6-4, 5-7, 6-2 on Saturday in the U.S. Open final, denying Sabalenka’s bid to win the tournament for a third straight year, The New York Times reported on Sept. 13.

“It is Rybakina’s first U.S. Open title, and her third Grand Slam title overall. It means she leaves the tournament as both the champion and the new world No. 1: Rybakina will replace Sabalenka at the top of women’s tennis on Monday,” reads the article.

Astana Arena in the capital of Kazakhstan selected to host 2028 UEFA Super Cup

The prestigious match, UEFA Super Cup, will take place at the Johan Cruyff Arena in Amsterdam, Netherlands, in 2027, before passing the baton to Astana Arena in Astana, Kazakhstan, in 2028. Kazakhstan has obtained the chance to host such a major match, marking a historic first for the country, Euronews reported on Sept. 15.

The decision was made and officially announced by the UEFA Executive Committee. Since 2013, the Super Cup venue has changed every year, moving to a new location each time. Kazakhstan has obtained the chance to host such a major match, marking a historic first for the country. For the uninitiated, the UEFA Super Cup is a single-match curtain-raiser where the Champions League and Europa League winners meet.

Kazakhstan is upgrading its oil export strategy: Here’s how

Astana is looking for more ways to move its oil. Russia, its principal export outlet, is rife with disruptions. Damage to the Caspian Pipeline Consortium’s (CPC) Black Sea terminal in November 2025 suppressed exports into early 2026, while the recent July attacks on tankers threatened roughly 1.5 million barrels per day, writes Joseph Shumunov for EU Reporter on Sept. 15.

The vulnerability would not be so enormous if 80% of Kazakh oil exports did not move through the CPC terminal near Novorossiysk. But is Kazakhstan merely searching for emergency alternatives amid instability? Or is this a transformation it has been preparing for? The answer is consequential: Kazakhstan is attempting a wholesale upgrade of its oil-export strategy, one befitting a rising regional power. It is moving from rational efficiency toward strategic resilience, from accepting routes toward shaping them, and from concentrated dependence toward managed interdependence.

World.title: Italy, Central Asia Launch B5+Italy Platform to Expand Regional Business Ties
World.content:
ASTANA – Government and business representatives from Central Asia and Italy convened on Sept. 16 in Astana for the launch of the B5+Italy platform aimed at turning growing political engagement into investment, industrial cooperation and stronger trade links across the region.

The forum in Astana brought together government officials and businesses from Italy, Kazakhstan, the Kyrgyz Republic, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan, with discussions focused on connectivity, sustainable growth and new opportunities for companies operating across Central Asia.
