The meeting follows the first Central Asia-Italy summit at the leaders’ level, held in Astana in May 2025, when Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni and the presidents of the five Central Asian states agreed to deepen cooperation across trade, investment, transport, energy and other sectors.

The platform, proposed by President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, is designed to complement the political dialogue in C5+1 format by giving businesses a more direct role in shaping economic cooperation.

Italian Undersecretary of State for Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation Maria Tripodi said the new business format was intended to give that political dialogue an economic dimension.

“We consider that today’s meeting is important because it is the beginning of a new era. (…) We want to transform the political dialogue into investments, partnerships and new opportunities for our countries,” Tripodi told the forum participants.

“It is the companies, in fact, that are subject to transform the political relationship into a more solid one, investing time and effort,” she said.

A dynamic market

Addressing the gathering, Kazakh Minister of Trade and Integration Arman Shakkaliyev said the forum gives an opportunity to Italian companies to approach Central Asia increasingly as a regional market rather than five isolated economies.

“Today, Central Asia is a market with a rapidly growing economy,” said the minister. “For Italian businesses, today’s forum represents an opportunity to work with the entire region and to expand production and market presence across several countries simultaneously.”

He said Central Asia should increasingly be viewed as an interconnected economic space where companies can establish production in one country while reaching consumers and supply chains across several neighboring markets.

For Kazakhstan, the regional format also offers an opportunity to use existing business infrastructure with Italy more broadly. Shakkaliyev highlighted the Kazakh-Italian Trade House that opened in Almaty earlier this year, saying it could serve not only bilateral commerce but wider links between Italian companies and Central Asia.

Growing interest from businesses

The push toward a regional format is also coming from companies and business associations that have traditionally worked through bilateral Kazakhstan-Italy ties. Marco Beretta, president of the Italian-Kazakh Trade Association, said the leaders’ summit in May 2025 convinced businesses that cooperation could be expanded beyond the two countries.

“In the last three years, we have been working very hard in order to promote collaboration between Italy and Kazakhstan,” Beretta told The Astana Times. “But after the visit of our prime minister last year in May, we understood that a much wider scope of work can be executed.”

He described Central Asia as an increasingly important economic link for Europe and said the expansion toward a five-country regional format represented a significant shift. Beretta said the association now wants to expand its Kazakh-Italian business forum into a broader Central Asian platform while keeping Kazakhstan as its base.

Diversifying trade structure

The forum comes at a time as Italy expands its economic engagement with Central Asia, with Kazakhstan accounting for a large share of that relationship. Italy was Kazakhstan’s third-largest trading partner last year, with bilateral trade reaching almost $17 billion in 2025, according to Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Trade and Integration. Trade reached $9.79 billion in January-July this year, including $9 billion in Kazakh exports to Italy and $789.6 million in imports.

But Shakkaliyev said maintaining high trade volumes alone was not enough. He pointed to the big role of commodities in the current structure of bilateral commerce.

Kazakhstan is seeking to expand exports of higher-value goods and estimates that it has an additional $307.5 million in export potential on the Italian market, particularly in metallurgy, petrochemicals, food products, chemicals and machinery.

Shakkaliyev said Kazakhstan was interested in changing the structure of trade by increasing exports of processed and higher-value products. He pointed to opportunities in agriculture, chemicals, manufacturing and industrial cooperation, while Tripodi emphasized Italian expertise in engineering, machinery and advanced industrial technologies.

This ambition reflects a broader challenge for Central Asian economies of moving from exports of raw materials toward local processing, manufacturing and bigger participation in international value chains.

Connectivity as central theme

Transport and logistics featured prominently in the forum as Central Asian states seek to strengthen links between Asian and European markets. Kazakhstan, which has invested around $35 billion in this area in the past 15 years, has promoted its position along transcontinental trade routes, particularly the Middle Corridor across the Caspian Sea. The Middle Corridor, formally known as the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, links China and Central Asia with Europe through the Caspian Sea, the South Caucasus and Türkiye.

Shakkaliyev said the region’s transport infrastructure could provide Italian producers and investors with access not only to Central Asian markets but also to wider international supply chains.

Tripodi said Italy was ready to share technology and experience to support Kazakhstan’s economic diversification, pointing to logistics as one area for cooperation.

“Our connectivity depends on growth and on being connected in a safe, self-sufficient way in large international markets,” she said. “We want Italy to be at the same time the driver of this new road to Europe and also the protagonist of its realization. Our companies are ready to contribute.”

Diversifying economic ties

Beretta pointed to logistics, agriculture, technology and petrochemicals as areas where Italian companies could work across the region. He also tied diversification to the development of higher-value production in Kazakhstan rather than continued reliance on raw-material exports.

“We need to create added value,” Beretta said.

Beretta also said one project under discussion is the development of a logistics hub in Kazakhstan accompanied by local production, including sustainable aviation fuel. He said such projects could also be part of a wider push into decarbonization, renewable power generation, sustainable development and water treatment.

“Decarbonization, power generation in a green way, sustainable development and water treatment are very important for Central Asia,” he said, stressing that Italian companies could bring technologies and industrial experience in those areas.

According to Tripodi, Italian companies have built extensive presence in oil and gas, but they are also looking to expand into renewable energy, critical minerals and areas linked to energy transition.

Shakkaliyev also noted Italy’s experience with small and medium-sized industrial companies could be particularly relevant for Central Asia, where governments are seeking investment that creates production capacity and jobs.

In her remarks, Tripodi noted the region offered a large and relatively young market of around 80 million people, combined with energy resources, critical materials and a strategic position between Europe and Asia. The country sees potential for its companies in sectors where Central Asian governments are trying to move further up value chains, she said.

Tripodi said Italian companies could contribute through design, engineering and industrial technologies as Central Asian economies seek greater diversification.

World.title: Apple TV Launches in Kazakhstan
World.content:
ASTANA — Apple TV has officially launched in Kazakhstan, giving users direct access to Apple Original films and series for the first time.

The streaming service is included in all iCloud+ plans alongside Apple Arcade, with no separate Apple TV subscription required.

The basic iCloud+ plan costs 499 tenge (US$1) per month and includes 50 gigabytes (GB) of cloud storage.

The service is available on Apple devices, compatible smart TVs, gaming consoles and other platforms.

World.title: Expert: Astana’s Financial Center Rating Rises 18 Points on Structural Progress
World.content:
ASTANA – Astana’s eight-place rise in the Global Financial Centers Index 40 (GFCI 40) should ultimately be measured by whether growing international confidence translates into more investment, deeper capital markets and greater cross-border financial activity, Bakhtiyar Tleubekov, chairman of the Management Board of Astana International Financial Centre, told The Astana Times on Sept. 18.

In the 40th edition of the Global Financial Centers Index, Kazakhstan’s capital ranked 57th among 117 financial centers worldwide, climbing eight places from 65th. Astana’s rating increased by 18 points, from 684 to 702.

Astana retains regional leadership

The city retained its leading position in Eastern Europe and Central Asia, which it has held for more than three years. Astana was followed by Cyprus, which ranked 72nd globally, and Warsaw, which placed 78th.

Astana’s rise came against a 1.09% decline in the average rating of financial centers in Eastern Europe and Central Asia. It was also named among the ten financial centers survey participants expected to play a more significant role in the global financial system over the next two to three years, ranking ninth with 45 mentions.

In the separate FinTech ranking, Astana rose four places from 55th to 51st.

“Astana’s eight-place rise and continued regional leadership send an important signal of growing confidence in the AIFC and Kazakhstan among the international financial community. For us, a position in the ranking is not an end in itself, but an independent assessment of the work we are consistently pursuing: improving the legal and regulatory environment, developing capital markets and financial technologies, and expanding international ties,” said AIFC Governor Renat Bekturov.

From ranking to capital flows

“The real measure of success is whether growing international confidence translates into more investment, deeper capital markets, more international financial institutions operating in Kazakhstan, and greater cross-border financial activity,” Tleubekov said.

According to him, over the next two to three years, the priority is to reinforce the conditions that international investors value most: political and macroeconomic stability, a predictable and transparent regulatory environment, consistent application of the law, and effective protection of investor rights.

Astana and Kazakhstan also need to continue strengthening their role as a regional gateway connecting international capital with opportunities across Central Asia and the wider Eurasian region.

“Kazakhstan’s geographic position and growing role in trans-Caspian transport and logistics create an opportunity to complement physical connectivity with financial connectivity,” he said.

Structural progress and international confidence

Tleubekov noted that the GFCI combines assessments from financial-sector professionals with quantitative indicators from more than 80 external sources covering the business environment, human capital, infrastructure, financial-sector development and reputation.

“Therefore, an 18-point increase cannot be attributed solely to improved perception, nor can it be explained by any single indicator,” he said.

He attributed Astana’s performance to both external conditions and structural progress, including Kazakhstan’s relative political and economic stability, regulatory continuity and openness to international investment.

The AIFC has been consistently developing a legal and regulatory framework based on international standards, independent dispute-resolution institutions, capital-market infrastructure, fintech and digital-asset regulation, and mechanisms for international and regional investors.

“Ultimately, progress should be measured not only by rankings, but by new investment, international companies choosing the AIFC, and new opportunities for Kazakhstan’s businesses,” Bekturov said.

The GFCI is published twice a year by the Z/Yen Group in partnership with the China Development Institute and assesses financial centers across five areas: business environment, financial sector development, infrastructure, human capital and reputation.

Continuing the conversation

The Astana Times has been following the AIFC’s development and Kazakhstan’s evolving role in the international financial system through its coverage and interviews with AIFC leadership.

At the recent Astana Finance Days, Bekturov joined discussions on the future of finance and Kazakhstan’s role in the next digital frontier.

The AIFC also recently shared the results of its first 10 years with The Astana Times team, offering a closer look at the centre’s development, growing international presence and priorities for the next decade. Also watch our YouTube interview with AIFC leadership.

World.title: South Ossetia election: as expected, former Moscow official Marat Kambolov becomes new president
World.content:
Kambolov becomes South Ossetia president

As expected, Marat Kambolov, the prime minister and acting president of South Ossetia who previously held senior positions in the Kremlin, is winning the snap presidential election held on 18 September.

According to preliminary results, he is securing a convincing victory over his formal rivals – state security officer Murat Valiev, South Ossetian University rector’s state adviser Kazbek Kodoev, and Unity party chairman Zurab Kokoev.

After 40% of the ballots had been counted, CEC head Emilia Gagieva said Kambolov had received 88.4% of the vote. Valiev had 4.3%, Kodoev 1.1%, and Kokoev 1.0%.

Marat Kambolov is a former Moscow official who first appeared in South Ossetia in May 2026 as an adviser to then-President Alan Gagloev. He was quickly granted South Ossetian citizenship and, within a month, rose from minister to prime minister, and then became acting president after Alan Gagloev resigned.

Polling stations were also open in Russia – in North Ossetia and Moscow. According to Emilia Gagieva, turnout was high at all polling stations and no violations were recorded.

According to the CEC, the election was monitored by 66 observers from 15 countries: Russia, Abkhazia, Nicaragua, Belarus, Armenia, Venezuela, Germany, Zimbabwe, Kenya, Mexico, Serbia, Tanzania, Turkey, Uganda and South Africa.

CEC member Dina Ostaeva said that “no complaints or appeals related to violations of electoral legislation or the organisation of voting” had been received during the day.

After polling stations closed at 8pm, a celebratory concert and lottery were held in the city centre, with household appliances, smartphones, TVs, bicycles, vacuum cleaners and the grand prize – a Russian-made Niva Legend car – raffled off.

As soon as the prizes had been handed out, Marat Kambolov took the stage, thanked the people of South Ossetia for taking part in the election and said that, in terms of voter turnout, the election had broken all records.

“Preliminary data show that we have broken all records. Never before have so many people taken part. More voters participated in this election than in any previous one. Only together can we strengthen our Tskhinvali and our Ossetia,” Kambolov said.

One of the voters who cast his ballot for Marat Kambolov believes that the high turnout and the large share of votes he received were not so much the result of political strategists’ work as of people believing in Kambolov and voting “for his authority, for the authority of Russia”.

Blogger Alik Pukhaev expressed hope that the new president would “finally make South Ossetia a state for all Ossetians”.

By this, he means the possibility for all ethnic Ossetians to obtain a South Ossetian passport.

At present, the law provides for citizenship only for people born in South Ossetia and their descendants. Under previous governments, however, there were repeated scandals over the illegal issuance — and even sale — of passports to residents of Chechnya, Ingushetia and Dagestan.

Russian State Duma MP Kazbek Taisaev, who observed the election, said it had been organised “at the highest level – transparently, fairly and openly”.

He also stressed that Russia would continue to provide South Ossetia with comprehensive support.

And that is almost certainly what will happen, given that Marat Kambolov is a Russian official who was clearly sent by the Kremlin with the specific aim of taking the presidency and governing in Russia’s interests rather than those of local politicians pursuing their own agendas.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

World.title: EU does not recognise “presidential election” in Georgia’s Russian-occupied Tskhinvali region
World.content:
EU condemns Russia and South Ossetia election

The European Union does not recognise the so-called “presidential election” held on 18 September in Georgia’s Russian-occupied Tskhinvali region (South Ossetia). In a statement, the EU Delegation said the results of the election have no legal effect.

Georgia’s Foreign Ministry also condemned the so-called “presidential election”, calling it a violation of Georgia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity.

The EU statement says it does not recognise the constitutional and legal framework, including recent amendments, under which the election was held in the Russian-occupied region, which unilaterally declared its secession from Georgia.

“The EU strongly condemns Moscow’s actions aimed at installing a Russian official as the de facto president of South Ossetia, Georgia’s occupied breakaway region,” the statement said.

The EU also expressed concern over the signing of the so-called “Treaty on Deepening Allied Cooperation” on 9 May 2026 and criticised Russia’s attempts to strengthen its control over South Ossetia in the political, military, economic and judicial spheres.

The EU considers these steps contrary to a peaceful resolution of the conflict and paving the way for the future illegal annexation of the Russian-occupied region.

“Such actions systematically deepen divisions, threaten regional security and stability, and constitute a flagrant violation of international law,” the EU statement said.

The bloc reaffirmed its commitment to a peaceful resolution of the conflict in Georgia, including through its co-chairmanship of the Geneva International Discussions and the activities of the European Union Monitoring Mission in Georgia.

The EU called on Russia to respect Georgia’s sovereignty and cease all actions undermining its territorial integrity.

“The European Union reaffirms its unwavering support for Georgia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity within its internationally recognised borders,” the statement said.

On 18 September, snap “presidential elections” were held in Russian-occupied “South Ossetia”. Four candidates took part.

However, calling it an “election race” would only be accurate in a very loose sense, as it was clear from the outset that the overwhelming favourite was so-called “acting president” and “prime minister” Marat Kambolov, who arrived in the region from Russia in May 2026.

Unlike Kambolov, the other three candidates were residents of South Ossetia. But that was where their advantage ended. Most experts described them as “technical candidates” — people who were not seriously trying to compete for the presidency:

Zurab Kokoev, leader of the Unity party;

Kazbek Kodoev, an independent candidate and adviser to the rector of South Ossetia University;

Murat Valiev, a candidate nominated by the Patriots of Alania party and an employee of the state security service.

None of them campaigned among the population. They presented their views on the development of so-called South Ossetia only during live televised debates.

News in Georgia

World.title: Pashinyan’s salary to nearly double as Armenian civil servants set for pay rises from 2027
World.content:
Salary increases for public officials in Armenia

From 1 January 2027, senior Armenian officials will receive higher salaries. Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan, for example, will earn 2,662,000 drams ($7,353), up from the current 1.5 million ($4,143). Deputy prime ministers’ salaries will rise to 2,163,000 drams ($5,975), from 1,289,000 ($3,560).

The increases will apply not only to the executive branch, but also to the legislative and judicial branches. The state budget will allocate 25 billion drams ($69 million) for this purpose. The government has already approved the draft. Parliament must now approve it.

“How does this public official live? How does he buy a suit and a watch? We never assess the negative impact [of this factor] on the development of our state. But the effect is highly negative. If we do not solve this problem, it will lead to disasters,” Nikol Pashinyan said during a discussion of the draft.

The ruling party views the decision as a reform. The prime minister said he was confident that failing to implement the project would mean “keeping Armenia stuck in place and continuing to subordinate the logic of the state to the logic of corruption”.

However, the opposition warns that such decisions will further deepen the sense of social injustice.

“Citizens often become disillusioned and leave the country not only because of economic difficulties, but also because of a sense of injustice,” former MP Garnik Danielyan said.

Salary increases in figures

Under the proposed amendments to the law “On remuneration for persons holding public office”:

the president of Armenia will earn 2,662,000 drams ($7,353), up from the current 1,664,000 drams ($4,596);

the speaker of the National Assembly will earn 2,496,000 drams ($6,895), up from 1,497,600 drams ($4,137);

MPs will earn up to 1,497,600 drams ($4,137), up from 832,000 drams ($2,311);

the president of the Constitutional Court will earn 2,412,800 drams ($6,665), up from 1,664,000 drams ($4,596);

the prosecutor general will earn 1,830,400 drams ($5,056), up from 1,248,000 drams ($3,447);

the ombudsman will earn 1,830,400 drams ($5,056), up from 998,400 drams ($2,758).

Governors, deputy ministers and deputy speakers of parliament will also receive higher salaries.

The stated amounts include taxes and other mandatory payments.

Ruling party representative’s assessment and opposition response

Eduard Aghajanyan, an MP from the ruling party, told journalists:

“The public administration system has consistently faced difficulties attracting highly qualified specialists. The issue became particularly acute after the 2018 revolution, when the logic of working within the system changed radically. Systemic corruption was eradicated, and the motivation mechanisms were completely restructured.

At the same time, pay levels made the public administration system unattractive to highly qualified professionals.

We have been at the helm of government for eight years now. I believe that the decision to address this issue is somewhat overdue.

I welcome the government’s decision. I am confident that it will produce the desired results in attracting highly qualified professionals.”

Former MP from the opposition Armenia bloc Garnik Danielyan wrote on his Facebook page:

“According to official data for 2024, Armenia’s poverty rate stands at 21.7%. One in four children lives in poverty, while thousands of families continue to face severe social hardship. People struggle to meet their basic needs. Moreover, in the 21st century, Armenia has recorded cases of people dying from hunger.

In your 2021 election programme, you [addressing the authorities] promised to halve the poverty rate by 2026. Poverty has not declined. But you yourselves are now living better. You no longer buy vacuum cleaners or televisions on instalment plans. Instead, you are accumulating assets.

Of course, no one objects to high salaries for public officials. But given this level of poverty, should the priorities not be addressing social problems, creating new jobs and ensuring decent living conditions for people?

And this is happening while Armenia’s public debt has already exceeded $14 billion. Housing and employment remain critical issues for thousands of Karabakh Armenians. Hundreds of people still live in temporary shelters, and many are forced to buy groceries on credit.

Clearly, political calculations also lie behind this decision — namely, preserving loyalty within the state system.”

Comments from Armenian residents on social media

The decision to raise the salaries of senior public officials has sparked heated discussions on social media. Most users criticised the authorities. Here are some of their comments:

“Of course, raising the salaries of civil servants and public officials is important. But we must not forget a phenomenon that is shameful for Armenia. Librarians receive the lowest salaries [75,000 drams — $208]. Raise them!”

“After spending days and nights thinking about the people, the ‘democratic’ government decided to raise its own salaries by 60–80%. Meanwhile, citizens earning 80,000–150,000 drams ($220–414) can continue entering shops full of goods. As prices rise rapidly, they must painfully choose whether to buy food for their child or shoes for themselves.”

“They are setting their salaries higher than those of members of the British royal family. And they are paying for all this with our taxes. They will bleed us dry. This is only the beginning.”

“The [prime minister] claims that raising his salary and those of other officials is necessary to prevent a catastrophe. According to this passionate speaker, a ‘catastrophe’ is when someone asks where an official got his suit or watch. I wonder who will ask him what he plans to spend those 2,662,000 drams — around $7,400 — a month on, considering how expensive he is for the state. For nine years now, you have paid neither rent nor utility bills, car expenses, petrol or maintenance costs.”

Salary increases for public officials in Armenia

World.title: Tbilisi condemns “presidential election” in Georgia’s Russian-occupied Tskhinvali region
World.content:
Georgia condemns Russia over South Ossetia election

Georgia’s Foreign Ministry condemned the so-called “presidential election” held on 18 September in the Russian-occupied Tskhinvali region (South Ossetia), calling it a violation of Georgia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity.

According to the ministry’s statement, “the opening of polling stations by Russia in the occupied territory without the consent of the Georgian government is a gross violation of Georgia’s sovereignty and another manifestation of Russia’s policy aimed at the de facto annexation of Georgia’s regions.”

Georgia’s Foreign Ministry said that holding the so-called election violates fundamental norms and principles of international law and cannot legitimise the occupation regime in Tskhinvali or change the region’s status under international law as part of Georgia.

“Holding any so-called elections in Georgia’s occupied territories, which are under military occupation and the effective control of the Russian Federation, while internally displaced persons and refugees are not given the opportunity to return to their homes safely and with dignity, is illegal and cannot have any international legal consequences,” the ministry said.

Tbilisi also condemned Russia’s decision to open polling stations for the Russian State Duma election in occupied Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region from 18 to 20 September.

The Foreign Ministry called on the international community to properly assess and condemn Russia’s actions and ensure an appropriate international legal and political response.

“Georgia continues to call on the international community to firmly protect Georgia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity within its internationally recognised borders and support a peaceful resolution of the conflict,” the statement said.

On 18 September, snap “presidential elections” were held in Russian-occupied “South Ossetia”. Four candidates took part.

However, calling it an “election race” would only be accurate in a very loose sense, as it was clear from the outset that the overwhelming favourite was so-called “acting president” and “prime minister” Marat Kambolov, who arrived in the region from Russia in May 2026.

World.title: Armenia’s anti-corruption campaign: law on confiscating illicit assets takes effect
World.content:
Armenia’s law on confiscating illicit property

A large-scale anti-corruption campaign is unfolding in Armenia . As part of the campaign, the state is confiscating assets belonging to members of the country’s former financial and political elite.

The authorities say they are moving from high-profile political accusations to a systematic effort to recover illegally acquired property. The list of people accused of corruption whose numerous properties and business assets have been frozen includes former Armenian president Robert Kocharyan , Prosperous Armenia party leader Gagik Tsarukyan, and former finance minister and ex-head of the State Revenue Committee Gagik Khachatryan. Prosecutors accuse those involved in these high-profile cases of money laundering, bribery and abuse of office.

At the same time, the debate in Armenia goes beyond how they managed to amass such wealth. It also concerns whether the process complies with the law, whether the authorities apply the law equally to everyone, and whether the confiscated property is genuinely being returned to the people.

About the law

Armenia’s Law on Confiscation of Property of Illicit Origin has been in force since 2020. The authorities adopted it “to strengthen the fight against corruption and restore social justice”. The law applies to assets worth more than 50 million drams ($132,120). It allows the state to confiscate property if its owner cannot prove that the income used to acquire it came from legal sources.

According to the Prosecutor General’s Office, between 2018 and the first half of 2026, the state and local communities recovered assets worth approximately 304 billion drams (around $840 million). More than two-thirds of that amount — about $562 million — was recovered over the past three and a half years.

Comment from lawyer Aram Orbelyan

“The Law on Confiscation of Property of Illicit Origin contains fundamental contradictions. In international practice, confiscation models are clearly separated. One involves checking declarations: if a person cannot explain their income, the state confiscates the property. The other involves confiscation following proof of a crime. Our lawmakers, however, have mixed everything together into complete confusion.

The grounds for an investigation are chaotic. Half of the provisions are linked to criminal cases, including cases that authorities have suspended or closed on non-exonerating grounds. The other half allows officials to launch confiscation proceedings based simply on ‘operational information’. As soon as any intelligence report appears, law-enforcement agencies immediately begin examining a person’s property, going back as far as 1991.”

The factual vacuum of the 1990s

“What political statements describe as ‘plunder’ is often impossible to prove in court because the circumstances of that era were different. In the 1990s, non-monetary transactions, including agricultural exchanges, were widespread. There was no clear system of tax and customs control. Vehicle databases only appeared in the early 2000s, while electronic tax records emerged in 2013.

Moreover, the law at the time did not require businesses to keep documents for more than five years. This has naturally created an information vacuum today. Young prosecutors fail to take this historical context into account, leading to dead ends in court.”

Intrusion into private life and the political context

“The extent of the intrusion into private life raises serious questions. The law allows investigators to examine years of bank statements belonging to any relatives of a person under investigation. As a result, investigators and prosecutors gain access to strictly personal spending unrelated to corruption: where people went on holiday, what they ordered in cafés and what illnesses they received treatment for.

Society sees this mechanism exclusively as a ‘law to recover what former [authorities] stole’. Legally, however, the law should target corruption as such, rather than individuals. To ensure that anti-corruption tools do not appear politically selective, they must operate universally. They should apply to all elites, regardless of their current political status or affiliation with the ruling camp.

Authorities must examine both the past and the present transparently, without politically motivated cases, while taking limitation periods and the economic realities of earlier years into account. The process should objectively target illicit property, rather than serve as a selectively applied repressive tool.”

Comment from Varuzhan Hoktanian, an expert at Transparency International’s Anti-Corruption Centre

“The law sparked legal disputes from the outset, which led to a review of its constitutionality by the Constitutional Court. The court, in turn, sought an expert opinion from the Venice Commission. International experts offered two key recommendations. First, the confiscation of property for the benefit of the state should take place through separate civil proceedings, rather than criminal prosecution resulting in imprisonment. Second, some responsibility for proving the lawful origin of assets should fall on the owner.

It is often extremely difficult to prove that property has a corrupt origin. For example, Kocharyan’s case involves the signing of government decisions. For the charges to stand, the prosecution must prove that he deliberately approved specific decisions in the expectation that the assets would eventually pass to his family. This is extremely difficult to establish, so the evidence often appears unconvincing. The situation is compounded by the absence of a mandatory declaration system in the 1990s. As a result, it is now virtually impossible to confirm that property was acquired legally.”

Discrimination or fight against corruption?

“Applying legal mechanisms exclusively to one group of people discredits the anti-corruption institution itself, turning the law into a tool of political pressure. Attempts to deprive opponents of financial resources by seizing their property create a risk of completely clearing the political field. If this is combined with double standards during elections — harsh punishment, including arrests, for vote-buying while ignoring the abuse of administrative resources — the system of checks and balances itself collapses. Ignoring any of these abuses leads to dictatorship.”

What happens to confiscated property?

“The legal question is only one side of the problem. The question of what happens to confiscated property after the state receives it is no less important.

I recall a similar confiscation from Soviet history — the dekulakisation campaign of the late 1920s and early 1930s. We later learned about the grave consequences it caused, including the Holodomor. As it turned out, the party nomenklatura ultimately received everything that the authorities had seized. Today, these assets could likewise pass to new wealthy individuals or another nomenklatura. Once again, ordinary people would receive nothing.

When people talk about confiscating property, they mean both financial assets and movable and immovable property. For example, someone may have built a luxurious house and live in it. If we return to the Soviet example, after the October Revolution, the authorities seized property from wealthy people and turned luxury homes into communal apartments. That will not happen in our case. No one plans to move an ordinary citizen into someone else’s mansion. This raises the question: who received the mansion belonging to formerprimeministerformer prime minister Hovik Abrahamyan, or the Golden Palace hotel in Tsaghkadzor?

The situation is also problematic here. Even if a new wealthy owner buys these properties, a change of government could lead to their seizure again, with the authorities claiming that the original confiscation was unlawful.

Moreover, the phrase ‘returning property to the people’ sounds somewhat abstract to me. The trend shows that confiscated real estate goes not to the people, but to another wealthy person close to the authorities. And the public will ask: ‘What do we get out of it?’

Let me give you an example. There used to be a kindergarten in our courtyard. A newly wealthy owner acquired it through an illegal transfer. If the state takes the building back today and restores its former status as a kindergarten, then yes, that would mean ‘returning it to the people’.

In other cases, this could become a vicious circle in which each successive government dispossesses the previous one. This is quite dangerous, especially in the context of investment. Investors should not have to fear that the authorities might dispossess them tomorrow.”

How can confiscated funds be used?

“As for monetary confiscations, the seized funds go into the budget, into what is known as a ‘common pot’. It is unclear how the authorities then spend this money. These are not earmarked revenues, so the authorities decide how to use them.

It would be better to classify these revenues as earmarked funds and regulate them by law, directing the money towards social programmes designed to improve citizens’ welfare.”

Armenia’s law on confiscating illicit property

World.title: Poll: Do Abkhazia residents consider voting in Russia’s State Duma elections important? Video
World.content:
Russia’s State Duma elections will take place on 20 September. As most residents of Abkhazia hold dual Abkhaz-Russian citizenship, they can also take part in the vote. In the republic, which has a population of 250,000, as many as 35 polling stations have opened, and campaigning is in full swing.

Ahead of the election, we asked residents of Sukhum whether they planned to vote and whether they believed doing so would make a real difference.

The poll produced highly contradictory responses. Some people do not want to spend their day off voting in another country. Others consider it very important because, “if things go badly in Russia, things will get very hot here in Abkhazia too”.

Rustam: “For some reason, Russia is placing great importance on Abkhazia at the moment, and they really want all residents to take part in these elections. Perhaps it does not even matter how people vote, because there is no alternative. What matters is showing the turnout — that people are actively and collectively going to the polls, thereby acknowledging the assistance Russia provides to Abkhazia.

Personally, I will not vote because I see no point in it. If the [Yabloko party] had not been barred from the election, I would definitely have voted. Or I would have supported the Communists. As things stand, I do not want to spend my day off that way.”

Eliso: “I will definitely go to the polls and vote.

I will not say whom I will vote for. But as a Russian passport holder, I have the right to influence the composition of the State Duma, because the decisions made there directly affect us.

As a woman and a future mother, I want Abkhazia residents with Russian citizenship to be able to receive child benefits. I believe this bill should be among the first issues considered by the new parliamentary term.”

Timur: “I always vote in every election, both ours and Russia’s. My choice may almost never win, but I want to feel involved and have at least some opportunity to influence events. Russia directly affects us, and by voting I make my small contribution to what is happening in Abkhazia today.”

Almaskhan: “I will not vote. I never take part in elections and I am not interested in politics. I do not even know which parties are currently running or what they decide. Everything is done without us anyway. We live in a reality that we simply have to adapt to. It is impossible to change anything with a ‘tick’ on a ballot — everything has already been decided.”

Liana: “I will see how things go on Sunday, but I am not particularly keen. I do not even know whom to choose. The only party I hear about is United Russia, because its s are everywhere. Everyone says it is the strongest party. And Kiriyenko (the Kremlin’s overseer of Abkhazia — JAMnews) is a member, so apparently everything here is done through them. If I go, I will probably vote for them.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

World.title: Investigation launched into dozens of children falling ill at Tbilisi nurseries
World.content:
Children poisoned at Tbilisi kindergartens

Fourteen children were taken to hospitals from state-run nurseries in Tbilisi with symptoms of intoxication. The agency responsible for managing the capital’s kindergartens said seven state-run nurseries had suspended operations “to prevent epidemiological risks”.

According to the agency, the children had developed high temperatures, while some also experienced nausea and vomiting.

The Investigation Service of the Ministry of Finance has launched an inquiry into the incident. Searches reportedly continued throughout the night at four kindergartens and three companies supplying food to them. Relevant teams from the Interior Ministry and the Ministry of Environmental Protection and Agriculture also took part in the investigative activities.

At this stage, it is unclear what caused the children’s condition or whether the cases were linked to food served at the nurseries. Some parents said their children had eaten a beef cutlet at the kindergarten. However, doctors say investigators will only be able to establish the exact cause through clinical tests.

The investigation is being conducted under Article 198, Part 2 of the Criminal Code. The provision concerns the production and sale of products that pose a danger to human life or health, where this creates a risk to life or health.

According to the information available so far, 55 children and one staff member from 20 Tbilisi kindergartens have sought medical attention. However, the number of children and staff showing signs of poisoning may be higher, as not all of them have visited medical facilities.

Maya Chkhaidze, director of the Tsitsishvili Children’s Clinic, said 14 children from different kindergartens had been brought to the clinic. They had experienced vomiting, abdominal pain and symptoms typical of gastroenteritis.

“This could be a symptom of a viral infection or intoxication. At this stage, it is impossible to determine the exact cause,” Chkhaidze said.

According to her, none of the patients is in serious condition. Several children have already stabilised and are in satisfactory condition, although they remain in the clinic under medical observation.

Saba Buadze, a former Tbilisi City Council member from the opposition Lelo party, wrote on social media that companies which win tenders supply food products to kindergartens, while staff prepare meals directly on the premises.

According to him, the estimated value of procurement in this sector exceeded 100 million lari (around $40 million) in 2024–2025.

Buadze recalled corruption cases uncovered in the sector, including during the investigation into the case of recently convicted former State Security Service chief Grigol Liluashvili. One of the corruption episodes for which authorities charged him involved allegedly taking kickbacks from commercial organisations when awarding kindergarten food procurement contracts, using his official position.

“During my time on the Tbilisi City Council, we summoned officials accused of corruption to the council several times. But they failed to attend the hearings, violating the law. Recently, the quality of food in kindergartens has improved compared with previous years,” Buadze wrote.

Children poisoned at Tbilisi kindergartens

World.title: Council of Europe Committee of Ministers urges Russia to withdraw troops from Georgia’s occupied territories
World.content:
Council of Europe urges Russia to withdraw troops

The Council of Europe’s Committee of Ministers has again called on Russia to withdraw its troops from Georgia’s occupied regions and end so-called “borderisation” – the installation of border signs along the dividing lines in the Georgian-Ossetian and Georgian-Abkhaz conflict zones.

According to the Georgian Justice Ministry, at its September meeting the Committee of Ministers discussed the implementation of European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) judgments in the interstate case Georgia v Russia.

● The Committee reaffirmed its support for Georgia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity within its internationally recognised borders and called on the Russian Federation to fulfil its international obligations.

● Among its demands, the Committee called for the withdrawal of Russian troops from Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region and an end to so-called “borderisation”.

● The Committee also called on Russia to ensure the free and safe movement of the local population, access to property and the opportunity to receive education in the Georgian language in the Russian-occupied regions.

● The Committee of Ministers called for the necessary conditions to be created for the safe, voluntary and dignified return of displaced people to their homes and for an end to killings, abductions, torture, unlawful detention and other serious violations.

The Georgian Justice Ministry said the government had secured rulings in several major interstate cases against Russia at the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg, including cases concerning Russia’s deportation of Georgian citizens, the August 2008 war and Russia’s continuing occupation of Georgian territories.

According to the ministry, the Georgian authorities continue to work to secure the full implementation of the ECHR judgments through legal and diplomatic mechanisms.

World.title: Azerbaijan’s ACG fields produce over 628M tonnes of oil, 253B cubic meters of gas over 32 years
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 20. As part of the development of the Azeri-Chirag-Gunashli (ACG) field, one of Azerbaijan’s key oil and gas sector projects, more than 628 million tonnes of oil and 253 billion cubic metres of gas had been produced as of September 1, 2026.

Azerbaijan’s Minister of Energy Parviz Shahbazov wrote this on his X page.

“Thirty-two years have passed since the signing of the ‘Contract of the Century.’ On September 20, 1994, a 30-year Production Sharing Agreement on the joint development of the Azeri-Chirag-Gunashli (ACG) fields and the sharing of production was signed with the participation of 11 international oil companies from seven countries. At the initial stage, the target was set to produce 500 million tonnes of oil from the ACG fields.

On September 14, 2017, the agreement on the ACG fields was amended and revised, following which a new Production Sharing Agreement was signed. Under the amended agreement, the development period of ACG was extended until the end of 2050. At the same time, SOCAR’s participating interest was increased from 11.65% to 25%, while Azerbaijan’s share of profit oil was set at 75%,” the minister wrote.

P. Shahbazov recalled that on April 19, 2019, the final investment decision was made on the Central East Azeri (ACE) project.

“The first oil from the ACE platform was produced on April 16, 2024. Over the project’s operating life, the target is to produce 300 million barrels of oil. On September 20, 2024, an agreement was signed on the production of natural gas from the ACG fields. Free natural gas production at ACG began on June 1, 2026. As of September 1, 2026, more than 628 million tonnes of oil and 253 billion cubic metres of gas had been produced from the ACG fields. More than 63 billion cubic metres of the gas produced was delivered to the state,” he noted.

Currently, the participating interests in the ACG project are distributed as follows: SOCAR — 35.30%, bp — 30.37%, MOL Group — 9.57%, INPEX — 9.31%, ExxonMobil — 6.79%, TPAO — 5.73%, and ONGC Videsh — 2.92%.

The minister stressed that the “Contract of the Century” is a historic agreement authored by National Leader Heydar Aliyev.

“It transformed the Caspian’s oil wealth into Azerbaijan’s economic strength, international confidence and strategic energy partnership. Today, building on this strong foundation, we are writing the next chapter of our country’s energy history through new energy projects and ‘green’ energy corridors,” the publication says.

World.title: Restoration of Azerbaijan's state sovereignty creates new political reality in region - MFA
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, September 20. The restoration of Azerbaijan's state sovereignty has opened up new opportunities for lasting peace.

This was reflected in the statement of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Azerbaijan on the occasion of September 20 - State Sovereignty Day.

It is noted that 20 September is a historic day marking the restoration of our state sovereignty that inscribed in golden letters in the centuries-old statehood chronicle of our nation:

"20 September is a historic day marking the restoration of our state sovereignty that inscribed in golden letters in the centuries-old statehood chronicle of our nation.

On 19-20 September 2023, local anti-terrorist measures were carried out in the Garabagh region of Azerbaijan to disarm and withdraw the remnants of the Armenian armed forces from our territories. Consequently, as a result of the measures completed in less than 24 hours, state sovereignty over the territories was restored.

The high professionalism, courage, and heroism of the Azerbaijan’s Armed Forces under the leadership and resolute political will of the President of the Republic of Azerbaijan, Victorious Commander-in-Chief H.E. Ilham Aliyev, played a decisive role in achieving this historic victory.

During the anti-terrorist measures, the Azerbaijani side paid special attention to the safety of the civilian population, targeting only the legitimate military facilities and infrastructure of illegal armed formations, rather than civilians and civilian infrastructure.

The restoration of Azerbaijan's state sovereignty created a new political reality in the region, opening new opportunities for the normalization of Azerbaijan-Armenia relations and for lasting peace. Demonstrating its commitment to the peace agenda, our country has taken consistent and purposeful steps toward normalizing relations.

The historic meeting held in Washington D.C. on 8 August 2025, with the participation of the leaders of Azerbaijan, the United States, and Armenia, marked an important milestone in the peace and normalization process.

Today, the agreements reached during the meetings between the leaders of Azerbaijan and Armenia are of great importance not only for ensuring lasting peace and stability in the region, but also for realizing the regional economic potential.

The restoration of economic- trade ties in the region and the implementation of confidence-building measures in this direction, as well as the promotion of regional integration of international transport and logistics routes, will create new economic dividends and cooperation opportunities not only for Azerbaijan and Armenia, but also for all interested parties.

Building upon the historic opportunity for peace, resolving the issues lying ahead to sign a peace agreement and fully normalize relations between Azerbaijan and Armenia is of paramount importance.

Today, Azerbaijan is carrying out large-scale efforts towards the restoration of the liberated territories, ensuring the return of former internally displaced persons to their native lands, and promoting the sustainable development of these areas. At the same time, eliminating the landmine threat and determining the fate of missing persons are among our country's main priorities.

State Sovereignty Day is a symbol of the Azerbaijani people’s commitment to their statehood, national will and territorial integrity. This significant day is an important occasion to pay deep respect to the dearest memory of our martyrs, and to always preserve and pass on to future generations the value of the historic Victory achieved at the cost of their lives.

The state sovereignty of the Republic of Azerbaijan is eternal, indivisible and inviolable.

Happy State Sovereignty Day, Azerbaijan!"

World.title: Alex de Minaur fires as Aussie pair clicks in Davis Cup triumph
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Alex de Minaur has returned to form to seal Australia's Davis Cup progression, with the hosts beating Poland 3-1 in Brisbane also thanks to some earlier doubles brilliance.

The world No.9 found top gear on Sunday at Pat Rafter Arena, beating Kamil Majchrzak 6-3 6-3 to clinch a 3-1 result that sends Australia into the Cup's penultimate round next year.

With his backhand and serve firing, de Minaur followed up his 57-minute annihilation of Maks Kasnikowski on Saturday with another therapeutic response to a disappointing second-round US Open exit earlier this month.

Earlier, Max Purcell's scintillating tiebreak tennis alongside rock-solid Rinky Hijikata swung their doubles match, and the tie, in Australia's favour.

The pair's 7-6 (7-3) 6-3 defeat of Jan Zielinski and Karol Drzewiecki followed the win and the loss posted in singles by de Minaur and James Duckworth respectively on Saturday.

Purcell, on the comeback from a controversial 18-month anti-doping ban, turned the match on its head after a tight first set progressed to an inevitable tie break.

He drilled a backhand return to win the opening point on the Polish serve, then produced a pair of aces to shoot the hosts clear 3-0.

De Minaur wins Davis Cup opener After a long and winding road to Brisbane in 2026, Alex de Minaur rides a partisan home crowd to an impressive victory in the first rubber of Australia's Davis Cup tie against Poland.

An unforced error from Poland was followed by two more Purcell winners, and he then held his nerve on a series of low volleys to eventually clinch the set.

Hijikata then held impressively and, after missing two break-point chances, nailed a forehand return to nab the match's only service break.

That was all Australia needed, with the composed pair energising the sold-out Pat Rafter Arena to secure a pressure-relieving victory in 77 minutes.

Australia's win followed a shock loss on the road to Ecuador earlier this year that plunged it into the must-win encounter against Poland.

The Aussies still need to win next year's qualifying round, against an opponent still to be decided, to progress to the finals in Italy in November, 2027.

AAP

World.title: 'Needle in haystack': Expert says little chance of finding shark that killed Greg O'Neill
World.content:
A behavioural biologist and shark drone expert has criticised the WA government's response to the state's most recent fatal shark attack, saying the chances of finding the shark responsible for a 63-year-old swimmer's death are slim to none.

WA Fisheries Minister Jackie Jarvis on Saturday took an "extraordinary" step of issuing a catch-and-kill order for the shark that killed Greg James O'Neill at Sorrento Beach in Perth's north.

Ms Jarvis said the decision was made under "the exceptional circumstances of the attack" where "the hazard posed by the shark" and "the potential recovery of coronial evidence" were taken into consideration.

Culum Brown is not convinced that the WA government will catch the shark responsible for Mr O'Neill's death. (Supplied: Culum Brown)

Culum Brown, from Macquarie University's Ecology and Evolution of Fishes Laboratory, said the chances of finding the shark responsible for Mr O'Neill's death were like finding "a needle in a haystack".

" The reality is that white sharks move a long, long way, they are literally on the move all the time … by now, that shark could be hundreds of kilometres away. "

The only way to determine whether a shark is responsible, according to Mr Brown, is to kill and gut it to see if it has human remains in it.

"So what are they going to do? Catch every white shark on the west coast until they find the one? I mean, it's a bit ridiculous."

The NSW government announced a further $34 million in shark-spotting drones this June. (ABC News: Berge Breiland)

Mr Brown said he believed a better response would be to invest more funds in shark-spotting drones, an approach the New South Wales government took after a shark attack at Sydney's Coogee Beach in June.

"They [drones] are just a very highly effective technology," Mr Brown said.

Third person killed by sharks in WA this year The often-heated debate over how to protect beachgoers from sharks is likely to get hotter after the death of a third person this year.

"They are a lot cheaper than fixed-wing or helicopters … and one of the many benefits is that you can intervene before the shark attacks anybody and … there's no bycatch as there is with shark nets and things like that."

He said that it was a "win-win" situation for swimmers and sharks.

The Fisheries Minister Ms Jarvis added that deploying more drones to spot sharks along WA's vast coastline was "absolutely under consideration".

She said the government would first review its current mitigation strategies — which focus on tagging and tracking, an app for notifications, warning sirens, shark enclosures and personal deterrents — to see what more could be done to protect beachgoers.

Body yet to be recovered

Mr O'Neill was swimming close to the Sorrento Beach shoreline when a suspected three-metre great white took him on Friday morning.

Authorities soon began a wide-scale search for his body and the white shark responsible, which they believed they had located before losing track of it.

The body of the 63-year-old is yet to be recovered.

A woman lays a floral tribute alongside others at Sorrento Beach after the fatal shark attack. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

The Department of Primary Industries and Regional Development (DPIRD) has set shark capture gear, a type of drum line normally used to tag sharks, about 1.5 kilometres off Sorrento Beach.

Loading...

On Sunday, WA Deputy Premier Rita Saffioti said she "100 per cent" supported Ms Jarvis's response to the attack, including the catch-and-kill order.

"The minister made a decision based on advice. That advice was given by, as I understand, both police and fisheries," Ms Saffiotti said.

WA Greens healthy oceans spokeswoman Sophie McNeill earlier criticised the order, describing it as cruel and ineffective.

Ms McNeill instead called for more funding for shark-spotting drones and helicopters, and an expansion of the shark tagging program.

World.title: Hot, dry day ahead for Qld with unusually high temps in some areas
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Hot and dry weather is forecast for the start of the week across much of Queensland, with unusually high temperatures predicted in some parts of the state.

On Monday, some areas of the Darling Downs could see their hottest September day since 2017, according to the Bureau of Meteorology (BOM).

Maximum temperatures for Brisbane could reach 32 to 34 degrees Celsius on Monday, about 5 degrees above average.

Warm temperatures coupled with school holidays are delivering crowds to beaches across the Gold Coast. (ABC News: Emily Dobson)

The Gold Coast and Sunshine Coast will be spared that kind of heat, with both regions expecting a top of 28C. Bundaberg is headed for 29C.

While Toowoomba's forecast top is 31C, some areas of the Lockyer Valley could be among the hottest parts of the state, with highs of up to 36C forecast.

"We're expecting around 28 in Cairns, 28 in Townsville, 26 for Mackay [and] 32 for Rockhampton," BOM senior meteorologist Steve Hadley said.

Hot and dry weather is set to continue in north Queensland. (ABC News: Isabella Garrido)

In the very north, there could be cloud and shower activity, mainly north of Ingham.

Early-morning fog patches are forecast for eastern areas south of Cairns, clearing to a fine day.

To the north of Townsville, temperatures are expected to be average for this time of year.

South of Longreach may see temperatures about 5 to 10 degrees above the September average.

"Longreach is expected to be on a high of 36 degrees, Mount Isa on 34, and we could see some areas getting up to around 36 or 37 in the Channel Country," Mr Hadley said.

Fire warnings

Mr Hadley said there was a broadscale fire risk across most of the state, with dry conditions and elevated temperatures, especially in the south.

A high fire danger means fires can be difficult to control under some circumstances. (ABC News: Isabella Garrido)

"Places like Townsville, where they get regular sea breezes in that part of the world, you can see quite drastic changes through the day as temperatures warm up," he said.

"The winds then can change, and come in from a different direction in the afternoon as the sea breeze comes in and that presents challenges for people fighting fires."

On Saturday, firefighter crews worked through "extreme winds" to contain a grass fire beside Townsville Airport.

Windy conditions posed a challenge for firefighters in Townsville. (ABC News: Isabella Garrido)

Station Officer Chris Maguire said crews had to work through volatile conditions to contain the flames and heavy plumes of smoke.

He said the grass fire was fast-moving, with challenging, windy conditions fuelling the flames.

Wind changes across other parts of the state are expected for the next few days, including sea breezes along the east coast.

World.title: Lions star to challenge grand final ban, Hawks pair handed massive fines
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

The Brisbane Lions will challenge a one-match ban handed to Lachie Neale, which would rule the two-time premiership captain out of the AFL grand final.

Neale was offered the suspension after being charged with striking during the Lions' controversial nine-point win over Hawthorn in Saturday night's preliminary final at the MCG.

Hawks fans throw bottles at umpires Hawthorn fans are condemned for their behaviour after the siren following a heart-stopping preliminary final against the Brisbane Lions at the MCG.

Meanwhile, Hawks pair James Sicliy and Tom Barrass have been fined $10,000 and $5,000 respectively for approaching umpire Hayden Meyer following the frenetic finish to the match.

Neale's off-the-ball incident involved a gut punch to the Hawks' Jack Ginnivan in the first quarter.

Vision showed Ginnivan wrestling with Lions forward Eric Hipwood, before Neale jogs over and hits the Hawks player with a left-handed punch to the stomach.

It was graded intentional conduct, medium impact and body contact.

Within minutes of the AFL releasing the match review findings on Sunday, the Lions confirmed they will challenge the ban.

Neale will front the tribunal but, if unsuccessful, will miss Saturday's grand final against Fremantle at the MCG.

New match review guidelines state intentional strikes to the stomach are automatically graded as medium impact rather than low, resulting in one-match bans.

Lachie Neale has won two flags with the Lions. (Getty Images/AFL Photos: Robert Cianflone)

Neale may attempt to lean on the "exemplary record" clause to clear himself for the grand final.

He has never been suspended in his 320-match career and could use the same clause that helped Scott Pendlebury escape suspension for his bump on Adelaide's Josh Worrell this season.

Under AFL regulations, "a player with an exemplary record may argue that their good record constitutes exceptional and compelling circumstances".

Players can no longer use the so-called "good bloke" defence that helped Brisbane's Charlie Cameron overturn a ban in 2024.

Neale's other option is to attempt to have the impact grading reduced, though that route would be unlikely to be successful.

A suspension would also mean Neale may have played his final match for the Lions.

The 33-year-old, who has twice won the Brownlow Medal, is set to make an off-season move to Collingwood as a free agent.

Neale and Harris Andrews were co-captains when the Lions won the 2024 and 2025 premierships.

Should the Lions defeat the Dockers, they will match the feat of the club's 2001-03 squad, which won three straight flags.

James Sicily was fined $10,000 by the AFL. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

Sicily and Barrass were handed their massive fines for misconduct after their heated conversation with Meyer immediately after the final siren.

It followed a controversial finish, in which a holding-the-ball free kick paid against Hawthorn's Jarman Impey gifted Brisbane's Hugh McCluggage the match-clinching goal in the dying stages.

Sicily and Barrass were not offered an early plea.

The AFL determined the fixed financial sanction for abusive language towards an umpire was inadequate, and so charged Sicily and Barrass under the "other misconduct'' provision.

Hawks midfielder Jai Newcombe was cleared over his first-quarter contact with Neale in a collision that involved opponents pushing the two players into each other.

ABC/AAP

World.title: Suns surge to victory, Tigers survive Giants comeback in AFLW
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Gold Coast's band of youngsters have strengthened their grip on a third AFLW finals berth, beating Essendon by 41 points at Windy Hill.

The Suns have surprised many this season after starting the campaign as one of the more youthful and inexperienced sides in the league.

Their 7.9 (51) to 1.4 (10) win over Essendon on Sunday was their third consecutive victory and moved them into fifth spot, just four points behind second-placed defending champions North Melbourne.

Gold Coast's defence was resolute in the blustery conditions, and the Bombers did not score a point until late in the second quarter.

At the same time, the visitors were dominating territory and snagged three goals courtesy of a trio of players all aged under 21.

After leading by 20 points at half-time, Suns forward Anne Hatchard and midfielder Charlie Rowbottom added their names to the scoresheet, before Emily Gough found the Bombers' only major late in the third period.

The visitors grabbed another two goals in the final term to complete the win.

Defender Niamh McLaughlin (33 disposals, 506 metres gained) and Rowbottom (36 disposals, one goal) were busy for Gold Coast (4-2), while Hatchard and Havana Harris scored two majors each.

The loss kept the Bombers (0-6) winless, although midfielder Madison Prespakis was outstanding with a game-high 38 disposals.

At Manuka Oval, Richmond survived an almighty scare to claim a stirring 9.14 (68) to 10.1 (61) win over a pinpoint-accurate GWS.

Do you have a story idea about women in sport? Email us abcsport5050@your.abc.net.au

Fresh off a 15-point win over St Kilda last Sunday, the Tigers (4-2) raced out of the gates and led by 16 points at quarter-time in Canberra.

Richmond continued to run riot in the second term, booting five goals in 12 minutes to balloon their advantage to 55-18 at the main break.

But the Giants completely transformed after half-time, scoring six majors, including a double from Georgia Garnett, to give themselves a glimmer of hope at three-quarter time.

Leading by eight points, the visitors sprayed a flurry of opportunities wide, but their defence held off the Giants' desperate attack to claim the win and go equal with the Suns on victories.

Finals hopes are fading for the Giants (1-5), but midfielders Alyce Parker (27 disposals) and Rebecca Beeson (23 disposals, two goals) were prolific, while Garnett finished with three goals.

Forward Gabby Seymour (16 hit outs) posted a career-best three majors for Richmond, while Olivia Wolmarans also had three goals.

AAP
