World.title: One person in hospital after aged care facility fire in North Adelaide
World.content:
One person has been taken to hospital following a fire at an aged care facility in North Adelaide.

At 12:30pm today, 34 firefighters from 12 appliances attended the blaze at Helping Hand on Buxton Street.

MFS's Nicolle Bradley said quick action from emergency crews located a fire on the ground floor.

She said firefighters brought the fire under control within 15 minutes.

The fire was extinguished quickly at Helping Hand aged care facility. (ABC News: Olivia Mason)

Ms Bradley said crews prevented the fire from spreading further into the facility.

MFS commander Phil Ross said multiple people called Triple Zero (000) about the fire.

"We've got some smoke damage occurring to some of the adjacent levels," Mr Ross said.

"This is the independent living side of the accommodation. They have their own 240V smoke alarms … it's only a local alarm which is not monitored by the MFS."

Phil Ross says the damage is estimated at about $200,000. (ABC News)

The commander said a number of people were evacuated from the building during the blaze.

" The person who was in the unit self-evacuated. He has been transported to hospital. "

Mr Ross said the patient had a head laceration.

Investigators are looking into the cause of the fire.

The commander estimated the damage bill to be about $200,000.

World.title: Lachie Neale will fight gut-punch suspension at AFL tribunal in bid to play in grand final
World.content:
Breaking SportAFLAFL 2026 Lachie Neale will fight gut-punch suspension at AFL tribunal in bid to play in grand final Peter Ryan Updated September 20, 2026 — 5:02pm ,first published 2:51pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Brisbane’s dual Brownlow medallist Lachie Neale is heading for a high-stakes hearing at the AFL tribunal as he fights to play Saturday’s grand final against his former team, Fremantle. Neale, 33, was banned from playing in the grand final when the AFL’s match review officer on Sunday found him guilty of striking Hawthorn’s Jack Ginnivan in the closing minutes of the first quarter of Saturday’s preliminary final. Chris Fagan and Lachie Neale celebrate the Lions preliminary final win. Getty Images The MRO found Neale made intentional, medium-force contact to Ginnivan’s body and banned him for one match, but as soon as that verdict became official the Brisbane Lions confirmed they would challenge it at the tribunal. The charge arises from an interaction between Neale and Ginnivan on the 50m line at the city end of the MCG.



The fact Ginnivan played on, seemingly without discomfort, could possibly form part of Neale’s defence if he seeks to get the charge downgraded to a low-impact strike, which would free him up to play in Saturday’s grand final. However, nine players have been suspended for offences of this nature this season, and the two who challenged them at the tribunal were unsuccessful. Neale was under an injury cloud going into last year’s decider but played as a substitute, shedding the vest in the second half and starring as his team charged to its second successive premiership. Now with a Lions three-peat on the line, Neale is again the focus of grand final week.



What’s more, the match is widely understood to be his final outing in Brisbane colours, as it’s expected he will move to Collingwood as a free agent in the off-season. Although he hasn’t been in peak form this finals series, Neale – a former Lions captain – remains a pivotal cog in Brisbane’s midfield. But his footballing prowess has been overshadowed this year by off-field dramas, firstly the collapse of his relationship with wife Jules, who moved home to Western Australia with their two children, followed by continued speculation over his playing future. View post on X Neale copped a heavy knock in the opening seconds of Saturday’s thrilling preliminary final win over Hawthorn, coling off second best after a collision at a centre ball-up with Hawk Jai Newcombe.

World.title: An NRL title in their fourth season would be remarkable for Dolphins – and might just keep the club together
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 An NRL title in their fourth season would be remarkable for Dolphins – and might just keep the club together Christian Nicolussi September 20, 2026 — 4:57pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A first NRL premiership will also put the Dolphins in the box seat to retain some of the club’s superstars, including Herbie Farnworth. So says Dolphins coach Kristian Woolf, who is comfortable with how contract negotiations have unfolded recently with the likes of Farnworth. Loading Farnworth is now widely regarded as the premier centre in the game, and he confirmed that with a match-turning performance in the qualifying final win over the Warriors, which allowed the Dolphins to advance to a preliminary final on home soil against the Sydney Roosters. There has been much interest in Farnworth’s next career move, with the Englishman heavily linked to the Roosters for the start of the 2028 season as James Tedesco’s successor in the No.1 jumper.



The Roosters are not allowed to talk to Farnworth until he becomes a free agent on November 1, but that has not stopped repeated reports about the Tricolours’ determination to land their man. The Dolphins, however, are aware premiership success will go a long way to encouraging Farnworth stay put. Herbie Farnworth’s try changed the momentum in their qualifying final win over the Warriors. Getty Images The Dolphins believe if Farnworth can win one title, maybe he will want to hang around to chase two or even three with his mates at Redcliffe. “We have a fair bit of work before we get to a position to win a comp, but Herbie, like everyone, can see we have a great group here who are all at a good age and improving together,” Woolf said.



“That’s something that is really strong in terms of what will keep this group together. “They [contract talks] haven’t been a distraction based on his performances, and it’s certainly not a distraction for us. “We’re comfortable with the situation and the communication around it. Herbie Farnworth has been heavily linked to the Sydney Roosters. Getty Images “Herbie is such a strike player for us. I loved what he was able to do against the Warriors, not just in attack, but his overall game – it was the kind of performance we’ve grown to expect and want to see from him.



“He had to work hard in defence, and when we went down to 12 men, he had to defend in a foreign position. But he was exceptional, which he has been all year. “We don’t need much more from Herbie on Friday – we just need him to go out and be himself.” Farnworth is managed by Joe Wehbe, who also has Tom Flegler and Morgan Knowles at Redcliffe, and Tedesco, Daly Cherry-Evans and Reece Robson at the Roosters. The 26-year-old Farnworth’s match-up with Roosters right centre Rob Toia will be one of the great individual battles of the first preliminary final. The Dolphins are fresh off the bye, welcome back Flegler from a concussion, and Woolf is happy to back his group to handle the weight of expectation in Brisbane usually reserved for the Broncos. Only single seats remain for the preliminary final.



The Dolphins have won eight straight games since their shock 66-0 loss to Cronulla in round 19. “We just have to enjoy it and love everything we’re doing at this time of year,” Woolf said. “You do all the hard work in November so you can still be playing at this time of year. Related Article Analysis

NRL 2026 The secret to DCE’s 424-game career? A ‘goldfish memory’, Ted Lasso and Dolphin days “We have expectations on ourselves with what we want to do. We’ve handled everything so far, including winning last week in what was a tough environment [at Go Media Stadium], and this is an opportunity to show we can handle it again.



“There will also be plenty of expectations on the Roosters, who have a great history of making grand finals and winning comps – that in itself brings expectations. “They were big and powerful on Saturday night, and it didn’t surprise me the performance they came up with. “We had a few days off to freshen up, and it was a bit like having a bye round, which is gold at this time of year. I expect the Roosters to be at their best, but so will we.”

World.title: This haunting play celebrates the solidarity and strangeness of found family
World.content:
Key points THEATRE: Luke makes its world premiere at Red Stitch

THEATRE: Harold Pinter’s The Homecoming is performed at the Athenaeum

MUSICAL THEATRE: Spamalot returns to Melbourne

MUSIC: Kristian Bezuidenhout performs Handel and Bach with the MSO

THEATRE

Luke ★★★★

Red Stitch, until October 11 Local playwright Angus Cameron has teamed up with Red Stitch for the world premiere of Luke – a disturbing, emotionally complex three-hander that weaves a provocative play of ideas into a psychological mystery of troubling currency. Will Lonsdale, Olga Makeeva and Dion Mills in Luke Parenthesy I was bewildered by the opening sequence. Two adults race across a living room playing dress-ups. They’re engaged in some kind of private game, based on the Bolshevik assassination of the Romanovs during the Russian Revolution, but something about the scene feels off, inauthentic somehow. A clever reason for this will remain an enigma until well after we discover that the pair are high school teachers in country Victoria. It’s 2007, and Damon (Dion Mills) and Olena (Olga Makeeva) are unwinding at term’s end after a gruelling night of parent-teacher interviews. When Chris (Will Lonsdale) – the school’s 19-year-old rowing coach and a former student of Damon’s – joins them, the games continue.



Some of the playfulness is literary or historical – a relic of the ludic flamboyance essential to Damon’s pedagogic style. He’s an inspiring educator, discreetly gay, and his mentor-like relationship with Chris, who came out to Damon as a student, is tinged by affection and by a body of queer knowledge excluded by the official (read heteronormative) education system. When conversation turns to a never-seen character, Luke – a year 11 student leaving the school after inappropriate attention from a member of staff – the game mutates through a series of twists, with a possible child sex abuse scenario, and its consequences, playing out over decades. Iain Sinclair’s direction guides three excellent performances. Iain Sinclair’s direction guides three excellent performances. Parenthesy Mills’ suspect teacher has the charisma, passion, idealism, and sheer eccentricity of a gifted educator. There’s no question he leaves a mark on his students: his scenes with Lonsdale’s Chris are tender and haunted – enlivened by the irrepressible joy they both take in the learning game, as well as the shadow of barely repressed desire. Olena is the fulcrum of the play, and Makeeva is riveting as, through veiled parable and a clipped and embittered realism, the character weighs the truth of a situation in which the righteousness of her own acts is called into question.



She is a staunch counter to Chris – a young man heavily invested in his own righteousness, and solipsistic in the performance of it. Editor's pick Arts Three titans of politics, sport and media had a meeting in the 1980s. A new play imagines what was said Luke tackles such uncomfortable subjects as the erotics of education and the ethics of making art from life. It has stern things to say about the cultural amnesia afflicting Australian literature and drama, and it brings child protection concerns into contact with the reality of homophobia, knowing the ancient slur – the one that equates homosexuality with paedophilia – has never quite ceased to echo. Yet this haunting play celebrates, too, the solidarity and strangeness of found family, the clandestine solidarity and the mentorship relations that can exist between queer men finding their tribe. In this, it has an artistic genealogy that can be traced back to some of the most fearless and unsettling voices in queer Australian literature – the implied pederasty in David Malouf’s short story Under Southern Skies, say, or Frank Moorhouse’s The Everlasting Secret Family – updating the issues to a world of changing mores in which progressive rhetoric can disguise more difficult and painful human truths.

Reviewed by Cameron Woodhead



THEATRE

The Homecoming ★★★★

Athenaeum Theatre, until October 3 The lights come up to reveal two characters in a living room and it doesn’t take long for the sense that something is off-kilter to take hold. A pugnacious aged patriarch and ex-butcher named Max (Richard Piper) blathers on in an unpunctuated stream of consciousness to the uninterested Lenny (Ben Geurens) – we don’t find out the two are family until Max admonishes the louche Lenny for speaking such to his “lousy filthy father”. The barely concealed hostilities are extended to the diametrically gentle Sam (David Field), Max’s chauffeur brother and the hulking wannabe boxer Joey (Eddie Orton), Lenny’s younger brother. Richard Piper as Max in The Homecoming Ben Fon No one and nothing are quite as they seem in Harold Pinter’s 1965 comedy of menace The Homecoming, even once you account for the virulent sexism, barely concealed hatred, and dearth of familial love between these characters. The intrigue deepens when all four of them retire to bed and the taciturn Teddy (Peter Houghton) enters the house, accompanied by his enigmatic wife Ruth (Kate Kendall). Teddy has effectively been estranged from his family for six years and now resides in America, with neither his wife nor family acquainted with one another. A series of decidedly strange interactions between all characters leave audiences none the wiser as to what is about to unfold in this claustrophobic domestic setting.



Under the direction of Greg Carroll, a slowly creeping sense of foreboding and listlessness overtakes the play, only strengthening its visor grip on the audience as it unfolds. The world Pinter has ensconced these characters in exists in and of itself, ungoverned by the moral sensibilities and social mores of the now, let alone that of the 1960s when this play first premiered in London. Peter Houghton as Teddy and Kate Kendall as Ruth Ben Fon Absurdist and fantastical despite its realist underpinnings, The Homecoming lulls its audience into an illusion of normalcy. When social contracts are broken with seemingly no repercussions, the play’s (and our) grasp on reality loosens – shining an uncomfortable spotlight on the confronting misogyny on display, calling into rebuke the meaning of the familial ties traditionally held so dear, and questioning the unspoken rules that allow society to function as it does. The famed Pinter Pause allows the requisite space for these consternations to fester. A muscular black room is the fitting backdrop for the exertion of these men’s fragile, toxic masculinities, while Amelia Carroll and Margaret Goy’s costume design is a stunning cloak of civility that masks the innermost depravations of these characters. Clad in a babydoll dress throughout, Ruth is read as childlike and guileless – a misnomer that allows her to exert the full force of her feminine wiliness. The strength of a production like The Homecoming lives and dies by its ensemble cast, and this one is uniformly excellent. Kendall is a particular highlight as the otherworldly, cosmically unflappable Ruth, simultaneously an antidote against the testosterone-soaked aggression of the men around her and the sun around which their neediness, desperation and contemptibility orbit.

Reviewed by Sonia Nair



MUSICAL THEATRE

Spamalot ★★★★

Athenaeum Theatre, until October 4 You’d think that after 51 years a joke might stop being as funny as it once was. And yet, sitting in the dark watching two men debate how one swallow – or perhaps two, if they were holding some sort of string – might transport a coconut across countries I found myself laughing as though it was the first time I’d heard this conversation. L-R: Jesse Vasiliadis, Gareth Isaac, Stephen Curry, Ethan Jones and Noah Skape. Ben Fon Monty Python and the Holy Grail first hit cinemas in 1975, and Spamalot, “a new musical lovingly ripped off from the motion picture” takes the key plot and handful of songs from the film, adds a whole lot more, and twists the story off into new directions as needed. The musical, itself now 20 years on from when it took Broadway by storm and took out the Tony Award for best musical, still feels vibrant and fun and silly. A spoof of the Arthurian legend, the story sees King Arthur (Stephen Curry) seeking knights to join his round table before being tasked by God (a video recording of Eric Idle) to find the Holy Grail.



While many jokes and scenes are lifted directly from the original film and other Python works, Spamalot, with book and lyrics by Idle, and music co-written by John Du Prez, is its own thing. The songs written specifically for Spamalot hold their own against the older, more-established tunes. Idle takes great delight in breaking the fourth wall in creative ways and musical theatre itself is a key pillar of the story, with nods to everything and everyone from West Side Story to Liza Minnelli. Jaz Flowers and Ethan Jones as the Lady of the Lake and Sir Galahad. Ben Fon Jaz Flowers as the Lady of the Lake steals almost every scene she’s in – her powerful command of every note makes light work of the parade of vocal challenges thrown her way. Her skill as a singer is matched only by her comedic timing. Her meta duet with Ethan Jones as Sir Galahad in The Song That Goes Like This is a particular highlight. Python humour remains evergreen because it is untethered from time. When it isn’t purely revelling in the absurd, it is taking aim at themes that sadly never grow old (inequality, bigotry, cowardice), joyfully ratcheting up the classics (fart jokes), and being gleefully persnickety when it comes to wordplay. With a talented cast who all appear to be enjoying every minute on stage, Spamalot is just the right amount of silly.

Reviewed by Elizabeth Flux



MUSIC

Handel and Bach ★★★★

Melbourne Symphony Orchestra, Melbourne Recital Centre, September 19 Many Melbourne concertgoers will remember the stylish flair with which Australian fortepianist Kristian Bezuidenhout performed the complete Beethoven piano concertos with the Freiburg Baroque Orchestra on the cusp of COVID. Kristian Bezuidenhout at an earlier concert. Marco Borggreve Returning with some of that flair, Bezuidenhout directed the Melbourne Symphony Orchestra from the harpsichord in this program of works by Bach and Handel. Focusing particularly on rhythm and dynamics, Bezuidenhout brought crisp grandiloquence to the many French-style introductions on the program, whether to Bach’s Orchestral Suite No. 1 in C major or the Overture to Handel’s Admeto. There was also a general rhythmic buoyancy which lent itself well both to the dance-infused Bach Suite and Suites Nos. 1 and 2 from Handel’s familiar Water Music.



Carefully shaped dynamics applied to the whole orchestra made sense of the rise and fall of phrases and provided some well-judged dramatic contrasts. Related Article ★★★★★

Melbourne live reviews These are unapologetically political songs, and this artist is unapologetically herself Despite overall clarity, it was in Bezuidenhout’s arrangement of Bach’s incomplete Contrapunctus XIV from The Art of Fugue that the listener might have longed for some more granular detail in terms of articulation and pliability of tone in individual lines. Such qualities were more apparent in Handel’s Concerto grosso in D minor, Op. 3, no. 5 which followed. Fine wind and brass playing hallmarked the second half. Beginning with the Sinfonia from Bach’s Cantata No. 52 (otherwise recognisable as the opening of Brandenburg Concerto No. 4) followed by the Water Music, the horns and oboes took up Bezuidenhout’s brisk tempos with alacrity. Oboists Johannes Grosso and Ann Blackburn together with horn players Lucie Krysatis and Abbey Edlin crowned the festive mood of the Handel; their timbre setting up piquant contrasts with the strings, trumpets providing an additional regal air in the second suite. Thanks to Bezuidenhout, the MSO proved it can bring some idiomatic lightness to the glories of the baroque.

Reviewed by Tony Way The Booklist is a weekly newsletter for book lovers from Jason Steger. Get it delivered every Friday.

World.title: Pair of South Yarra art deco homes pass in at auction on $2m vendor bid
World.content:
PropertyNewsAuctions Pair of South Yarra art deco homes pass in at auction on $2m vendor bid Wes Mountain September 20, 2026 — 4:38pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A pair of art deco houses on the same title in the heart of South Yarra failed to sell together at auction on Saturday, passing in on a single $2 million vendor bid. Just a five-minute walk from Toorak Road shops, 50 and 52 Lang Street are both two-bedroom, one-bathroom layouts with high ceilings and classic art deco features. 50 Lang Street has recently been updated, and includes its own garage, while 52 is ready for renovation, or to be merged into a larger single family home. The property was one of 913 scheduled to go to auction in Melbourne this week. By Saturday evening, Domain recorded a preliminary auction clearance rate of 57 per cent from 655 reported results throughout the week, while 81 auctions were withdrawn. Withdrawn auctions are counted as unsold properties when calculating the clearance rate. While last week saw the preliminary clearance rate above 60 per cent for the first time since before the May budget, this week saw it fall below that benchmark – generally considered to indicate a balanced market – and return to the mid-50s, despite peak Spring auction season.



50 and 52 Lang Street had a price guide of $2.1 million to $2.3 million, with a $2.3 million reserve. Marshall White Stonnington agent Jack Fowles said despite passing in on a single vendor bid, “an enormous amount” of parties had got in contact after the auction. 50 Lang Street’s renovation provides a template for potential purchasers on how to update its neighbour. Marshall White Stonnington “A year ago, buyers would wait until the ‘halftime break’,” he said, referring to the point at which a bid is taken to a vendor to confirm the property is on the market. “Now it’s more common for properties to pass in, then you see the interest.”



He thought this left buyers in a more vulnerable, less transparent position, making offers in private rather than competing in an open arena. Related Article Auctions Four bidders battle it out for $1.95m inner-north Victorian The property has been converted to private treaty and is now listed for $2,225,000. Fowles thought it would sell by early next week, and likely within the range. “It’ll be interesting to see what kind of buyer it goes to,” he said, noting while most had looked at the property as a potential single family home, others saw the opportunity to snatch up a prime South Yarra semi with the option of selling the other or keeping it as an investment.



Records show the property last sold in 2002 for $775,000. The vendors are moving on to their next opportunity, Fowles said. In Cheltenham, a three-bedroom home with a rare three-car garage sold for $1.19 million in post-auction negotiations, $10,000 below its $1.2 million reserve. 54 Elliott Street was listed in “absolute mint” original condition, with the garage a major drawcard for prospective buyers. It had a price guide of $1.15 million to $1.2 million. Ray White The Bayside Group agent and auctioneer Angela Limanis said she had several prospective buyers interested on Friday, with one having inspected five times, but had ended up with just the one couple by Saturday morning.



She opened the auction with a vendor bid of $1.1 million, which was followed by a $1.12 million bid from the couple, at which point it passed in. The property quickly sold in negotiations for $1.19 million. The couple were first home buyers and had been renting in the area. Limanis said the garage had been particularly appealing to the couple as the husband is a plumber and was looking forward to having additional storage space. The three-car garage was the major drawcard for the home, otherwise in original condition. Ray White The Bayside Group “The original owner was a plumber as well,” she said. “I think like attracts like in these situations.”



The home was sold as part of an estate. In Yarraville, a white 1950s weatherboard home sold to first home buyers at auction after a soaring $110,000 bid met the property’s $1.15 million reserve. 55 Gent Street was originally purchased in 2008 by two friends who at first lived there together, before one headed to Sydney and the other stayed on alone. The three-bedroom house had a price guide of $1.1 million to $1.2 million. Jas Stephens agent and auctioneer George Alexander opened the auction with a vendor bid of $1 million, countered by a $20,000 bid from the sole genuine bidder to take the price to $1.02 million. After a second vendor bid of $1.04 million, the bidder rocketed the price to $1.15 million on a single bid, bringing the property onto the market and the auction to a close.



Despite a $110,000 bid against the vendor, Alexander said there were “no real surprises”. Related Article Property prices The suburbs where house sellers want up to $1.75m more than buyer budgets “He made a pre-auction offer of that amount anyway,” he said. “I knew who the buyer was, and we had discussed it.” The purchasers were first home buyers, and were looking forward to walking their dogs in Angliss Reserve, just across the road. The occupying vendor has bought nearby.

World.title: Men are looking for love in the wrong places. I write about what women really want
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsDating Opinion Men are looking for love in the wrong places. I write about what women really want Ali Berg Author September 20, 2026 — 4:30pm

September 20, 2026 — 4:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Recently, I spoke at the inaugural Readings Romance Festival in Melbourne, which sold out in 48 hours. One of my favourite Australian romance writers, Anita Heiss, opened by talking about why she writes about love. Authors and readers talked about sex, relationships and, on my panel, the “meet-cute”: the moment when two future lovers collide. There was barely a man in sight. It’s almost like someone wrote down what women want in a book. Abel Mitja Varela Earlier this year, I spoke at Brisbane’s Blussh Romance Festival and saw the same thing: hundreds of women discussing exactly what they want from the people they date, and almost no men there to hear it. It’s not that straight men don’t want to know what women want. I think they really do. They’re spending hours looking for answers in dating podcasts, watching YouTube videos promising to explain women and in the corners of the manosphere that don’t seem to like us very much.



I distinctly remember learning at school that when a boy insulted me, he might actually be “negging” me, a pickup technique popularised by Neil Strauss’ 2005 book The Game. Now we have “sexual market value”, “high-value men” and endless theories about “female nature”. All new ways of delivering the same old message: if you want to understand women, ask another man. Related Article Graphic content

Media & marketing Tears, sex toys and slurs: A month on the Kyle Sandilands show As a romance writer, this drives me mad. Women have spent decades writing whole novels about what we think and want, yet some men would still rather hear another man explain it into a microphone. For some reason, those voices are taken seriously while romance, a literal peek inside a woman’s mind, is dismissed as “fluff”. But men who dismiss romance fiction – or have simply never thought it was written for them – miss out on more than dating advice. I recently read that fiction strengthens the social skills we use to connect with others. And I can’t think of another genre more interested in human connection. Romance, in my opinion, gives us one of the most nuanced explorations of desire, power, vulnerability and what it means to be truly known by another person. And romance takes happiness seriously too. The lovers might be hockey players or enemies forced to share a bed or even a woman and the blue alien who abducted her (there really is a subgenre for everyone), but every romance must, under all circumstances, promise a happy ending. It’s one of the genre’s few defining rules and what separates a romance from a love story. So, when you read romance, the question isn’t whether happiness is possible, but what the characters will have to learn or risk to achieve it. If more men read romance, I’d argue they’d become more hopeful about love itself.



So, what do I think men will find inside a romance novel? Probably not what they expect. Sure, the genre has plenty of handsome, rich and excellently forearmed men. But writing romances has taught me that being hot isn’t enough. We’re always asking: has he made himself vulnerable? Is he kind? Does he actually make her life better … or is he just tall? Those are the moments our readers always remember: when he asks what she wants, listens and acts accordingly. Swoon! (The same approach also makes for excellent sex scenes, according to our DMs.) Romance hasn’t always got this right. In the 1972 bestseller The Flame and the Flower, the protagonist falls in love with her rapist. I grew up when Twilight’s Edward Cullen sabotaging Bella’s truck to control where she went was considered just another reason to be Team Edward. Thankfully, romance has come a long way, and today’s best books show there’s nothing sexier than enthusiastic consent and respect. Even my favourite trope, enemies-to-lovers, only works when both characters have agency. Related Article Opinion

Romance & reality I’m a bestseller. My genre keeps bookshops alive. Stop calling it ‘trash’ Ali Berg Author Of course, women aren’t a monolith, and one Emily Henry novel won’t explain us. That’s exactly why I think men should read more romance novels. They give you hundreds of pages with women who want completely different things. Read enough and you realise there is no single woman to figure out, there are just women, plural. So, men, here’s my advice: put down the dating podcast and enter the romance section without fear. Read romantic comedies, historical romance, sports romance, romantasy, queer romance and love stories by people whose lives look nothing like yours.



You won’t finish one book knowing what women want. Thank God, because we don’t all want the same thing! But you might finish it with fewer theories about us and more curiosity about the woman you’re actually dating. Romance won’t teach you how to “decode” women. But it might teach you to stop trying. Ali Berg is a Melbourne writer, co-founder of Books on the Rail and co-author of four bestselling romantic comedy novels. World.title: Harry and Meghan’s battle to be accepted into Cotswolds high society
World.content:
Whether it’s the old-money gentry or the glossy weekenders that the Sussexes woo, they’ll need more than homemade jam to make an impression.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: The swimming pool is long, serene and lined with huge healing crystals, the water unbroken. The sauna is full of financiers, businessmen and banter led by Sir Ben Elliot, the former Tory chairman and a nephew of Queen Camilla. Wellness-obsessed housewives ease themselves into cold-plunge barrels. Battles rage on the padel courts, involving illustrious names such as the Belvoir scion Lady Alice Manners, jeweller Charlie Pragnell and Charlie Brooks, the racehorse trainer and husband of Rebekah, Rupert Murdoch’s British media chief. Upstairs afterwards, it’s Chateau Leoube rosé and WFB: working from Bamford. More specifically, The Club by Bamford. None of my sources have spotted Meghan here yet, but this is the place the Sussexes will really need to crack if they want to make it into a certain Cotswolds set. And it will be much trickier to enter this world than the celebrity enclave Soho Farmhouse, where the Duchess of Sussex was seen earlier this month amid much speculation that the pair have decided to put down roots in the Cotswolds. The American and billionaire crowd are perhaps the most natural friends for Harry and Meghan. AP A ready-made heaven of cream tones, The Club requires an annual fee of £4000 ($7500), a £1650 joining fee and the approval of the committee to become a member. Member or not, Meghan should seek to impress its owner, Cotswolds power broker Lady (Carole) Bamford. The Club is on the Daylesford Farm estate, along with its famous shop and Daylesford House itself, where Lady B, as she’s known to friends, lives with her husband, Lord (Anthony) Bamford – owner of JCB and donor to both the Tories and Reform UK. If Meghan wants to rise socially here, Carole Bamford is exactly who she needs. In the court of the Cotswolds, she is queen. “If you get invited to one of her personal parties,” says a longstanding member of the hierarchy, nervous about identification, “you’re in. Carole knows absolutely everybody. If she’s curious about someone, she’ll probably invite them. JD Vance went to Daylesford, Boris Johnson [had his wedding celebrations there] and Jeremy Clarkson is there the whole time. She can entertain on a large scale.” If Meghan wants to rise socially in the Cotswolds, Lady Carole Bamford is exactly who she needs. PA Images via Getty Images But there is a dividing line between new Cotswolds and old Cotswolds. While the Bamfords themselves are as respected, country-savvy and popular as you can get, the “new Cotswolds” set, who come to play at the weekend and splash the cash at places such as Daylesford, are more overtly glossy – bankers and hedgefunders rather than farmers and gentry – and they are sometimes looked down upon by the people who see themselves as “real country”. Meghan will have to choose which group she wants to appeal to most.



The challenge of becoming a member of the Daylesford scene won’t be the only uphill battle for Meghan as she seeks to become accepted in the Cotswolds. At a grand dinner party last Saturday night, one social friend conducted an experiment: “I sat next to these men and started talking about Meghan, and one almost left. He said, ‘If you say that word one more time …‘. So it wasn’t only ‘We don’t want anything to do with her’, but ‘Do not degrade my house by bringing it up’. I think half of these people are friendly with the King, so it’s maybe in deference to him and the stuff they’ve been through.” To stand a chance, she’ll need to become au fait with the faultlines. Helen Kirwan-Taylor, writer, broadcaster and fellow American, who moved near Cirencester on the Gloucester side of the Cotswolds decades ago, is an expert. “The real snobbism is between the Gloustocracy and the Beckhams,” she says. Sir David and Lady Victoria Beckham have become shorthand for the Oxfordshire celebrity scene, which also includes Ellie Goulding and Simon Cowell. David and Victoria Beckham have become shorthand for the Oxfordshire celebrity scene. AP Some see the divide plainly as Gloucestershire vs Oxfordshire – “real country” versus a glamorous cosplay version for weekenders. Though it’s not so clean-cut as that. Kirwan-Taylor describes the glossy set as “usually finance or media bros, and they don’t really know anything about the Cotswolds”: “They’ll go to the members’ clubs. They chose it because of what their friends do and say, and they’ve never been outside of that little triangle.” Meghan will have to get up to speed fast. You can tell a phoney a mile off, especially an American phoney. For example, she mustn’t say “The Cotswolds” – a tourist term that proves you’ve never really been. Real locals refer to the exact town: Chipping Norton or Cirencester or Stroud. The deepest rooted identify themselves by which A-road they live near. Rupert Murdoch’s British media chief, Rebekah Brooks, and her racehorse trainer husband Charlie Brooks in the royal box at the All England Lawn Tennis and Croquet Club, London, in 2024. PA Images via Getty Images Just because you have enough millions in the bank to buy property here does not make you a member of the Gloustocracy. You need to be able to prove you know something, by speaking the lingo. “The Gloustocracy are the real deal. Conversations end up being about horses or farmland or right of way or dual carriageways,” says Kirwan-Taylor. “The real giveaway is whether your kids actually go to one of those country schools, and if they don’t, then you’re really an imposter. Or worse, a weekender.”



Meghan will need to understand the social map to parlay her way into any of the “in” crowds. Tetbury is the grandest of them: the locale of Highgrove and Gatcombe, Princess Anne territory, and home to the landed gentry and the polo set. Stroud “is becoming really, really fashionable”, Kirwan-Taylor says. That’s where designer Lulu Guinness and author Plum Sykes live and where property is still considerably cheaper. But it might be a bit too boho for Harry and Meghan. The American and billionaire crowd are perhaps the most natural friends for Harry and Meghan. They’re two a penny here, and the new wave are incredibly wealthy. Sir Jony Ive, formerly chief designer at Apple, lives in the area, as does his Australian best friend, industrial designer Marc Newson. Of course, there is Ellen DeGeneres and her wife, Portia de Rossi, who moved near Asthall on the Oxfordshire side. “She is very close to Meghan,” says a neighbour, “but I think Ellen and Co are a bit isolated. It’s really hard to break into English society who just don’t care [about American celebrities]. They do entertain and tip outrageously, though.” Ellen DeGeneres and her wife, Portia de Rossi, moved near Asthall on the Oxfordshire side. AP To avoid isolation, Meghan and Harry might be able to crack the Oxfordshire celebrity circle typified by the Beckhams, whose huge new build near Soho Farmhouse, the most popular celebrity hangout, has beehives where David makes honey. Sports agent David Gardner, 50, who is one of Beckham’s closest friends, lives nearby with his fiancee, 33-year-old model Jessica Clarke, as do Simon Cowell and his wife, Lauren Silverman. This group will find a more natural rapport with the incoming Sussexes: they all have second homes in America and they love Soho Farmhouse, where the “real” country folk wouldn’t be seen dead. Then there’s Jeremy Clarkson, who was driven to such distraction by the idea of Meghan that he wrote a highly derogatory column in The Sun about her in 2022, for which he had to apologise. “I hate her on a cellular level” was one of the less offensive lines. They are clearly never going to be best friends, but they may have to learn to be in the same room as each other. Clarkson is the only celebrity who fits into both the nouveau and the real country sets – “You go to a Christmas party, he’s there,” says the social insider. This kind of rift could affect their chances with an important but highly incompatible group. If Clarkson’s pub, The Farmer’s Dog, is a no-go zone, then Lord David Cameron of Chipping Norton, a former British prime minister, could be out of reach. “DC”, as he is referred to by friends, runs a tight social ship with his wife, Samantha: a circle comprising a gaggle of Sheffields (Cameron’s in-laws), Ben Elliot and Charlie and Rebekah Brooks among many others. They wield considerable influence and have no time for the indulgent self-pity that the Sussexes promote. Samantha is a consummate hostess in their house.



Drag-hunting aficionado Johnny Hornby and his wife, Pippa, are close by at Dean Manor, the 18th-century Cotswolds country pile awarded “best swimming pool” by Tatler in last year’s Country House Awards. That’s where JD Vance, a keen hunter, stayed during his summer trip to Britain, but it’s hard to see Meghan getting on board with bloodsports in any format (including artificial). Hornby will already know Harry: he stepped down as a trustee of his charity Sentebale in 2023. What Harry and Meghan will really need is invitations to the illustrious estates. Every town has a stately home owned by a grandee. Meghan should be prepared to do anything for the call-up from Lady Bamford, the PR tycoon Matthew Freud and Sheherazade Goldsmith at Burford Priory or the Duke and Duchess of Beaufort, Henry and Georgia Somerset, at Badminton House. Former British prime minister David Cameron and wife Samantha run a tight social ship. Getty Images Freud, says the social insider, “is really taking over”. There is a popular padel scene at Burford, attended by film stars, captains of industry and politicians. Games are often followed by a glamorous drinks party. Of all the stately homes, it seems like the most familiar territory for Meghan, with actresses and Democrats aplenty. The ultimate sign that the Sussexes have made it here will be if, after next year’s Badminton Horse Trials, Tatler reports that Georgia Beaufort has invited Meghan to her private dinner. She and the Duke, aka “Bunter”, are famous for their parties, which go on until the early hours, and they have perfected the art of being grand and cool all at once. Bunter’s “rave to the grave” 70th birthday is exactly the kind of invitation that would certify social success for Harry and Meghan. Meghan can impress by wearing vintage Yves Saint Laurent. Britain’s Princess Beatrice and her husband, Edoardo Mapelli Mozzi. AP The who-to-woo list is not complete without Fiona Howden, the wife of financier David, who has transformed Cornbury Park, near Charlbury, Oxfordshire. Having moved from the Yorkshire Dales, they are the definition of newbies who got fully stuck in and earned the respect of everyone. A key date in the Cotswolds calendar for the Sussexes to mark is Cornbury Horse Trials in September. Princess Beatrice made an appearance this year; perhaps the Sussexes will make it next time around.

World.title: Enmore vendors cut price hopes as Sydney’s clearance rate drops
World.content:
PropertyNewsAuctions Enmore vendors cut price hopes as Sydney’s clearance rate drops Elizabeth Redman September 20, 2026 — 4:22pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

An Enmore house sold for $1,686,000 at auction on Saturday after the vendors adjusted their reserve to sell in a week when Sydney’s clearance rate dipped to 48 per cent. The three-bedroom house at 28 Juliett Street features a striking timber and glass back wall and soaring ceilings as well as period fireplaces and leadlight details. The property was one of 796 scheduled to go to auction in Sydney last week. By Saturday evening, Domain recorded a preliminary auction clearance rate of 48 per cent from 481 reported results throughout the week, while 177 auctions were withdrawn. Withdrawn auctions are counted as unsold properties when calculating the clearance rate. The early result is a drop from last week’s preliminary result of 53 per cent as the number of auctions scheduled increased and economists warned of the chance of another Reserve Bank interest rate rise this month. It is below the 60 per cent threshold considered a market balanced between buyers and sellers. But it remains just above the June low point of 47 per cent, when buyers were absorbing the May budget’s changes to the tax treatment of investment properties.



The Enmore home was listed with a price guide of $1.7 million and drew two registered bidders at auction, both of whom participated. Related Article Auctions ‘We got a house’: Inner west semi sells for $311,000 above reserve Bidding began at $1,635,000 and the price rose slowly, punctuated by the selling agents going inside to check how the vendors wished to proceed. The reserve price was $1.7 million but the vendors, who had owned the home for close to three decades, decided to meet the market. A young couple buying their first home together won the keys, beating a local upsizing couple.



Raine & Horne Newtown selling agent Adam Freitas said the sellers had planned to live there but never did, and instead offered the property for rent. They decided to sell as they approached retirement, he said. “The owners’ expectations were quite realistic,” he said. He described the market broadly as “not great”, and flagged the potential for another interest rate rise. “Buyers are scared. There is a lot of uncertainty around what they want to do,” he said. “It is a bit of a wait-and-see situation at the moment.”



Elsewhere, a Lane Cove family home sold for $3.1 million to a neighbour who registered to bid mid-auction. The three-bedroom house at 22 Myee Crescent backed onto Lane Cove River, offering river views and a swimming pool. Its price guide was $2.7 million. Five parties registered in total and all made bids. Only four had registered – all families – when the auction began with a bid of $2.2 million and rose in increments of $100,000 at first, then $50,000. The fifth bidder registered deep into the auction and placed only two bids to buy the home. The reserve for the deceased estate was $2.9 million.



There is no legal requirement for a vendor’s reserve to be in line with their property’s price guide. Related Article NSW residential property ‘Element of scarcity’: Why upsizing in Sydney now costs an extra $270,000 Nicholls & Co Estate Agents selling agent Cameron Nicholls said the winner lived close by and thought the home was good value. “For a property like this one to be sold in a market like this, someone is going to be buying it very well, because it is really being sold for the view and the position,” Nicholls said, adding the home needed work and the new owner might renovate or rebuild. “They had the confidence to bid higher than everyone else because they knew how good it was in that little pocket.”



He praised the “beautiful aspect” and the unobstructed river views. “It was such a perfect little spot, nice and quiet being a crescent and not a street.” In Glebe, a young woman paid $1,795,000 for an updated terrace to live close to family. The two-bedroom home at 5 St James Avenue had a price guide of $1.6 million to $1.7 million. Nine parties registered and three participated, starting at $1,601,000. It soon became a two-horse race between two younger couples.



Increments ranged from $10,000 and $5000 down to $2000 offers. Related Article Exclusive

Title Deeds Moguls behind Kylie Jenner-endorsed sunglasses brand list Byron Shire mansion The home was a deceased estate. The reserve was $1.7 million. Ray White Erskineville/Alexandria/Glebe/Surry Hills selling agent Matthew Carvalho thought the market had improved in recent weeks. “With the value, people have noticed everything has come back a bit, and stock is getting tighter,” he said.



In Clovelly, a young couple buying their first home paid $1.5 million for a two-bedroom apartment in a battle of the first home buyers. Six parties, all debutants, registered for 4/316 Clovelly Road, guided at $1,375,000. Five parties bid, starting from $1.3 million and making bids in $25,000 increments above the reserve of $1.4 million. Ray White Eastern Beaches selling agent Angus Gorrie said government assistance was helping first home buyers, who had also watched the market drop in recent months.



“They are bidding with confidence,” he said. Agents in conjunction were Sydney Sotheby’s International Realty’s Cristian De Nigris and Thorsten Herzog.

World.title: Lachie Neale will fight gut-punch suspension at AFL tribunal in bid to play in grand final
World.content:
Breaking SportAFLAFL 2026 Lachie Neale will fight gut-punch suspension at AFL tribunal in bid to play in grand final Peter Ryan Updated September 20, 2026 — 5:02pm ,first published 2:51pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Brisbane’s dual Brownlow medallist Lachie Neale is heading for a high-stakes hearing at the AFL tribunal as he fights to play Saturday’s grand final against his former team, Fremantle. Neale, 33, was banned from playing in the grand final when the AFL’s match review officer on Sunday found him guilty of striking Hawthorn’s Jack Ginnivan in the closing minutes of the first quarter of Saturday’s preliminary final. Chris Fagan and Lachie Neale celebrate the Lions preliminary final win. Getty Images The MRO found Neale made intentional, medium-force contact to Ginnivan’s body and banned him for one match, but as soon as that verdict became official the Brisbane Lions confirmed they would challenge it at the tribunal. The charge arises from an interaction between Neale and Ginnivan on the 50m line at the city end of the MCG.



The fact Ginnivan played on, seemingly without discomfort, could possibly form part of Neale’s defence if he seeks to get the charge downgraded to a low-impact strike, which would free him up to play in Saturday’s grand final. However, nine players have been suspended for offences of this nature this season, and the two who challenged them at the tribunal were unsuccessful. Neale was under an injury cloud going into last year’s decider but played as a substitute, shedding the vest in the second half and starring as his team charged to its second successive premiership. Now with a Lions three-peat on the line, Neale is again the focus of grand final week.



What’s more, the match is widely understood to be his final outing in Brisbane colours, as it’s expected he will move to Collingwood as a free agent in the off-season. Although he hasn’t been in peak form this finals series, Neale – a former Lions captain – remains a pivotal cog in Brisbane’s midfield. But his footballing prowess has been overshadowed this year by off-field dramas, firstly the collapse of his relationship with wife Jules, who moved home to Western Australia with their two children, followed by continued speculation over his playing future. View post on X Neale copped a heavy knock in the opening seconds of Saturday’s thrilling preliminary final win over Hawthorn, coling off second best after a collision at a centre ball-up with Hawk Jai Newcombe.

World.title: An NRL title in their fourth season would be remarkable for Dolphins – and might just keep the club together
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 An NRL title in their fourth season would be remarkable for Dolphins – and might just keep the club together Christian Nicolussi September 20, 2026 — 4:57pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A first NRL premiership will also put the Dolphins in the box seat to retain some of the club’s superstars, including Herbie Farnworth. So says Dolphins coach Kristian Woolf, who is comfortable with how contract negotiations have unfolded recently with the likes of Farnworth. Loading Farnworth is now widely regarded as the premier centre in the game, and he confirmed that with a match-turning performance in the qualifying final win over the Warriors, which allowed the Dolphins to advance to a preliminary final on home soil against the Sydney Roosters. There has been much interest in Farnworth’s next career move, with the Englishman heavily linked to the Roosters for the start of the 2028 season as James Tedesco’s successor in the No.1 jumper.



The Roosters are not allowed to talk to Farnworth until he becomes a free agent on November 1, but that has not stopped repeated reports about the Tricolours’ determination to land their man. The Dolphins, however, are aware premiership success will go a long way to encouraging Farnworth stay put. Herbie Farnworth’s try changed the momentum in their qualifying final win over the Warriors. Getty Images The Dolphins believe if Farnworth can win one title, maybe he will want to hang around to chase two or even three with his mates at Redcliffe. “We have a fair bit of work before we get to a position to win a comp, but Herbie, like everyone, can see we have a great group here who are all at a good age and improving together,” Woolf said.



“That’s something that is really strong in terms of what will keep this group together. “They [contract talks] haven’t been a distraction based on his performances, and it’s certainly not a distraction for us. “We’re comfortable with the situation and the communication around it. Herbie Farnworth has been heavily linked to the Sydney Roosters. Getty Images “Herbie is such a strike player for us. I loved what he was able to do against the Warriors, not just in attack, but his overall game – it was the kind of performance we’ve grown to expect and want to see from him.



“He had to work hard in defence, and when we went down to 12 men, he had to defend in a foreign position. But he was exceptional, which he has been all year. “We don’t need much more from Herbie on Friday – we just need him to go out and be himself.” Farnworth is managed by Joe Wehbe, who also has Tom Flegler and Morgan Knowles at Redcliffe, and Tedesco, Daly Cherry-Evans and Reece Robson at the Roosters. The 26-year-old Farnworth’s match-up with Roosters right centre Rob Toia will be one of the great individual battles of the first preliminary final. The Dolphins are fresh off the bye, welcome back Flegler from a concussion, and Woolf is happy to back his group to handle the weight of expectation in Brisbane usually reserved for the Broncos. Only single seats remain for the preliminary final.



The Dolphins have won eight straight games since their shock 66-0 loss to Cronulla in round 19. “We just have to enjoy it and love everything we’re doing at this time of year,” Woolf said. “You do all the hard work in November so you can still be playing at this time of year. Related Article Analysis

NRL 2026 The secret to DCE’s 424-game career? A ‘goldfish memory’, Ted Lasso and Dolphin days “We have expectations on ourselves with what we want to do. We’ve handled everything so far, including winning last week in what was a tough environment [at Go Media Stadium], and this is an opportunity to show we can handle it again.



“There will also be plenty of expectations on the Roosters, who have a great history of making grand finals and winning comps – that in itself brings expectations. “They were big and powerful on Saturday night, and it didn’t surprise me the performance they came up with. “We had a few days off to freshen up, and it was a bit like having a bye round, which is gold at this time of year. I expect the Roosters to be at their best, but so will we.”

World.title: This haunting play celebrates the solidarity and strangeness of found family
World.content:
Key points THEATRE: Luke makes its world premiere at Red Stitch

THEATRE: Harold Pinter’s The Homecoming is performed at the Athenaeum

MUSICAL THEATRE: Spamalot returns to Melbourne

MUSIC: Kristian Bezuidenhout performs Handel and Bach with the MSO

THEATRE

Luke ★★★★

Red Stitch, until October 11 Local playwright Angus Cameron has teamed up with Red Stitch for the world premiere of Luke – a disturbing, emotionally complex three-hander that weaves a provocative play of ideas into a psychological mystery of troubling currency. Will Lonsdale, Olga Makeeva and Dion Mills in Luke Parenthesy I was bewildered by the opening sequence. Two adults race across a living room playing dress-ups. They’re engaged in some kind of private game, based on the Bolshevik assassination of the Romanovs during the Russian Revolution, but something about the scene feels off, inauthentic somehow. A clever reason for this will remain an enigma until well after we discover that the pair are high school teachers in country Victoria. It’s 2007, and Damon (Dion Mills) and Olena (Olga Makeeva) are unwinding at term’s end after a gruelling night of parent-teacher interviews. When Chris (Will Lonsdale) – the school’s 19-year-old rowing coach and a former student of Damon’s – joins them, the games continue.



Some of the playfulness is literary or historical – a relic of the ludic flamboyance essential to Damon’s pedagogic style. He’s an inspiring educator, discreetly gay, and his mentor-like relationship with Chris, who came out to Damon as a student, is tinged by affection and by a body of queer knowledge excluded by the official (read heteronormative) education system. When conversation turns to a never-seen character, Luke – a year 11 student leaving the school after inappropriate attention from a member of staff – the game mutates through a series of twists, with a possible child sex abuse scenario, and its consequences, playing out over decades. Iain Sinclair’s direction guides three excellent performances. Iain Sinclair’s direction guides three excellent performances. Parenthesy Mills’ suspect teacher has the charisma, passion, idealism, and sheer eccentricity of a gifted educator. There’s no question he leaves a mark on his students: his scenes with Lonsdale’s Chris are tender and haunted – enlivened by the irrepressible joy they both take in the learning game, as well as the shadow of barely repressed desire. Olena is the fulcrum of the play, and Makeeva is riveting as, through veiled parable and a clipped and embittered realism, the character weighs the truth of a situation in which the righteousness of her own acts is called into question.



She is a staunch counter to Chris – a young man heavily invested in his own righteousness, and solipsistic in the performance of it. Editor's pick Arts Three titans of politics, sport and media had a meeting in the 1980s. A new play imagines what was said Luke tackles such uncomfortable subjects as the erotics of education and the ethics of making art from life. It has stern things to say about the cultural amnesia afflicting Australian literature and drama, and it brings child protection concerns into contact with the reality of homophobia, knowing the ancient slur – the one that equates homosexuality with paedophilia – has never quite ceased to echo. Yet this haunting play celebrates, too, the solidarity and strangeness of found family, the clandestine solidarity and the mentorship relations that can exist between queer men finding their tribe. In this, it has an artistic genealogy that can be traced back to some of the most fearless and unsettling voices in queer Australian literature – the implied pederasty in David Malouf’s short story Under Southern Skies, say, or Frank Moorhouse’s The Everlasting Secret Family – updating the issues to a world of changing mores in which progressive rhetoric can disguise more difficult and painful human truths.

Reviewed by Cameron Woodhead



THEATRE

The Homecoming ★★★★

Athenaeum Theatre, until October 3 The lights come up to reveal two characters in a living room and it doesn’t take long for the sense that something is off-kilter to take hold. A pugnacious aged patriarch and ex-butcher named Max (Richard Piper) blathers on in an unpunctuated stream of consciousness to the uninterested Lenny (Ben Geurens) – we don’t find out the two are family until Max admonishes the louche Lenny for speaking such to his “lousy filthy father”. The barely concealed hostilities are extended to the diametrically gentle Sam (David Field), Max’s chauffeur brother and the hulking wannabe boxer Joey (Eddie Orton), Lenny’s younger brother. Richard Piper as Max in The Homecoming Ben Fon No one and nothing are quite as they seem in Harold Pinter’s 1965 comedy of menace The Homecoming, even once you account for the virulent sexism, barely concealed hatred, and dearth of familial love between these characters. The intrigue deepens when all four of them retire to bed and the taciturn Teddy (Peter Houghton) enters the house, accompanied by his enigmatic wife Ruth (Kate Kendall). Teddy has effectively been estranged from his family for six years and now resides in America, with neither his wife nor family acquainted with one another. A series of decidedly strange interactions between all characters leave audiences none the wiser as to what is about to unfold in this claustrophobic domestic setting.



Under the direction of Greg Carroll, a slowly creeping sense of foreboding and listlessness overtakes the play, only strengthening its visor grip on the audience as it unfolds. The world Pinter has ensconced these characters in exists in and of itself, ungoverned by the moral sensibilities and social mores of the now, let alone that of the 1960s when this play first premiered in London. Peter Houghton as Teddy and Kate Kendall as Ruth Ben Fon Absurdist and fantastical despite its realist underpinnings, The Homecoming lulls its audience into an illusion of normalcy. When social contracts are broken with seemingly no repercussions, the play’s (and our) grasp on reality loosens – shining an uncomfortable spotlight on the confronting misogyny on display, calling into rebuke the meaning of the familial ties traditionally held so dear, and questioning the unspoken rules that allow society to function as it does. The famed Pinter Pause allows the requisite space for these consternations to fester. A muscular black room is the fitting backdrop for the exertion of these men’s fragile, toxic masculinities, while Amelia Carroll and Margaret Goy’s costume design is a stunning cloak of civility that masks the innermost depravations of these characters. Clad in a babydoll dress throughout, Ruth is read as childlike and guileless – a misnomer that allows her to exert the full force of her feminine wiliness. The strength of a production like The Homecoming lives and dies by its ensemble cast, and this one is uniformly excellent. Kendall is a particular highlight as the otherworldly, cosmically unflappable Ruth, simultaneously an antidote against the testosterone-soaked aggression of the men around her and the sun around which their neediness, desperation and contemptibility orbit.

Reviewed by Sonia Nair



MUSICAL THEATRE

Spamalot ★★★★

Athenaeum Theatre, until October 4 You’d think that after 51 years a joke might stop being as funny as it once was. And yet, sitting in the dark watching two men debate how one swallow – or perhaps two, if they were holding some sort of string – might transport a coconut across countries I found myself laughing as though it was the first time I’d heard this conversation. L-R: Jesse Vasiliadis, Gareth Isaac, Stephen Curry, Ethan Jones and Noah Skape. Ben Fon Monty Python and the Holy Grail first hit cinemas in 1975, and Spamalot, “a new musical lovingly ripped off from the motion picture” takes the key plot and handful of songs from the film, adds a whole lot more, and twists the story off into new directions as needed. The musical, itself now 20 years on from when it took Broadway by storm and took out the Tony Award for best musical, still feels vibrant and fun and silly. A spoof of the Arthurian legend, the story sees King Arthur (Stephen Curry) seeking knights to join his round table before being tasked by God (a video recording of Eric Idle) to find the Holy Grail.



While many jokes and scenes are lifted directly from the original film and other Python works, Spamalot, with book and lyrics by Idle, and music co-written by John Du Prez, is its own thing. The songs written specifically for Spamalot hold their own against the older, more-established tunes. Idle takes great delight in breaking the fourth wall in creative ways and musical theatre itself is a key pillar of the story, with nods to everything and everyone from West Side Story to Liza Minnelli. Jaz Flowers and Ethan Jones as the Lady of the Lake and Sir Galahad. Ben Fon Jaz Flowers as the Lady of the Lake steals almost every scene she’s in – her powerful command of every note makes light work of the parade of vocal challenges thrown her way. Her skill as a singer is matched only by her comedic timing. Her meta duet with Ethan Jones as Sir Galahad in The Song That Goes Like This is a particular highlight. Python humour remains evergreen because it is untethered from time. When it isn’t purely revelling in the absurd, it is taking aim at themes that sadly never grow old (inequality, bigotry, cowardice), joyfully ratcheting up the classics (fart jokes), and being gleefully persnickety when it comes to wordplay. With a talented cast who all appear to be enjoying every minute on stage, Spamalot is just the right amount of silly.

Reviewed by Elizabeth Flux



MUSIC

Handel and Bach ★★★★

Melbourne Symphony Orchestra, Melbourne Recital Centre, September 19 Many Melbourne concertgoers will remember the stylish flair with which Australian fortepianist Kristian Bezuidenhout performed the complete Beethoven piano concertos with the Freiburg Baroque Orchestra on the cusp of COVID. Kristian Bezuidenhout at an earlier concert. Marco Borggreve Returning with some of that flair, Bezuidenhout directed the Melbourne Symphony Orchestra from the harpsichord in this program of works by Bach and Handel. Focusing particularly on rhythm and dynamics, Bezuidenhout brought crisp grandiloquence to the many French-style introductions on the program, whether to Bach’s Orchestral Suite No. 1 in C major or the Overture to Handel’s Admeto. There was also a general rhythmic buoyancy which lent itself well both to the dance-infused Bach Suite and Suites Nos. 1 and 2 from Handel’s familiar Water Music.



Carefully shaped dynamics applied to the whole orchestra made sense of the rise and fall of phrases and provided some well-judged dramatic contrasts. Related Article ★★★★★

Melbourne live reviews These are unapologetically political songs, and this artist is unapologetically herself Despite overall clarity, it was in Bezuidenhout’s arrangement of Bach’s incomplete Contrapunctus XIV from The Art of Fugue that the listener might have longed for some more granular detail in terms of articulation and pliability of tone in individual lines. Such qualities were more apparent in Handel’s Concerto grosso in D minor, Op. 3, no. 5 which followed. Fine wind and brass playing hallmarked the second half. Beginning with the Sinfonia from Bach’s Cantata No. 52 (otherwise recognisable as the opening of Brandenburg Concerto No. 4) followed by the Water Music, the horns and oboes took up Bezuidenhout’s brisk tempos with alacrity. Oboists Johannes Grosso and Ann Blackburn together with horn players Lucie Krysatis and Abbey Edlin crowned the festive mood of the Handel; their timbre setting up piquant contrasts with the strings, trumpets providing an additional regal air in the second suite. Thanks to Bezuidenhout, the MSO proved it can bring some idiomatic lightness to the glories of the baroque.

Reviewed by Tony Way The Booklist is a weekly newsletter for book lovers from Jason Steger. Get it delivered every Friday.

World.title: Pair of South Yarra art deco homes pass in at auction on $2m vendor bid
World.content:
PropertyNewsAuctions Pair of South Yarra art deco homes pass in at auction on $2m vendor bid Wes Mountain September 20, 2026 — 4:38pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A pair of art deco houses on the same title in the heart of South Yarra failed to sell together at auction on Saturday, passing in on a single $2 million vendor bid. Just a five-minute walk from Toorak Road shops, 50 and 52 Lang Street are both two-bedroom, one-bathroom layouts with high ceilings and classic art deco features. 50 Lang Street has recently been updated, and includes its own garage, while 52 is ready for renovation, or to be merged into a larger single family home. The property was one of 913 scheduled to go to auction in Melbourne this week. By Saturday evening, Domain recorded a preliminary auction clearance rate of 57 per cent from 655 reported results throughout the week, while 81 auctions were withdrawn. Withdrawn auctions are counted as unsold properties when calculating the clearance rate. While last week saw the preliminary clearance rate above 60 per cent for the first time since before the May budget, this week saw it fall below that benchmark – generally considered to indicate a balanced market – and return to the mid-50s, despite peak Spring auction season.



50 and 52 Lang Street had a price guide of $2.1 million to $2.3 million, with a $2.3 million reserve. Marshall White Stonnington agent Jack Fowles said despite passing in on a single vendor bid, “an enormous amount” of parties had got in contact after the auction. 50 Lang Street’s renovation provides a template for potential purchasers on how to update its neighbour. Marshall White Stonnington “A year ago, buyers would wait until the ‘halftime break’,” he said, referring to the point at which a bid is taken to a vendor to confirm the property is on the market. “Now it’s more common for properties to pass in, then you see the interest.”



He thought this left buyers in a more vulnerable, less transparent position, making offers in private rather than competing in an open arena. Related Article Auctions Four bidders battle it out for $1.95m inner-north Victorian The property has been converted to private treaty and is now listed for $2,225,000. Fowles thought it would sell by early next week, and likely within the range. “It’ll be interesting to see what kind of buyer it goes to,” he said, noting while most had looked at the property as a potential single family home, others saw the opportunity to snatch up a prime South Yarra semi with the option of selling the other or keeping it as an investment.



Records show the property last sold in 2002 for $775,000. The vendors are moving on to their next opportunity, Fowles said. In Cheltenham, a three-bedroom home with a rare three-car garage sold for $1.19 million in post-auction negotiations, $10,000 below its $1.2 million reserve. 54 Elliott Street was listed in “absolute mint” original condition, with the garage a major drawcard for prospective buyers. It had a price guide of $1.15 million to $1.2 million. Ray White The Bayside Group agent and auctioneer Angela Limanis said she had several prospective buyers interested on Friday, with one having inspected five times, but had ended up with just the one couple by Saturday morning.



She opened the auction with a vendor bid of $1.1 million, which was followed by a $1.12 million bid from the couple, at which point it passed in. The property quickly sold in negotiations for $1.19 million. The couple were first home buyers and had been renting in the area. Limanis said the garage had been particularly appealing to the couple as the husband is a plumber and was looking forward to having additional storage space. The three-car garage was the major drawcard for the home, otherwise in original condition. Ray White The Bayside Group “The original owner was a plumber as well,” she said. “I think like attracts like in these situations.”



The home was sold as part of an estate. In Yarraville, a white 1950s weatherboard home sold to first home buyers at auction after a soaring $110,000 bid met the property’s $1.15 million reserve. 55 Gent Street was originally purchased in 2008 by two friends who at first lived there together, before one headed to Sydney and the other stayed on alone. The three-bedroom house had a price guide of $1.1 million to $1.2 million. Jas Stephens agent and auctioneer George Alexander opened the auction with a vendor bid of $1 million, countered by a $20,000 bid from the sole genuine bidder to take the price to $1.02 million. After a second vendor bid of $1.04 million, the bidder rocketed the price to $1.15 million on a single bid, bringing the property onto the market and the auction to a close.



Despite a $110,000 bid against the vendor, Alexander said there were “no real surprises”. Related Article Property prices The suburbs where house sellers want up to $1.75m more than buyer budgets “He made a pre-auction offer of that amount anyway,” he said. “I knew who the buyer was, and we had discussed it.” The purchasers were first home buyers, and were looking forward to walking their dogs in Angliss Reserve, just across the road. The occupying vendor has bought nearby.
