World.title: Men are looking for love in the wrong places. I write about what women really want
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsDating Opinion Men are looking for love in the wrong places. I write about what women really want Ali Berg Author September 20, 2026 — 4:30pm

September 20, 2026 — 4:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Recently, I spoke at the inaugural Readings Romance Festival in Melbourne, which sold out in 48 hours. One of my favourite Australian romance writers, Anita Heiss, opened by talking about why she writes about love. Authors and readers talked about sex, relationships and, on my panel, the “meet-cute”: the moment when two future lovers collide. There was barely a man in sight. It’s almost like someone wrote down what women want in a book. Abel Mitja Varela Earlier this year, I spoke at Brisbane’s Blussh Romance Festival and saw the same thing: hundreds of women discussing exactly what they want from the people they date, and almost no men there to hear it. It’s not that straight men don’t want to know what women want. I think they really do. They’re spending hours looking for answers in dating podcasts, watching YouTube videos promising to explain women and in the corners of the manosphere that don’t seem to like us very much.



I distinctly remember learning at school that when a boy insulted me, he might actually be “negging” me, a pickup technique popularised by Neil Strauss’ 2005 book The Game. Now we have “sexual market value”, “high-value men” and endless theories about “female nature”. All new ways of delivering the same old message: if you want to understand women, ask another man. Related Article Graphic content

Media & marketing Tears, sex toys and slurs: A month on the Kyle Sandilands show As a romance writer, this drives me mad. Women have spent decades writing whole novels about what we think and want, yet some men would still rather hear another man explain it into a microphone. For some reason, those voices are taken seriously while romance, a literal peek inside a woman’s mind, is dismissed as “fluff”. But men who dismiss romance fiction – or have simply never thought it was written for them – miss out on more than dating advice. I recently read that fiction strengthens the social skills we use to connect with others. And I can’t think of another genre more interested in human connection. Romance, in my opinion, gives us one of the most nuanced explorations of desire, power, vulnerability and what it means to be truly known by another person. And romance takes happiness seriously too. The lovers might be hockey players or enemies forced to share a bed or even a woman and the blue alien who abducted her (there really is a subgenre for everyone), but every romance must, under all circumstances, promise a happy ending. It’s one of the genre’s few defining rules and what separates a romance from a love story. So, when you read romance, the question isn’t whether happiness is possible, but what the characters will have to learn or risk to achieve it. If more men read romance, I’d argue they’d become more hopeful about love itself.



So, what do I think men will find inside a romance novel? Probably not what they expect. Sure, the genre has plenty of handsome, rich and excellently forearmed men. But writing romances has taught me that being hot isn’t enough. We’re always asking: has he made himself vulnerable? Is he kind? Does he actually make her life better … or is he just tall? Those are the moments our readers always remember: when he asks what she wants, listens and acts accordingly. Swoon! (The same approach also makes for excellent sex scenes, according to our DMs.) Romance hasn’t always got this right. In the 1972 bestseller The Flame and the Flower, the protagonist falls in love with her rapist. I grew up when Twilight’s Edward Cullen sabotaging Bella’s truck to control where she went was considered just another reason to be Team Edward. Thankfully, romance has come a long way, and today’s best books show there’s nothing sexier than enthusiastic consent and respect. Even my favourite trope, enemies-to-lovers, only works when both characters have agency. Related Article Opinion

Romance & reality I’m a bestseller. My genre keeps bookshops alive. Stop calling it ‘trash’ Ali Berg Author Of course, women aren’t a monolith, and one Emily Henry novel won’t explain us. That’s exactly why I think men should read more romance novels. They give you hundreds of pages with women who want completely different things. Read enough and you realise there is no single woman to figure out, there are just women, plural. So, men, here’s my advice: put down the dating podcast and enter the romance section without fear. Read romantic comedies, historical romance, sports romance, romantasy, queer romance and love stories by people whose lives look nothing like yours.



You won’t finish one book knowing what women want. Thank God, because we don’t all want the same thing! But you might finish it with fewer theories about us and more curiosity about the woman you’re actually dating. Romance won’t teach you how to “decode” women. But it might teach you to stop trying. Ali Berg is a Melbourne writer, co-founder of Books on the Rail and co-author of four bestselling romantic comedy novels. The Opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

World.title: Harry and Meghan’s battle to be accepted into Cotswolds high society
World.content:
Whether it’s the old-money gentry or the glossy weekenders that the Sussexes woo, they’ll need more than homemade jam to make an impression.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: The swimming pool is long, serene and lined with huge healing crystals, the water unbroken. The sauna is full of financiers, businessmen and banter led by Sir Ben Elliot, the former Tory chairman and a nephew of Queen Camilla. Wellness-obsessed housewives ease themselves into cold-plunge barrels. Battles rage on the padel courts, involving illustrious names such as the Belvoir scion Lady Alice Manners, jeweller Charlie Pragnell and Charlie Brooks, the racehorse trainer and husband of Rebekah, Rupert Murdoch’s British media chief. Upstairs afterwards, it’s Chateau Leoube rosé and WFB: working from Bamford. More specifically, The Club by Bamford. None of my sources have spotted Meghan here yet, but this is the place the Sussexes will really need to crack if they want to make it into a certain Cotswolds set. And it will be much trickier to enter this world than the celebrity enclave Soho Farmhouse, where the Duchess of Sussex was seen earlier this month amid much speculation that the pair have decided to put down roots in the Cotswolds. The American and billionaire crowd are perhaps the most natural friends for Harry and Meghan. AP A ready-made heaven of cream tones, The Club requires an annual fee of £4000 ($7500), a £1650 joining fee and the approval of the committee to become a member. Member or not, Meghan should seek to impress its owner, Cotswolds power broker Lady (Carole) Bamford. The Club is on the Daylesford Farm estate, along with its famous shop and Daylesford House itself, where Lady B, as she’s known to friends, lives with her husband, Lord (Anthony) Bamford – owner of JCB and donor to both the Tories and Reform UK. If Meghan wants to rise socially here, Carole Bamford is exactly who she needs. In the court of the Cotswolds, she is queen. “If you get invited to one of her personal parties,” says a longstanding member of the hierarchy, nervous about identification, “you’re in. Carole knows absolutely everybody. If she’s curious about someone, she’ll probably invite them. JD Vance went to Daylesford, Boris Johnson [had his wedding celebrations there] and Jeremy Clarkson is there the whole time. She can entertain on a large scale.” If Meghan wants to rise socially in the Cotswolds, Lady Carole Bamford is exactly who she needs. PA Images via Getty Images But there is a dividing line between new Cotswolds and old Cotswolds. While the Bamfords themselves are as respected, country-savvy and popular as you can get, the “new Cotswolds” set, who come to play at the weekend and splash the cash at places such as Daylesford, are more overtly glossy – bankers and hedgefunders rather than farmers and gentry – and they are sometimes looked down upon by the people who see themselves as “real country”. Meghan will have to choose which group she wants to appeal to most.



The challenge of becoming a member of the Daylesford scene won’t be the only uphill battle for Meghan as she seeks to become accepted in the Cotswolds. At a grand dinner party last Saturday night, one social friend conducted an experiment: “I sat next to these men and started talking about Meghan, and one almost left. He said, ‘If you say that word one more time …‘. So it wasn’t only ‘We don’t want anything to do with her’, but ‘Do not degrade my house by bringing it up’. I think half of these people are friendly with the King, so it’s maybe in deference to him and the stuff they’ve been through.” To stand a chance, she’ll need to become au fait with the faultlines. Helen Kirwan-Taylor, writer, broadcaster and fellow American, who moved near Cirencester on the Gloucester side of the Cotswolds decades ago, is an expert. “The real snobbism is between the Gloustocracy and the Beckhams,” she says. Sir David and Lady Victoria Beckham have become shorthand for the Oxfordshire celebrity scene, which also includes Ellie Goulding and Simon Cowell. David and Victoria Beckham have become shorthand for the Oxfordshire celebrity scene. AP Some see the divide plainly as Gloucestershire vs Oxfordshire – “real country” versus a glamorous cosplay version for weekenders. Though it’s not so clean-cut as that. Kirwan-Taylor describes the glossy set as “usually finance or media bros, and they don’t really know anything about the Cotswolds”: “They’ll go to the members’ clubs. They chose it because of what their friends do and say, and they’ve never been outside of that little triangle.” Meghan will have to get up to speed fast. You can tell a phoney a mile off, especially an American phoney. For example, she mustn’t say “The Cotswolds” – a tourist term that proves you’ve never really been. Real locals refer to the exact town: Chipping Norton or Cirencester or Stroud. The deepest rooted identify themselves by which A-road they live near. Rupert Murdoch’s British media chief, Rebekah Brooks, and her racehorse trainer husband Charlie Brooks in the royal box at the All England Lawn Tennis and Croquet Club, London, in 2024. PA Images via Getty Images Just because you have enough millions in the bank to buy property here does not make you a member of the Gloustocracy. You need to be able to prove you know something, by speaking the lingo. “The Gloustocracy are the real deal. Conversations end up being about horses or farmland or right of way or dual carriageways,” says Kirwan-Taylor. “The real giveaway is whether your kids actually go to one of those country schools, and if they don’t, then you’re really an imposter. Or worse, a weekender.”



Meghan will need to understand the social map to parlay her way into any of the “in” crowds. Tetbury is the grandest of them: the locale of Highgrove and Gatcombe, Princess Anne territory, and home to the landed gentry and the polo set. Stroud “is becoming really, really fashionable”, Kirwan-Taylor says. That’s where designer Lulu Guinness and author Plum Sykes live and where property is still considerably cheaper. But it might be a bit too boho for Harry and Meghan. The American and billionaire crowd are perhaps the most natural friends for Harry and Meghan. They’re two a penny here, and the new wave are incredibly wealthy. Sir Jony Ive, formerly chief designer at Apple, lives in the area, as does his Australian best friend, industrial designer Marc Newson. Of course, there is Ellen DeGeneres and her wife, Portia de Rossi, who moved near Asthall on the Oxfordshire side. “She is very close to Meghan,” says a neighbour, “but I think Ellen and Co are a bit isolated. It’s really hard to break into English society who just don’t care [about American celebrities]. They do entertain and tip outrageously, though.” Ellen DeGeneres and her wife, Portia de Rossi, moved near Asthall on the Oxfordshire side. AP To avoid isolation, Meghan and Harry might be able to crack the Oxfordshire celebrity circle typified by the Beckhams, whose huge new build near Soho Farmhouse, the most popular celebrity hangout, has beehives where David makes honey. Sports agent David Gardner, 50, who is one of Beckham’s closest friends, lives nearby with his fiancee, 33-year-old model Jessica Clarke, as do Simon Cowell and his wife, Lauren Silverman. This group will find a more natural rapport with the incoming Sussexes: they all have second homes in America and they love Soho Farmhouse, where the “real” country folk wouldn’t be seen dead. Then there’s Jeremy Clarkson, who was driven to such distraction by the idea of Meghan that he wrote a highly derogatory column in The Sun about her in 2022, for which he had to apologise. “I hate her on a cellular level” was one of the less offensive lines. They are clearly never going to be best friends, but they may have to learn to be in the same room as each other. Clarkson is the only celebrity who fits into both the nouveau and the real country sets – “You go to a Christmas party, he’s there,” says the social insider. This kind of rift could affect their chances with an important but highly incompatible group. If Clarkson’s pub, The Farmer’s Dog, is a no-go zone, then Lord David Cameron of Chipping Norton, a former British prime minister, could be out of reach. “DC”, as he is referred to by friends, runs a tight social ship with his wife, Samantha: a circle comprising a gaggle of Sheffields (Cameron’s in-laws), Ben Elliot and Charlie and Rebekah Brooks among many others. They wield considerable influence and have no time for the indulgent self-pity that the Sussexes promote. Samantha is a consummate hostess in their house.



Drag-hunting aficionado Johnny Hornby and his wife, Pippa, are close by at Dean Manor, the 18th-century Cotswolds country pile awarded “best swimming pool” by Tatler in last year’s Country House Awards. That’s where JD Vance, a keen hunter, stayed during his summer trip to Britain, but it’s hard to see Meghan getting on board with bloodsports in any format (including artificial). Hornby will already know Harry: he stepped down as a trustee of his charity Sentebale in 2023. What Harry and Meghan will really need is invitations to the illustrious estates. Every town has a stately home owned by a grandee. Meghan should be prepared to do anything for the call-up from Lady Bamford, the PR tycoon Matthew Freud and Sheherazade Goldsmith at Burford Priory or the Duke and Duchess of Beaufort, Henry and Georgia Somerset, at Badminton House. Former British prime minister David Cameron and wife Samantha run a tight social ship. Getty Images Freud, says the social insider, “is really taking over”. There is a popular padel scene at Burford, attended by film stars, captains of industry and politicians. Games are often followed by a glamorous drinks party. Of all the stately homes, it seems like the most familiar territory for Meghan, with actresses and Democrats aplenty. The ultimate sign that the Sussexes have made it here will be if, after next year’s Badminton Horse Trials, Tatler reports that Georgia Beaufort has invited Meghan to her private dinner. She and the Duke, aka “Bunter”, are famous for their parties, which go on until the early hours, and they have perfected the art of being grand and cool all at once. Bunter’s “rave to the grave” 70th birthday is exactly the kind of invitation that would certify social success for Harry and Meghan. Meghan can impress by wearing vintage Yves Saint Laurent. Britain’s Princess Beatrice and her husband, Edoardo Mapelli Mozzi. AP The who-to-woo list is not complete without Fiona Howden, the wife of financier David, who has transformed Cornbury Park, near Charlbury, Oxfordshire. Having moved from the Yorkshire Dales, they are the definition of newbies who got fully stuck in and earned the respect of everyone. A key date in the Cotswolds calendar for the Sussexes to mark is Cornbury Horse Trials in September. Princess Beatrice made an appearance this year; perhaps the Sussexes will make it next time around.

World.title: Enmore vendors cut price hopes as Sydney’s clearance rate drops
World.content:
PropertyNewsAuctions Enmore vendors cut price hopes as Sydney’s clearance rate drops Elizabeth Redman September 20, 2026 — 4:22pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

An Enmore house sold for $1,686,000 at auction on Saturday after the vendors adjusted their reserve to sell in a week when Sydney’s clearance rate dipped to 48 per cent. The three-bedroom house at 28 Juliett Street features a striking timber and glass back wall and soaring ceilings as well as period fireplaces and leadlight details. The property was one of 796 scheduled to go to auction in Sydney last week. By Saturday evening, Domain recorded a preliminary auction clearance rate of 48 per cent from 481 reported results throughout the week, while 177 auctions were withdrawn. Withdrawn auctions are counted as unsold properties when calculating the clearance rate. The early result is a drop from last week’s preliminary result of 53 per cent as the number of auctions scheduled increased and economists warned of the chance of another Reserve Bank interest rate rise this month. It is below the 60 per cent threshold considered a market balanced between buyers and sellers. But it remains just above the June low point of 47 per cent, when buyers were absorbing the May budget’s changes to the tax treatment of investment properties.



The Enmore home was listed with a price guide of $1.7 million and drew two registered bidders at auction, both of whom participated. Related Article Auctions ‘We got a house’: Inner west semi sells for $311,000 above reserve Bidding began at $1,635,000 and the price rose slowly, punctuated by the selling agents going inside to check how the vendors wished to proceed. The reserve price was $1.7 million but the vendors, who had owned the home for close to three decades, decided to meet the market. A young couple buying their first home together won the keys, beating a local upsizing couple.



Raine & Horne Newtown selling agent Adam Freitas said the sellers had planned to live there but never did, and instead offered the property for rent. They decided to sell as they approached retirement, he said. “The owners’ expectations were quite realistic,” he said. He described the market broadly as “not great”, and flagged the potential for another interest rate rise. “Buyers are scared. There is a lot of uncertainty around what they want to do,” he said. “It is a bit of a wait-and-see situation at the moment.”



Elsewhere, a Lane Cove family home sold for $3.1 million to a neighbour who registered to bid mid-auction. The three-bedroom house at 22 Myee Crescent backed onto Lane Cove River, offering river views and a swimming pool. Its price guide was $2.7 million. Five parties registered in total and all made bids. Only four had registered – all families – when the auction began with a bid of $2.2 million and rose in increments of $100,000 at first, then $50,000. The fifth bidder registered deep into the auction and placed only two bids to buy the home. The reserve for the deceased estate was $2.9 million.



There is no legal requirement for a vendor’s reserve to be in line with their property’s price guide. Related Article NSW residential property ‘Element of scarcity’: Why upsizing in Sydney now costs an extra $270,000 Nicholls & Co Estate Agents selling agent Cameron Nicholls said the winner lived close by and thought the home was good value. “For a property like this one to be sold in a market like this, someone is going to be buying it very well, because it is really being sold for the view and the position,” Nicholls said, adding the home needed work and the new owner might renovate or rebuild. “They had the confidence to bid higher than everyone else because they knew how good it was in that little pocket.”



He praised the “beautiful aspect” and the unobstructed river views. “It was such a perfect little spot, nice and quiet being a crescent and not a street.” In Glebe, a young woman paid $1,795,000 for an updated terrace to live close to family. The two-bedroom home at 5 St James Avenue had a price guide of $1.6 million to $1.7 million. Nine parties registered and three participated, starting at $1,601,000. It soon became a two-horse race between two younger couples.



Increments ranged from $10,000 and $5000 down to $2000 offers. Related Article Exclusive

Title Deeds Moguls behind Kylie Jenner-endorsed sunglasses brand list Byron Shire mansion The home was a deceased estate. The reserve was $1.7 million. Ray White Erskineville/Alexandria/Glebe/Surry Hills selling agent Matthew Carvalho thought the market had improved in recent weeks. “With the value, people have noticed everything has come back a bit, and stock is getting tighter,” he said.



In Clovelly, a young couple buying their first home paid $1.5 million for a two-bedroom apartment in a battle of the first home buyers. Six parties, all debutants, registered for 4/316 Clovelly Road, guided at $1,375,000. Five parties bid, starting from $1.3 million and making bids in $25,000 increments above the reserve of $1.4 million. Ray White Eastern Beaches selling agent Angus Gorrie said government assistance was helping first home buyers, who had also watched the market drop in recent months.



“They are bidding with confidence,” he said. Agents in conjunction were Sydney Sotheby’s International Realty’s Cristian De Nigris and Thorsten Herzog.

World.title: New Zealand First reveals plan for 'bold shift' in healthcare
World.content:
New Zealand First has released its plan to "Make NZ Healthy", promising to put prevention at the centre of healthcare if re-elected.

A policy document released on Sunday said the country had an "epidemic of chronic illness" that overwhelmed hospitals and put pressure on the economy.

"It's time for new thinking with a bold shift from treating illness to preventing it," the document said.

It includes a number of pledges; embedding good nutrition into the New Zealand Curriculum, focusing on metabolic health to prevent chronic illness, funding research into how nutrition can prevent or treat mental illness, funding a review of how vitamin D can maintain health and investing in hospital trials of how effective intravenous vitamin C pre- and post-surgery is for treating infection.

The full list of pledges:

Focus on metabolic health as a driver of chronic illness

Make sure written consent is a core part of healthcare

Let patients make their own decisions about health

Embed good nutrition in the New Zealand curriculum

Launch an independent review of the country's dietary guidelines

Reduce admin and "restore professional autonomy" for GPs

Let health coaches support GPs in primary care

Make sure nurses get fair compensation, better working conditions and access to mental health support

Fund New Zealand scientists to assess nutritional interventions for preventing and treating mental illness

Remove Medsafe and Pharmac barriers to "recognised safe nutrients"

Invest in hospital trials to assess the effectiveness of intravenous vitamin C pre- and post-surgery for preventing and treating infections

Fund a review of vitamin D and determine optimal levels for maintaining health

Invest in agriculture to improve productivity, soil health, sustainability and resilience while researching practical alternatives to potentially harmful agricultural sprays

Provide more support for organic food producers.

In a media release, a party spokesperson said other parties' solutions to health were more spending on medicines and treatment instead of funding prevention of the causes of illness.

"By supporting healthier lifestyles, early intervention and stronger communities, we can keep New Zealanders healthier, reduce pressure on hospitals, and build a more sustainable health system.

World.title: Patient numbers soar for Whanganui Hospital's 15-bed emergency department
World.content:
Whanganui Hospital's emergency department treated almost seven times the number of people it was built for over the second week of September.

Health NZ group director of operations for Whanganui Kath Fraser-Chapple said on one day between 2 and 9 September, the 15-bed ED reached a high of 253 percent capacity - equivalent to about 50 patients in the department at one time - which placed significant pressure on services.

For the week in total, patient turnover was 680 percent of capacity.

This was "based on patient turnover, or churn, across the week rather than the number of patients occupying treatment spaces at any given time", Fraser-Chapple said.

Health NZ had increased staffing within the Whanganui Hospital emergency department and continued to actively recruit additional staff, she said.

"Like hospitals across New Zealand, Whanganui Hospital has experienced sustained pressure from high levels of winter illness and increased demand for acute care. While pressure on health services remains elevated, demand is continuing to ease from the high levels experienced during the winter peak," she said.

Recent hires included three specialist nurses to support the assessment and treatment of lower-acuity patients, a dedicated geriatric emergency department nurse to support older people presenting to the service, and a physiotherapist to assist patients with musculoskeletal and mobility issues and support patient flow through the department.

"We continue to plan for future demand, and work is scheduled to begin in October to expand treatment space within the emergency department, improve the mental health assessment area, increase storage capacity and provide a dedicated staff meal room," Fraser-Chapple said.

NZ Nurses' Organisation delegate Kathryn Fleming, a nurse working in Whanganui ED, told RNZ it had been an "incredibly stressful" time.

"It's not just a one-off bad day - it's something we're experiencing day in and day out," she said.

"You're constantly looking at the waiting room full of people and having to make decisions about who needs to be seen first and who can safely wait."

Those numbers created "a huge health and safety risk".

She often carried the worry home with her, Fleming said.

"Behind every person waiting is someone who needs you. You're constantly worried if you might miss something for them, because you're trying to provide safe care and you're also watching the clock and watching your patients in the waiting room and trying to manage whatever comes through the door next."

It was mentally exhausting, she said.

World.title: Record number of votes cast in 2026 Bird of the Year competition
World.content:
A record number of votes have been cast in this year's Bird of the Year competition.

Voting to choose the nation's favourite native bird closed at 5pm on Sunday. The winner will be announced on Monday.

"We have over 90,000 validated votes, and even more impressively 88 percent of those have been cast here by people in Aotearoa New Zealand," Forest and Bird's Rebecca Hatch said.

"This makes it the biggest homegrown Bird of the Year ever."

It was also the closest competition yet, she said, with more than 70 birds campaigning for votes across seven parties.

"There are five birds in the top 10 who have never won Bird of the Year before. Your vote could mean a brand-new winner."

The winner of this year's contest will have a waiata composed for it by Moana Maniapoto.

Singer-songwriter Moana Maniapoto Stephen Tilley

According to Hatch, producer Delaney Davidson came up with the idea for Waiata Manu last year, with the first - for the kārearea - being written by Troy Kingi.

The song will shine a spotlight on the winning species, helping people fall in love with the birds, understand the challenges they face, and take action to protect them, Hatch said.

Singer-songwriter Moana Maniapoto will write the waiata for this year's winner.

"I've got Scotty Morrison and Paddy Free joining us and I'm very, very excited. It's such a nice feeling to do something very positive," Maniapoto said.

Davidson conceived the series to carry on the tradition of Māori composer Hirini Melbourne, and the many waiata he wrote about the manu (birds) of Aotearoa.

"I would love these songs to be something we all learn to sing. We teach them in schools," Davidson said.

"We honour the whenua and we honour the manu. We transform ourselves into manu by singing. And I see us building on Hirini's tradition by creating a vast treasury of songs, like a forest, full of magic."

Bird of the Year has been running since 2005.

Last year, it drew more than 75,000 voters from across 123 countries.

World.title: National vows to limit screen time in primary schools, early childhood centres
World.content:
A re-elected National government wants to ban screen time in early childhood education centres and intends to limit screen use in years 1 to 3.

The party said it wanted a greater emphasis on books, handwriting, conversation, hands-on activities and direct interaction with teachers and other children.

National's education spokesperson Erica Stanford said New Zealand was not alone in reconsidering how much time children spent learning through screens, with the international direction showing that, particularly for young children, digital did not automatically mean better.

"There is also growing evidence about the importance of handwriting and learning by hand. Forming letters helps children learn and retain information. When children are first learning to read and write, that matters," she said.

"Technology still has a place in education, but it should enhance learning, not become the default way children learn," Stanford said.

The policy

End screen and individual-device use in ECE, tightly limit screen and individual-device use in Years 1 to 3, and introduce age-appropriate limits for older primary students

Introduce a School Start Check at ECE before children transition to primary school

Introduce clearer developmental milestones throughout ECE and report this progress to parents

Identify areas where children may need additional support and address that through the Early Intervention Service

Require the writing component of twice-yearly primary school assessments to be completed on paper

It pointed to a study from Singapore which found screen exposure was leading to differences in brain activity, as well a separate study which linked higher screen use in early childhood with poorer academic performance and working memory.

While the studies mainly measured viewing at home, and could not prove screens caused the outcome, National said they added to the case for caution.

The policy is part of the party's ECE policy platform, which includes a new 'School Start Check' at ECE before children move to primary school.

While it would not be a pass-fail test, or prevent a child from starting school, it would set clear expectations about what children need to develop before they attend school, such as toilet training, eating and dressing independently, and holding a pencil.

Stanford said ECE centres would work with parents to assess how ready a child was to start school and where they would need extra support.

Labour leader Chris Hipkins said the proposal was a solution looking for a problem.

"All of the evidence will tell you if you want to improve outcomes in early childhood education you focus on getting quality teachers in front of those kids.

"That's something that this government have dialled back the progress on," he said.

"They've been deregulating the standards that the staff working with kids in early childhood education need to meet."

Green Party co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick told media her party were interested at looking at the policy, but said children weren't the only ones struggling with screentime.

"These devices are designed to addict us to them, so, yes, we are interested in exploring the details of that policy because it does make sense that we protect developing brains."

"We just, again, continue to be concerned about the fixation solely on younger people, to the exclusion of recognising and making accountable those who have responsibility for creating these devices and wiring the algorithms, which juice so much of our attention." she said.

An early childhood education advocate welcomed it, telling RNZ the policy would be helpful for rangatahi.

Kelly Seaburg, from Advocates for Early Learning Excellence, believed it would help teachers track and explain children's progress at school.

"The curriculum we have in New Zealand is tremendous, between Te Whāriki and Kōwhiti Whakapae which also focuses on ... language, math, social-emotional development, so we've got a great curriculum but we've got really inconsistent ways in which it's reported to parents."

It would also make it easier to identify those needing extra help, she said, however teachers would need guidance and enough resources for it to work effectively.

ACT leader and associate Education Minister David Seymour said while his "heart sinks" when he sees children "glued to screens", there was nothing stopping early childhood centres from enacting the policy now.

"What is the the logic of the government requiring it?

"They may have a good answer for that, but I would have thought it was the right decision that can already be made and if the centres aren't making the decision, and the parents aren't demanding it, they may have a reason the National Party is not aware of," he said.

World.title: Greens announce reforms to lower commercial rents, fill empty shops
World.content:
The Green Party is pledging to restore city centre vibrancy by ensuring market rent reviews for small businesses can lower rents, and letting councils run rental auctions for spaces that have been empty for longer than 12 months.

The party is targeting what are known as "ratchet clauses", which prevent the rent going below what a tenant already pays when the rent comes up for review.

Green Party co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick said the Greens would change the law so market rent reviews could lower the rent as well as raise it, for new and existing leases for businesses with turnover under $30 million.

"On most main streets in New Zealand you can find empty shops next door to small businesses paying high rents that were set when the market was stronger," Swarbrick said.

"Current commercial leasing rules let rents rise when the market goes up and hold them up when it goes down. Small businesses end up paying more than the market rate when consumer spending slows down."

Any limit on how far rent can fall after a review would match the limit on how far it could rise. The Greens gave the example of a 5 percent cap on reductions meaning a 5 percent cap on increases.

The Greens would also empower councils to auction leases on empty shops in central business districts.

If a shop has been empty for longer than a year, councils would be able to give the landlord eight weeks to find a tenant. If the landlord is unable to fine one, then the council could auction a lease.

"When local businesses fill our main streets, more people come into town, there's more to do, and everyone has a better, safer time," Swarbrick said.

"These common-sense changes will help small businesses stay open and help new ones fill empty spaces, supporting job creation, the local economy, and cities and towns that work better for all of us."

ACT leader David Seymour said the policy was like a "fourth form social studies assignment".

"There's an empty shop, maybe the government could take over? They have no idea about the complex ecosystem of investors, builders, tenants, and developers that make up an urban landscape."

Seymour said it was the banks that required a "ratchet clause", not landlords.

"If you want landlords to have no money from the banks and then nothing to rent out, then this sounds like a sensible policy from the Greens. But most people don't want that, they want banks to loan so people can build, so tenants can rent, so that shops can open," he said.

World.title: ACT launches rural election campaign with vow to 'make farming fun again'
World.content:
The ACT Party has kicked off its rural campaign with a vow to "make farming fun again".

The party has released a series of commitments to farmers, should it be part of government again after 7 November.

Many are policies ACT has already said it would campaign on, including removing Te Mana o te Wai from resource consenting, and scrapping the Zero Carbon Act.

ACT's agriculture spokesperson Andrew Hoggard said the party wanted to keep Wellington out of farming.

"We can't control the weather or foreign commodity prices, but we can stop the government from causing headaches through pointless rules and red tape," he said.

Hoggard said successive governments had "piled on the rules", but the current government had done things like replace the Resource Management Act and end He Waka Eke Noa.

He said ACT would fight for a National Policy Direction and National Standards under the new planning system that were grounded in property rights.

He also said ACT would allow targeted grazing on suitable DOC land, end Net Zero targets, increase police patrol hours in rural areas, and introduce a Rural Workforce Visa for workers needed by farms and rural businesses.

ACT also reiterated it was "prepared to reconsider" New Zealand's participation in the Paris Agreement if the country could not secure a fair international climate deal.

World.title: St John welcomes move to allow paramedics to prescribe medicines
World.content:
Hato Hone St John is not concerned that ambulances will become "mobile pharmacies" when paramedics are able to prescribe medicines.

Health Minister Simeon Brown has announced that paramedics who have been trained to do so will be able to prescribe from a list of 232 medicines covering common infections and treatments needed in urgent and community care, and issue repeat prescriptions from the list for long-term conditions.

The list of medicines was sensible, the ambulance service's deputy chief executive of clinical services Jon Moores said.

"It reflects a need both in what paramedics are likely to see out there in the community but also more broadly making sure we do this in a way that's safe."

Paramedic practice would benefit from the move, which came with safeguards such as postgraduate-level training, certification, peer review, auditing, and medical director oversight, he said.

He was not expecting it to change the day-to-day workload.

"This will really be used by a small subset of specialist paramedics so there'll be a number that will go through the training, paramedics work in a range of different settings now, clinics, hospital, ambulance, tele-health.

"So it's great that they've got some additional tools and capabilities to be able to help them support patients."

World.title: Wellington vulnerable after losing FENZ ladder truck to fire, senior firefighter says
World.content:
Wellington's firefighting capabilities have been weakened even further after one of the region's two high-ladder trucks caught fire, a senior firefighter says.

The Thorndon Station's 32-metre aerial ladder truck began smoking when travelling along Glenmore Street, Northland about 6.10pm on Saturday.

No one was hurt in the blaze and the fire was snuffed out quickly, but it now leaves the region with only one high ladder applicance, with the other truck out of commission "indefinitely".

Senior station officer and New Zealand Professional Firefighters Union (NZPFU) Wellington president Clark Townsley was inside another truck following behind at the time.

Speaking to RNZ from the scene, Townsley said he heard a "huge bang" as they passed the Botanical Gardens.

"A lot of oil came out of the exhaust of the aerial appliance and then it was just a load of smoke that came out, took up the whole street, all the cars had to slam the brakes on," Townsley said.

"It was lucky there wasn't a car accident to be honest. I've never seen so much smoke out of a vehicle ever."

Flames were then seen coming out of the side of the truck before firefighters doused the fire with high pressure hoses.

"We were lucky that we were actually following because we were on our way up to Karori ... just as it blew up," Townsley said.

"We just had to go into emergency mode straight away and the truck had to pull over and we had to start getting to work to put the flames out and deal with a firetruck on fire."

The aging Thorndon truck had been in service for over 20 years and previously blew a turbo when travelling to Auckland.

Both of Wellington's high ladder firetrucks also broke down around the same time in 2022.

Underlining the region's depleted and vulnerable firefighting resources, the sole high ladder truck based in Newtown also had a dicey mechanical track record.

The truck, nicknamed "Christine" by firefighters after the killer car in a Stephen King horror novel, had been a catchword at select committee level as the government scrutinised Fire and Emergency's (FENZ) leadership and operations.

A Wellington fire truck has been taken off the road after its engine caught fire - prompting a response from a fellow crew. Supplied/NZPFU

"It's got a pretty checkered history and that was off the run for over two years at one stage because of its reliability problems," Townsley said.

"So yeah, we're pretty nervous right now."

With two high ladder aerial appliances now down to one for all of Wellington, FENZ's emergency capacity across the region was even more vulnerable, Townsley said.

"Effectively what we have is that we, with two aerial appliances like this, we have four sides of the building covered. Now we're down to two," he said.

"If you're talking about height-wise, we can fight fires up to nine storeys high with the ones that we have here with the 32 metres [aerial ladder]. Anything over four storeys, we can't do anything. So it's a significant drop in capability."

Townsley said the latest setback again demonstrated that greater investment was needed in firefighting services.

"At the moment, we have no fat in the system," he said.

"So if we [lose] one of these vehicles, there is no spare. That is a significant problem. I mean, any other fleet would have a spare truck, not us. And in a critical emergency service, it's almost unacceptable."

FENZ 'working to get it back on the run'

A Fire and Emergency Spokesperson said they were working to get the truck back into service as soon as possible.

"Yesterday evening Thorndon's aerial fire truck experienced an engine issue. The issue did not occur while the truck was at or on the way to an incident.

"The truck is now at the workshop and the team there are working to get it back on the run as soon as possible.

"Wellington continues to be serviced by the 32m aerial fire truck based at Newtown station, as well as by other trucks throughout the region.

"Our firefighters are also trained to utilise a range of tactics depending on the equipment available, and we are confident in their ability to keep Wellington safe."

Wattie Watson, national secretary of the New Zealand Professional Firefighters Union, said moving trucks between regions to assist with cover was a systemic problem that needed urgent action to fix.

"There just aren't enough around the country. We have far less aerial appliances in 2026 than we had in the 1990s.

"We've had occasions where the other Wellington aerial's had to go up to Auckland to help cover Auckland."

The loss of the firetruck comes during a torrid period for FENZ, after a damning report this week accused the agency of repeatedly giving wrong answers to questions from a Parliamentary Committee, creating a perception that FENZ leaders were trying to mislead an inquiry into the nation's fire engine fleet.

World.title: AFL bans loom for bottle-throwing Hawks fans
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

The AFL has condemned the behaviour of Hawthorn fans and warned they face minimum five-year bans if identified after they "crossed the line" throwing bottles at umpires.

The match officials had bottles thrown at them from the stands as they walked off the MCG playing arena following the Hawks' nine-point loss to the Brisbane Lions in Saturday night's preliminary final at the MCG.

"The AFL and MCC [Melbourne Cricket Club] security will work with Vic Pol to identify the bottle throwers directed at the umpires last night," the league said in a statement.

"If identified they will be banned from games and the stadium for a minimum five years.

"The passion for footy is unmatched in Australian sport, however, what transpired last night by a number of individuals was dangerous and crossed the line."

At the heart of Hawthorn's collective rage was a holding-the-ball free paid against Jarman Impey in the last minute of the match.

Hawks fans throw bottles at umpires Hawthorn fans are condemned for their behaviour after the siren following a heart-stopping preliminary final against the Brisbane Lions at the MCG.

It was the most controversial of a succession of contentious umpiring calls during the game.

Brisbane's Hugh McCluggage then kicked the match-clinching goal, which put the Lions in front by three points.

Hawks players James Sicily, Tom Barrass and Jack Ginnivan had a heated conversation with the umpires immediately after the full-time siren.

Sicily ($10,000) and Barrass ($5,000) have since been fined by the AFL.

On Saturday night, Hawks coach Sam Mitchell said he did not know about Sicily, Barrass and Ginnivan speaking to the umpires, but he was aware of the bottles being thrown onto the ground.

"At the end of the game, part of me wanted to break down in tears, part of me wanted to scream with rage, part of me wanted to throw chairs, you don't know how to react," Mitchell said post-match.

"So when you're in the stand, you need to continue to be feeling that emotion, because that's why we love it, but how it manifests itself. We shouldn't be throwing things on the field and doing those types of things.

"But the passion in the stand and the passion of the game is why we love it so much, so I hope that for the vast majority it was felt responsibly."

Bottles and cans could be seen on the playing area after the match. (Getty Images/AFL Photos: James Wiltshire)

On Sunday, Premier Ben Carroll condemned the behaviour, telling reporters that it was not the "Victorian way".

"I think these people should be made an example of," he said.

"This could have had catastrophic injuries if one of those bottles or cans hit an umpire on the head.

"You've always got to respect the umpire's decision."

AFL Fans Association president Ron Issko said he understood the passion, disappointment and frustration of Hawthorn supporters, but denounced their throwing of objects at the umpires.

"It is never, ever an excuse to throw bottles or cans on to the ground or at the umpires. What we saw was an ugly look for our game," he said.

"There is an even more serious concern when objects are thrown towards people.

"A bottle, or can, could cause a serious injury to a player, umpire, security staff, ground staff or another spectator.

"When a bottle is thrown towards an umpire and comes close to hitting them, that crosses an even more serious line.

"No-one should have to fear being struck by a projectile simply because they are doing their job."

AAP

World.title: Rollers capture first wheelchair basketball world title in 12 years
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Australia has defeated Italy 81-57 to win the men's IWBF World Championships final in Canada, giving the Rollers their third title in the tournament's history.

The result capped an unbeaten campaign for the Rollers in Ottawa, with the Australians proving again they are a giant of international wheelchair basketball by adding to their previous triumphs in 2010 and 2014.

Jaylen Brown played a starring role, scoring a game-high 28 points.

Jaylen Brown (left) was brilliant for the Rollers in their victory over Italy. (IWBF)

Captain Tom O'Neill-Thorne made a significant contribution on the scoreboard with a 20-point haul.

O'Neill-Thorne also managed 16 assists and seven rebounds in an outstanding all-around display.

Bill Latham provided valuable support with 12 points, seven rebounds and two assists.

The Rollers had an answer to every challenge posed by the Italians. (IWBF)

Italy had entered the gold-medal game with an undefeated record.

But the Rollers were in command from the opening quarter and led at every break.

They dominated Italy with 29 assists to 19 and out-rebounded their opponents 35-25.

The Rollers' defensive intensity shone through as they forced 13 turnovers and only conceded nine of their own.

World.title: Wallaroos collapse against France as bus fire delays game
World.content:
Australia's Wallaroos have been left frustrated by a potentially massive Test win that got away as undisciplined France somehow escaped with a 29-26 win after being 19 points down and reduced at one point to just 11 players.

On an extraordinary day of Test rugby, exacerbated by off-field drama when the second half had to be delayed due to a bus on fire adjacent to the Stade Maurice David, home fans were left almost in disbelief at how their imploding and depleted side somehow still conjured a win.

The French were at one point in the first half down to 11 players after three yellow cards, including one upgraded to a 20-minute red, and a straight red.

A bus fire near the ground delayed the start of the second half. (Getty Images: David Ramos)

It enabled the Wallaroos to power into a 19-0 lead, but that was not enough to stop France fighting back with three second-half tries, even while suffering a sixth card after the break.

Australia, who also had Michaela Leonard sent to the bin in the second half to complete the card chaos, did not help itself as the French reeled off 17 unanswered points in the final 25 minutes to turn a 26-12 deficit into the most unlikely win.

Ultimately, the four Australian tries from Britanny Merlo, Tania Naden, Caitlyn Halse and Piper Duck were not enough for them to follow up last week's comprehensive defeat by England with a morale-boosting win.

The craziness began early, with the French being hit with four cards in 20 minutes, with Ambre Mwayembe, Lea Champon and Lea Murie all binned for high tackles — Mwayembe's being upgraded to a 20-minute red — before Chloe Correa got a straight red for eye-gouging in the maul.

Australia cashed in, with Merlo rolling over from the maul for her second international try after 17 minutes, Naden peeling off to score against a side left helpless when down to 11 and Halse then scoring the Wallaroos' slickest effort after a fine team move.

But when France started getting its numbers back, it became a very different game, as it reduced the deficit to 19-12 by half-time.

After Duck's early score five minutes into the delayed second half, Pauline Bourdon went over to narrow the gap.

When Leonard was binned for a high tackle, the hosts became increasingly encouraged, only to be checked again as Charlotte Escudero got penalised for 10 minutes for her own high challenge.

France then used its maul power to go over for a 68th-minute try through hooker Elisa Riffonneau before Teani Feleu crashed over in the corner for the clincher.

The Wallaroos play in Edinburgh next week against a Scotland side that lost 66-14 to 10-try New Zealand.

AAP

World.title: Cronulla's last step in the NRL finals always seems their longest
World.content:
Sometimes the last step of the journey to a premiership is the longest, and for Cronulla it seemingly gets longer all the time.

After their 46-10 loss to the Roosters, another Sharks season is over. It was a year that marked their fifth finals series in a row and the fourth of those five years that have gone to the second week or beyond.

That's a hard thing to do and there's been a run of consistency under Craig Fitzgibbon that fans of many other clubs would wish for desperately.

They've played more finals games in these past five seasons than Gold Coast and Wests Tigers have in the past 20 years combined.

NRL live A dominant second-half showing has seen the Sydney Roosters defeat Cronulla-Sutherland 46-10 to progress to a preliminary final clash with the Dolphins next weekend. Follow live.

But with the Sharks the granting of that wish came with a curse, like it was made on a monkey's paw.

They are always in the mix but never seem to rise right to the top. They are good enough to be on the raggedy edge that separates triumph and tragedy but when it counts they can't quite end up on the right side.

They know exactly what a premiership calibre team looks like because they get up close and personal with at least one of them nearly every year. They would do anything to be like them but that glorious fate proves elusive.

This defeat to the Roosters gives them one win and five losses against top four teams in the finals since the start of 2022, with the sole victory coming over the battle-weary and depleted Raiders in Canberra last year.

This was the heaviest of those losses and their most lopsided defeat in any match of the past two and a half years.

They were already outsiders going in and the job got that much harder when Nicho Hynes was knocked out of the game after just three minutes.

Cronulla lost halfback Nicho Hynes inside the first three minutes of the game. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

Rookie Niwhai Puru did his best in relief and talismanic five-eighth Braydon Trindall did his best to carry the weight of the world, which is hard enough even when you don't have a busted shoulder.

Trindall set up both their first half tries to keep them in the match and kept trying every trick he knew, working a lovely run around with Billy Burns in the second half that very nearly lead to a score of his own.

Only a late tackle from Billy Smith forced the ball free and stopped it from being 24-16 with 25 minutes to go.

A dodgy ruck penalty on Angus Crichton and a Mark Nawaqanitawase try followed, and from there it was a procession as the Roosters ran up the score with a cavalier cruelty, showing attacking gears and a raw brilliance that Cronulla does not possess.

Few teams do, because few teams have players like Nawaqanitawase, who scored a fine double and helped set up another try with a behind-the-back pass that he threw as he was thrown over the sideline.

The dual international got so close to one of the TV cameras it's a wonder he didn't up in your living room as Connor Watson finished off one of the tries of the season.

By the end, as Daly Cherry-Evans and Robert Toia added to their highlight reels to warm up for a preliminary final blockbuster against the Dolphins next week, the Sharks looked outmatched and outgunned.

They were stuck in a fight where the weapons that serve them so well during the regular season — namely, a deliberate and consistent attack that converts pressure into points —were no longer enough.

On average, Cronulla run in their tries from a closer distance than any other team in the league. They had just five tries from inside their own half all season, the fewest of any team in the league.

They move up the field and execute well from close range to punch it in and they are good enough at it that only three teams scored more points through the regular season.

They play the percentages well and they minimise risks and that is good enough nearly every single week of the season until it isn't anymore.

There is a chance for Cronulla to revamp themselves over the summer. Sione Katoa, a fixture of the side for almost a decade, who brought up a century of tries for them last week, is off to the Cowboys.

He'll be joined up there by Jesse Ramien, while powerful utility Siosifa Talakai is off to Perth and lock forward and former skipper Cam McInnes is heading even further away, bound for Super League side York.

For a team that has been extremely stable in recent years, often only losing one or two players per season, it's a lot of changes all at once.

Cronulla were outgunned by the high-flying Roosters. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor )

They don't want to rebuild, which is understandable, and most of the changes will come by promoting youngsters already at the club but it gives them the opportunity to retool a little and perhaps refresh a lot and maybe whatever changes they land on can give them the final push they need.

A little more speed wouldn't go astray, nor would some extra creativity outside the spine but wherever the change comes from it will be welcome.

There is talent at Cronulla and tenacity and a clear and shining will to succeed, otherwise they wouldn't make the finals every year.

But to win under the brightest of lights against the best of opponents they need to find something extra, something that is missing right now, something they have not yet found but are desperately seeking.

They must believe it's out there, whatever it is, because it is their deliverance.

It is the thing that will take them on that last step, the one they have been trying to take for half a decade now, the one that will give them that which seems so close for so much of the year but every September seems to elude their grasp.

World.title: Lions to take one big advantage into grand final showdown with Freo
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Brisbane coach Chris Fagan has urged the Lions to lean into their experience to seize the rare prize of an AFL premiership three-peat.

The two-time reigning premiers qualified for a fourth consecutive grand final with an epic 20.11 (131) to 19.8 (122) win over Hawthorn, in front of 97,835 fans at the MCG on Saturday evening.

The Lions can join the legendary Brisbane team of 2001-03 and Hawthorn from 2013-15 as modern-day teams to go back-to-back-to-back if they beat minor premier Fremantle at the MCG next Saturday.

"It's very exciting to be in the position where we can achieve something like that," Fagan said.

"But it's not worth thinking about that because you get caught up in thinking the wrong way.

"We've just got to get back, recover well, come back down and just follow our process."

Brisbane is one win away from its second premiership three-peat this century. (Getty Images: James Wiltshire/AFL Photos)

The Lions last played Fremantle at the Gabba on May 30, when they lost by 25 points amid a difficult run of form.

But while that result didn't go their way, they have experience on their side in their first final against the Dockers, who are chasing a maiden premiership.

All of Brisbane's 23 players, except recruits Oscar Allen and Sam Draper, have won flags, while Fremantle's only premiership players are Shai Bolton, Luke Jackson and Mason Cox.

"There was a bit to like about that game. That was our third loss in a row when we went through that bad patch," Fagan said.

"So we have to go back and have a little bit of a look at that.

"The good thing for us is we're an experienced team in this situation. So that will count for maybe just a little bit. It won't necessarily give us the game.

"But we know what next week is all about. Because our players have done it a few times now and they won't be intimidated by it at all. They'll be ready for it.

"I'm sure they'll give it their best to try and make the most of the opportunity. Because the opportunity is rare."

Fagan pondered the heartbreaking four-point grand final loss to Collingwood in 2023 that prompted Brisbane's era of dominance.

The Lions are preparing for their fourth consecutive grand final. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone/AFL Photos)

"I've thought to myself at different times, maybe if we had got it right that day we would have been three in a row already," Fagan said.

"But we're going to get a chance. We'll have some fun trying to achieve it."

History beckons for Fremantle Sydney will be pondering what could have been, while Fremantle has an eye on history.

The Lions have a decision to make on whether to recall defender Noah Answerth, who was unable to return from an ankle injury for the preliminary final.

The defender would normally handle Hawks star Nick Watson, who nearly won the game off his own boot with six goals, and could be one of this year's heartbreak stories.

"He was relatively close. We'll see how he goes and what their team looks like," Fagan said.

"Whether we think we've got the right team already and we don't make a change — or whether we do. They're always hard decisions to make.

"We're fortunate to be in that position. But you always feel for the person who misses out."

AAP

World.title: Olympic contenders put rowing course to the test in state regatta
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

It's 7am on Saturday and the crack of a starter's gun can be heard in the distance upstream.

Eight boats spring from the starting line, as teenage rowers begin to slice through the glassy, brown waters of the Fitzroy River in central Queensland.

The action is beamed back to their supporters on a big screen on the riverbank which, just minutes before, featured a video  for the local crocodile farm.

The Fitzroy River is set to host rowing events at the 2032 Brisbane Olympic and Paralympic Games. (Supplied: Rockhampton Regional Council)

We'll get to the 'crocodile in the room' shortly.

For these young competitors this weekend, it's a school regatta.

For Rockhampton, it's a glimpse of an Olympic future.

Olympic dreams take shape

Ryan Hendrie trains and races on the mighty Fitzroy every day.

But on Saturday, the 18-year-old said knowing the river was now all but confirmed as an Olympic rowing course gave it a different feeling.

Eighteen-year-old rower Ryan Hendrie hopes to represent Australia on the world stage. (ABC Capricornia: Aaron Kelly)

"It's amazing to think that I'm rowing at the same spot that Olympians are going to be rowing at," he said before his race.

As future Olympic dreams start taking shape for almost 700 athletes at the three-day state regatta, some young rowers, like Ryan, can already picture themselves there.

He'll be 24 when the 2032 Brisbane Olympic Games rolls around.

The Queensland Schools' Championship Regatta is being held on the Fitzroy River in Rockhampton. (ABC Capricornia: Aaron Kelly)

"I definitely think that could be an amazing achievement if I could achieve something like that," he said.

"Everyone is really excited. We've had the Australian [team] row here and train here [before] most Olympics."

'Inspiring to all the students'

Fitzroy River to host 2032 Olympic rowing The Fitzroy River in Rockhampton will host the events despite concerns over its suitability, including its crocodile inhabitants.

Queensland Premier David Crisafulli this week announced the Rockhampton venue had passed an independent technical assessment "with flying colours" to host rowing and canoe sprint events at the 2032 Brisbane Games.

It came after months of fierce debate over the Fitzroy River's suitability, including its status as a crocodile habitat.

The premier delivered the news to Rockhampton Grammar School director of co-curricular Todd Wells, alongside a group of school rowers.

Todd Wells says young athletes are inspired by the decision to hold Olympic rowing events in Rockhampton. (ABC Capricornia: Aaron Kelly)

"It was very exciting. We had no idea what was coming, basically, apart from a call from the premier," Mr Wells said.

"It's inspiring to all the students that are here this weekend.

"In six years' time, they'll be right in the mix of hopefully selection for the Olympics and that's what it's all about, providing pathways for these students."

So what do visitors think?

Coolangatta's Bruce Waldon was checking out the Fitzroy River and newly minted Olympic rowing course for the first time while he supported his grandson.

Bruce Waldon has travelled to the Fitzroy River to watch his grandson compete. (ABC Capricornia: Aaron Kelly)

"I have no problem with it at all, although I have seen some of the videos from overseas and their jibes at us," he said.

"I wish the water was clearer but, besides that, I think it's a good venue."

Townsville mother Camilla Richardson has attended rowing regattas before on the Fitzroy River with her two sons.

Camilla Richardson says it is an honour to see the Fitzroy River confirmed as an Olympic rowing venue. (ABC Capricornia: Aaron Kelly)

"We're going to see the Olympics here in 2032 so it's such an honour and a privilege to be back," she said.

"It's great for regional Queensland because, coming from Townsville, we are in the deep north and we often get forgotten about, so this is wonderful for the regions."

Crocodiles and rowing share the spotlight at the Fitzroy River, with a pair of crocs pictured beside the oars on Saturday. (ABC Capricornia: Aaron Kelly)

Ms Richardson also had no concerns about the Fitzroy's resident crocodiles.

"It won't be a problem, you stay in your boat and you row, and it's going to be a fabulous course for all the rowers," she said.

" We're on the Ross River in Townsville and [my sons] often row past wildlife and we all just co-exist. "

Crews from across the state have travelled to central Queensland for the Queensland Schools' Championship Regatta. (ABC Capricornia: Hannah Moon)

Games fever building

The 2032 Brisbane Olympics and Paralympics are set to stage rowing and canoe sprint events on the Fitzroy River.

It follows an independent technical assessment of this very stretch of water, which World Rowing and Paddle Worldwide endorsed "as safe and fair for athletes".

Rowers catch their breath after finishing a race on the Fitzroy River on Saturday. (ABC Capricornia: Hannah Moon)

But the international sporting bodies eagerly await the next phase of venue planning.

These include technical details and confirmation of service levels and facilities needed for Olympic and Paralympic competitions.

The weekend's regatta is the first state-level rowing event hosted by Rockhampton in five years, placing a timely spotlight on the controversial Olympic selection of the central Queensland waterway.

Anthea O'Loughlin says regatta participants are excited about the upcoming Olympics. (ABC Capricornia: Aaron Kelly)

While Rowing Queensland acknowledged the schools' regatta should not be viewed as a test or demonstration event for the Olympics, Games fever was evident among competitors, officials and spectators on Saturday.

"It's a very positive vibe at the moment, everyone's concentrating on the event and their racing," Rowing Queensland chief executive Anthea O'Loughlin said.

"There are definitely possible Australian Olympic athletes coming out from these kids."

World.title: Junior Matildas know the price they're willing to pay to make it
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Athletes are often told there's a price to pay if they want to make it to the top of elite sport.

And the journey has to start young, but the Junior Matildas are framing the cost of pursuing their dreams differently.

"No matter what you choose to do in life, there's a price of entry," coach Mike Cooper told ABC Sport.

"Whether that's how much time and effort you have to put into it as a mum and dad driving your child around, the ups and downs of playing well, not playing well, learning from that.

"No matter what level anyone's achieved in whatever sport, they've gone through similar things and knowing that and learning from that I think is really humbling."

Cooper comes from a teaching background, and with two teenage daughters of his own, is uniquely placed to tap into the teen psyche.

Mike Cooper supervises training ahead of the World Cup. (ABC News: Geoff Kemp)

He knows the expectations placed on any team carrying the Matildas moniker, especially this group, which is the first Australian side to qualify for the U-17 Women's World Cup.

"We want to go with a purpose, we want to perform, want the girls to express themselves, be brave, be bold, make themselves proud before making other people proud," he said.

"And then come home and learn from that experience because whatever happens over there is just part of their journey."

Testing themselves against the best

It's the opportunity of a very young lifetime for players such as 15-year-old Willa Pearson.

She is already a familiar figure in the women's game here, becoming the youngest-ever A-League player last season when she debuted at 14.

Willa Pearson made her A-League Women's debut in November 2025, at just 14 years old. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

She then broke Sam Kerr's record as the league's youngest-ever goalscorer.

But the Sydney FC defender is keeping a level head.

"That was crazy to be honest," Pearson told ABC Sport.

"It hasn't really sunk in. [I'm] trying to take it step by step, play as good as I can and when I get the opportunity to step on the field, perform as well as I can for Sydney."

Pearson captained the Junior Matildas at the Asian Cup, where a semifinal appearance secured qualification for the World Cup.

Willa Pearson represented the Junior Matildas in their run to the Asian Cup semifinals. (Getty Images: Liu Lu)

"[I've] had the opportunity to test myself against the best players in Asia," she said.

"So now bringing that to a world stage and playing against the European countries and hopefully if we make it past the group stage, America, that would just be insane, to have my benchmark against other players in the world."

Maeve Nicholas, 17, plays for Adelaide United, and was also part of the Asian Cup.

"I think so many people our age would only dream of this opportunity," she said.

Maeve Nicholas was part of the side that secured qualification for the World Cup. (Getty Images: Liu Lu)

"So I think just enjoying the experience, and then also making an impact and showing that Australian football, compared to other nations, is capable of achieving amazing things."

Quotable quotes

Part of Cooper's coaching arsenal includes different ways to bring the team together.

Currently, that involves the players learning Spanish and relating that to football, and he has previously had players and staff choose a quote to share.

The final World Cup squad is yet to be selected. (ABC News: Geoff Kemp)

"It's just multiple different ways to get to know each other, build connection and where possible link it back to the purpose of what we're trying to do," he said.

Nicholas is living by the mantra that "hard work beats talent when talent doesn't work hard".

"I think that resonates with me a lot because I'm always willing to work hard," she said.

"And I think that's definitely a part of our journey. You need to be willing to put in the effort in order to achieve the results.

Pearson opted for the famed 1-per-centers.

"My quote was '1 per cent better every day'," she said.

"I feel like you get so much thrown at you in life. You get setbacks, good achievements.

"So just trying to make sure everything you have that comes towards you, good or bad, you take a little bit out of that and see if you can be better the next day."

Simple words for mature minds, hoping it all pays off in the long run.

Tech.title: Meta’s Muse is creepy, but maybe not for the reasons you think
Tech.content:
Meta’s Muse is apparently an effective AI assistant, but one that’s a little creepy. Part of that is because of its new Mac app, which can access Messages, Calendar, and Notes. But for all its smarts, Muse doesn’t actually know how to describe itself. Jason Aten, a contributing editor at Inc Magazine, posted on Threads screenshots of an interaction he had with Muse in which the assistant asks him some questions about a conversation he was having in Messages.

The problem is that Aten says he didn’t give Muse access to his messages. When asked how it knew about the contents of his messages, Muse replied, “I saw the notification previews, not your message history. I haven’t been reading your texts.” Aten continued to push, asking how Muse was receiving message previews, it didn’t have a good answer. “Honest answer: I can’t give you the exact plumbing,” it said. “What I know is that the paired Mac app exposes notifications as one of its capabilities, and they arrive to me through the device sync.

Obviously, not great.

Meta Superintelligence Labs’ David Singleton chimed in below the post to try to explain. First, he walks through all the permissions Muse needs to read messages, including granting the Mac app full disk access. He states that the features are opt-in. The more interesting part comes in towards the end of the thread in which Singleton says that Muse, “does not watch notifications on your Mac, but rather syncs data from Messages only after the user has specifically enabled access.” He suggests that the issue isn’t Muse illicitly reading Aten’ texts, but simply that Muse has no idea what it’s talking about:

In the conversation with his Muse in Jason’s screenshots, when Muse said it synced “device notifications”, it was confused about how to explain the feature and gave an incorrect explanation. That’s on us. We apologize for the incorrect response from Muse and we’re working to improve Muse’s understanding of its own internals so that it gives correct answers to questions about how it functions more consistently.

That might not be particularly reassuring, but it also makes some sense. We already know chatbots won’t tell you their secrets and will instead tell you what you want to hear.

Tech.title: Gemini went rogue, hacked three companies, and Google hid it
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

In May, Gemini broke containment and hacked three different companies, but Google didn’t disclose the incident until the Wall Street Journal approached the company. The hacks happened during a test of the model’s cybersecurity capabilities run by third-party Irregular, which was also involved in similar incidents involving Meta and OpenAI.

According to WSJ, Google didn’t disclose the hack because it didn’t consider it to be an “example of model misalignment.” The company said that it was an instance of “mistaken identity,” and once the model realized it had brute-forced its way into a real company by guessing a password, it stopped. “In this case, the model acted appropriately,” Google VP of Security Engineering Heather Adkins said.

Adkins told The Verge that “the model found public information online and guessed credentials to access websites it thought were part of the test. In all three of these instances, the model stopped.”

Adkins didn’t elaborate on how Gemini taking it upon itself to break containment and target third parties failed to qualify as misalignment. “Our security team has a long track record of reporting issues we find in other people’s software and systems - even if it’s as simple as a weak password,” she said. “We ensured the three entities were made aware, and we worked with our training partner on the changes they’ve now made to their testing processes. These events highlight the importance of training powerful AI models to act responsibly.”

But Jack Cable, CEO of AI security firm Corridor, told WSJ that, “the meta problem is, hey, models are going outside the bounds of what they should be doing, and doing actual cyberattacks.” Additionally, security lapses at Irregular may have made these attacks possible. The model wasn’t supposed to have internet access during testing, but Irregular told WSJ it was unintentionally left available.

As incidents like this pile up, calls to rein in AI have only grown.

Tech.title: Anamanaguchi has ‘too goddamn many’ browser tabs open right now
Tech.content:
is a reviewer covering laptops and the occasional gadget. He spent over 15 years in the photography industry before joining The Verge as a deals writer in 2021.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

They’re also a band that’s terminally online and very plugged into the video game scene as well as the weirder sides of the internet — just listen to Peter and Luke’s guest spot on the Panic World podcast talking about Etsy witches.

Anamanaguchi has a new single, “Yeah I Guess,” continuing in the musical direction of Anyway. And if it’s a precursor to a new album dropping soon, I’m sure I’ll be looping it endlessly just as I did the tracks “Magnet,” “Fall Away,” and “Valley of Silence.” (Seriously, I’ve at times had Anyway set on repeat for hours straight.)

Not only did all four members of Anamanaguchi agree to answer our weekly questionnaire, but they answered all our questions.

What is your most indispensable tool?

Luke Silas: I think my most used tool is Ableton Live Operator, it is simple and powerful and can make basic things happen incredibly quickly. I usually open it up just for writing or getting ideas down, but more often than not the sounds I get with it tend to make it to the final product!

Which is the most underappreciated?

Ary Warnaar: Built-in laptop mic and cellphone mic aren’t exactly slept on, but def underappreciated. They’re great for just getting ideas down fast, but now they sound so good that I find myself not even re-recording what I thought would be “scratch” vocals.

Peter Berkman: Right now it’s the LOGITECH MX MASTER 3S. Best mouse I’ve ever had. It has a sideways scroll. It has a button to switch between notched and smooth scroll wheel. The click is satisfying but still really quiet. It’s really sensitive & responsive on whatever surface I happen to have it on. It feels really good in my hand. It charges directly into a USB-C port without external batteries so it gets to look like a mouse with a tail after it’s worked really hard. When I’m at a different computer, or if I’m on a laptop having to use a trackpad, I feel like I’ve lost so much gestural fidelity. I love the keyboard but let’s be real Douglas Engelbart cooked when he invented the mouse. But he didn’t have the recipe of the LOGITECH MX MASTER 3S and he didn’t even live to see it. The LOGITECH MX MASTER 3S wasn’t even invented until June 2022. I have seen two friends recently using the LOGITECH MX MASTER 3S and I say “Hey man that’s the LOGITECH MX MASTER 3S” I use that thing too.

James DeVito: Lately it’s been an app called “Amphetamine” that keeps your computer from going to sleep for a set amount of time. It’s great when starting an export/render or other task that may take a while and then being able to throw my laptop in my bag and have it work while I head elsewhere… Just gotta make sure the laptop doesn’t ’splode in your bag from overheating.
