In Connections, you look at a grid of 16 words and pick four words that have a connection to each other. You do this four times until all 16 words in the puzzle are grouped. The tough part is that Times associate puzzle editor Wyna Liu chooses words that could fit in multiple groups. The obvious guess — hey! Those are four animals! — is almost always going to be wrong. I’ve compiled my favorite tips for Connections if you need a boost.

The Times has a Connections Bot, like the one for Wordle. Go there after you play to receive a numeric score and to have the program analyze your answers. Players who are registered with the Times Games section can nerd out by following their progress, including the number of puzzles completed, win rate, number of times they nabbed a perfect score and their win streak.

Today’s NYT Connections puzzle was a little tricky, I thought. Let’s hope you remember your high school math terms. I do love the era depicted in the blue group, so that was a fun one. For the purple group, however, I wonder if anyone in the US uses the term “cos lettuce.” (Is this another “sausage dog” situation?) Read on for hints and today’s Connections answers.

Hints for today’s Connections groups

Yellow group hint: Think more broadly.

Green group hint: Often made with crayons.

Tech.title: Battery Replacement Has Gotten Pricier for Apple’s Latest iPhone 18 Pro Models
Tech.content:
Swapping the battery on Apple’s newest flagship iPhone models just got a little more expensive. As noted by sites including MacRumors, the fee to replace the battery on the iPhone 18 Pro or iPhone 18 Pro Max has gone up by $10, from $119 to $129, compared to previous models (such as the iPhone 17 and iPhone 16 Pro and Max models or the iPhone Air).

Apple’s latest iPhone 18 Pro models feature larger battery capacities, which is likely behind the price increase.

Apple’s policy strongly pushes users toward official channels to get an iPhone battery replaced, whether in or out of warranty, by visiting an Apple store or Apple Authorized Service Provider, or by shipping the phone to an Apple Repair Center.

The critical metric in Apple’s policy is the 80% maximum capacity mark. Apple officially considers a battery “healthy” if it retains 80% or more of its original capacity. If you have an active AppleCare Plus plan and your battery health drops below 80%, Apple will replace the battery at no additional cost. But if your battery drops below 80% without AppleCare, you’ll have to pay out of pocket.

The standard one-year limited warranty doesn’t cover batteries that naturally wear down from everyday use.

According to its device pricing page, Apple can still replace batteries for much older devices, all the way back to the iPhone 6 and the original iPhone SE — those batteries are the cheapest at $69. The page also lists fix-it prices for rear glass or screen damage (or both), rear camera damage or “other damage.”

A representative for Apple did not immediately return a request for comment.

Why do batteries even wear out?

Along with phones from OnePlus and Motorola, the batteries on Apple’s high-end phones, like the Pro and Pro Max, do very well in testing. In recent years, smartphone-makers like Apple have continued to eke out additional battery life even as batteries shrink to accommodate new designs.

But advanced phones with up-to-date battery tech perform a wider array of energy-sucking tasks, functioning as cameras, wallets, GPS systems, AI data crunchers and more. That’s why most of us still complain about limitations and feel frustrated with our current phone’s battery life. A recent CNET survey found that better battery life is the top reason most people upgrade to a new device.

Turning off some features, such as widgets, animations or keyboard haptics, is one way to keep your device from draining its battery too quickly. You can also try to extend a smartphone’s battery life by using the phone’s battery optimizations, avoiding extreme temperatures that can damage the battery, and choosing a phone case that doesn’t trap heat.

But even with optimized charging settings, keeping your phone plugged in at 100% all night can wear out the battery faster. Overall, rechargeable batteries always degrade over time, reducing their capacity and, in some cases, requiring replacement.



Aren’t batteries getting cheaper?

You might think that with the increased popularity of electric vehicles and the ubiquity of smartphones and other battery-powered devices, there’s a shortage or price spike for batteries, as with other electronics components like memory and storage. But the opposite is actually true.

According to Bloomberg, battery prices were already dropping steeply late last year, and that trend continues as Chinese companies flood the market with cheaper batteries.

The price collapse is largely due to companies increasing battery production capacity over the last few years. Quartz reports that price drops also result from “a shift toward cheaper battery chemistry, a crash in lithium prices, and a decades-long accumulation of manufacturing improvements.”

Tech.title: iPhone 18 Pro Launch Could Be the First of Many for Apple’s New CEO This Year
Tech.content:
New Apple CEO John Ternus welcomed buyers of the new iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max to the company’s flagship Fifth Avenue store in New York on Friday, and it’s likely to be just the first of several major product launches for the former hardware lead’s first year in the top job.

Dressed in a dark gray shirt and blue jeans, Ternus immediately took to taking selfies, giving handshakes and signing phone boxes for the hundreds of fans who chose to preorder the new iPhone or Apple Watch.

Ternus, formerly Apple’s senior vice president of hardware engineering, took a casual and personable approach to the launch — even gently laughing as one excited Apple fan accidentally dropped his iPhone 17 Pro Max onto the concrete while walking into the store.

“It’s fine, it’s got a little ding, no crack, thank you, Ceramic Shield,” Dallen Frutchey, 18, from Virginia, said about the accidental drop just ahead of moving his data to his new iPhone 18 Pro Max. This is his fourth time attending one of Apple’s Fifth Avenue store openings, where he had met prior CEO Tim Cook a number of times. At today’s event, he got a selfie with Ternus just before the phone drop.

“I’m excited to have someone who is down in the details with the products working on things now,” Frutchey said, wearing a blue sweater that matched his new glacier blue phone.

Dallen Frutchey, 18, with his new iPhone 18 Pro Max in glacier blue. Mike Sorrentino/CNET

The very first person to come out of the Apple store — Harry Sun, 21, from New Jersey — walked out with a burgundy phone while wearing a Believe pin from the Apple TV show Ted Lasso. Eric Morgan, the second person in line, came all the way from Guatemala. He was buying several phones for his family, who also made the trip but were staying at their hotel, away from the iPhone launch-day madness.

Harry Sun, 21, was the first person to walk out of Apple’s Fifth Avenue store with a new iPhone in hand. Bridget Carey/CNET

The glacier blue hue appeared to be an early crowd favorite at this store, and Apple’s flagship location had a number of visible changes to mark the occasion. The outside of the store had a color blend of burgundy along with that shade of blue — giving no love to the more traditional silver and black color variants that are also available for the 18 Pro and Pro Max.

Apple decorated the entrance to its Fifth Avenue store for the launch. Mike Sorrentino/CNET

Inside, the Apple store took on more of a party vibe as it filled with the crowds that had been waiting outside. A DJ booth spinning Lady Gaga songs blasted in front of a large blue carpet area that served as a showroom for the new phones, as well as the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4.

The blue carpet showroom area for Apple’s iPhone 18 Pro phones, Apple Watch Series 12, Apple Watch Ultra 4 and the AirPods 5. Mike Sorrentino/CNET

At the opposite end of the store, without many passersby, a small photography exhibit featuring photos taken on the iPhone 18 Pro was on display in an area that formerly served as the Apple HomePod demo area. We will see over the next few months whether new products will take over that real estate, since today’s event also marks a shift in how Apple conducts its iPhone launches.

Apple has a photography exhibition spotlighting images taken on the iPhone 18 Pro at its Fifth Avenue store. Mike Sorrentino/CNET

Apple’s set to do at least one more store launch like this when the iPhone Duo goes on sale on Oct. 23 — marking the company’s first entry into the foldable phone space. It’s also rumored to be launching a number of new home entertainment products, with the decreased floor space for the HomePod possibly hinting at a relaunch of the speaker now that the new Siri AI assistant is rolling out to the iPhone 15 Pro and later.

And that’s not to mention the rumors hinting that a non-Pro iPhone 18 and an iPhone Air sequel may be set up for a spring launch, anchoring what could be a new annual launch event early in the year to contrast with premium phones coming later in Apple’s typical September window.

Apple’s current lineup consists of (left to right) the iPhone 17, iPhone Air, iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max. Not pictured but also available are the iPhone 17E and iPhone 16. Mike Sorrentino/CNET

So while this is the first iPhone launch under Ternus, it’s likely that several more of these are to come over the next year.

Bridget Carey contributed to this story.
